- [F026: Compare PPO, DPO and GRPO using their training requirements.](../03_training_and_alignment.md#f026)
- [F027: Write and interpret the DPO loss.](../03_training_and_alignment.md#f027)
- [F028: Explain a clipped PPO update in plain language.](../03_training_and_alignment.md#f028)
- [F029: Calculate group-relative advantages and diagnose zero-variance rewards.](../03_training_and_alignment.md#f029)

title: LoRA and PEFT Variants
question: Concept round on LoRA and its variants — the rank parameterization, how it composes with full fine-tuning, QLoRA quantization, DoRA, AdaLoRA, and practical hyperparameter trade-offs.

steps: LoRA: parameterize the update and count the memory
QLoRA, DoRA and AdaLoRA are different changes
solution.example: 4096x4096 rank8 LoRA trains65536 adapter weights versus16777216 full weights; QLoRA additionally quantizes the frozen base.
solution.trap: Frozen weights still consume base/activation memory; training W plus LoRA loses standard optimizer-memory savings.
solution.teaching_notes_markdown:
### LoRA: parameterize the update and count the memory

For W:(d_out,d_in), freeze W and train $W'=W+(\alpha/r)BA$ with A:(r,d_in),B:(d_out,r). Count r(d_in+d_out) adapter parameters, not r. A4096×4096 matrix at r8 has65,536 trainable adapter entries versus16,777,216 base entries. Random A/zero B starts with a zero update while allowing B gradients; both zero would stall both factors. Savings mainly concern trainable gradients/optimizer states and checkpoint size; base weights and forward/backprop activations still occupy memory.

LoRA is a constrained alternative to full fine-tuning. A model already fully fine-tuned can be a frozen base for another adapter; a compatible trained adapter can be merged into W for deployment, then later full-tuned if desired. Training W freely alongside BA removes most of the usual optimizer-memory benefit and makes the decomposition nonidentifiable. Several adapters can share one base and be selected per task; merging multiple deltas is possible algebraically but their combined behavior needs evaluation.

### QLoRA, DoRA and AdaLoRA are different changes

[QLoRA](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.14314) freezes a4-bit quantized base and backpropagates through dequantized computation to adapters; its NF4, double-quantized scales and paged optimizer address memory. It does not mean all activations/gradients/optimizer state are4-bit. Quantization error and kernel/dequantization overhead must be measured; merging may require higher-precision reconstruction and requantization.

[DoRA](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.09353) separates weight magnitude and direction, learning magnitude plus a low-rank directional update. With output-row normalization as the stated convention, write $W'_j=m_j(V_j+\Delta V_j)/\|V_j+\Delta V_j\|$. It adds trainable magnitude values and normalization overhead during adaptation while a merged dense inference representation can avoid a separate adapter path.

[AdaLoRA](https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.10512) allocates a fixed parameter budget unevenly across matrices using an SVD-like update parameterization and importance-based pruning of singular components. It can spend rank where useful rather than setting identical r everywhere, at the cost of importance estimates, budget schedules and more implementation complexity. It is not automatic proof that a smaller rank is better.

### Practical selection and tests

Tune rank, alpha/scaling, targeted Q/K/V/O/FFN matrices, adapter dropout, learning rate and training tokens on a held-out task set. Larger rank or more targeted layers adds capacity/optimizer state; low rank can underfit a large domain shift. Compare equal token/compute budgets, multiple seeds when feasible, target quality plus retention/safety slices, and end-to-end memory/latency. Verify frozen weights stay frozen, initial delta is zero, adapter gradients exist and merged/unmerged outputs match within the precision tolerance. Track base/tokenizer/quantization/adapter versions together; an adapter trained for one base is not automatically compatible with another.

### Further study

- [F024: Explain LoRA and calculate its trainable parameter count.](../03_training_and_alignment.md#f024)

title: ML Research Orals: Self-Attention, LoRA, Optimizers
question:
A rapid-fire ML-knowledge oral for research/MLE roles, usually after a 30-minute project deep-dive. Give crisp, correct one-paragraph answers to:

Describe self-attention. Why is the attention score divided by sqrt(d_k)?
Describe LoRA and its benefits. Why does LoRA reduce GPU memory consumption?
Difference between Adam and SGD.
ViT vs CNN — pros/cons, and what influences the ViT patch size.
Difference between MSE loss and cross-entropy loss.

Usually closes with a trivial coding task (e.g. count word occurrences over a stream — a dict/Counter suffices).

steps: ViT versus CNN and patch size
solution.example: For image patches, halving p makes4x tokens and about16x dense attention interactions; streaming word counts return the2/cat2/dog1.
solution.trap: MSE on probabilities is a valid Brier objective; it is different from MSE on raw logits.
solution.teaching_notes_markdown:
### Self-attention

From token states X form Q=XWq,K=XWk,V=XWv, compute $\operatorname{softmax}_{keys}(QK^T/\sqrt{d_k}+M)V$ and mix heads. Queries match keys and copy weighted values; a causal mask blocks future keys. Independent zero-mean unit-variance query/key coordinates give dot-product variance d_k, so division by sqrt(d_k) controls scale/saturation. Softmax max subtraction separately prevents overflow. Unlike an RNN hidden-state recurrence, teacher-forced attention evaluates positions in parallel; autoregressive generation still depends on previously generated tokens.

### LoRA and GPU memory

Freeze W and learn $\Delta W=(\alpha/r)BA$, with r(d_in+d_out) entries instead of d_in·d_out trainable weights. This saves gradient/Adam-state memory and per-task checkpoints, while the frozen base and activations remain necessary; 4-bit base storage is an additional QLoRA choice. Initialize only one factor zero to permit gradients, validate target tasks and merge-compatible adapters for inference if useful. It may underfit compared with full tuning and does not guarantee a fixed whole-GPU memory factor.

### Adam versus SGD

SGD subtracts eta times the minibatch gradient; momentum smooths a velocity across steps. Adam tracks exponential first/second gradient moments, bias-corrects them and divides the first by the square root of the second plus epsilon, adapting per-coordinate scales. It often handles noisy/sparse signals conveniently but stores two moment tensors and needs learning-rate/decay tuning. SGD can use less memory and generalize well after scheduling; neither universally wins. AdamW decouples weight shrinkage from adaptive moments.

### ViT versus CNN and patch size

A CNN shares local kernels, building locality/translation equivariance and often good data efficiency. A ViT embeds image patches and attends globally, offering flexible long-range relationships but weaker built-in locality and data/compute demands. For H×W images and patch side p, token count is about HW/p²; halving p makes4× tokens and about16× dense attention interactions. Small patches preserve detail useful for small objects but cost more; large patches are cheaper and may erase fine structure. Choose by resolution, objects, data/pretraining, positional scheme, memory/latency and validation, not a universal patch size.

### MSE versus cross-entropy

Squared error targets a conditional mean and corresponds to Gaussian observation noise for regression. Cross-entropy is negative log likelihood for categorical/Bernoulli outcomes and acts on normalized class probabilities, preferably computed from logits. For sigmoid BCE the logit gradient is p-y, whereas MSE on probability includes an extra p(1-p) factor that can shrink updates when confidently wrong. MSE/Brier loss is still a valid probability scoring rule; it is a different objective. Compare calibration and task cost, not just raw loss magnitudes across incompatible scales.

### A stream word-count implementation

```python
from collections import Counter


def count_words(records):
    counts = Counter()
    for record in records:
        counts.update(record.lower().split())
    return dict(counts)


assert count_words(iter(["The cat", "the dog cat"])) == {"the": 2, "cat": 2, "dog": 1}
assert count_words(iter([])) == {}
```

This explicitly chooses lowercase whitespace words, keeping punctuation attached; replace that policy if the interviewer specifies a different tokenizer. It scans once, storing O(distinct words) counts rather than the full stream.

### Further study

- [F002: Why divide attention logits by the square root of the head dimension?](../01_llm_internals.md#f002)
- [F003: Trace every shape in multi-head self-attention.](../01_llm_internals.md#f003)
- [F005: Why do Transformers need positional information, and what does RoPE do?](../01_llm_internals.md#f005)

title: LLM Fundamentals: Quantization, FlashAttention, Parallelism
question:
A set of five open-ended questions on how large language models are made smaller, faster and trainable at scale: quantization, FlashAttention, RNNs versus Transformers, and parallelism. Answer each question as you would in a technical interview, with mechanisms and trade-offs rather than definitions alone.

Questions
1.
Quantization approaches. What quantization approaches are commonly used for LLMs? Compare them on numerical precision, training requirements, deployment complexity and accuracy or speed trade-offs. Name at least two concrete post-training methods and say when quantization-aware training is worth its cost.
2.
FlashAttention. What is FlashAttention? Which compute and memory bottlenecks of standard attention does it remove, and which algorithmic ideas (tiling, fused kernel, online softmax, recomputation) make that possible? State what it does to memory use and whether the result is exact.
3.
RNNs versus Transformers. Compare the two architectures: how information flows across positions, training parallelism, cost in sequence length, handling of long-range dependencies, and the advantages and disadvantages of each.
4.
Parallelism. How are Transformer models parallelized for training and for inference? Cover data, tensor, pipeline, sequence or context, and expert parallelism, the memory sharding used for optimizer state (ZeRO or FSDP), and the inference-time techniques that raise throughput.
5.
Where to quantize. Which parts of an LLM system are quantized, and where should quantization be prioritized in training versus in inference? Discuss weights, activations and the KV cache, which components stay in higher precision, and the hyperparameters that matter.
Expectations
Each answer covers its stated points and ends with the main trade-off.
Use correct terminology; where numbers are quoted (bit widths, memory factors) they must be accurate.
Questions 1 and 5 both involve quantization: question 1 is about the methods, question 5 is about placement and priorities.

steps: 1. Compare quantization methods, not only bit widths
5. Place precision where the bottleneck is
solution.example: 4-bit raw weight storage is one quarter of16-bit, but KV/activations/scales and kernel overhead prevent assuming4x end-to-end gains.
solution.trap: Flash-style exact attention removes HBM score storage/traffic, not the quadratic dense interaction arithmetic.
solution.teaching_notes_markdown:
### 1. Compare quantization methods, not only bit widths

Post-training quantization converts a pretrained model with no full gradient-based retraining, often using a representative calibration sample. Weight-only INT8/INT4 reduces bandwidth/storage, but dequantization and kernel support decide speed; W8A8 also quantizes activations and must handle activation outliers. GPTQ uses approximate second-order reconstruction to choose low-bit weight values; AWQ uses activation information to preserve salient weights through scaling. Both require calibration/versioned kernels and may regress unusual domains. SmoothQuant moves activation quantization difficulty into offline weight scaling for integer weight/activation execution. These are distinct methods, not interchangeable formats.

QAT inserts fake-quantization/quantization effects during training so weights adapt to deployment error, costing training data/compute and often straight-through gradient approximations. Use it when low-bit PTQ fails quality targets at an important deployment footprint and compatible runtime kernels exist. BF16/FP16 are ordinary reduced floating precision, while FP8 training/inference needs format/scaling support; “4-bit model” does not imply every tensor is4-bit. Trade-off: PTQ is cheaper to prepare; QAT can recover quality but needs training and operational complexity.

### 2. FlashAttention changes memory scheduling

Naive attention writes $S=QK^T/\sqrt d$ and P=softmax(S) to HBM, each T×T/head, then reads P to multiply V. Tiling keeps small Q/K/V blocks and running row maxima/normalizers/output accumulators in SRAM/registers, fuses operations and avoids full score/probability HBM storage. When a new block increases max m to m', rescale old sum/output by exp(m-m') before adding new exponentials; this is online softmax, not independent block softmax. Backward can recompute blocks rather than store P. Dense-attention arithmetic remains O(T²d); activation score storage falls from quadratic to linear-size stored state plus tiles. It is mathematically exact attention up to floating-point order differences. Trade-off: faster/lower memory on supported hardware, with specialized kernels and shape-dependent performance.

### 3. RNN/LSTM versus Transformer

An LSTM uses recurrent hidden/cell state, costing O(T(dh+h²)) and sequential dependence across positions; it has bounded streaming state but long-range signals pass through many updates. A Transformer projects in O(TD²) and mixes all positions in O(T²D), allowing parallel teacher-forced training and short information paths but needing positional information and growing context/KV memory. Autoregressive generation remains token-sequential for both. RNNs can suit compact streaming/low-state tasks; Transformers exploit parallel hardware/data and direct context access. Trade-off: bounded recurrence/state versus parallel training and expensive long-context attention.

### 4. Parallelism and sharding

Data parallel replicas process different batches and synchronize gradients. Tensor parallel splits matrix operations with intra-layer collectives, best on fast links. Pipeline parallel splits layers with activation/gradient transfers and microbatch bubbles. Sequence parallel partitions token activations for suitable operations; context parallel partitions attention context and exchanges K/V or partial softmax state. Expert parallel routes MoE tokens to expert-owning devices with all-to-all and load-balance costs. ZeRO1 shards optimizer state, ZeRO2 also gradients, ZeRO3/FSDP also parameters with all-gather/reduce-scatter around layer computation. Sharding saves persistent memory at communication/transient-gather cost.

Inference uses request replicas, tensor/pipeline/expert splitting for large models, KV caching, continuous batching, chunked prefill and prefix-cache reuse. It usually has no optimizer state to shard. Trade-off: enough partitioning to fit memory versus synchronization, latency, pipeline bubbles and failure complexity.

### 5. Place precision where the bottleneck is

Training often uses BF16/FP16 matrix operations with higher-precision reductions, master/optimizer states and loss/normalization calculations; FP16 commonly needs loss scaling. Activation checkpointing/sharding can matter more than weight-only compression for training memory. In inference prioritize weight bytes when low-batch decode is bandwidth-bound, activation precision when prefill kernels benefit, and KV cache when long context/concurrency dominates. Keep sensitive norms, softmax/log-sum-exp, accumulations and outlier channels in appropriate precision if tests require it.

Tune bit width, symmetric/asymmetric representation, per-tensor/channel/group scales, group size, calibration mixture/length, clipping/outlier thresholds and cache quantization block policy. For a fixed weight count,4-bit raw weights are one quarter of16-bit bytes before scales/packing; this is not a4× whole-service speed claim. Evaluate target/rare/long-context tasks, calibration, hardware throughput and p99 under realistic shapes, with rollback to a known precision. Trade-off: compression improves fit/bandwidth only if numerical error and kernel overhead remain acceptable.

### Further study

- [F038: Choose a quantization approach and validate its cost.](../04_serving_and_training_systems.md#f038)
- [F008: What makes attention quadratic, and what does FlashAttention change?](../01_llm_internals.md#f008)
- [F035: Compare data, tensor and pipeline parallel training.](../04_serving_and_training_systems.md#f035)

title: LLM Questions: Training Systems, Hardware, and Scaling

steps: Partition the work at the correct boundary
What transfers from small to large
solution.example: TP8 within a fast-link node, PP across nodes and DP across complete groups partition communication by frequency and tensor ownership.
solution.trap: A small-model learning-rate ranking or kernel bottleneck need not persist at large scale.
solution.teaching_notes_markdown:
### Partition the work at the correct boundary

Data parallelism replicates weights for different examples and all-reduces gradients; it scales throughput when the model fits per replica, but replicated weights/optimizer consume memory. FSDP/ZeRO shard persistent state and gather layer units, exchanging memory for communication. Tensor parallelism splits operators/weights and communicates partial outputs/gradients each layer, favoring within-node fast interconnects. Pipeline parallelism puts layer groups on different devices and exchanges boundary activations/gradients, with microbatch bubbles and load-balance constraints; it can cross slower links more efficiently than frequent tensor collectives. Context/sequence parallelism partitions long-token activations and attention work; expert parallelism partitions MoE experts with token dispatch/all-to-all.

For example,8 GPUs/node can form one tensor-parallel group; several nodes can be pipeline stages; many such model groups can be data-parallel replicas. Tune that decomposition from model/activation/optimizer memory, batch/context size and measured interconnect. Within one GPU, thousands of threads execute SIMD/SIMT work, blocks tile matrices through registers/shared SRAM, and matrix units execute supported small matrix operations. This intra-device parallelism is distinct from assigning model shards across devices. A collective cannot be justified merely by saying “gather”: concatenate disjoint output rows, but sum contributions to the same derivative.

### CPU, GPU and TPU architecture

| Device | Design and memory | Suitable work and trade-off |
|---|---|---|
| CPU | Relatively few complex latency-oriented cores, branching/speculation, large caches and DRAM; vector units; cache-coherent sockets | Data/control, irregular workloads, modest batches, orchestration; lower large-dense-matmul throughput per watt |
| GPU | Many throughput-oriented execution lanes, registers/shared SRAM, high-bandwidth memory, matrix/tensor units and device links | Dense batched matmul/attention and parallel kernels; launch/transfer overhead, divergence and memory pressure can dominate small work |
| TPU | Specialized matrix/systolic units with vector/scalar support, on-chip buffers, HBM and pod interconnect under a compiler/runtime | Large dense ML and supported distributed graphs; strong throughput when compiler/layout/sharding fit, with less general execution flexibility |

Compare actual generations/capacity/bandwidth/topology and supported FP32/BF16/FP16/FP8/integer modes rather than quoting an eternal core count. Host–device links and cross-device links differ; a fast chip with an unsuitable network can underperform. A roofline gives $\min(peak\ FLOP/s,bandwidth\cdot arithmetic\ intensity)$; batching/tiling improves reuse but does not fix every control-bound path.

### What transfers from small to large

Target alignment, leakage prevention, shape/mask correctness and controlled ablations transfer as invariants. Initialization/normalization, activation and gradient statistics, optimizer moment behavior and schedule design transfer as mechanisms, but best learning rates/batch sizes do not transfer unchanged. Use parameterization-aware scaling rules as hypotheses, then staged pilots with loss-versus-tokens/compute and stability logs.

Generalization/evaluation discipline transfers: decontamination, independent test families, uncertainty and calibration/safety slices. Small-model benchmark order can reverse at large scale, and rare failures/capabilities may appear only with longer training/context. Data provenance/dedup/quality/mixture design matter at every size, while filter thresholds and source balance need scaling audits.

Architectural ablations should hold parameters/tokens/compute as appropriate, change one mechanism, and repeat at several scales rather than extrapolate one point. What often fails to transfer is hardware efficiency: large tensors alter compute/bandwidth balance, collectives and input/checkpoint IO emerge, and failures become normal over weeks. Pilot a representative distributed slice, measure scaling efficiency and communication, extrapolate with explicit bounds, then validate before committing the full training budget.

title: Matmul Arithmetic Intensity and Roofline Performance Modeling
question:
Estimate how fast matrix multiplications run on one GPU using the roofline model, then scale the estimate to a 72-layer network and compare two ways of splitting it over two GPUs. This is a pen-and-paper performance-modelling question: show the formula, the arithmetic and the conclusion for each part.

Hardware (one GPU, all numbers given)
Peak compute: 312 TFLOP/s (BF16)
HBM bandwidth: 1.5 TB/s
VRAM: 40 GB (take 1 GB = 10^9 bytes)
Link between two GPUs: 300 GB/s per direction
All tensors are BF16 (2 bytes per element). A matmul C = A @ B with A: m x k, B: k x n, C: m x n reads A and B once and writes C once.
1. Cost of a single matmul

For each shape (m, k, n) below, derive:

1.
FLOPs: 2 * m * k * n
2.
Bytes moved: 2 * (m*k + k*n + m*n)
3.
Arithmetic intensity: FLOPs / bytes (FLOP/byte), and the ridge point peak FLOP/s / bandwidth
4.
Bound regime: memory-bound below the ridge point, compute-bound above it
5.
Predicted time: max(FLOPs / peak FLOP/s, bytes / bandwidth)

Shapes: (1, 8192, 8192), (64, 8192, 8192), (512, 8192, 8192), (4096, 4096, 4096).

2. A 72-layer network on one GPU

The network has 72 layers that alternate between two matmul patterns, 36 layers of each. Every layer reads its own weight matrix, and layers are costed independently.

Pattern A: (m, k, n) = (2048, 8192, 8192)
Pattern B: (m, k, n) = (2048, 8192, 32768)

Compute: (a) the total compute time sum FLOPs / peak, (b) the total data-transfer time sum bytes / bandwidth, (c) the predicted end-to-end time as the sum of the per-layer predicted times from Part 1's rule, and (d) whether all weights plus the largest input and output activation of any one layer fit in 40 GB.

3. Splitting over two GPUs

Compare, for the same network and a single batch of m = 2048 rows:

Pipeline parallelism: layers 1-36 on GPU 0 and layers 37-72 on GPU 1. Only the m x 8192 activation crosses the link once.
Tensor parallelism: every weight matrix is split along n into two halves, one per GPU, so each GPU runs (m, k, n/2). After every layer each GPU sends its half of the output (m * n * 2 / 2 bytes) to the other GPU over the link, with no overlap with compute.

Report end-to-end latency, per-GPU weight memory, and the trade-off (latency against communication volume and memory). Ignore pipeline bubbles: one batch, no micro-batching.

Constraints
Use exactly the numbers above; round results to three significant figures.
State the bound regime of each matmul before computing its time.

solution.example: 72-layer baseline158.583ms; two-GPU pipeline158.695ms; stipulated tensor-parallel89.358ms, eachGPU12.080GB weights.
solution.trap: One-batch pipeline stages run serially; full-duplex300GB/s per-direction transfer latency is not doubled.
solution.teaching_notes_markdown:
### 1. One-GPU roofline arithmetic

Use decimal units, P=312×10¹² FLOP/s, BW=1.5×10¹² byte/s. For shape(m,k,n), F=2mkn, bytes B=2(mk+kn+mn), intensity I=F/B and time=max(F/P,B/BW). The ridge is P/BW=**208 FLOP/byte**. Classify by intensity before choosing the larger time.

| (m,k,n) | FLOPs | Bytes | I (FLOP/B) | Regime | Compute time | Memory time | Predicted |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---|---:|---:|---:|
| (1,8192,8192) |1.34×10⁸|1.34×10⁸|1.00|Memory|.000430ms|.0895ms|**.0895ms**|
| (64,8192,8192) |8.59×10⁹|1.36×10⁸|63.0|Memory|.0275ms|.0909ms|**.0909ms**|
| (512,8192,8192) |6.87×10¹⁰|1.51×10⁸|455|Compute|.220ms|.101ms|**.220ms**|
| (4096,4096,4096) |1.37×10¹¹|1.01×10⁸|1.37×10³|Compute|.441ms|.0671ms|**.441ms**|

For example, first shape has F=134,217,728 and B=134,250,496, so I=.999756 and memory dominates. Rounding in the table is to three significant figures; use unrounded values for totals.

### 2. Sum the 72 independent layer costs

Pattern A: F_A=274,877,906,944, B_A=201,326,592, I_A=1365.33>208, hence compute-bound, time .881019ms (memory .134218ms).

Pattern B: F_B=1,099,511,627,776, B_B=704,643,072, I_B=1560.38>208, hence compute-bound, time3.524076ms (memory .469762ms).

Total pure compute=36(F_A+F_B)/P=**159ms** (unrounded158.583ms). Total pure transfer=36(B_A+B_B)/BW=**21.7ms**. Sum of per-layer roofline times=36(.881019+3.524076)=**159ms**; generally sum(max) need not equal max(sum), but here every layer is compute-bound.

Weights occupy 36·2(8192²+8192·32768)=24,159,191,040 bytes=**24.2GB**. Largest simultaneous input+output is2(2048·8192+2048·32768)=167,772,160 bytes=.168GB. Combined **24.3GB** fits40GB under the stipulated single-layer activation model; training gradients/optimizer and other runtime buffers were not requested. Alternating raw shapes are not a self-contained dimension-compatible neural architecture; this is the question's independent-layer cost model, with no invented bridging operations.

### 3. Pipeline versus tensor splitting

Pipeline: GPU0 and GPU1 each hold18 A and18 B weights, **12.1GB/GPU**. One batch visits both halves sequentially, so compute latency remains158.583ms. Boundary bytes=2·2048·8192=33,554,432 bytes=.0336GB, transfer=.111848ms. End-to-end **159ms** (158.695 unrounded). No microbatch overlap means no single-batch2× speedup; adding throughput overlap would be a different scenario.

Tensor: each GPU computes A'=(2048,8192,4096), I=1170.29 and time.440509ms; B'=(2048,8192,16384), I=1489.45 and time1.762038ms. Both remain compute-bound. Sum local compute=36(.440509+1.762038)=**79.3ms**. Per-direction output transfer per layer is m·n bytes: A16,777,216 and B67,108,864. Across all layers each GPU sends36(16,777,216+67,108,864)=3,019,898,880 bytes=**3.02GB**. Full-duplex per-direction300GB/s gives **10.1ms**, not twice that latency; total bidirectional traffic is6.04GB. With no overlap, end-to-end **89.4ms**. Weight storage is again**12.1GB/GPU**, plus temporary gathers/activations.

Tensor parallelism reduces this modeled latency about1.78× versus pipeline while sending about180× the pipeline's total link bytes (6.04GB/.0336GB). Pipeline has much less communication and can improve throughput with microbatches, but not this single-batch latency. All times are optimistic roofline estimates excluding launches, collectives/software and contention; no achieved benchmark is implied.

title: Roofline Analysis and Mixed-Precision Gradients for Matmul
question:
A GPU has a peak FP16 throughput of 312 TFLOP/s and an HBM bandwidth of 1.5 TB/s. Use the roofline model to analyse matrix multiplications on it, then reason about the gradient of a residual connection and about where casting from FP32 to FP16 causes trouble.

Questions
1.
Roofline for a matmul. For (M,K)·(K,N) in FP16 (2 bytes per element, each matrix moved once), derive the FLOP count, the bytes moved, the arithmetic intensity, and the roofline time bound max(compute_time, memory_time). Compute the ridge point of this GPU.
2.
Two shapes. Apply this to M = K = N = 4096 and to M = 1, K = N = 4096 (a matrix-vector product). Classify each as compute-bound or memory-bound and give both time estimates.
3.
Residual gradient. For y = x + f(x), derive dL/dx in terms of dL/dy and explain why the identity branch keeps the gradient from vanishing as depth grows.
4.
FP32 to FP16. Name where casting to FP16 hurts (gradient underflow, normalisation denominators, accumulation, weight updates) and give the standard mitigation for each. Explain why bf16 often needs no loss scaling.
Expected deliverable

Worked arithmetic with units for parts 1 and 2, a short derivation for part 3, and a list of pitfalls with their mitigations for part 4.

steps: Residual gradient: a useful direct path, not an absolute guarantee
Where FP16 casting hurts and what to do
solution.example: 4096-cube intensity1365FLOP/B is compute-bound at.440509ms; M1 vector case intensity~1 is memory-bound at.0223805ms.
solution.trap: Residual identity paths help but Jf=-I can still cancel gradients; loss scaling does not repair forward overflow.
solution.teaching_notes_markdown:
### Derive and apply the roofline

For FP16 matmul, F=2MKN and B=2(MK+KN+MN) bytes under the specified once-read/once-write assumption. I=F/B FLOP/byte; compute time=F/(312×10¹²), memory time=B/(1.5×10¹²), lower-bound time=max of the two. Ridge=312/1.5=**208 FLOP/byte**.

For M=K=N=4096: F=137,438,953,472, B=100,663,296, I=1365.33>208, so **compute-bound**. Compute time=.440509ms, memory time=.0671089ms, roofline=.440509ms.

For M=1,K=N=4096: F=33,554,432, B=33,570,816, I=.999512<208, so **memory-bound**. Compute=.000107546ms=.107546microseconds; memory=.0223805ms=22.3805microseconds; roofline=.0223805ms. The matrix-vector operation does far less work but still rereads almost the same weights. Batching improves their reuse; real tiny-kernel latency also includes launch overhead.

### Residual gradient: a useful direct path, not an absolute guarantee

For y=x+f(x), column-vector upstream g=dL/dy gives $dL/dx=(I+J_f(x))^Tg=g+J_f(x)^Tg$. Across depth, products of `(I+J)` include identity paths, so information/gradients need not pass only through a long product of small branch derivatives. This makes learning corrections easier. It does **not** mathematically prevent vanishing: J_f=-I cancels the direct derivative, and other spectra can still explode. Initialization/normalization/residual scale remain important.

### Where FP16 casting hurts and what to do

| Failure point | Mechanism | Mitigation |
|---|---|---|
| Tiny gradients | Values below representable subnormal/normal ranges round toward zero | Dynamic loss scaling before backward; unscale before clipping/update, detect nonfinite gradients and skip/reduce scale |
| Normalization/loss denominator | Squaring/reduction/epsilon may overflow or lose precision; small epsilon can round away | Compute mean/variance/log-sum-exp/denominator in FP32 with suitable epsilon and stable formulas |
| Accumulation | Many low-precision additions lose increments or overflow | FP32 matmul/reduction/gradient accumulation where supported and verify kernel behavior |
| Weight updates | Small update disappears when added directly to a large FP16 weight | FP32 master parameters/optimizer moments, update in FP32 then cast a compute copy |
| Large values | FP16 maximum finite magnitude65504 can be exceeded | Monitor activations/gradients, correct scaling/initialization, keep sensitive paths FP32 or use BF16 |

FP16 has5 exponent bits and10 fraction bits, BF16 has8 exponent bits and7 fraction bits. BF16's exponent range is similar to FP32, making gradient underflow/overflow much less common and often removing the need for loss scaling; its mantissa is coarser, so it still needs careful accumulation and master/update precision. Loss scaling does not cure an already-overflowing forward or a wrong derivative. Benchmark convergence and task quality against a higher-precision baseline before claiming a mixed-precision win.

### Further study

title: Design a GPU Inference Serving System
question:
Design a high-throughput inference serving system that hosts large models behind an API on a fixed fleet of expensive GPUs. Maximize throughput (requests / tokens per second) while keeping p99 latency low.

In your design, address:

the request lifecycle and batching strategy (static vs continuous / dynamic batching),
model loading and GPU-memory management,
routing, replication, and autoscaling across GPU workers,
hosting multiple models on shared hardware,
absorbing load spikes and overload,
the key bottlenecks and trade-offs.

The crux to nail: keeping the GPUs saturated through batching without blowing the latency target.

steps: Load models and allocate against live memory
solution.example: One4k-token32-layer8-KV-head BF16 request consumes512MiB raw cache; twenty consume10GiB before weights.
solution.trap: A high batch count cannot excuse violating memory/deadline admission or p99 constraints.
solution.teaching_notes_markdown:
<!-- architecture:W026:start -->
### Architecture and request flow

![W026 question-specific component flow](../diagrams/W026_architecture.svg)

A version-pinned request passes deadline/token-memory admission, a bounded continuous batch and a warm GPU worker before its ordered stream is delivered.

[Open full-size diagram](../diagrams/W026_architecture.svg).
<!-- architecture:W026:end -->

### Request path and bounded batching

Assume autoregressive text generation with a fixed fleet, several versioned models and separately defined p99 TTFT/inter-token/completion budgets. `POST /v1/generate` carries request id, model alias, text, max output and deadline; returns a stream with ordered request-scoped events. Status/cancel endpoints handle disconnects and retries. Gateway authenticates, tokenizes, resolves an immutable model version and rejects unsupported lengths or quotas before enqueueing. Request state records version, prompt/output token counts, deadline, worker/attempt, status and usage; the registry stores digest, precision, tokenizer/runtime compatibility and resource profile.

Static batches wait for all members or waste finished slots. Dynamic batching collects a short bounded window for compatible independent work. For generation use continuous batching: admit/remove requests between decode iterations, with maximum active tokens and per-iteration work budget. Chunk long prefills so one huge prompt does not stall all active decodes. Prioritize imminent deadlines and age long jobs; batching is constrained by latency and memory, not merely a target batch size. A queue full of work beyond its deadlines is overload, not useful GPU utilization.

### Load models and allocate against live memory

Download verified weight shards to local disk, load/warm a new replica, run health/parity checks, then mark ready. Never route to a half-loaded model. Track memory as weights + runtime/temporary buffers + live KV + allocator headroom. KV bytes/token=$2LH_{KV}d_hs$; for L32,Hkv8,dh128,s2 it is131,072 bytes, so4k cached tokens use512MiB/request. Twenty such requests need10GiB cache before weights/buffers. Reserve or conservatively bound future output growth; paged blocks reduce fragmentation but not logical cache bytes. Release on EOS/cancel/deadline and validate prefix-cache keys by model/tokenizer/positions/tenant policy.

Route to compatible warm workers using live-token load, queue delay and prefix locality, with bounded affinity to avoid hot spots. Replicate popular models; tensor-shard models that cannot fit on one GPU, preferring fast-link groups. On a fixed fleet “autoscaling” reallocates replicas/partitions between models and may shed work; it cannot create unprovided GPUs. Model swaps cost transfer/warmup and must be rate-limited. Small models may share a GPU with hard budgets; large models/strict tails may need isolation. Avoid opportunistic evictions that repeatedly destroy a popular model's warm cache.

### Overload, failures and tuning

Use per-tenant weighted queues/quotas, short admission windows, token caps,429/503 with Retry-After and an explicitly permitted fallback. A worker crash terminates that generation attempt; retries must not splice different nondeterministic text into an already delivered stream. Event ids support reconnect replay; duplicate client keys return the existing request. Canceling queued/running work frees resources promptly.

Prefill often benefits from compute parallelism; low-batch decode often rereads weights/cache and is bandwidth-bound. Quantization can reduce bytes, fusion removes intermediates, and larger batches amortize weight reads, but all need matched quality/latency measurements. Monitor useful completed tokens/s, p99 queue/TTFT/inter-token, OOM/preemption, cache fragmentation/hits, model load times and fairness. Load-test length distributions and bursts, choose a throughput–p99 operating point below saturation, canary and rollback. The existing diagram's gateway, registry, queue and workers are the lifecycle above; the central correctness rule is that memory/deadline admission precedes dispatch.

### Further study
