solution.teaching_notes_markdown:
### Define the decision and its cost

Score a payment before authorization and choose allow, challenge or reject. Confirm the allowed extra latency, peak transaction rate, geographical requirements and which losses are counted. Optimize prevented fraud loss after subtracting customer friction, lost legitimate sales and review cost. A chargeback label arrives later than the transaction and may reflect disputes other than fraud.

![W061. Design an ML Fraud Detection System — architecture](../diagrams/W061_review_architecture.svg)

[Open the architecture diagram](../diagrams/W061_review_architecture.svg).

### Build point-in-time training data

Join transaction, account, merchant and device facts as known at authorization time. Useful features include amount relative to the account's history, account age, device novelty, recent failed attempts, merchant risk and cross-account device velocity. Deduplicate transaction events, preserve missingness, and prevent future chargeback or post-decision information from leaking into features. Keep late-arriving labels out of prematurely classified negatives.

Start with rules plus gradient-boosted trees on tabular features. Compare a neural or graph-enhanced model when shared-device/account relationships provide measurable gains. Fraud imbalance calls for class weighting or negative downsampling during training, with correction/calibration on representative prevalence. Never report evaluation on an artificially balanced test set as production precision.

Measure PR-AUC, recall and fraud value caught at a fixed false-positive/challenge rate, expected monetary loss, calibration and subgroup/merchant slices. Use chronological splits, leave an appropriate label-maturation gap and consider entity grouping to assess generalization to new fraud rings.

### Serve, fail and improve

Keep model weights local to horizontally scaled risk workers; precompute aggregates in a low-latency feature store and update velocity features from streams. Attach freshness timestamps and choose documented missing-feature defaults. Let peak QPS be $Q$, per-instance tested capacity $q$ at the latency target and utilization target $u$; provision at least $\lceil Q/(qu)\rceil$ instances plus failure headroom. “Massive volume” is not a numerical capacity requirement, so ask for $Q$ and benchmark $q$.

A transaction ID makes repeated scoring auditable; it does not by itself prevent duplicate payment authorization, which belongs to the payment ledger. On feature timeouts, use a tested reduced-feature model or risk-tier policy rather than silently allowing everything. Shadow new versions, then canary with rollback. Monitor score shifts, missing/stale features, model latency/errors, challenge completion, mature fraud loss and legitimate declines. Route uncertain cases within review capacity and audit allowed payments to detect blind spots. Retrain with delayed, reviewed outcomes and investigate adversarial adaptation instead of treating drift alerts as automatic retraining orders.

title: Design an Account Takeover Prediction System
question:
Design a machine learning system to predict Account Takeover (ATO) risk for a payments platform. ATO occurs when an attacker steals login credentials or uses a fake identity to break into a real user's account. The prompt is deliberately open-ended — clarify rules and requirements up front.

The interview covers three areas:

Modeling (~20 min): feature engineering (login time/location/device, transaction amount and velocity, IP/network signals), preprocessing (missing values, scaling, categorical encoding), model choice and evaluation metrics, and risks (class imbalance, duplicate/leaky features, overfitting).

System (~15 min): architecture (ingestion, feature store, model serving, health monitoring), low-latency inference at high QPS, handling data-fetch delays, live model updates, and production monitoring of both prediction quality and system speed.

Business value (~15 min): proving impact (fewer compromised accounts, higher trust), the cost of false positives (blocking a legitimate user), and future improvements.

Follow-up on data splitting: how to train on heavily imbalanced data — oversampling, SMOTE, stratified sampling.

solution.example: Worked examples and checks are included in the complete answer.
solution.trap: Do not substitute a related generic method for this question’s specified contract.
solution.teaching_notes_markdown:
### Clarify account takeover

Predict whether the current login or account action is controlled by an attacker. Ask whether the decision occurs at login, account-setting changes or payment, what challenge methods exist, and the latency/false-positive budget. ATO differs from payment fraud: a new device may be a legitimate owner, and a low-value login can precede a high-value theft.

![W062. Design an Account Takeover Prediction System — architecture](../diagrams/W062_review_architecture.svg)

[Open the architecture diagram](../diagrams/W062_review_architecture.svg).

### Features, preprocessing and labels

Use device novelty, recent credential failures, IP/network reputation, impossible-travel estimates, hour relative to usual activity, password-reset recency, account age, transaction amount deviation and velocity. Treat VPNs, shared networks and travel as noisy evidence rather than proof. Collect labels from confirmed compromises, recoveries and adjudicated investigations; a blocked login is not automatically an attacker.

Deduplicate repeated events and join only facts available before scoring. Add missing-value indicators, encode categories with training-only vocabularies and scale continuous inputs for linear/neural models. Trees usually need no scaling. Remove near-duplicate or post-outcome features that inflate offline quality. Start with boosted trees and compare a calibrated logistic baseline; add sequence/graph models only if they improve the intended decision.

### Handle imbalance without leaking

Use chronological train/validation/test periods with enough label delay and evaluate important user/device splits. Preserve real prevalence in validation and test. Class weighting or training-only negative downsampling is a practical first choice. Oversampling must happen **after** the split; otherwise copies can land in both training and test. SMOTE can create unrealistic mixtures of IP/device categorical features and should not be the default for this event data. A stratified random split preserves class proportion but does not protect against temporal leakage or repeated-user overlap.

Report PR-AUC, recall at a fixed legitimate-user challenge rate, calibrated probability, confirmed loss and account recovery burden. Choose thresholds using the cost of an undetected compromise versus a challenge or false block. Where uncertainty is manageable, step-up authentication is less disruptive than denial.

### Production and business proof

Keep a low-latency online feature store and in-process model, with versioned schemas and an atomic model switch. Bound feature lookups; fall back to an evaluated reduced-feature model or explicit risk-tier policy when signals are unavailable. Monitor p95/p99 latency, QPS, timeouts, feature age and score shifts alongside delayed confirmed ATO, legitimate-user lockouts and challenge abandonment.

Use a guarded experiment on eligible traffic, preserving strong protections for high-risk actions. Measure fewer confirmed compromises and lower loss together with successful legitimate logins, support contacts and trust/recovery outcomes. Interpret early results cautiously because compromise confirmation is delayed. Future work includes better device linking, sequence signals and friction-aware challenges, with access limits and retention rules for sensitive login data. Retraining and canary deployment must keep calibration and customer-friction guardrails intact.

title: ML System Design: Search & Ranking
question:
Family of design prompts: Pin search, Pin ranking, home-feed retrieval, search input suggestions. Interviewers expect a candidate-generation -> ranking stage architecture with explicit embedding sourcing, loss choice (pair-wise vs point-wise), offline metrics, and candidate-pool sizing math.

Requirements

Design one of:

A search engine for Pins (the most common framing): candidate generation, ranking, query understanding, personalization.
Pin ranking / home feed: surface relevant pins to a user in real time, responsive to engagement.
Search input suggestions / typeahead: low-latency query autocompletion with personalization signal.
A recommender system end-to-end: data storage, candidate generation, ranking model serving.

The interviewer typically asks for explicit answers to: How do you efficiently generate candidates? What models / loss function (pair-wise vs point-wise vs list-wise)? What features and how are they constructed? Offline vs online metric? How many candidates pass to the ranker (justify the number)? Where is data stored / how are models served? For a 60GB GPU, how do you compute the serving batch size?

Notes
The standard reference architecture: two-tower retrieval (user tower, item tower; dot-product similarity) for candidate generation, plus a heavier ranker (DLRM / DCN / MMoE) for the top-N candidates. Pinterest's published PinSAGE / PinnerSAGE family is the relevant embedding work.
Candidate-count math: candidate pool is sized as inference_complexity_per_item x items_per_inference_batch x number_of_instances against the per-request latency budget. Be ready to derive it from a stated 100ms latency budget.
Batch size for a 60GB GPU: model weights + activation memory + intermediate buffers must fit; max_batch = (60GB - weights - KV) / activation_per_sample.
Embedding training is the most common driver: positive pairs (co-engaged pins, user-pin engagement), negative sampling (in-batch negatives, hard negatives), label-noise handling.
Pair-wise (BPR / RankNet) for ranking with implicit feedback; point-wise (cross-entropy on click) for retrieval when calibrated probabilities matter.

steps: Pick Pin search and define the stages
solution.contract_notes: Read the worked solution for the exact assumptions, constraints and missing-input limitations.
solution.example: Worked examples and checks are included in the complete answer.
solution.trap: Do not substitute a related generic method for this question’s specified contract.
solution.teaching_notes_markdown:
### Pick Pin search and define the stages

Given a query and permitted user context, return relevant Pins within an assumed 100 ms serving budget. Use lexical and embedding retrieval for broad recall, a heavier ranker for relevance/engagement, and a final diversity/policy pass. The other proposed products need different targets: a home feed has no explicit query, while typeahead prioritizes prefix matching and much tighter latency.

![W063. ML System Design: Search & Ranking — architecture](../diagrams/W063_review_architecture.svg)

[Open the architecture diagram](../diagrams/W063_review_architecture.svg).

### Train retrieval and ranking differently

Build item embeddings from Pin text/images and co-engagement data; build a user/query representation from permitted history and the current query. Train retrieval on positive query–Pin or user–Pin pairs with sampled/in-batch negatives. A contrastive softmax loss makes positives score above sampled alternatives. Filter accidental positives among negatives and add hard negatives carefully. Graph/co-engagement representations can complement content embeddings, particularly for established items; content is essential for cold starts.

The ranker combines lexical match, embedding similarity, user/item features, freshness and quality. Pointwise binary cross-entropy on clicks can estimate click probability **after** accounting for exposure and calibration. Pairwise RankNet/BPR losses prefer a positive over a negative:

$$L_{\mathrm{pair}}=-\log\sigma(s^+-s^-).$$

A listwise loss can optimize a whole displayed slate. Pairwise scores are not automatically calibrated probabilities, and retrieval is not restricted to pointwise training. Choose the objective for the stage and target, rather than memorizing one loss per architecture.

### Derive candidate and memory budgets

Suppose measured non-ranking work consumes 45 ms of the 100 ms budget and the ranker processes 64 candidates in 8 ms. With no extra overhead, at most $\lfloor55/8\rfloor\times64=384$ candidates fit sequentially on one reserved lane. Start around 300 and validate tail latency under contention. Parallel lanes reduce per-request latency only when spare capacity exists; multiplying instance count alone does not make each request faster. Measure recall@K to see whether that pool preserves relevant items.

For a 60 GB GPU, estimate

$$B_{\max}\le\left\lfloor\frac{60-W-R}{A}\right\rfloor,$$

where $W$ is resident weight/embedding memory, $R$ is runtime/workspace/reserve and $A$ is measured incremental activation memory per example, all in consistent units. A feed-forward ranker normally has no autoregressive KV cache. With illustrative $W=12$ GB, $R=8$ GB and $A=0.05$ GB, memory permits 800 examples, but latency may require a much smaller batch. Load-test dynamic batching and queue delay.

### Storage and evaluation

Keep versioned training tables in object storage, item vectors in sharded ANN indexes, lexical documents in a search index and hot user/item features in an online store. Publish model and embedding-index versions compatibly. Evaluate retrieval recall, ranker NDCG and slices for rare queries/new Pins, then run an online experiment on useful saves/long-term satisfaction with latency, diversity and negative-feedback guardrails. Log the actual displayed slate and its propensity/exploration context to reduce position and feedback bias.

title: ML System Design: Dynamic K in Retrieval Stage
question:
In a recommendation stack (retrieval, then ranking, then re-ranking), the retrieval stage hands a fixed number K of candidate items to the ranking stage for every request. A static K wastes ranking compute on easy requests and starves ranking on ambiguous ones. Design a model or system that chooses K dynamically for each request.

Requirements

Your design must cover these parts:

1.
Goal metric: define how you decide that the chosen K was right for a request, and which guardrail metrics (latency, ranking cost, engagement) bound it.
2.
Model output: decide whether the model predicts K directly or predicts a per-candidate quantity from which K is derived, and justify the choice, including where the training labels come from.
3.
Features: list the request-level, session-level, retrieval-stage and system-level signals the controller uses.
4.
Calibration and thresholds: explain how scores are made trustworthy enough to turn into a count, and how the threshold is tuned.
5.
Serving and safety: explain how worst-case latency is bounded, how the controller stays cheap, and how the learning loop is run.
6.
Evaluation and trade-offs: give an online experiment plan and compare static K with dynamic K, including failure modes.
Constraints
Ranking cost grows roughly linearly with K; p99 latency is a hard ceiling.
The controller adds negligible latency compared with the compute it saves.
A regression in downstream engagement must be caught before full rollout.

steps: Choose the smallest useful candidate count
Learn a quantity with an interpretable decision
solution.contract_notes: Read the worked solution for the exact assumptions, constraints and missing-input limitations.
solution.example: Worked examples and checks are included in the complete answer.
solution.trap: Do not substitute a related generic method for this question’s specified contract.
solution.teaching_notes_markdown:
### Choose the smallest useful candidate count

The controller should save ranking work while preserving downstream value and a hard latency limit. Start with a small menu, for example $K\in\{100,200,400,800\}$, rather than regressing an arbitrary integer that may be unstable or unsupported by training data.

![W064. ML System Design: Dynamic K in Retrieval Stage — architecture](../diagrams/W064_review_architecture.svg)

[Open the architecture diagram](../diagrams/W064_review_architecture.svg).

### Learn a quantity with an interpretable decision

For each adjacent menu step, predict the expected marginal gain from adding that block of candidates. Offline, run the expensive downstream ranker on a sampled maximum pool and compare the best final slates attainable at each K. That provides a teacher signal, but is limited to the maximum retrieved pool and inherits the teacher's biases. Online engagement labels require randomized exploration or suitable propensity-aware estimation: unranked candidates do not have observed clicks.

A policy can select

$$K^*=\arg\max_{K\in\mathcal K,\ T_{99}(K)\le D}
[\widehat U(x,K)-\lambda C(K)],$$

where utility comes from the downstream task, $C$ is measured ranker cost and $D$ is the latency ceiling. Predicting marginal gains makes the reason for spending another block understandable. Direct multiclass prediction of the best menu item is a simpler alternative, but its labels still need reliable counterfactual comparisons.

### Features and calibration

Use query ambiguity, user/session history length, current intent, retrieval-score gaps/entropy, source disagreement, candidate diversity and recent repetition. Include current queue depth, available ranker capacity and feature freshness. A controller that saves 5 ms but itself consumes 10 ms fails the purpose; use a tiny tree or shallow model and precomputed statistics.

On held-out requests, group predicted marginal gains and compare them with measured gains. Calibrate by request type and time, especially for tail queries and cold users. Tune $\lambda$ and menu boundaries against a utility–cost frontier, then validate latency on production-like load. A probability threshold alone is insufficient unless the predicted event and its relation to downstream value are defined.

### Enforce safety outside the model

Clamp K between a minimum-quality floor and a capacity-dependent hard maximum. Reserve time for feature retrieval, reranking and network overhead; if the controller fails, use a tested static K. A fixed Kmax retrieval still costs something, so include it when estimating total savings. Avoid rapidly changing K with noisy queue depth; use bounded adjustments and stable admission control.

First shadow the policy and measure recall loss, ranking cost and tail latency. Then randomize users/requests as appropriate between static and dynamic K with a small exploration allocation. Primary success is lower cost at prespecified engagement noninferiority, or higher engagement at equal cost. Monitor rare-intent slices, p99, fallback frequency and controller drift. Roll back if it repeatedly starves ambiguous queries, learns from biased exposure labels or increases p99 during load spikes.

title: Video Recommendation
question:
ML system-design round: architect a video recommendation system covering candidate generation, ranking, serving, and feedback loops. The interviewer pushes hard on infrastructure: service split, data flow end to end, and especially event logging, pipelines, and observability that power the feedback loop.

Areas to cover
Candidate generation: embedding-based / two-tower retrieval, recency and engagement sources, filtering.
Ranking: scoring model(s), features, multi-objective balancing.
Serving: request-time flow with bounded latency.
Feedback loops: how observed engagement improves model quality.
Interviewer emphasis

Service split (where boundaries sit), data flow (interaction -> event bus -> training data + features -> serving; training-serving skew), and event logging + observability as the central deep-dive (Kafka -> offline store -> training/feedback; metrics and monitoring).

steps: Follow a recommendation from request to training
Prevent the feedback loop from corrupting training
solution.contract_notes: Read the worked solution for the exact assumptions, constraints and missing-input limitations.
solution.example: Worked examples and checks are included in the complete answer.
solution.trap: Do not substitute a related generic method for this question’s specified contract.
solution.teaching_notes_markdown:
### Follow a recommendation from request to training

Recommend a diverse set of eligible videos with useful watch time and satisfaction, rather than maximizing clicks on misleading thumbnails. Separate the online latency path from the durable feedback pipeline; event quality is as important as the ranker.

![W065. Video Recommendation — architecture](../diagrams/W065_review_architecture.svg)

[Open the architecture diagram](../diagrams/W065_review_architecture.svg).

### Candidate and ranking services

A two-tower model retrieves videos close to the user's current interests. Item embeddings combine content and engagement so new videos can enter before they have many clicks. Add recency, subscriptions and popularity sources to avoid relying on one representation. Merge and filter removed, already watched or ineligible videos before expensive ranking.

The ranker predicts click/start, useful watch duration, completion, skip and negative feedback. Combine these with explicit weights or constraints; raw duration alone favors long videos. A slate stage limits repeated creators, introduces diversity and respects product policies. Set candidate counts from measured recall and ranker latency rather than an unexplained constant. Serve a cached eligible slate or lightweight popularity fallback if an optional source misses its deadline.

### Design the event contract

Each recommendation response has a request ID, model/index versions, experiment assignment, candidate sources, displayed item IDs, positions and scores. The client emits actual impressions, starts, heartbeats, stops and feedback with unique event IDs, event time, receive time and session/request IDs. An API response is not proof that the user saw every item.

The event gateway validates schemas and writes to a partitioned durable bus. Consumers deduplicate event IDs and handle out-of-order/late playback events with event-time windows. Heartbeats can overlap or be missing: compute bounded watch intervals rather than blindly summing every reported second. Persist immutable raw events for replay; derive versioned feature tables and training labels from them.

### Prevent the feedback loop from corrupting training

Use one feature definition for offline point-in-time joins and online aggregates. Store feature timestamps and freshness; never join a user's future watch history into an earlier impression. Exposed-but-unwatched items can be negatives after a defined window; unexposed items are not known negatives. Add controlled exploration and log its probabilities when using counterfactual methods.

Monitor event drop/duplicate rates, client/server count reconciliation, consumer lag, label maturation, feature skew, source recall, score drift and per-stage p99. Offline metrics include recall@K and ranking quality; online tests measure satisfied watch time, skips/complaints, creator diversity and long-term retention with cost/latency guardrails. Train on a schedule, validate, canary and roll back model and index versions together where compatibility requires it.

title: Homepage Video Recommendation System
question:
Open ML-system-design prompt: recommend videos for the Netflix home page. Reported rounds skew toward high-level service architecture (how many services, how they communicate) over feature engineering / modeling / evaluation.

Clarify whether the prompt wants an ML-system-design treatment or a product-serving architecture treatment before diving into model internals.

steps: State the product and service boundary
solution.contract_notes: Read the worked solution for the exact assumptions, constraints and missing-input limitations.
solution.example: Worked examples and checks are included in the complete answer.
solution.trap: Do not substitute a related generic method for this question’s specified contract.
solution.teaching_notes_markdown:
### State the product and service boundary

Assume the task is the serving architecture for a personalized streaming-video homepage. Return rows of eligible titles and their order, not just one globally ranked list. Ask about catalog size, regions, peak requests/s, profile privacy, device types and latency before assigning machine counts. Model details can be a follow-up; the core design must explain how a page arrives reliably.

![W066. Homepage Video Recommendation System — architecture](../diagrams/W066_review_architecture.svg)

[Open the architecture diagram](../diagrams/W066_review_architecture.svg).

### What each service owns

The edge authenticates the profile and passes a request deadline. Catalog/eligibility owns region rights, maturity constraints and playable versions. Candidate services retrieve personalized, continue-watching, trending and editorial pools. The ranker scores candidates, while the row composer chooses coherent rows, orders them and removes excessive duplication across rows. Metadata hydration batches title/artwork fields and uses a CDN for assets. These are responsibility boundaries; a small deployment can combine some processes.

Store durable viewing history and progress separately from low-latency derived recommendation features. Version item embeddings and precomputed per-profile candidate sets. Use event-driven updates for recent viewing and batch computation for expensive long-term interests. Content publication and rights changes invalidate eligibility caches promptly; cached personalization must still pass current rights checks.

### One request and its failures

The orchestrator fetches independent candidate sources concurrently with individual deadlines. It does not wait indefinitely for one source. Rank the merged eligible pool, compose rows, hydrate metadata and return a response with request/model/experiment IDs. Continue-watching can be returned early if progressive rendering is supported.

If personalization is unavailable, use cached candidates or region-appropriate popular/editorial rows. If a metadata lookup fails, omit the affected card or use an already validated cached representation. Fail closed for unknown playback rights. Bound fan-out and use bulk feature/metadata reads; one RPC per item creates a latency and load explosion. Cache stable profile/context combinations briefly, respecting recent viewing and ownership boundaries.

### Capacity and proof

Let peak homepage traffic be $Q$ requests/s. If a source receives one call per page, it must sustain roughly $Q$ calls/s; multiplying five source calls means total downstream demand near $5Q$, before retries. Estimate response bytes, candidate counts and ranker throughput from measurements, and size each service for failure headroom. Do not equate catalog size with online ranking load.

Test end-to-end p99 under slow dependencies and a lost zone. Monitor source deadlines, fallback rate, page completeness, rights violations and feature freshness. Log actual card visibility and play completion, not just returned candidates. A/B tests use profile-level assignment and compare useful viewing, row interaction, long-term satisfaction and abandonment with latency guardrails. Daily model updates can proceed through shadow/canary rollout without making homepage availability depend on the training pipeline.

title: Design Meta Ads Ranking
question:
Design the Meta ads-ranking system. Given a user impression slot, select and rank ads to show, optimizing advertiser value (bid × pCTR × pCVR) while respecting user experience.

The three reported deep-dive zones are feature engineering, model architecture, and calibration. Be ready to go deep on the data pipeline (how training data is sourced, logged, labeled) as well.

steps: Define the probability and value being ranked
Serve and evaluate the complete decision
solution.contract_notes: Read the worked solution for the exact assumptions, constraints and missing-input limitations.
solution.example: Worked examples and checks are included in the complete answer.
solution.trap: Do not substitute a related generic method for this question’s specified contract.
solution.teaching_notes_markdown:
### Define the probability and value being ranked

For a conversion-valued ad, an illustrative expected advertiser value per impression is

$$v=b\,P(\mathrm{click}\mid x,a)\,
P(\mathrm{conversion}\mid\mathrm{click},x,a).$$

Here the bid $b$ is value per conversion and the conversion probability is **conditional on a click**. If a model already predicts conversion per impression, multiplying by pCTR again double counts the click probability. This is a ranking-value component, not a complete specification of auction payments.

![W067. Design Meta Ads Ranking — architecture](../diagrams/W067_review_architecture.svg)

[Open the architecture diagram](../diagrams/W067_review_architecture.svg).

### Features and architecture

User/context features include permitted recent interests, device, time and placement. Ad features include creative text/image embeddings, category, destination quality and campaign history. Interaction features capture user–ad similarity, prior exposure and frequency. Fast-changing budget/pacing state belongs in the serving policy; do not infer spend solely from a stale training feature. Apply privacy/consent constraints before feature access.

Retrieve eligible campaigns with cheap representations, then rank a bounded candidate pool. A shared-bottom or multi-task network can share sparse embeddings while separate heads estimate click, conversion and negative feedback. Compare with strong simpler baselines. Model conditional conversion carefully because clicked impressions are a selected sample; all-impression multitask formulations can reduce some selection issues but still require correct label definitions.

### Data and calibration are central

Log unique impression IDs, displayed positions, eligible context, model versions, predictions and experiment assignment. Join clicks and attributed conversions by stable IDs with an explicit attribution window. A recent impression with no conversion yet is censored, not a mature negative. Deduplicate events, handle late arrivals and prevent post-impression information from leaking into features. Correct training negative sampling when recovering production probabilities.

Evaluate log loss, calibration curves and predicted/observed ratios by placement, advertiser cohort and traffic slice in addition to AUC. A model that orders ads correctly but doubles pCVR can misallocate spend. Fit Platt/isotonic or other suitable calibration on a separate, representative period; validate again after model or traffic changes. Small slices require smoothing and uncertainty, not independent overfit calibrators.

### Serve and evaluate the complete decision

Fetch hot features in bulk and enforce deadlines; keep a reduced-feature fallback. Budget reservation and pacing need their own concurrency-safe state. Combine expected value with user-quality penalties/constraints such as repetitive exposure and hide/report risk. Candidate filtering, ranking and auction eligibility must use consistent policy versions.

Offline use time-based mature labels, ranking metrics and calibration. Online measure advertiser outcomes and spend efficiency together with user engagement, hides/reports, frequency, latency and budget correctness. Controlled exploration provides evidence beyond ads the old model preferred. Canary model/calibration changes, monitor delayed outcomes, and retain rollback versions. A short-term click increase does not establish improved conversion value or user experience.

title: Design App Store Search and Ranking
question:
Design the search and ranking system for the Apple App Store: a user types a query and receives a ranked list of relevant apps.

Requirements
1.
Scope and scale — state the catalog size, query volume, latency budget and objectives (relevance, install conversion, quality and anti-spam) you design for.
2.
Query understanding — how you normalize the query, detect its language, embed it, and classify its intent (navigational vs. exploratory).
3.
Retrieval — how you produce a candidate set of a few hundred apps from millions, covering both exact and semantic matches.
4.
Ranking — the model, the features it uses (from the sources below), and the training objective.
5.
Feature freshness and serving — how static and fast-changing features are computed, stored and served within the latency budget.
6.
Risks and trade-offs — cold-start apps, spam and keyword stuffing, optimizing clicks vs. installs, and privacy limits on user features.
Available feature sources
Static app features (recomputed when the app is updated): title, subtitle, description, category, keywords, icon and preview-image embeddings, price, in-app-purchase presence, developer reputation.
Dynamic app features (updated every minute): rating, review count, install velocity, recent click-through and uninstall rates.
Query features: normalized tokens, language, query embedding, inferred intent, query popularity.
Query-app interaction features: BM25 score, semantic cosine similarity, historical click-through and install rate for the (query, app) pair, lexical overlap.
User and context features (subject to privacy constraints): locale, device, prior downloads, cohort.
Constraints
Catalog of several million apps; end-to-end latency of roughly 200 ms per query.
Deliverable

A design that answers parts 1–6: the pipeline stages, the features and model used at each stage, and the main trade-offs.

### Scope the search request

Assume a catalog of five million apps and an illustrative peak of 10,000 queries/s; confirm the actual traffic. Return organic results for the user's locale/device within roughly 200 ms. Optimize useful installs and relevant discovery with quality/anti-spam constraints. A navigational query such as an exact app name needs different handling from “offline photo editor.”

![W068. Design App Store Search and Ranking — architecture](../diagrams/W068_review_architecture.svg)

[Open the architecture diagram](../diagrams/W068_review_architecture.svg).

### Retrieve broadly, then score carefully

Normalize Unicode and spelling while preserving the original query and brand names. Detect language, classify navigational/exploratory intent and produce a query embedding. Retrieve several hundred candidates from BM25/title-prefix matching and semantic ANN search; merge, deduplicate and filter apps unavailable for the device/region. Exact title matches should remain available even when embedding similarity is imperfect.

Build static item features at app update: title, subtitle, description, category, keywords, image/icon embeddings, price, purchase model and developer quality. Index text lexically and embed it semantically. Stream minute-level rating counts, install velocity, recent CTR and uninstall rate into a timestamped online feature store. Smooth low-count rates so one click does not make a new app appear perfect.

A tree or neural ranker combines BM25, cosine similarity, lexical overlap, intent, locale/device compatibility, static quality and query-app install history. Use only permitted prior-download/cohort features. Start with pointwise install prediction on exposed results; add relevance labels or a pairwise/listwise component so pure popularity does not overwhelm query matching. Account for position/exposure bias and conversion delay.

### Meet 200 ms with explicit ownership

An illustrative critical-path allocation is 25 ms for understanding, 50 ms for parallel retrieval, 25 ms for bulk feature lookup, 55 ms for ranking/policy and 25 ms for transport/slack: 180 ms total. Benchmark actual end-to-end p99; sums of allocated budgets do not substitute for measurement. Cache popular normalized queries by locale/device, with short freshness bounds. Keep static vectors in the index, changing aggregates in the online store and raw events/training tables in durable analytical storage.

### Handle product risks and prove improvement

New apps use content relevance and developer priors with controlled exposure; absence of installs is not evidence of low quality. Detect keyword stuffing, manipulated reviews and abnormal install patterns separately from relevance. Uninstall rates are delayed and context-dependent; define their observation window. A click-optimized model can reward misleading icons, so monitor useful installs, retention and user complaints.

Offline measure recall@K, NDCG from relevance judgments, install calibration and tail-query/new-app slices. Online randomize stable users and compare useful install conversion with relevance, spam, latency and privacy guardrails. Audit navigational success separately. Version model/index/features, shadow new versions and fall back to a filtered lexical baseline when semantic retrieval or personalization times out.

### Training data and features

Create one row per displayed candidate with request ID, position, model version and feature timestamps. Define a booking label and attribution window; recent unbooked impressions remain immature. Join later cancellations separately to distinguish low-quality bookings from durable ones. Unexposed listings are not observed negatives. Retrieve current availability from an authoritative service or short-lived cache. Do not train on a booking confirmation field or a price that changed after the impression.

A boosted tree is a strong baseline; a neural ranker can combine sparse IDs, content embeddings and interactions at larger scale. Minimize booking cross-entropy, optionally adding auxiliary click loss or a pairwise/listwise ranking objective. Calibrate probabilities on representative time-separated data. Cold-start Experiences rely on content and smoothed priors rather than a nonexistent booking history.

Precompute static features, update behavioral aggregates incrementally and fetch all candidate features in batches. Keep the model resident in replicated workers. A proposed 100 ms ranking budget might reserve 25 ms for features, 50 ms for batched scoring and 15 ms for postprocessing, leaving 10 ms slack; validate p99 under peak load. On optional-feature failure, use a tested fallback rather than waiting indefinitely. Availability must be rechecked before purchase even if it was fresh at ranking time.

### Define relevance under real delivery constraints

Given a query, delivery location, time and permitted history, rank restaurants or store items that can actually be ordered. Optimize completed satisfactory orders; high predicted conversion is less useful if delivery is consistently late. Confirm whether the result is a restaurant list or an item list because inventory, embeddings and attribution differ.

![W070. ML System Design: Restaurant / Store Recommendation — architecture](../diagrams/W070_review_architecture.svg)

[Open the architecture diagram](../diagrams/W070_review_architecture.svg).

### Separate slow representations from fast facts

Train a two-tower retriever on user/query–item engagement and completed-order pairs with carefully sampled negatives. Refresh expensive item embeddings less frequently, using content features for new entries and incremental index updates where possible. Retrieve hundreds to low thousands from millions. Query lexical matching protects exact food/store intents; personalized ANN sources provide discovery.

A daily ranker combines relevance, user cuisine preferences, price, fees, distance, estimated arrival, store quality and recent conversion/cancellation rates. The online feature store serves recent aggregates; the authoritative availability/fulfillment services provide open status, stock and current ETA. A yesterday embedding is tolerable for taste similarity, but yesterday's stock or serviceability cannot decide whether an item is orderable.

### Make the objective explicit

An illustrative score is

$$S=P(\mathrm{completed\ order}\mid x,i)
\cdot V_i-\lambda\,\widehat{\mathrm{late\ minutes}}-\mu\,P(\mathrm{cancel}\mid x,i).$$

Choose interpretable weights through offline trade-off curves and online tests, or enforce lateness as a constraint rather than hiding everything in one number. Do not multiply dollars and minutes without defining conversion weights. Preserve minimum query relevance so personalization does not show unrelated cuisine. Separate ad eligibility/auction decisions and label sponsored slots; ad insertion still must respect serviceability and quality rules.

### Serve inside 100–200 ms

Parallelize independent retrieval sources, batch feature lookup and scoring, and cap candidate count from measured ranker throughput. Precompute slow features, set per-source deadlines and use an eligible popular/lexical fallback. Monitor the end-to-end p99, not just model inference. Cache by location/time/query carefully and invalidate serviceability and inventory changes; long-lived cached results can violate the product's core promise.

Log actual impressions, source, position, model/index versions and experiment assignment. Join orders, delivery times, cancellations and refunds with explicit attribution/maturation windows. Offline use retrieval recall, ranking quality and calibration with time-separated data; online compare completed orders and repeat use with ETA error, lateness, cancellations, cost, diversity and latency guardrails. Audit new stores, sparse neighborhoods and feedback loops so popular nearby restaurants do not permanently crowd out reasonable alternatives.

title: Build a Simplified Image-Text Retrieval Training and Evaluation Pipeline
question:
eBay uses multimodal intelligence (image + text) to retrieve relevant products for a user's text query. Build a simplified image-text retrieval model training and evaluation pipeline.

What you are given
A dataset of product images (assume one image per product)
Product title/description text for each product
Query text with associated positive product IDs

Text encoder: sentence-transformers/all-MiniLM-L6-v2
What to implement

Image and text embedding models

Use resnet50 to extract image features, then a trainable projection head to map them into a shared embedding space of dimension D.
Use all-MiniLM-L6-v2 to extract text features, then a trainable projection head to map them into the same embedding space.
Apply L2 normalization to the final embeddings so cosine similarity can be used for retrieval.

A joint-embedding loss function

Implement a contrastive objective that aligns query text with its positive product (image and/or product text representation).
Must support in-batch negatives.
You may choose InfoNCE / softmax cross-entropy / triplet loss, etc., but provide a runnable implementation.

Retrieval evaluation

Given a query text, score all products by similarity (e.g., cosine similarity) and return Top-K product IDs.
Implement an offline evaluation over a set of queries, computing Top-K quality such as Recall@K.
Constraints / requirements
Use Python (PyTorch recommended).
Include a training loop (forward, loss, backprop, optimizer step).
Evaluation must be callable independently and return Top-K results.
Describe/implement how you build training batches (at minimum query-positive-product pairs).
Deliverables
Clean code structure (clear classes/functions).
A minimal runnable example (you may mock data with random tensors; the interfaces and data flow must be realistic).
Example
Input:  query="red nike shoes", k=5, (products: precomputed embeddings)
Output: top_k=[103, 998, 42, 77, 501]

solution.teaching_notes_markdown:
### Put queries and products in the same space

A query is text; a product has an image and title/description. Their original encoder outputs have different dimensions, so train projections into a shared $D$-dimensional space. Freeze the supplied backbones for a simple first implementation, cache their outputs, and train only the projection heads. This is a genuine training pipeline, but not full backbone fine-tuning.

For product $j$, normalize each projected modality, average them, then normalize again. For query $i$, normalize its projected text vector. Their dot product is cosine similarity. With temperature $\tau$, the single-positive loss is

$$L_i=-\log\frac{\exp(q_i^\top v_i/\tau)}{\sum_j\exp(q_i^\top v_j/\tau)}.$$

Other products in the batch provide negatives. Repeated positive product IDs must not become false negatives; the implementation sums probability over all matching columns. Additional known positives outside that ID require an expanded positive mask.

### Complete PyTorch implementation

[Download and run the training/evaluation example](../multimodal_retrieval_071.py).

```python
"""W071: frozen backbone features, trainable image/text projections."""

import torch
from torch import nn
from torch.nn import functional as F


def load_backbones(device="cpu"):
    # Optional: downloads pretrained weights on first use; not needed by demo.
    from torchvision.models import resnet50, ResNet50_Weights
    from sentence_transformers import SentenceTransformer

    weights = ResNet50_Weights.IMAGENET1K_V2
    image_model = resnet50(weights=weights)
    image_model.fc = nn.Identity()
    image_model = image_model.to(device).eval().requires_grad_(False)
    text_model = SentenceTransformer(
        "sentence-transformers/all-MiniLM-L6-v2", device=device
    )
    text_model.eval().requires_grad_(False)
    return image_model, text_model, weights.transforms()


@torch.no_grad()
def extract_features(image_model, text_model, image_batch, product_texts, queries):
    # image_batch must already use the returned weights.transforms().
    image_model.eval()
    text_model.eval()
    image = image_model(image_batch)
    title = text_model.encode(product_texts, convert_to_tensor=True)
    query = text_model.encode(queries, convert_to_tensor=True)
    return image.detach(), title.detach(), query.detach()


class JointEmbedding(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, image_dim=2048, text_dim=384, dimension=128):
        super().__init__()
        self.image_projection = nn.Linear(image_dim, dimension)
        self.text_projection = nn.Linear(text_dim, dimension)

    def queries(self, features):
        return F.normalize(self.text_projection(features), dim=-1)

    def products(self, image, text):
        image = F.normalize(self.image_projection(image), dim=-1)
        text = F.normalize(self.text_projection(text), dim=-1)
        return F.normalize((image + text) / 2, dim=-1)


def contrastive_loss(query, product, product_ids, temperature=0.1):
    if temperature <= 0:
        raise ValueError("Temperature must be positive")
    logits = query @ product.T / temperature
    # Same product may appear twice: both columns are positives, not negatives.
    positive = product_ids[:, None].eq(product_ids[None, :])
    positive_logits = logits.masked_fill(~positive, float("-inf"))
    return (
        torch.logsumexp(logits, dim=1) - torch.logsumexp(positive_logits, dim=1)
    ).mean()


def train_epoch(model, batches, optimizer):
    model.train()
    total = 0.0
    count = 0
    for query, image, text, product_ids in batches:
        optimizer.zero_grad(set_to_none=True)
        loss = contrastive_loss(
            model.queries(query), model.products(image, text), product_ids
        )
        loss.backward()
        optimizer.step()
        total += loss.item() * len(query)
        count += len(query)
    return total / count


@torch.no_grad()
def evaluate(model, query_features, images, texts, catalog_ids, positive_sets, k=5):
    if len(set(catalog_ids)) != len(catalog_ids) or not catalog_ids or k < 1:
        raise ValueError("Need unique catalog IDs and positive k")
    if len(positive_sets) != len(query_features) or any(not p for p in positive_sets):
        raise ValueError("Each query needs at least one positive ID")
    was_training = model.training
    try:
        model.eval()
        scores = model.queries(query_features) @ model.products(images, texts).T
        indices = scores.topk(min(k, len(catalog_ids)), dim=1).indices.cpu().tolist()
        top_ids = [[catalog_ids[j] for j in row] for row in indices]
        recall = sum(
            len(set(row) & set(pos)) / len(set(pos))
            for row, pos in zip(top_ids, positive_sets)
        ) / len(top_ids)
        return top_ids, recall
    finally:
        model.train(was_training)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    torch.manual_seed(7)
    torch.set_num_threads(1)
    # Random, frozen feature fixtures simulate encoder outputs, not actual images.
    n = 8
    query = torch.randn(n, 384)
    image = torch.randn(n, 2048)
    text = query.clone()
    ids = torch.arange(n)
    model = JointEmbedding(dimension=16)
    optimizer = torch.optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=0.01)
    batch = [(query, image, text, ids)]
    first = train_epoch(model, batch, optimizer)
    for _ in range(79):
        last = train_epoch(model, batch, optimizer)
    top, recall = evaluate(
        model, query, image, text, list(range(n)), [{i} for i in range(n)], k=1
    )
    assert last < first and recall == 1.0
    assert (
        contrastive_loss(torch.eye(2), torch.eye(2), torch.tensor([1, 1])).item() == 0
    )
    print("Fixture loss", first, "->", last, "Recall@1", recall)
```

`load_backbones` uses ResNet-50 without its classification head (2048 features) and the specified MiniLM text encoder (384 features). Apply the returned image transform to every image, concatenate each product's title and description as text, and call `extract_features`. The first pretrained run needs the optional libraries and cached/downloadable weights; the included random-feature demo is offline and does not download anything.

Build training rows as `(query, positive_product_id)`, look up that product's cached image/text features, and shuffle pairs into batches with several distinct products. Split queries/products appropriately before tuning, and keep test relevance labels out of training. During real evaluation, project the complete unique product catalog once and reuse it; the simple function recomputes it for clarity. For very large catalogs use chunked exact scoring or an ANN index and measure approximation recall separately.

### Read the output correctly

`evaluate` returns actual catalog IDs for each query plus mean Recall@K. With several relevant products, a query's recall is the fraction of its relevant IDs present in the returned set; it is not simply a binary hit. A positive ID absent from the available catalog cannot be retrieved and lowers recall under this definition.

The executable fixture overfits eight synthetic pairs and checks Recall@1 equals one, decreasing training loss and duplicate-positive handling. This validates shapes, gradients and data flow. It does not establish retrieval quality on real product images. Use held-out queries, hard negatives, category/language slices and an actual relevance set to establish that.

title: Implement a Vision Transformer (ViT) from Scratch
question:
Implement a Vision Transformer (ViT) from Scratch

Implement the forward pass of a Vision Transformer image classifier using only NumPy. The model cuts an image into square patches, turns every patch into a token, adds one extra classification token (CLS) and a learned position embedding, runs the tokens through a stack of pre-norm transformer encoder blocks, and predicts the class from the final CLS token. The weights are given; you write the computation.

What to implement
import numpy as np

def softmax(x, axis=-1): ...
def layer_norm(x, gamma, beta, eps=1e-5): ...
def gelu(x): ...
def patch_embed(images, w, b, patch_size): ...
def multi_head_attention(x, w_qkv, b_qkv, w_out, b_out, num_heads): ...
def encoder_block(x, p, num_heads): ...
def vit_forward(images, params, patch_size, num_heads): ...

Do not use any deep-learning library or ready-made attention or transformer layer; only NumPy. B is the batch size, N the number of patches, D the embedding size.

Rules
1.
softmax(x, axis): subtract the maximum along axis before exponentiating, so large inputs do not overflow.
2.
layer_norm(x, gamma, beta, eps): normalize over the last axis: (x - mean) / sqrt(var + eps) * gamma + beta, with the biased variance (divide by the count).
3.
gelu(x): the tanh form 0.5 * x * (1 + tanh(sqrt(2 / pi) * (x + 0.044715 * x^3))).
4.
patch_embed(images, w, b, patch_size): images has shape (B, C, H, W) with H and W divisible by P = patch_size. Patches are taken row by row (left to right, then top to bottom), and the pixels of one patch are flattened in (C, P, P) order into a vector of length C*P*P. The result is flat @ w + b with w of shape (C*P*P, D), shape (B, N, D), N = (H/P) * (W/P).
5.
multi_head_attention(x, ...): x has shape (B, N, D). Compute qkv = x @ w_qkv + b_qkv with w_qkv of shape (D, 3D). Columns [0, D) are the queries, [D, 2D) the keys, [2D, 3D) the values. Head h uses columns [h*d, (h+1)*d) of each, where d = D / num_heads. Per head, the attention weights are softmax(Q K^T / sqrt(d)) over the keys (no mask), and the head output is the weights times V. Concatenate the heads in order and return concat @ w_out + b_out, shape (B, N, D).
6.
encoder_block(x, p, num_heads) is pre-norm with residual connections: x = x + attention(layer_norm(x)), then x = x + mlp(layer_norm(x)), where mlp(h) = gelu(h @ fc1_w + fc1_b) @ fc2_w + fc2_b. The dictionary p has the keys ln1_g, ln1_b, qkv_w, qkv_b, proj_w, proj_b, ln2_g, ln2_b, fc1_w, fc1_b, fc2_w, fc2_b.
7.
vit_forward(images, params, patch_size, num_heads): embed the patches with params["patch_w"], params["patch_b"]; put the CLS vector params["cls"] (shape (D,)) in front of the tokens as token 0; add params["pos"] (shape (N+1, D)); apply the blocks in params["blocks"] (a list of dictionaries as in rule 6); apply layer_norm with params["ln_g"], params["ln_b"]; and return the logits of token 0: token0 @ params["head_w"] + params["head_b"], shape (B, num_classes).
Examples

Example 1: images of shape (2, 3, 16, 16), patch_size = 4, D = 8, 10 classes. patch_embed returns shape (2, 16, 8), the sequence has 17 tokens after the CLS token is added, and vit_forward returns shape (2, 10).

Example 2: layer_norm(np.array([1.0, 2.0, 3.0]), 1.0, 0.0, eps=0.0) returns [-1.2247, 0.0, 1.2247]. The mean is 2 and the biased variance is 2/3.

Example 3: images = [[[[1, 2], [3, 4]]]] (one image, one channel, 2 x 2 pixels), patch_size = 1, w = [[2.0]], b = [1.0] returns [[[3.0], [5.0], [7.0], [9.0]]]. Each pixel is a patch and is mapped to 2 * pixel + 1, in row-major order.

Constraints
1 <= B <= 8; images up to 224 x 224; 1 <= C <= 3.
D is divisible by num_heads; D <= 768; up to 12 blocks.
The inputs and the parameters are not modified.

solution.teaching_notes_markdown:
### Follow the shape changes

This exercise asks for a forward computation with supplied weights, not training. Keep the required NumPy implementation separate from a library model. Start with images `(B,C,H,W)`, rearrange them into `(B,N,C*P*P)` patches, project to `(B,N,D)`, prepend CLS and add positions. Each pre-norm block preserves `(B,N+1,D)`. Only token zero goes into the final classifier.

The subtle part is patch order: grid row, grid column, channel, patch row, patch column. A plain reshape without transposing can mix pixels from different patches. The other common error is combining Q/K/V heads in the wrong order. Split the three contiguous Q/K/V column ranges first, then split each into heads.

### NumPy forward pass

[Download the complete numerical implementations](../exact_numeric_51_100.py).

```python
"""Exact NumPy contracts for W072, W076 and W079."""

import numpy as np


def softmax(x, axis=-1):
    shifted = x - np.max(x, axis=axis, keepdims=True)
    exps = np.exp(shifted)
    return exps / exps.sum(axis=axis, keepdims=True)


def layer_norm(x, gamma, beta, eps=1e-5):
    centered = x - x.mean(axis=-1, keepdims=True)
    variance = (centered**2).mean(axis=-1, keepdims=True)
    return centered / np.sqrt(variance + eps) * gamma + beta


def gelu(x):
    return 0.5 * x * (1 + np.tanh(np.sqrt(2 / np.pi) * (x + 0.044715 * x**3)))


def patch_embed(images, w, b, patch_size):
    B, C, H, W = images.shape
    P = patch_size
    if P <= 0 or H % P or W % P:
        raise ValueError("Patch size must divide both image dimensions")
    # B,C,patch-row,pixel-row,patch-col,pixel-col
    patches = images.reshape(B, C, H // P, P, W // P, P)
    patches = patches.transpose(0, 2, 4, 1, 3, 5)  # B,grid-H,grid-W,C,P,P
    flat = patches.reshape(B, (H // P) * (W // P), C * P * P)
    return flat @ w + b


def multi_head_attention(x, w_qkv, b_qkv, w_out, b_out, num_heads):
    B, N, D = x.shape
    if num_heads <= 0 or D % num_heads:
        raise ValueError("Heads must divide embedding dimension")
    h, d = num_heads, D // num_heads
    qkv = x @ w_qkv + b_qkv
    q, k, v = [
        part.reshape(B, N, h, d).transpose(0, 2, 1, 3)
        for part in np.split(qkv, 3, axis=-1)
    ]
    weights = softmax((q @ k.swapaxes(-1, -2)) / np.sqrt(d), axis=-1)
    combined = (weights @ v).transpose(0, 2, 1, 3).reshape(B, N, D)
    return combined @ w_out + b_out


def encoder_block(x, p, num_heads):
    h = layer_norm(x, p["ln1_g"], p["ln1_b"])
    x = x + multi_head_attention(
        h, p["qkv_w"], p["qkv_b"], p["proj_w"], p["proj_b"], num_heads
    )
    h = layer_norm(x, p["ln2_g"], p["ln2_b"])
    return x + gelu(h @ p["fc1_w"] + p["fc1_b"]) @ p["fc2_w"] + p["fc2_b"]


def vit_forward(images, params, patch_size, num_heads):
    tokens = patch_embed(images, params["patch_w"], params["patch_b"], patch_size)
    B, N, D = tokens.shape
    cls = np.broadcast_to(params["cls"], (B, 1, D))
    x = np.concatenate([cls, tokens], axis=1) + params["pos"]
    for block in params["blocks"]:
        x = encoder_block(x, block, num_heads)
    x = layer_norm(x, params["ln_g"], params["ln_b"])
    return x[:, 0] @ params["head_w"] + params["head_b"]
```

For head dimension $d=D/h$, each head computes

$$A=\operatorname{softmax}(QK^\top/\sqrt d),\qquad O=AV.$$

The key axis is the final axis of the score matrix; there is no causal mask for this image encoder. Layer normalization uses the population variance across features, and both residual additions use the unnormalized residual input. Final normalization applies to all tokens before selecting CLS.

### Check values, not just output shape

For the one-channel 2×2 example and patch size one, `patch_embed` produces `[3,5,7,9]` with the given weight/bias. For a larger patch, compare one flattened patch directly against `images[b,:,row:row+P,col:col+P].reshape(-1)`. Check layer normalization of `[1,2,3]` against `[-sqrt(1.5),0,sqrt(1.5)]` when epsilon is zero.

Validate attention against a slow per-head reference and confirm that a zero attention/MLP branch leaves its residual unchanged. Save copies of input/parameter arrays and compare them afterward to check the no-mutation rule. The companion tests exercise those cases and a complete small classifier. The normal computation costs roughly $O(BN^2D+BND^2)$ per block and stores attention of size $O(BhN^2)$, so patch size strongly affects memory.

A PyTorch equivalent for study is shown below; it is **not** the answer to the NumPy-only constraint. Convert NumPy linear weights with `.T` because `nn.Linear` stores `(out,in)` weights. PyTorch's `gelu(..., approximate="tanh")` and `LayerNorm(eps=1e-5)` match the specified formulas.

```python
import torch
from torch import nn


class StudyViT(nn.Module):
    def __init__(
        self,
        channels,
        image_size,
        patch_size,
        dimension,
        heads,
        hidden,
        layers,
        classes,
    ):
        super().__init__()
        self.patch = nn.Conv2d(channels, dimension, patch_size, patch_size)
        count = (image_size // patch_size) ** 2
        self.cls = nn.Parameter(torch.zeros(1, 1, dimension))
        self.pos = nn.Parameter(torch.zeros(1, count + 1, dimension))
        self.blocks = nn.ModuleList(
            [
                nn.TransformerEncoderLayer(
                    dimension,
                    heads,
                    hidden,
                    dropout=0.0,
                    activation=lambda x: torch.nn.functional.gelu(
                        x, approximate="tanh"
                    ),
                    batch_first=True,
                    norm_first=True,
                )
                for _ in range(layers)
            ]
        )
        self.norm = nn.LayerNorm(dimension)
        self.head = nn.Linear(dimension, classes)

    def forward(self, images):
        tokens = self.patch(images).flatten(2).transpose(1, 2)
        x = torch.cat([self.cls.expand(len(images), -1, -1), tokens], dim=1) + self.pos
        for block in self.blocks:
            x = block(x)
        return self.head(self.norm(x)[:, 0])
```

solution.teaching_notes_markdown:
### 1. What are we actually building?

For every input token, predict the token immediately after it. This exercise deliberately uses **only the current token**. It does not ask for a Transformer, attention, a recurrent network or a causal mask.

For the sequence `[2, 3, 4, 0]`, the training pairs are:

| Current token | Next-token target |
|---|---|
| 2 | 3 |
| 3 | 4 |
| 4 | 0 |

Feed `[2, 3, 4]` and supervise `[3, 4, 0]`. The model estimates $p(x_{t+1}\mid x_t)$, not a distribution conditioned on the whole prefix. The same current token always produces the same logits under fixed weights, regardless of its neighboring tokens.

### 2. The exact model implementation

`nn.Embedding` turns an integer token id into a trainable feature vector. The first linear layer and ReLU transform that vector; the final linear layer produces one raw score per vocabulary token.

```text
integer tokens (B, L)
    → embedding (B, L, H)
    → hidden linear + ReLU (B, L, H)
    → vocabulary linear (B, L, V)
```

Use these imports for the code below:

```python
import torch
from torch import nn
from torch.nn import functional as F
from torch.utils.data import Dataset, DataLoader
```

```python
class TinyNextTokenModel(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, vocab_size, hidden_dim):
        super().__init__()
        self.embedding = nn.Embedding(vocab_size, hidden_dim)
        self.hidden = nn.Linear(hidden_dim, hidden_dim)
        self.output = nn.Linear(hidden_dim, vocab_size)

    def forward(self, token_ids):
        embeddings = self.embedding(token_ids)  # (B, L, H)
        hidden_states = torch.relu(self.hidden(embeddings))
        return self.output(hidden_states)
```

For one position, the computation is

$$
e_t=E[x_t],\qquad h_t=\operatorname{ReLU}(W_1e_t+b_1),\qquad
z_t=W_2h_t+b_2.
$$

There is no operation combining different positions. `nn.Linear` transforms the final dimension and leaves batch and sequence dimensions intact. Consequently, a full input of shape `(B, T)` produces `(B, T, V)`; the shifted training input has length `T-1` and produces `(B, T-1, V)`.

### 3. Shift once, then calculate the actual loss

```python
def next_token_loss(model, sequences):
    if sequences.ndim != 2 or sequences.size(1) < 2:
        raise ValueError("sequences must have shape (batch, length >= 2)")
    inputs = sequences[:, :-1]
    targets = sequences[:, 1:]
    logits = model(inputs)
    vocabulary_size = logits.size(-1)
    return F.cross_entropy(
        logits.reshape(-1, vocabulary_size),
        targets.reshape(-1),
    )
```

The first slice removes the last input token. The second removes the first target token. Flattening preserves the pair order:

```text
inputs:  [[2, 3, 4], [0, 1, 2]]
targets: [[3, 4, 0], [1, 2, 3]]

logits.reshape(-1, V): 6 rows, each containing V class scores
targets.reshape(-1):  [3, 4, 0, 1, 2, 3]
```

Use `reshape` because sliced tensors can be noncontiguous. Pass raw logits directly to `F.cross_entropy`; it already computes the needed log-probabilities. Labels are integer class ids, not one-hot vectors.

With batch size $B$ and original sequence length $T$, the loss is

$$
\mathcal L=-\frac{1}{B(T-1)}\sum_{b=1}^{B}\sum_{t=0}^{T-2}
\log\operatorname{softmax}(z_{b,t})_{x_{b,t+1}}.
$$

A causal mask is unnecessary: this architecture cannot read any other position in the first place.

### 4. DataLoader and the completed training loop

When the interview skeleton supplies `SyntheticDataset`, retain that implementation and construct the loader exactly as requested:

```python
# Run after the supplied SyntheticDataset class has been defined.
dataset = SyntheticDataset(num_samples=256, seq_len=9, vocab_size=8)
loader = DataLoader(dataset, batch_size=32, shuffle=True)
```

Each batch must be a tensor of integer sequences shaped `(B, T)`. If a different provided dataset returns a tuple, unpack it according to that actual contract rather than guessing. The training function performs all five required operations in order:

```python
def train_one_epoch(model, loader, optimizer, device="cpu"):
    model.train()
    total_loss = 0.0
    total_targets = 0
    for sequences in loader:
        sequences = sequences.to(device)
        optimizer.zero_grad(set_to_none=True)
        loss = next_token_loss(model, sequences)
        loss.backward()
        optimizer.step()

        count = sequences.size(0) * (sequences.size(1) - 1)
        total_loss += loss.item() * count
        total_targets += count
    if total_targets == 0:
        raise ValueError("loader contains no target tokens")
    return total_loss / total_targets
```

`zero_grad` clears gradients from the previous minibatch, `backward` computes new ones, and `step` updates the registered parameters. `model.train()` selects training mode. On a GPU, move the model to the same device passed to this function; the batch is moved inside the loop.

### 5. A complete, reproducible demonstration

**The exercise does not include its `SyntheticDataset` implementation.** The following is a clearly chosen demonstration fixture, not a reconstruction of hidden data. Its rule is `next = (current + 1) % vocab_size`, which this current-token-only architecture can learn. If the supplied data has independent random next tokens, there is no such predictable rule; its population optimum is the next-token marginal, uniform loss $\log V$ when that marginal is uniform.

Define this fixture **before** constructing its DataLoader if you run the examples outside the original skeleton:

```python
class SyntheticDataset(Dataset):
    def __init__(self, num_samples, seq_len, vocab_size, seed=0):
        if num_samples < 1 or seq_len < 2 or vocab_size < 2:
            raise ValueError(
                "need samples > 0, sequence length >= 2 and vocabulary >= 2"
            )
        random = torch.Generator().manual_seed(seed)
        starts = torch.randint(vocab_size, (num_samples, 1), generator=random)
        offsets = torch.arange(seq_len).unsqueeze(0)
        # Demonstration rule: after token k comes (k + 1) modulo vocab_size.
        self.sequences = (starts + offsets) % vocab_size

    def __len__(self):
        return len(self.sequences)

    def __getitem__(self, index):
        return self.sequences[index]
```

Compare checkpoints on the same complete dataset, weighting by target count so a short last batch does not receive the same weight as a full batch:

```python
def evaluate_loss(model, loader, device="cpu"):
    was_training = model.training
    model.eval()
    total_loss = 0.0
    total_targets = 0
    with torch.no_grad():
        for sequences in loader:
            sequences = sequences.to(device)
            count = sequences.size(0) * (sequences.size(1) - 1)
            total_loss += next_token_loss(model, sequences).item() * count
            total_targets += count
    model.train(was_training)
    if total_targets == 0:
        raise ValueError("loader contains no target tokens")
    return total_loss / total_targets


def run_demo(seed=7, epochs=6):
    torch.manual_seed(seed)
    vocabulary_size = 8
    dataset = SyntheticDataset(
        num_samples=256, seq_len=9, vocab_size=vocabulary_size, seed=seed
    )
    loader = DataLoader(
        dataset,
        batch_size=32,
        shuffle=True,
        generator=torch.Generator().manual_seed(seed),
    )
    evaluation_loader = DataLoader(dataset, batch_size=32, shuffle=False)
    model = TinyNextTokenModel(vocabulary_size, hidden_dim=32)
    optimizer = torch.optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=0.02)
    history = [evaluate_loss(model, evaluation_loader)]
    for _ in range(epochs):
        train_one_epoch(model, loader, optimizer)
        history.append(evaluate_loss(model, evaluation_loader))
    return model, history
```

```python
model, losses = run_demo(seed=7, epochs=6)
print([round(loss, 6) for loss in losses])
# One tested CPU run:
# [2.177346, 0.043959, 0.000115, 0.000011, 0.000004, 0.000003, 0.000002]

with torch.no_grad():
    predictions = model(torch.arange(8).unsqueeze(0)).argmax(dim=-1)
print(predictions.squeeze(0).tolist())  # [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 0]
assert losses[-1] < losses[0]
```

Small numerical differences can occur across versions and devices. The important checks are that the final loss decreases on this fixed learnable fixture, the shape and shift are correct, and the model learns the stated transition. Minibatch SGD is not guaranteed to improve on every individual update; comparing unrelated minibatch losses is not a reliable correctness test.

### 6. Run the solution and verify the actual requirements

The [complete runnable script](../tiny_next_token.py) puts these definitions in the right order and includes the demonstration entry point. The [behavior tests](../test_tiny_next_token.py) check next-token alignment, position independence, gradient flow, final-batch weighting and reproducible learning.

From the chapter directory, with PyTorch installed:

```bash
python tiny_next_token.py
python -m unittest test_tiny_next_token -v
```

**Interview explanation:** “I embed each token independently, apply a hidden linear layer and ReLU, and output vocabulary logits. I align `sequences[:, :-1]` with `sequences[:, 1:]`, flatten the positions for cross-entropy, then run backward and Adam. No attention or causal mask is needed because positions never interact. I verify the exact shift and learning on a fixed, explicitly learnable dataset.”

title: Compute the Distribution of LLM Decoding Stopping Time and Build a Strategy Against Adversaries
question:
Problem: Model the Distribution of LLM Decoding Stopping Time and Implement a Minimax Strategy Against Adversaries

In a simplified LLM decoding process, at each step the model may emit a special token <STOP> and terminate. You must do two things.

Part A: Stopping-Time Distribution

Given a maximum length N (generation runs for at most N tokens; if it does not stop early, it is forced to stop at N) and a per-step stop probability sequence:

At step t (1-indexed), the probability of emitting <STOP> is p[t] (0 <= p[t] <= 1)
If it does not stop at step t, it proceeds to step t+1

Compute:

For all t = 1..N, the stopping-time probability P(T=t)
The expected stopping time E[T]

Note: If <STOP> is never emitted by step N, define T=N (forced stop).

Part B: Strategy Against Adversaries

There are multiple adversaries. Each adversary corresponds to a different mechanism that influences p[t] and/or the payoff. After observing p[1..N] (or its parametric form), your program must choose a decision (e.g., a cutoff step k, an early-stop policy, or an action a) to maximize the worst-case (minimax) expected reward.

Implement a program that takes:

N
p[1..N]
parameters for M adversaries (each defines a possible p[t] and/or reward function)
a reward function reward(decision, T, adversary)

Output:

the chosen decision
the expected reward under the worst adversary
I/O Spec

You must clearly specify:

stdin input format
stdout output format
constraints (N, M) and complexity requirements

Provide at least 5 test cases including edge cases.

Example

Input:

...

Output:

...

steps: Part B: state the missing decision contract

solution.example: Worked examples and checks are included in the complete answer.
