title: Improve Booking via Cover Photo Selection (ML Design)
question:
Pick the cover photo for each listing to maximize click-through and booking. Open-ended ML design — the candidate drives the framing.

Requirements
Functional
For each listing with >= 5 photos, choose the cover photo shown on the search results page.
Optimize for click-through to the listing page; secondary for booking conversion.
Non-functional
Batch inference acceptable; daily or weekly recompute.
Latency at serve time is negligible (cover photo is materialized in the listing record).

solution.example: Illustration only: photo A gets 30/1,000 clicks and B gets 40/1,000 under comparable randomized exposure; B's observed CTR is one point higher, but uncertainty and booking outcomes still matter. Assuming ten million listings with ten photos each, full scoring touches 100 million photos; cache embeddings by photo digest and rescore only changed listings or changed model versions. At 1,000 cached-photo scores/s the full pass is about 27.8 hours, so incremental updates or more workers are needed for a daily SLA. Validate deleted covers, missing embeddings, duplicate jobs, and drift in search traffic. Batch failures retain the previous valid cover instead of erasing it.
solution.trap: Photos never shown as covers have missing counterfactual CTR labels, not zero CTR.
solution.teaching_notes_markdown:
### Define the decision and comparison

For each listing with at least five eligible photos, choose one cover once per daily/weekly batch. The primary near-term objective is click-through per search impression; require booking conversion/booking-per-impression and misrepresentation complaints as guardrails so clickbait does not win. Clarify whether a single universal cover or a personalized cover is required; assume one materialized cover per listing as stated. A contextual personalized policy would need a different serving contract.

Create one training row per displayed listing-cover impression, with search context, listing, photo/version, position, current displayed price and exposure policy. Label click in-session and booking within a defined mature attribution window. Historic non-cover photos have no counterfactual CTR label; assigning them zero clicks creates severe selection bias. Run a controlled within-listing photo experiment with logged assignment probabilities to collect comparisons, respecting photo quality and safety eligibility.

### Model and batch pipeline

Extract image embeddings, scene type (bedroom, exterior, living room), brightness, sharpness, crop quality, resolution and visual clutter. Combine listing context such as property type, region, room count, price band and attributes; add search position/context only as observed at prediction time. A pretrained image encoder plus a small tabular ranker is a practical baseline, compared to a sharpness/room-type rule. Predict calibrated CTR and optionally booking conditional on click with shared features. Randomized cover exposures identify relative performance better than old owner-selected covers.

The diagram's candidate pool is the listing's own eligible photos, not the entire catalog. A daily job reads immutable photo/listing versions, scores each candidate under representative traffic contexts, aggregates expected CTR across that context distribution and selects the best subject to quality/bookings guardrails. Persist CoverChoice(listing,photo_id,photo_version,model_version,computed_at,expected_listing_version) using compare-and-swap. A concurrent photo deletion or listing edit invalidates the proposed choice. CDN thumbnails are generated before the new pointer goes live; serving just reads that pointer, with a safe previous/default cover fallback.

### Evaluation and operational checks

Split by listing/property owner and time to prevent near-duplicate photo leakage. Offline evaluate pairwise preference/CTR calibration on randomized holdout data and booking performance after label maturity, segmented by property type and geography. User- or search-session A/B tests compare the cover policy consistently, log actual rendered cover and prevent a user repeatedly switching variants mid-session. Listing-level randomization may be appropriate for a fixed global cover, but traffic interference and repeated impressions require clustered confidence intervals. Monitor CTR, booking per impression, click-to-book drop, complaint/cancellation signals and host overrides.

title: Learning / Job Recommendation Ranking
question:
Design a recommender that surfaces LinkedIn Learning courses (or jobs) based on a user's profile, recently applied jobs, and behavioral history.

Functional: return a ranked list of items the user is likely to engage with; handle cold-start for new users/items; provide explainability ("why is this recommended?").

Non-functional: sub-200 ms candidate generation + ranking; recall over the full catalog, precision over the top-10 served; online learning loop closes within hours.

LinkedIn twist: heavy feature engineering on the job/course side and explicit per-item explainability.

steps: Choose an outcome and preserve intent
solution.contract_notes: Job/learning recommendations require eligibility/prerequisite constraints, freshness and user intent; do not equate a click with a useful course completion or successful match.
solution.example: `GET /recommendations` returns IDs, model version, exposure_id and a structured reason. Retrieve across the full catalog using skill/inverted indexes, two-tower/content ANN, similar-career paths and fresh items. Merge roughly 1,000 candidates, rank a few hundred with a GBDT or multi-task neural model predicting start, completion and useful outcome, then diversify by skill, provider and difficulty. The diagram's candidate stage ensures broad recall; the final stage aims at top-10 precision under a sub-200-ms request budget. Allocate, illustratively, 30 ms features, 40 ms retrieval, 60 ms rank and 70 ms filtering/network/headroom.
solution.trap: Clicks are not useful completion/placement; explanations need supported authorized feature evidence.
solution.teaching_notes_markdown:
### Choose an outcome and preserve intent

Assume LinkedIn Learning courses; optimize useful starts followed by completion or skill progress, with seven/thirty-day return and user satisfaction. Jobs use the same funnel but labels become qualified application, recruiter response and eventual placement, with much longer delays. A course click is not a completed course, and a job click is not a successful match. Enforce content access, language and prerequisites; for jobs enforce location/work eligibility and current posting status where legally/product-appropriate.

User features include profile skills, role/seniority, declared career goals, recent applications and searches, completed courses and recent session behavior. Item engineering is central: normalized skills, prerequisites, difficulty, duration, syllabus/topic embeddings, language, credential, freshness and instructor quality; jobs add required/preferred skills, seniority, employment type and normalized location. Compute user-item skill gaps, role transitions, completion compatibility and explicitly requested versus inferred interest. Keep profile inferences separate from verified skills and protect sensitive attributes.

### Retrieval, ranking and explanation

`GET /recommendations` returns IDs, model version, exposure_id and a structured reason. Retrieve across the full catalog using skill/inverted indexes, two-tower/content ANN, similar-career paths and fresh items. Merge roughly 1,000 candidates, rank a few hundred with a GBDT or multi-task neural model predicting start, completion and useful outcome, then diversify by skill, provider and difficulty. The diagram's candidate stage ensures broad recall; the final stage aims at top-10 precision under a sub-200-ms request budget. Allocate, illustratively, 30 ms features, 40 ms retrieval, 60 ms rank and 70 ms filtering/network/headroom.

Reasons come from supported features, for example “builds SQL used in your recently applied analyst roles” or “next course after your completed introduction.” Store reason_code plus evidence IDs with the recommendation; do not ask a generator to invent causal explanations for a score. Suppress sensitive or stale evidence and allow users to correct preferences. A cold user gets profile/goal-based content matching; a cold item uses syllabus/skill embeddings with limited exploration.

### Learning and serving reliability

Exposure rows record user,item,time,position,source,feature/model versions and selection propensity. Deduplicate engagement events, retain label maturity and use point-in-time joins; application outcomes after the impression cannot be input features. Streams refresh recent actions within minutes, hourly jobs update aggregates and incremental embeddings, and a model refresh/shadow evaluation can close the loop within hours without forcing unsafe full retraining every event. Keep a slow mature completion/placement evaluator as well.

Forward-time splits plus new-user/new-item and skill-domain holdouts assess recall@1000, NDCG/precision@10, calibration and completion quality. Online user A/B tests measure useful outcomes with dismissal, unsubscribes, latency and opportunity-distribution guardrails; exposure bias needs exploration and careful propensity correction. Scale is unspecified: at assumed 10,000 QPS and 200 rank candidates, capacity is two million pair scores/s. Cache content embeddings and short-lived eligible candidates, but recheck expired job postings and user access. Model/index versions deploy together; fall back to goal/skill rules on failure. Test a prerequisite violation, revoked access, removed posting and an explanation whose evidence was deleted. Monitor skill-extraction drift, stale profiles, feature age and top-10 concentration.

title: Listing Lifetime Value — Estimation (ML Design)
question:
Estimate the lifetime value of a listing — projected revenue over the next 12 months. Used downstream for ranking, host outreach, and inventory acquisition decisions. The prompt is intentionally open and rewards strong scoping.

Requirements
Functional
Predict per-listing 12-month booking revenue (or a related target the candidate proposes).
Output consumed by ranking (boost high-LTV listings) and by host-success teams (prioritize outreach).
Non-functional
Batch inference is acceptable; daily refresh.
Predictions should be calibrated — absolute dollar values, not relative scores.

steps: Define dollars and the observation window
solution.example: Use rolling-origin splits, leaving a full label horizon before an untouched future test when necessary. Report dollar MAE, aggregate bias, RMSLE as a supplementary scale metric, calibration by predicted decile/cohort/age/market and interval coverage. A model can order listings well but systematically overpredict absolute dollars, violating this prompt. Example: 40 available nights at $100 and 50% expected occupancy give $2,000 for a month; sum month-specific values, not simply 12× a peak month. If predicted annual dollars sum to $10 million but mature revenue is $8 million, investigate systematic calibration and market shift.
solution.trap: Do not label one month of an immature listing as twelve-month value or confuse LTV with outreach uplift.
solution.teaching_notes_markdown:
### Define dollars and the observation window

Assume the target is gross completed-booking revenue in the next 365 days, net of cancellations/refunds but before platform fees, in a fixed reporting currency using a documented conversion convention. If the business wants platform margin instead, change both labels and cost model; these are different targets. At daily snapshot t, predict E[Y(t)|features available at t], where Y(t) sums eligible stay-night revenue in [t,t+365). Allocate bookings crossing the window by night, and avoid double-counting a future reservation already known at t. Clarify whether host churn/blocked nights are part of future value; assume they are.

Daily snapshot rows include listing age, location/property type/capacity/amenities, host reliability, available calendar nights, current prices and booked pipeline, historical occupancy/revenue/cancellations, review trends, local seasonality/events and market demand. Features are time-stamped; future calendar changes, future price corrections and final cancellation information are leakage. A new listing has sparse history but metadata and market priors.

### Baseline and stronger model

Start with cohort occupancy×available nights×average daily rate, adjusted for expected active survival and known booked revenue. Compare a two-part model P(active/bookable) times expected revenue conditional on activity, or a direct Tweedie/GBDT revenue regressor suited to nonnegative zeros and a long tail. A monthly decomposition predicts 12 revenue increments and sums them, making seasonality and survival explicit. Calibrate the summed dollar prediction on a held-out period rather than just ranking scores. Predict intervals/quantiles for outreach decisions with uncertain new listings.

Only snapshots whose complete next year and cancellation finalization are observed have an ordinary full label. An in-progress listing's first month is not its final 12-month revenue. Use mature cohorts for a simple baseline; if freshness demands recent cohorts, use a survival/censoring-aware likelihood or explicitly model observed monthly outcomes with censor masks. Administrative censoring differs from real listing churn, which may legitimately produce zero later revenue. Repeated daily snapshots of one listing require grouped/temporal evaluation and correlated-error handling.

### Evaluate downstream uses separately

Use rolling-origin splits, leaving a full label horizon before an untouched future test when necessary. Report dollar MAE, aggregate bias, RMSLE as a supplementary scale metric, calibration by predicted decile/cohort/age/market and interval coverage. A model can order listings well but systematically overpredict absolute dollars, violating this prompt. Example: 40 available nights at USD 100 and 50% expected occupancy give USD 2,000 for a month; sum month-specific values, not simply 12× a peak month. If predicted annual dollars sum to USD 10 million but mature revenue is USD 8 million, investigate systematic calibration and market shift.

The diagram's batch feature/model/output flow materializes ListingValue(listing,snapshot,horizon,currency,model_version,mean,quantiles) daily. Consumers reject stale/incompatible versions. Ranking boosts based on predicted LTV can create a feedback loop by increasing exposure; control the boost and A/B-test booking/satisfaction and host fairness. Outreach needs incremental treatment benefit or an experiment: high baseline LTV does not imply high outreach uplift.

Assume 20 million listings and one score/day: about 232 scores/s average, excluding feature construction. Incremental aggregates and partitioned daily output can support this with batch workers. Publish a complete version manifest atomically; a failed daily job leaves the prior valid snapshot. Monitor freshness, missing currencies, market drift and delayed mature-cohort calibration, not just daily proxy clicks.

title: ML News Recommendation System Design
question: Design a machine learning system to recommend email newsletter content to users of the Nextdoor platform. You need to outline the overall architecture of the system and the required machine learning models. Consider details on feature engineering, model selection, training, and evaluation.

solution.contract_notes: News needs time-aware evaluation, deduplication, freshness and source/content quality rules; avoid future-story leakage and popularity feedback loops.
solution.example: Scale is unspecified. Assuming ten million daily recipients, a two-hour send window requires about 1,389 sends/s, plus provider limits/retries. Precompute neighborhood candidate pools, personalize bounded sets offline and schedule per-region sends. If ranking fails, use a vetted local digest; if permission data is unavailable, omit uncertain content. If delivery stalls, expire time-sensitive items and avoid sending yesterday's emergency as fresh news. Monitor feature/content age, provider failure, duplicate sends, per-neighborhood no-content rates and mature quality metrics. A useful failure test is an event canceled after assembly but before send: invalidation or a final eligibility check must remove it.
solution.trap: Mail pixel opens are unreliable and private neighborhood content needs final permission checks.
solution.teaching_notes_markdown:
### Newsletter objective and locality

Assume a daily personalized Nextdoor email containing local news/posts/events. Optimize meaningful local engagement and sustained newsletter satisfaction, with unsubscribes, spam complaints, misinformation/safety, neighborhood diversity and send frequency as guardrails. Opens alone are unreliable because mail clients may prefetch tracking pixels; define clicked/qualified reading and subsequent local action separately. Enforce neighborhood access and privacy before ranking so a good embedding never leaks private posts.

Build content records with post/article ID, neighborhood/geography, author/source permissions, publish/expiry time, topic, event date and text/image embeddings. User features include consented home neighborhood, interests, language, recent local interactions, followed topics and historical email engagement. Batch jobs compute long-term affinities; streaming updates add new stories, remove expired/unsafe content and update recent actions. Labels come from actually sent/rendered content: click, qualified read, local participation, hide/report and unsubscribe with chosen mature windows. Log selected slate, position, send time, policy/model version and delivery status.

### Candidate generation, ranking and assembly

The diagram's retrieval stage unions geographically eligible recent stories, interest/content similarity, trusted-source editorial picks and controlled new-topic exploration. Group near-duplicate reports of one local event; expired event notices are removed. Start with a recency/locality/content baseline, then train a calibrated multi-task GBDT or neural ranker on impression rows to predict meaningful engagement and dissatisfaction. Collaborative embeddings can augment content once enough history exists, but recent local news still needs content retrieval and freshness.

Rank a few hundred candidates, then assemble a small newsletter with topic/source diversity, urgent local information and no duplicate story. Send-time selection can be a separate learned policy with explicit quiet hours and user preferences. The output is materialized Newsletter(user,edition,slate,versions,state); an idempotent send key (user,edition) and transactional outbox prevent ordinary duplicate dispatch. Provider timeouts are reconciled using provider message IDs; delivered/opened/clicked are different states. Membership, consent and takedowns are rechecked before send, not just during yesterday's batch.

### Evidence, capacity and recovery

Train/evaluate forward in time and hold out new stories/neighborhoods; a future story cannot enter the candidate set for an earlier email. Measure candidate recall on engaged local content, NDCG@newsletter size, click calibration, freshness and neighborhood coverage. Randomized positions/exploration help diagnose exposure bias. A user-randomized A/B test measures qualified engagement and weekly retention with complaint/unsubscribe guardrails, stratified by neighborhood/activity. Community spillovers may require cluster experiments; novelty and seasonal events can confound short tests.

Scale is unspecified. Assuming ten million daily recipients, a two-hour send window requires about 1,389 sends/s, plus provider limits/retries. Precompute neighborhood candidate pools, personalize bounded sets offline and schedule per-region sends. If ranking fails, use a vetted local digest; if permission data is unavailable, omit uncertain content. If delivery stalls, expire time-sensitive items and avoid sending yesterday's emergency as fresh news. Monitor feature/content age, provider failure, duplicate sends, per-neighborhood no-content rates and mature quality metrics. A useful failure test is an event canceled after assembly but before send: invalidation or a final eligibility check must remove it.

title: ML System Design - Predict Item Category
question:
Build an ML system that predicts the category of a new catalog item (e.g. "Outdoor -> Camping -> Tents") from its title, description, attributes, and images. Cover data, labels, model architecture, serving, and evaluation.

Requirements
Functional: given an unlabeled item (title + description + structured attributes + images), output a predicted category path within Walmart's taxonomy, plus a confidence score and (optionally) top-K alternatives.
Non-functional: latency in tens of milliseconds at write time (called during item onboarding); throughput sized for catalog ingest spikes; offline batch mode for back-filling historical items; observable per-category accuracy with drift detection.
Outputs: a single best leaf-level category, top-K alternatives, and a calibrated probability per output for downstream routing thresholds.

solution.example: The diagram's ingestion stage validates/canonicalizes an item, its model stage fuses modalities and its output stage writes a versioned prediction/review request. `POST /categorize` takes item fields plus image references or cached embeddings; synchronous tens-of-ms latency is plausible only if image upload/decode/embedding is already completed or tightly bounded. State that contract explicitly. An illustrative 40 ms budget is 5 ms validation/cache, 15 ms text/structured encoding, 10 ms cached-image fusion/scoring and 10 ms response/headroom. Uncached large images need a pending/asynchronous path, not a hidden SLA violation.
solution.trap: Top-K probabilities are not renormalized leaf mass, and uncached image preprocessing may violate tens-of-ms latency.
solution.teaching_notes_markdown:
### Output and labels

This version asks for one best leaf path plus top-K alternatives with calibrated probabilities. Define a taxonomy_version and emit {item_version,taxonomy_version,model_version,best_leaf,path,top_k:[(leaf,p)]}. A single leaf induces its ancestors; top-K probabilities are not renormalized to sum to one because omitted leaves retain mass. If confidence is low, return the prediction but route it for human confirmation rather than silently asserting certainty.

Training data combines adjudicated catalog labels and reliable merchant corrections, retaining label source/version. Map old taxonomy labels through explicit migration tables; ambiguous splits require relabeling. Group duplicate products/brands across train/test and use forward-time plus new-category/seller holdouts. Category text copied from a later correction is leakage. Rare categories need class-balanced sampling/weights and human review, evaluated at natural production prevalence.

### Multimodal model and serving

Encode title/description with a compact text transformer, images with a pretrained vision encoder, and attributes with categorical embeddings/numeric transforms. Concatenate pooled vectors plus missing-modality masks, then a small fusion MLP and leaf softmax or hierarchical conditional heads. Text-only TF-IDF/logistic regression is the baseline; compare image-only, text-only and fused ablations. Train cross-entropy for one leaf, optionally adding an ancestor-consistency loss. A hierarchical head multiplies conditional branch probabilities along the path; greedy traversal can miss the most likely leaf, so use beam search or compute all candidate path scores.

Calibrate with held-out temperature scaling or another validated method, checking rare-category reliability. A photo of a tent with title “replacement tent pole” should rely on attributes/text enough to avoid confusing the accessory with the entire product. Missing images use the text branch and a missingness mask, not a fabricated zero-confidence image prediction.

The diagram's ingestion stage validates/canonicalizes an item, its model stage fuses modalities and its output stage writes a versioned prediction/review request. `POST /categorize` takes item fields plus image references or cached embeddings; synchronous tens-of-ms latency is plausible only if image upload/decode/embedding is already completed or tightly bounded. State that contract explicitly. An illustrative 40 ms budget is 5 ms validation/cache, 15 ms text/structured encoding, 10 ms cached-image fusion/scoring and 10 ms response/headroom. Uncached large images need a pending/asynchronous path, not a hidden SLA violation.

### Batch, consistency and evaluation

Catalog change events carry item_id/version. Workers reuse the same model/feature package for write-time and historical backfill, batch GPU embedding jobs and conditionally write only if the item version still matches. Duplicate events are idempotent and old completions cannot overwrite a newer description. A model/taxonomy rollout publishes compatible versions atomically; on model outage store a pending classification or return a clearly marked prior prediction, depending on onboarding policy.

Throughput is unspecified: assuming a 10,000-item/s spike and 20 ms unbatched service time implies 200 concurrent inferences before headroom. Benchmark batching, cache reuse and backpressure, retaining an ingest queue for batch work. Measure leaf accuracy, hierarchical distance, top-K recall, macro/per-leaf F1, calibration and review coverage/error by confidence threshold. Monitor drift, unknown attributes, modality missingness, p99 latency and per-category corrections. Validate taxonomy migration, image absence, duplicate items, conflicting updates and cold rare leaves before claiming correctness.

title: ML System Design — Asset / Template Recommendation & Feed
question:
ML System Design — Asset / Template Recommendation & Feed

ML system-design round: build a recommender for Figma assets/templates, or a home feed. Treated as a fairly standard newsfeed-style recsys — candidate generation plus ranking — adapted to Figma's content.

MLE RS · tags: recommendation, feed, ranking, mlsd, system-design

Requirements

Design a recommendation/feed system for Figma:

Recommend assets / templates to users, or design the home feed.
Expected to look like a standard newsfeed recommender: candidate generation → ranking, with the usual feature, training, and serving discussion.
Notes
Candidates treated this like an FB-newsfeed recsys and that framing was accepted — cover candidate retrieval (e.g. two-tower / embedding retrieval), a ranking model, features (user, asset, context), training data and labels, online serving, and metrics.
Adapt the content specifics to Figma (design assets/templates, collaboration signals) rather than reciting a generic social feed.
Part of the longer ML onsite, usually alongside an ML model-design round and a project deep dive.

steps: Adapt the objective to design work
solution.contract_notes: Asset/template recommendation needs compatibility, licensing/access and editable format constraints; deduplicate near-identical variants and preserve diversity.
solution.example: Scale is not provided. Assume ten million assets at 256 fp16 dimensions: 5.12 GB raw vectors, excluding ANN and replicas. At 5,000 requests/s and 200 ranked candidates, score one million pairs/s. An illustrative 150 ms budget reserves 30 ms retrieval, 30 ms batch features, 50 ms rank and 40 ms policy/network. Version model/index together, canary changes and fall back to safe compatible curated assets on ranker failure. Idempotent insertion/export requests and content-version checks prevent retries creating duplicate copies unexpectedly. Test revoked team access, missing dependency/version mismatch, delayed takedown, near-duplicate leakage and a permission change during a cached session.
solution.trap: Private team assets and near-duplicate templates require access isolation and family-aware evaluation.
solution.teaching_notes_markdown:
### Adapt the objective to design work

Assume a Figma asset/template discovery feed. Optimize successful insert/duplicate followed by meaningful editing or retained use, with satisfaction, license violations, load time and creator diversity as guardrails. A thumbnail click is a weak label; accidental duplicates and immediate undo should not count as successful use. Log impressions, position, asset/version, workspace context, insert/duplicate, edits after a defined interval, undo/remove, save and delayed reuse. Never use private file content without permission.

Features include user role/interests, recent searches, preferred style and prior assets; asset category, tags, visual/text embedding, component type, editable format, dependencies, license, version compatibility, quality and freshness; context includes current design task, device and team-approved libraries. Collaboration features can use authorized team usage and shared-library relevance, but another team's private assets must not enter candidates or explanations.

### Retrieval and ranker

`GET /assets/recommendations` takes authorized workspace/task context and returns IDs, versions and structured reasons. Candidate generation unions content/two-tower ANN, related assets, team-library choices, editorial quality and a new-creator pool. Deduplicate near-identical templates and apply access, license and compatibility rules. Rank hundreds with a multi-task model predicting meaningful reuse, quality and negative outcomes; a GBDT over content and usage features is a fast baseline, with richer user-asset interaction models after enough data exists. Re-rank by style/category/creator diversity so a page is not twenty recolored copies of one template.

The diagram's retrieval is over versioned assets, its ranking uses user/task context, and its policy stage checks permissions and licensing. New users get role/task/onboarding-based content matches; new assets use embeddings and limited randomized exposure. Cache public item embeddings globally and team-private candidates only within the authorized tenant boundary. Index deletions and permission changes through monotonic versions/tombstones, with final access rechecks when opening/inserting.

### Training, evaluation and operations

Use point-in-time features, mature reuse labels and grouped splits by asset family/creator to prevent duplicate-template leakage. Measure candidate recall, NDCG@20 on useful inserts, calibration, compatibility rejection and new-creator coverage; human task relevance helps evaluate cold-start content. Exposure and position bias require logged propensities/randomized slots, not treating every unshown template as disliked. User-randomized A/B tests may contaminate teams through shared assets, so assign by workspace/team when collaboration spillover is material; monitor useful editing sessions, re-use, undo, complaints and creator concentration.

Scale is not provided. Assume ten million assets at 256 fp16 dimensions: 5.12 GB raw vectors, excluding ANN and replicas. At 5,000 requests/s and 200 ranked candidates, score one million pairs/s. An illustrative 150 ms budget reserves 30 ms retrieval, 30 ms batch features, 50 ms rank and 40 ms policy/network. Version model/index together, canary changes and fall back to safe compatible curated assets on ranker failure. Idempotent insertion/export requests and content-version checks prevent retries creating duplicate copies unexpectedly. Test revoked team access, missing dependency/version mismatch, delayed takedown, near-duplicate leakage and a permission change during a cached session.

title: ML System Design: Bad / Unsafe Content Detection
question:
Design a content-understanding pipeline that flags unsafe / bad pins (or bad images) at upload time and at re-evaluation time. Used by Trust & Safety / Content Signal teams; the framing changes between teams but the underlying ML system is recognizably one design.

Requirements

Design an end-to-end content-safety pipeline for Pinterest pins. Address:

How content (image + text + metadata) is represented as features.
Multi-modal embedding choice — image + caption + board context.
Labeling strategy: human review queue, weak labels from report signals, gold-set evaluation.
Model architecture and training (multi-label classification, threshold calibration per policy).
Inference pipeline: synchronous (block upload) vs asynchronous (post-publish takedown).
How the system handles model updates and re-scoring of historical content.
How human reviewers feed back into training.
Notes
Multi-modal embedding is the central design choice. The expected answer covers image embeddings (CNN / ViT) + text embeddings (transformer) + a fusion layer; many candidates underspecify the fusion and lose signal.
Calibration matters more than accuracy in this domain — policy thresholds are set per category, and miscalibrated probabilities translate to wrong policy enforcement. Mention temperature scaling or isotonic regression as the calibration step.
Asynchronous re-scoring of historical content is a common follow-up. The accepted answer: a Kafka-backed event log of all pins, a worker pool that consumes the log against the current model version, sharded by content-id to limit duplicate work.
Bias-and-fairness analysis is sometimes pushed — subgroup metric breakdowns and counterfactual evaluation.
One reported variant is bank/transaction fraud detection used as a generic real-time scoring system; the architecture overlaps (feature pipeline -> scoring -> threshold -> action).

solution.example: On model/storage outage, hold high-risk new content instead of issuing an unsupported safe verdict; preserve the prior decision for existing pins pending reevaluation. Canary/shadow new models against fixed gold and recent random samples, verify subgroup calibration and retain rollback compatibility. Review outcomes feed a versioned dataset after quality checks, with random audits to counter selection bias. Monitor upload p99, moderation lag, stale models, review age and reversal rates. Tests include image/text contradiction, missing caption, duplicate replay, simultaneous human override and a removed pin receiving an old allow result.
solution.trap: Unknown policy labels are not negatives; include model version in historical-rescore idempotency keys.
solution.teaching_notes_markdown:
### Representation and calibrated policy decisions

Treat Pinterest pin safety as multi-label classification: a pin can violate several policies, and the thresholds for removal, limited distribution and review differ. Inputs are image, caption/OCR text, board context, source URL and available metadata. Use a ViT/CNN image vector v, a text-transformer vector t over caption/OCR/board text, and structured features z. A concrete fusion is h=MLP([v;t;v⊙Pt;z;modality_masks]), with a projection P aligning dimensions; sigmoid heads output one score per policy. Compare image-only, text-only and concatenation versus interaction ablations. Board context is a signal, not permission to infer unrelated private attributes.

Train weighted binary cross-entropy with a mask for unannotated labels; unknown labels are not negative. Expert gold labels, adjudicated appeals and human review form trusted data. Reports, blocked URLs and heuristic rules are weak labels with provenance and measured noise. Sample uncertain/new-pattern content for active learning plus random production content for unbiased prevalence/error estimates. Reviewer disagreement requires guidelines and adjudication, not averaging away policy ambiguity. Split by time and near-duplicate/source clusters.

Calibrate each policy using held-out temperature scaling or isotonic regression where data supports it. Measure action precision, severe-harm recall, false removals per million, PR-AUC, calibration and appeal reversals by language, content type and subgroup. Choose thresholds under explicit harm costs and review capacity. A single aggregate accuracy number hides rare severe failures and cannot determine safe enforcement.

### Upload and historical paths

`POST /pins` stores media in quarantine, commits Pin(id,version,media_digest,state) and publishes an outbox event. Cheap hash/rule checks and a bounded fast model run synchronously; confidently unsafe content blocks, uncertain severe cases remain held, and lower-risk uncertain cases may publish with limited distribution only if policy allows. A slower model/reviewer can later take down published content. The diagram's model output is therefore followed by a policy/version-aware action service, not direct unconditional deletion.

Historical rescoring consumes a durable pin manifest/event log into partitioned workers keyed by pin_id. Deduplication key is (pin_id,pin_version,policy_version,model_version). Claim leases, retry transient media/model failures with backoff and dead-letter corrupt content. Conditional writes compare input version and current decision authority, so a late older model cannot undo a newer appeal or rescore. A new model version intentionally gets a new key; using only content_id+rule_version would mistakenly suppress it. Replay capacity is separated from upload capacity to protect latency.

### Sizing, failure handling and feedback

Traffic is unspecified. Assume 20 million uploads/day, fivefold peak: about 1,157/s. If 1% require human review, that is 200,000 reviews/day, so staffing becomes a major design constraint; at 30 seconds each that is 1,667 reviewer-hours/day. Measure rather than assume that threshold choice is operationally affordable. Persist Decision, Action, ReviewAssignment and Appeal with immutable versions and audit logs; reviewer claims and overrides use atomic state transitions.

On model/storage outage, hold high-risk new content instead of issuing an unsupported safe verdict; preserve the prior decision for existing pins pending reevaluation. Canary/shadow new models against fixed gold and recent random samples, verify subgroup calibration and retain rollback compatibility. Review outcomes feed a versioned dataset after quality checks, with random audits to counter selection bias. Monitor upload p99, moderation lag, stale models, review age and reversal rates. Tests include image/text contradiction, missing caption, duplicate replay, simultaneous human override and a removed pin receiving an old allow result.

title: ML System Design: Behavior Prediction from Sensor + Camera Data
question:
Design a machine learning system for an autonomous vehicle that predicts the future behavior of the vehicles, pedestrians and cyclists around it from the car's sensor and camera data, and hands calibrated uncertainty to the motion planner that consumes the predictions.

Requirements
1.
Inputs. Time-aligned LiDAR / radar data and camera streams from the ego vehicle, plus the tracked history of each surrounding agent.
2.
Outputs. For every agent, a trajectory prediction over a future horizon of about 3 to 8 seconds, with uncertainty: either a per-step covariance or a categorical distribution over trajectory modes.
3.
Planner contract. The motion planner needs (a) deterministic outputs at a fixed cadence, (b) uncertainty in a form it can use inside its cost functions, and (c) a bounded latency budget.
4.
Cover these parts of the design:
problem framing and the input and output representation;
model architecture and output head;
loss function;
uncertainty: aleatoric versus epistemic, and how each reaches the planner;
data collection and long-tail curation of rare, dangerous scenarios;
training stages;
evaluation, offline and in closed loop;
serving and latency.
Constraints
The planner runs at about 10 Hz, so the predictor must return a fresh batch of predictions in under 100 ms, with a bounded 99th-percentile latency.
Safety-critical use: a design that averages several plausible futures into one trajectory is not acceptable.
Follow-up 1: interactive prediction

Condition the predictions on the ego vehicle's planned action, so the forecast reflects how other agents react to what the ego plans to do. Say what changes in the inputs, the training data and the evaluation.

Follow-up 2: emergent dangers

Extend the system to flag emergent dangers that call for intervention, for example a pedestrian stepping into the road. Say how you would label, train and evaluate this.

solution.contract_notes: Synchronize sensor and camera timestamps, calibrate coordinate frames and define the prediction horizon. Split by drive/session/location rather than nearby frames, mask missing modalities and evaluate latency plus safety-critical slices. A multimodal fusion model must beat single-modality and simple temporal baselines under the same information availability.
solution.example: An illustrative <100 ms budget is 15 ms sync/preprocess, 30 ms shared sensor encoder, 20 ms interactions/head, 10 ms calibration/serialization and 25 ms headroom; if perception already supplies features, avoid double-counting it. Cap agent count with a conservative fallback for omitted actors, use fixed shapes/precision validation and monitor p99 under worst-case crowded scenes. On deadline miss the planner receives a failure flag and uses a validated conservative reachable-set/previous-prediction policy with age limits, not a silently stale confident forecast.
solution.trap: Never average incompatible futures or pretend marginal modes form a safe joint scene distribution.
solution.teaching_notes_markdown:
### Planner-facing representation

At each 10 Hz tick, form one synchronized scene in the ego coordinate frame at timestamp t: calibrated camera/point-cloud/radar features, ego pose/motion, map lanes/crosswalks and tracked agent histories with masks, velocity, heading and covariance. Motion-compensate asynchronous sensors and mark staleness; a future observation cannot enter a training feature. For each agent return K trajectory modes over an assumed five-second horizon at fixed steps, mode probabilities summing to one and optionally a positive-definite covariance per step. Include timestamp, coordinate frame, valid horizon, model version and out-of-distribution/quality flags. Deterministic inference means fixed inputs produce the same bounded, ordered output, not sampling a different future every call.

### Model, objective and uncertainty

A BEV sensor encoder fuses cameras/LiDAR/radar, a temporal encoder summarizes agent history, and an interaction/map encoder models agents and lane relations. A mixture head predicts πk, means μk,1:T and covariance Cholesky factors Lk,t with positive diagonals, giving Σ=LLᵀ. Train a trajectory mixture negative log likelihood:

$$L=-\log\sum_{k=1}^K\pi_k\,\mathcal N(y_{1:T};\mu_{k,1:T},\Sigma_k),$$

masking unobserved future steps and using log-sum-exp. If covariance is block-diagonal across time, state that approximation; it does not represent full temporal correlation. Add physical-feasibility/map losses carefully and inspect mode collapse. A constant-velocity baseline establishes how much complex interactions help. Turning left and going straight must remain separate modes; their average may point into a sidewalk.

Aleatoric uncertainty is represented by distinct futures and within-mode covariance. Epistemic uncertainty comes from a small ensemble evaluated within the latency budget, disagreement/distilled uncertainty, and OOD diagnostics; it should trigger a conservative planner response, not be mislabeled as calibrated mode probability. Calibrate likelihood/mode probabilities and coverage on held-out drives. The planner consumes the full mixture in collision-risk/expected-cost or chance constraints and receives an explicit stale/failure flag; marginal per-agent forecasts do not establish a safe joint scene distribution.

### Data, evaluation and latency

Train sensor encoders/self-supervised representations, then supervised forecasting and interaction fine-tuning; compare modalities and rare-scenario ablations. Curate turns, occlusions, emergency braking, unusual cyclists and pedestrian near-misses, retaining random driving for real prevalence. Correct for oversampling in evaluation/calibration. Split by drive, geography and time, never adjacent video frames. Track label noise from tracking and uncertain future identities.

Offline metrics include minADE/minFDE, miss rate, mixture NLL, probability/coverage calibration, collision/off-road rate and rare-event slices; minADE alone rewards many guesses. Closed-loop simulation with the actual planner measures collisions, near misses, progress and comfort under reactive agents, followed by guarded real-world validation. The diagram's predictor-to-planner boundary is an explicit safety contract.

An illustrative <100 ms budget is 15 ms sync/preprocess, 30 ms shared sensor encoder, 20 ms interactions/head, 10 ms calibration/serialization and 25 ms headroom; if perception already supplies features, avoid double-counting it. Cap agent count with a conservative fallback for omitted actors, use fixed shapes/precision validation and monitor p99 under worst-case crowded scenes. On deadline miss the planner receives a failure flag and uses a validated conservative reachable-set/previous-prediction policy with age limits, not a silently stale confident forecast.

For interactive prediction, condition the head on candidate ego trajectories/actions and learn responses from logged interactions. Logs cover only the executed ego policy; counterfactual reactions to untried actions are not identifiable without coverage, carefully validated simulation or controlled data. Evaluate reactive closed-loop outcomes and sensitivity to ego plans rather than only open-loop imitation. To flag emergent danger, add a time-to-conflict/intervention head with event/horizon labels from expert-adjudicated near misses and counterfactual collision risk; avoid leakage from the eventual intervention. Evaluate recall at a fixed false-alert rate, time-to-warning and subgroup/scenario calibration, including benign road-edge pedestrians. Intervention authority stays with a separately validated safety/planning policy.

Read the numbered path as Time-aligned sensor scene → BEV + agent/map encoders → Trajectory mixture head → Modes / covariance / flags → 10 Hz motion planner → Closed-loop safety evaluation. title: ML System Design: Notification Ranking & Ads CTR
question:
Two adjacent prompts that share an architecture: design the ML system for Pinterest notifications (which pin to push, when, with what frequency cap) or for ads CTR prediction (rank ad candidates for an impression slot). Both want explicit feature, loss, calibration, and online-experimentation design.

Requirements

Design one of:

Notification ranking — pick the best pin (or no pin) to surface to a user via push notification, given the user's history, the available pin pool, and a frequency-capping budget.
Ads CTR prediction — rank ad candidates for a given impression slot to maximize expected revenue (eCPM = bid x pCTR).

Address: feature engineering, model architecture, loss function, calibration, the send-or-not-send decision (notifications) or the floor-price interaction (ads), and the online experimentation strategy (A/B test design, online metric vs offline metric divergence).

Notes
The send-or-not-send decision is the key notification-specific design point: rank candidate pins by expected user engagement; apply a frequency cap (per-user, per-day, per-channel); use a calibrated probability threshold for the send / no-send gate. Mention the cold-start problem for new users.
For ads CTR, calibration is non-optional because the downstream auction multiplies bid x pCTR. Mis-calibrated CTR distorts the auction. Isotonic regression or Platt scaling on a held-out set is the standard answer.
Two-tower retrieval for the candidate pool + a heavier ranker for the top-N is the same skeleton as the search / ranking card; focus the round on what makes notifications / ads distinct.
Online-vs-offline metric divergence is a graded sub-thread. Common causes: position bias, novelty effects, A/B-test contamination.

solution.contract_notes: Notification ranking and ads CTR share exposure-aware probability modeling, but have different action/cost objectives. Explain each objective, its label window, and its independent budget/opt-out constraints.
solution.example: Scale is absent; assuming 5,000 opportunities/s and 200 ranked pins gives one million pair scores/s. An assumed 150 ms budget reserves 30 ms retrieval, 30 ms features, 50 ms rank and 40 ms policy/delivery enqueue. Test duplicate opportunities, rolling-window boundaries, opt-out while queued and stale pin removal; monitor latency, cap violations, delivery uncertainty and mature calibration.
solution.trap: Calibrated open probability does not establish incremental value; no-send is a real action.
solution.teaching_notes_markdown:
### Choose the notification variant

Rank Pinterest pins for a push opportunity and explicitly allow no-send. Optimize incremental meaningful visits/retained engagement, with opt-out, spam complaints, fatigue and safety guardrails. Required transactional messages have a separate delivery contract. `POST /notification-opportunities` accepts user, time and channel; return selected pin and decision_id or SKIP with reason. Store Decision, candidate snapshot, model/feature versions and budget reservation; retries of the same opportunity return the same result.

Retrieve fresh eligible pins through content/two-tower ANN, followed interests and a safe fresh pool. Filter access, removed content and previously sent duplicates. Features include user topic/creator affinity, recent browsing, pin visual/text embeddings and quality, recency, local time, recent sends, recent opens and current activity. A two-tower retriever is cheap over a huge catalog; a GBDT or multi-task neural ranker uses richer interactions over hundreds. Train binary cross-entropy heads for click/meaningful session/opt-out with mature windows and masks, and compare to a content/cohort baseline for new users.

### Calibration, send gate and frequency

Calibrate held-out predictions using Platt/isotonic scaling as data permits, by important activity/cohort/channel slices. High p(open) does not prove an incremental visit, so maintain randomized no-send holdouts and estimate incremental downstream value. Rank candidates by calibrated expected utility and send only when the best candidate exceeds an interruption-cost threshold, is eligible and fits the frequency budget. A conservative cold-start user gets declared-interest pins and low frequency, not an aggressively confident behavioral prediction.

The diagram's ranker feeds a separate send/skip policy and atomic cap check. For an assumed two promotional pushes per rolling day, two racing workers must conditionally reserve against one user/channel budget before enqueueing delivery. Outbox delivery carries a unique notification_id; distinguish reserved, provider-accepted, delivered and failed states. Recheck opt-out and content safety at dispatch. Timeouts do not prove nondelivery; reconcile provider IDs before resending or releasing budget. A model outage skips noncritical pushes or uses a validated conservative fallback, preserving quiet hours.

### Experiment and contrast with ads

Offline measure log loss, calibration, NDCG on mature meaningful-engagement labels and cold-start coverage using forward-time splits. User A/B tests assess incremental meaningful sessions and long-term retention with guardrails; test send rate as part of the policy, not just ranking among sent users. Check position/exposure bias, novelty, sample-ratio mismatch and cross-device contamination. An offline click win may fail online because it changes frequency, user fatigue or candidate distribution. Keep logging candidates, selection propensity and no-send outcomes.

If choosing the ads variant instead, replace send costs/caps with targeting, advertiser budget/pacing and auction constraints. Model calibrated pCTR from observed impression/click rows, with user/ad/context features; rank expected click revenue as bid×pCTR, converting to eCPM by ×1,000 when bids are per click. Apply floor and eligibility in consistent units and auction semantics, not a separate arbitrary probability threshold. A bid USD 2 and pCTR 0.01 yield expected USD 0.02/impression or USD 20 eCPM. Miscalibration changes auction allocation/revenue, so held-out calibration is essential. Evaluate revenue, advertiser value and user harm in an auction-aware experiment.

Scale is absent; assuming 5,000 opportunities/s and 200 ranked pins gives one million pair scores/s. An assumed 150 ms budget reserves 30 ms retrieval, 30 ms features, 50 ms rank and 40 ms policy/delivery enqueue. Test duplicate opportunities, rolling-window boundaries, opt-out while queued and stale pin removal; monitor latency, cap violations, delivery uncertainty and mature calibration.

title: ML System Design: Product Categorization / Taxonomy
question:
ML System Design: Product Categorization / Taxonomy

The MLE system-design round, most often a product-categorization problem over Shopify's product taxonomy (10,000+ hierarchical categories across 26+ business verticals): design real-time and streaming classification of merchant products into the taxonomy. Variants include search autocomplete and personalized product feeds.

Requirements
Design a system to classify merchant products into Shopify's Product Taxonomy: 10,000+ categories, hierarchical, spanning 26+ business verticals.
Cover both serving modes the interviewers push on:
Real-time categorization when a user/merchant submits a single product.
Streaming categorization that detects changes across many products and re-categorizes at scale.
Address the modeling side too: it is framed as a multi-class (multi-label) classification over a hierarchy. A known wrinkle: the hierarchical tags are not mutually exclusive, so a flat multi-class assumption breaks — discuss hierarchical/multi-label handling.
Notes
This round emphasizes serving and architecture (real-time vs. batch/streaming paths, latency, throughput) while still expecting sound modeling choices — distinct from the separate ML modeling round, which is modeling-only.
Interviewer fit is inconsistent: some panels are senior/disengaged and jump straight to "how do you handle real-time vs. batch," sometimes asserting "assume no labeled data" and asking how you'd bootstrap labels. Be ready to discuss label sourcing/weak supervision.
Reported variants in this slot: search autocomplete design, and personalized product feeds. One candidate strong in personalization was still failed for "insufficient depth," so push concrete detail (candidate generation, ranking, features, evaluation), not just a block diagram.
Useful framing references candidates mention: product-taxonomy classification writeups and large-catalog categorization papers.

steps: Real-time and streaming share one model contract
solution.example: Evaluate micro/macro F1, per-vertical/leaf precision-recall, hierarchical distance, path consistency, top-K recall, calibration and human-review coverage. Calibrate per-label or pooled families with enough support. Monitor taxonomy-specific drift, merchant disagreement, streaming lag, p99 and stale prediction rate. Test multi-path products, category migration, duplicate/reordered changes, no-label launch and a merchant edit racing a backfill. For autocomplete/feed variants, reuse taxonomy content features but define separate retrieval/ranking labels; classification quality alone does not measure search or recommendation success.
solution.trap: Hierarchical tags can overlap, so a single flat exclusive softmax violates the requested label contract.
solution.teaching_notes_markdown:
### Hierarchical multi-label output

The required contract permits multiple compatible tags; a single flat softmax over 10,000+ categories would force mutually exclusive labels incorrectly. Return product_version, taxonomy_version, model_version and a set of category paths with calibrated per-node/leaf probabilities. A selected child implies its ancestors; probabilities for sibling tags need not sum to one when several can apply. If a merchant UI requires a primary category, derive it separately from the tag set and document that rule.

Encode product title/description, structured attributes and images, with missing-modality masks. Fuse text/image embeddings with attributes into an MLP and sigmoid label heads, possibly first routing to several of the 26+ verticals and scoring candidate subtrees. Do not force a single vertical before classification if cross-vertical labels are possible. Train masked binary cross-entropy on observed positives/verified negatives, plus hierarchical consistency constraints such as p(child)≤p(parent). Unknown labels are not negatives. Compare lexical/content baselines and text-only versus multimodal ablations.

### Label bootstrap and taxonomy changes

When labeled data exists, use adjudicated merchant assignments/corrections and gold sets, retaining taxonomy version and provenance. With no labels, start from taxonomy descriptions, content-embedding retrieval, merchant metadata and high-precision weak rules; these are suggestions with measured uncertainty, not a claimed supervised classifier. Experts label a stratified seed set across verticals and rare categories. Active learning adds uncertain/disagreement cases, while random samples estimate true prevalence/error. Train and calibrate only after these labels exist. Splits hold out future time, duplicate product families and merchants; category-text leakage from later corrections is removed.

A taxonomy release records added/deprecated/moved nodes and migration mappings. Simple renames can migrate; category splits may need reclassification or human review. Version output schemas and model/index manifests together, and retain old mappings for audit.

### Real-time and streaming share one model contract

`POST /categorize` takes product fields/version and returns paths, scores or PENDING_REVIEW. For a chosen 50 ms online target, precompute/reuse image embeddings at upload and use a compact text/fusion model; uncached media cannot silently consume unbounded time. The diagram's online path goes directly through the shared feature/model service, while change events drive a separate batching worker pool. `ProductChanged(product_id,version)` is emitted through an outbox from the product database. Streaming workers coalesce rapid edits, fetch current content, score in batches and conditionally write only when source version matches. Unique (product,version,model,taxonomy) deduplicates retries, and tombstones prevent deleted products reappearing. Historical backfills use the same contract with lower-priority capacity.

### Capacity, failure and evaluation

Throughput is unspecified. Assume 2,000 updates/s and 10,000 label scores each: 20 million output scores/s before candidate pruning. At 4 bytes each, naively persisting every score would be 80 MB/s; store selected tags/top-K plus audit summaries and retain full scores only as needed. Queue lag/backpressure isolates bulk rescoring from interactive traffic. Transient failures retry with backoff; malformed inputs go to a dead-letter/review path. Model outage returns pending or a marked older prediction, never a fabricated confident category. Database CAS prevents stale completions overwriting newer merchant edits.

Evaluate micro/macro F1, per-vertical/leaf precision-recall, hierarchical distance, path consistency, top-K recall, calibration and human-review coverage. Calibrate per-label or pooled families with enough support. Monitor taxonomy-specific drift, merchant disagreement, streaming lag, p99 and stale prediction rate. Test multi-path products, category migration, duplicate/reordered changes, no-label launch and a merchant edit racing a backfill. For autocomplete/feed variants, reuse taxonomy content features but define separate retrieval/ranking labels; classification quality alone does not measure search or recommendation success.

title: ML System Design: Recsys, Chatbot, Image Classifier
question: Google MLE / AI-ML L4–L5 loops include a ~60-min ML System Design round. Prompts span: (1) a real-time recommendation system for an e-commerce/social platform; (2) a mobile app that photographs a leaf and classifies it into one of K species; (3) a chatbot grounded in mixed structured + unstructured data; (4) short-video duplicate detection at billions scale. Interviewers probe pipeline structure, feature engineering, training/serving split, cold start, A/B testing, and latency vs accuracy trade-offs. Design one and cover the key axes.

solution.example: The diagram's path is mobile capture → quality/preprocess → versioned classifier → calibrated top-K/retake. Batch training produces signed model and label-map artifacts; online inference uses the same resize/normalization package. Cache by image digest plus model version, enforce image size/decode limits and strip unnecessary location metadata. If offline use matters, ship a compact on-device model; a larger server model can offer an explicit second pass with network consent. Cold species require labeled examples and a taxonomy/model release, not collaborative filtering; unknown users need no behavior history.
solution.trap: Unknown species need abstention; do not present leaf identification as a safe-to-eat guarantee.
solution.teaching_notes_markdown:
### Choose one design: leaf-species identification

Design the mobile leaf-photo classifier rather than answering four different prompts incompletely. Assume K known species, one leaf/plant per image, a top-three result with calibrated probabilities and an UNKNOWN/RETAKE option for unsupported or unreadable photos. Clarify geography, poisonous-species consequences, offline use and target devices; this is identification assistance, not a safe-to-eat decision. Optimize verified species accuracy at chosen coverage, with dangerous-confusion rate, latency, battery and abstention quality as guardrails.

The app uploads a resized photo or runs an on-device quality gate; the response contains species IDs, taxonomy/model version, confidence and evidence-quality warnings. Image records retain consent/license, species, annotator confidence, capture time/location if permitted, plant/photographer identity and image digest. Expert/botanical labels form a gold set; user confirmations alone are noisy. Detect duplicate images and split by plant, photographer, geography and time, so near-identical shots do not inflate test accuracy. Cover seasons, leaf damage, lighting, backgrounds and class imbalance. Unknown species and non-leaf images need dedicated evaluation, not just K-way test data.

### Model and training/serving split

Start with a pretrained compact CNN/ViT encoder and a K-way head, trained with cross-entropy on verified labels and realistic crop/color/blur augmentations. Compare a nearest-embedding baseline and a quantized model at matched quality/latency. Train a quality/leaf-presence head and an out-of-distribution/abstention gate; maximum softmax alone is not a reliable unknown detector. Calibrate on held-out data, including rare species and lookalikes. Optional user region can define a transparent prior, but hard exclusion risks missing introduced plants and must be tested.

The diagram's path is mobile capture → quality/preprocess → versioned classifier → calibrated top-K/retake. Batch training produces signed model and label-map artifacts; online inference uses the same resize/normalization package. Cache by image digest plus model version, enforce image size/decode limits and strip unnecessary location metadata. If offline use matters, ship a compact on-device model; a larger server model can offer an explicit second pass with network consent. Cold species require labeled examples and a taxonomy/model release, not collaborative filtering; unknown users need no behavior history.

### Latency, evidence and operations

Assume a 300 ms server-side p95 target excluding upload on slow mobile links: 30 ms validation/decode, 100 ms encoder, 20 ms calibration/output and 150 ms queuing/network headroom. Report end-to-end upload separately. At an assumed 1,000 QPS and 0.1 GPU-seconds/image, at least 100 fully utilized GPU equivalents are required without batching gains, plus headroom; benchmark real hardware instead of assuming this rate. On timeout return retry/queued state, not a stale answer for a different image. Idempotent request IDs deduplicate uploads; versioned hashes prevent old results overriding a replacement photo.

Offline measure macro/per-species F1, top-1/top-3 accuracy, calibration, risk-coverage curves and dangerous lookalike confusion. Online randomize users/devices persistently between validated models and measure expert-audited identification success, retakes, abandonment and p95/battery guardrails; self-reported confirmation is biased. Canary releases, monitor image-quality/domain drift, unknown rates and geography slices, and keep rollback label-map compatibility. Test corrupt images, multiple leaves, rare species, offline fallback and model-update/cache mismatch. This explicitly chosen design covers the prompt's feature, training/serving, cold-start, experimentation and latency axes.

title: ML System Design: Search, Ranking, Experimentation
question:
Applied Scientist full-loop ML system design on search / ranking / experimentation. Pick a domain (often 'search ranking' or 'image generation for brand ads') and walk through the ML stack: retrieval, candidate generation, ranking, re-ranking, business-rule overlays, and online evaluation. Discuss offline metrics (NDCG, MRR), online metrics (CTR, conversion, brand-safety), and how to design an uncontaminated A/B test.

Recent prompts: 'How would you evaluate generation quality for image or text?' and 'If the image is for brand ads, how do you make sure the brand name is right in the image?'

steps: Labels and experiments are part of the stack
solution.contract_notes: Connect every proposed ranking improvement to assignment/exposure logging, an experiment unit, guardrails and a prespecified stopping rule.
solution.example: If an advertisement must show the exact brand name, generate the scene separately and composite an approved vector/raster wordmark or typeset text with known fonts, permissions and layout constraints. OCR/spelling checks and logo/template validation are gates, with human approval for high-risk output. A generative model merely prompted to spell correctly cannot guarantee exact text. Cache approved assets by input/spec/model/version and fail closed on failed brand validation. This turns brand-name correctness into a verifiable rendering contract rather than an unsupported model claim.
solution.trap: Correct brand text is a validated compositing/rendering contract, not guaranteed by a generative prompt.
solution.teaching_notes_markdown:
### Concrete domain: retail search ranking

Optimize completed satisfactory purchases per query, with relevance, returns, brand safety, price transparency and latency guardrails. `POST /search` accepts query, user context and filters; return eligible products, positions, exposure_id and model/index versions. Query understanding extracts brand/category/attributes and corrects spelling while preserving explicit constraints. Union lexical retrieval for exact names/SKUs, semantic ANN for intent, and category candidates; hard-filter stock, shipping eligibility, policy and explicit user filters before ranking.

Use query-product lexical/semantic match, price, availability, user purchase/intent features, product quality and context. A GBDT learning-to-rank baseline scores hundreds; a neural multi-task ranker can predict click, purchase and return-adjusted value. Re-rank for near-duplicate suppression, diversity and business rules with documented sponsored placement. The diagram's retrieval broadens recall, rank orders by relevance/value and re-ranking enforces list-level rules. Do not let revenue weights bypass brand-safety or availability constraints.

### Labels and experiments are part of the stack

Log all displayed impressions with position, retrieval source, feature timestamp/version, assignment and propensities where randomized. Join clicks/cart/purchases and mature returns using stable keys; unshown products are unlabeled rather than observed negatives. Build point-in-time features and forward-time/duplicate-family splits. Evaluate recall@candidate count, graded NDCG@10 for usefulness, MRR for navigational queries, calibration and per-query-type brand-safety/filter violations. A higher CTR can reflect clickbait rather than more satisfied purchases.

For an uncontaminated A/B test, randomize persistently by user/account across devices where possible, assign before candidate generation, and keep feature/index/eligibility logging compatible. Predeclare primary purchase/satisfaction metric, minimum effect, duration, guardrails and stopping rule; check sample-ratio mismatch and exclude internal bots consistently. Avoid training treatment and control on mixed treatment-generated feedback during an initial test unless this interference is intentionally modeled. Marketplace inventory and seller response can spill across users, so use cluster/geo or switchback designs for material supply effects. Novelty, position bias and delayed returns explain offline/online divergence.

Assume 10,000 QPS, 300 ranked products and a 150 ms budget: three million pair scores/s; allocate 30 ms retrieval, 30 ms features, 50 ms ranking and 40 ms policy/network. Use cached item embeddings, batch lookups and per-region indexes; stale stock is rechecked. On semantic/ranker failure fall back to lexical/relevance rules. Outbox updates and monotonic product versions handle retries/deletions; model/index rollout uses canaries and instant compatible rollback.

### Generation-quality follow-up

For generated text/images, create a blinded task-specific gold set and expert rubric for instruction adherence, factual/visual correctness, usefulness, safety and brand fidelity. Use pairwise human preferences with inter-rater agreement and confidence intervals; automated scores/model judges are proxies validated against humans and protected against prompt manipulation. Deduplicate evaluation prompts from training and segment difficult languages/brands. Online test downstream qualified conversions with complaint and safety guardrails, not just aesthetic ratings.

If an advertisement must show the exact brand name, generate the scene separately and composite an approved vector/raster wordmark or typeset text with known fonts, permissions and layout constraints. OCR/spelling checks and logo/template validation are gates, with human approval for high-risk output. A generative model merely prompted to spell correctly cannot guarantee exact text. Cache approved assets by input/spec/model/version and fail closed on failed brand validation. This turns brand-name correctness into a verifiable rendering contract rather than an unsupported model claim.

title: Model Delivery-Time Prediction for Online Orders
question:
An online retail platform wants to tell buyers when an order will arrive. Design the machine-learning model that predicts delivery time for each order. This is a modeling question, not a serving-architecture question.

What to cover

Answer each part with concrete details:

1.
Problem framing. Is this classification, regression or ranking? What is the prediction unit, and how would you quote a promised date to the buyer?
2.
Label. Define exactly what the target is and how it is obtained. Address orders still in transit and label noise.
3.
Data and features. Name the data sources and concrete features, grouped by entity, and call out leakage and freshness risks.
4.
Algorithm. Propose a baseline and a stronger alternative, with the trade-offs of each.
5.
Offline evaluation. Choose metrics tied to the business goal, define the train/validation/test split, and say how you would segment the error.
6.
Deployment and monitoring. Describe the online experiment, the success metric and guardrails, what you monitor after launch, and how you iterate.

State your assumptions explicitly where the problem is underspecified.

Constraints
Orders arrive at high volume and a prediction is needed at checkout and again after shipment.
Predictions feed a customer-facing promise, so late deliveries cost more than early ones.

steps: Regression with an asymmetric customer promise
solution.contract_notes: Use historical pickup/order times and geography to define a future demand or duration target, with only features available at prediction time. Compare seasonal/time-of-day baselines and use forward time splits plus spatial holdouts. For duration, predict quantiles or calibrated intervals when late-delivery costs are asymmetric. For demand/premium effects, distinguish forecasting demand from estimating the causal response to a price multiplier; historic price is confounded by the platform’s own demand policy.
solution.example: Example: checkout p50 is four days and calibrated p90 six days; a six-day promise may fit the assumed cost ratio. After a late departure scan, the remaining p90 can move to five more days; log the revision rather than rewriting the original promise. Failed feature updates use a conservative validated lane prior and an explicit freshness flag. This is chiefly a modeling design: capacity/architecture choices matter only insofar as they keep the two prediction-time contracts intact.
solution.trap: In-transit orders are censored; checkout and shipment-time features have different information contracts.
solution.teaching_notes_markdown:
### Regression with an asymmetric customer promise

Assume the prediction unit is a shipment, because one order may split across packages; quote an order date as the latest promised shipment date, explaining partial delivery. At checkout predict duration from order acceptance to customer delivery. After shipment predict remaining duration from the current timestamp, using newly available carrier events. The target is a duration distribution or selected quantiles, not ranking or a coarse on-time class alone.

Let y be realized delivery duration and a the quoted duration. If late cost is c_l(y-a)+ and early/overconservative cost is c_e(a-y)+, minimizing expected loss gives F_Y(a)=c_l/(c_l+c_e). With explicitly assumed costs c_l=9 and c_e=1, quote a calibrated p90 date. This trades lateness against unnecessarily pessimistic promises; it does not justify arbitrarily adding days. Customer-facing dates apply destination timezone/calendar/cutoffs and retain the underlying timestamp distribution.

### Labels, censoring and features

Use verified delivered timestamp minus the appropriate prediction timestamp, with event corrections and timestamp provenance. Still-in-transit shipments are right-censored: omit them only for a clearly mature-cohort baseline, or fit a survival/distribution model with censoring likelihood. A shipment delivered before horizon contributes density f(y); one still traveling at c contributes survival 1-F(c). Lost/canceled/returned-to-sender shipments need explicit competing outcomes, not fake delivery dates. Audit carrier scans, missing delivery confirmations and clock/timezone errors.

Order features: item size/weight, split shipment, order time/cutoff, fulfillment choice and inventory known at checkout. Warehouse/seller features: current backlog, handling-time distribution, processing calendar and reliability. Route/destination: origin/destination region, distance, customs, service level, holidays and weather forecast available then. Carrier features: lane transit history and operational incidents. Post-shipment features add actual dispatch, latest scan/location, time since scan and route progress. Actual dispatch or future traffic cannot appear in the checkout model; train separate contracts or explicitly masked stages.

### Baseline, stronger model and validation

A lane×carrier×service×weekday empirical median/p90 with pooled backoff is interpretable and strong. Quantile GBDTs capture nonlinear interactions and missingness at low cost; a survival/distributional model handles censoring and supports coherent updated intervals but adds complexity/calibration work. Train pinball loss for selected quantiles, enforce noncrossing quantiles and calibrate held-out coverage. Do not multiply independent stage quantiles and call the result an order quantile without checking dependence.

Use rolling-origin train/validation/test by order time with mature outcomes and no future aggregate leakage. Test holiday peaks, new lanes/warehouses and carriers separately. Measure MAE for typical accuracy, pinball loss for promise quantiles, late-delivery rate, mean days late, excess quoted days and interval coverage/width. Segment by lane, service, basket/seller, region and censoring age. MAPE is unstable for near-zero durations and is supplementary at best.

### Launch and iteration

Shadow the model, then randomize users/orders consistently for promise display with a prespecified primary outcome such as conversion with promised-date adherence. Guard cancellations, support contacts, late rate and overly pessimistic promises; carrier/warehouse capacity interference may require cluster/switchback analysis. Store prediction timestamp, feature/model version and quoted date for honest backtesting. Monitor input freshness/missing carrier scans, drift, p90 coverage after maturity and cost-weighted error; early proxy scan delays cannot replace delivered outcomes.

Example: checkout p50 is four days and calibrated p90 six days; a six-day promise may fit the assumed cost ratio. After a late departure scan, the remaining p90 can move to five more days; log the revision rather than rewriting the original promise. Failed feature updates use a conservative validated lane prior and an explicit freshness flag. This is chiefly a modeling design: capacity/architecture choices matter only insofar as they keep the two prediction-time contracts intact.
