title: Post-Comment Ranking System
question:
Design a ranking system for a post's discussion tree (and a subreddit post feed): when a user opens a post with a large thread, quickly surface the most relevant, highest-quality comments without loading and re-sorting the whole tree.

Requirements
Functional: rank top comments per post (personalized + stable global order), rank posts in a subreddit feed, paginate, refresh scores as votes/comments arrive.
Non-functional: P99 < 150ms; freshness within seconds; consistent read stream during pagination; graceful degradation.
Design anchors

Blended pluggable score (Wilson score interval / hot formula, recency decay, reputation, personalization, moderation); denormalized comment_score table keyed by (post_id, score DESC); event-driven recompute on vote/comment change + cached per-post top-K; cursor pagination over (score DESC, comment_id); rank within a parent (per-subtree top-K) rather than a global flat sort; Wilson interval resists brigading.

steps: Score within the tree, then store ordered results
solution.contract_notes: Comment ranking needs moderation, conversation/thread context, freshness and protection against engagement bait. Do not use later upvotes as a feature available when the comment was first ranked.
solution.example: P99<150 ms can use an illustrative 15 ms auth/cache, 30 ms ordered-index lookup, 35 ms batch body/features, 30 ms bounded personalization and 40 ms network/headroom. Personalization only re-ranks a stored bounded candidate pool; full arbitrary personalization over millions of comments conflicts with this target. A stable global fallback remains available. For assumed 20,000 reads/s, top-K caches reduce hot-post database load; 10,000 vote events/s requires keyed aggregation, not a full tree sort for each vote. Large threads distribute by parent/subtree while preserving post lookup metadata.
solution.trap: Wilson is not anti-brigading security and a mutable (score,id) cursor alone does not ensure stable paging.
solution.teaching_notes_markdown:
### Score within the tree, then store ordered results

Store Comment(id,post_id,parent_id,author,created_at,body_version,moderation_state), Vote(user,comment,value,version) and CommentScore(post,parent,comment,rank_epoch,global_score,features_version). A unique user/comment vote prevents duplicate votes; vote edits emit idempotent versioned events. Rank siblings within each parent and cache top children for popular parents. A global flat sort destroys reply context. A subreddit PostScore table uses the same approach keyed by subreddit rather than parent.

A pluggable global score combines a conservative quality estimate, recency, author reputation and moderation. For binary helpful/unhelpful votes, Wilson's lower bound is

$$W=\frac{\hat p+z^2/(2n)-z\sqrt{\hat p(1-\hat p)/n+z^2/(4n^2)}}{1+z^2/n},$$

with a stated z, e.g. assumed 1.96, and a prior rule for n=0. Blend W with time decay and bounded personalization; logged voting propensity matters if interpreting votes as quality. Wilson penalizes uncertainty at small n; it does **not** prevent coordinated brigading or sybil voters. Add rate limits, reputation, graph/anomaly signals and moderation independently. Raw score terms need explicit normalization/weights, tested against quality judgments and satisfaction.

### Events, indexes and stable pagination

The diagram's event stream recomputes affected comment/post scores in bounded batches and updates a denormalized ordered index (post_id,parent_id,rank_epoch,score DESC,comment_id). Update high-traffic parents in microbatches and cache their top-K lists. Event consumers track source versions so delayed votes cannot revert newer aggregates. A materialized score/read model can lag seconds while the canonical vote records remain authoritative.

`GET /posts/{id}/comments?parent=&cursor=` returns a ranked sibling page and continuation. A cursor with only (score,id) is insufficient when scores change between pages: rows can jump past the cursor. Pin the first page to rank_epoch/snapshot_id, user/model version and filters; paginate within that immutable order using (score DESC,id) and retain it for a short TTL. If the snapshot expires, explicitly restart. New-score refresh creates a new snapshot. Read-time moderation/access checks can remove items even from old snapshots; fetch extra candidates to fill gaps. Expand child subtrees separately to bound work.

### Latency, scale and race example

P99<150 ms can use an illustrative 15 ms auth/cache, 30 ms ordered-index lookup, 35 ms batch body/features, 30 ms bounded personalization and 40 ms network/headroom. Personalization only re-ranks a stored bounded candidate pool; full arbitrary personalization over millions of comments conflicts with this target. A stable global fallback remains available. For assumed 20,000 reads/s, top-K caches reduce hot-post database load; 10,000 vote events/s requires keyed aggregation, not a full tree sort for each vote. Large threads distribute by parent/subtree while preserving post lookup metadata.

Example: page one pins epoch 42. A comment gaining votes appears higher in epoch 43, but page two continues epoch 42 and therefore does not repeat/skip it due to score movement. A new deleted comment remains hidden through a tombstone even in epoch 42. Cache eviction falls back to the indexed snapshot; scorer failure serves the last valid global order and reports freshness. Monitor score lag, p99, duplicate/skip rates, parent coverage and moderation propagation. Test equal-score tie-breaks, vote deduplication, score movement between pages, snapshot expiry and a million-comment post. User A/B tests evaluate helpful replies found, meaningful participation and complaint/moderation rates, not votes alone.

title: Premium Product Recommendation System
question:
Design a recommendation or prediction system for Intuit products. One variant recommends premium-product content or offers; a newer staff+ variant predicts the top-selling items in a user-selected category and future time window, with explicit discussion of LLM/agent design, latency estimates, data flow, and caching.

Functional requirements
Recommend premium-product content, offers, or next-best actions to eligible users.
Personalize using customer and product-context signals.
Support feedback loops (impressions, clicks, conversions, dismissals, downstream outcomes).
Keep recommendations explainable for product and compliance review.
Allow experiments measured against conversion and customer-trust metrics.
Staff+ forecasting variant
User picks a product category and a future time window.
Predict the best-selling items in that category for the selected period.
Explain the data flow when items sell (sales events -> features/aggregates).
Provide per-component latency estimates and an end-to-end latency target.
Include a caching strategy for repeated category/window queries and expensive model outputs.
Decide whether a traditional ML/service architecture or an LLM/agent architecture is appropriate.
Notes

A strong answer starts with product objective and measurement, then decomposes the ML system: data sources, feature pipelines, candidate generation or forecasting, ranking, serving, experimentation, monitoring, and human/product guardrails. GenAI is one possible component inside a measurable recommendation product, not the whole system; if the estimated path exceeds interactive latency, move expensive computation offline and cache hot results.

steps: Two product variants need different targets
solution.contract_notes: A premium-product objective needs expected value and long-term satisfaction, not price alone; evaluate selection effects and whether the product was actually available to the user.
solution.example: An illustrative 200 ms interactive target is 10 ms auth/validation, 5 ms cache, 40 ms forecast-store/aggregation, 25 ms ranking/explanation lookup and 120 ms network/headroom. Cache keys include category, interval, metric, permissions, inventory/forecast generation; version keys avoid stale invalidation races. Popular windows precompute top lists, and late sales corrections trigger a new forecast generation rather than silently mutating an old as_of result. Assuming one million items×90 forecast days×4 bytes, means alone take 360 MB per generation, before keys/quantiles/replicas; size retention accordingly.
solution.trap: Forecasted sales and personalized premium-offer uplift are different targets; stockout sales censor demand.
solution.teaching_notes_markdown:
### Two product variants need different targets

For premium recommendations, assume the objective is incremental useful adoption/retention, with conversion as a near-term metric and complaints, cancellations, affordability and trust as guardrails. Eligibility, entitlements and compliance are hard filters. Features include consented customer needs, product usage, current plan, context and offer attributes; do not infer financial distress as a reason to pressure upgrades. Retrieve eligible offers/content and rank calibrated adoption/value predictions, then diversify/cap contact. Reasons come from supported product facts, e.g. “this feature addresses the workflow you selected,” and are logged for review. A randomized offer/no-offer test estimates incremental value; high propensity to buy is not the same as uplift.

For the staff forecasting variant, define best-selling as expected net units sold during [start,end) in a category, not clicks or gross dollars; if revenue is wanted, model price×units explicitly. Output ranked items, expected units, uncertainty and as_of/model versions. These outcomes are future forecasts, not personalized offer recommendations.

### Sales-to-forecast data flow

Deduplicate SalesEvent(event_id,item,category,quantity,price,event_time) and negative return/cancel adjustments, then maintain event-time hourly/daily aggregates with late-event corrections. Durable sales and item/version records feed a stream/warehouse; features include lagged sales, rolling averages, seasonality, price/promotion, stock, category trend and new-item content. Forecast demand separately from observed sales when stockouts censor demand, or clearly state the target is sales conditional on planned stock. Rolling-origin splits train/evaluate without seeing future promotions unless those plans are actually available at forecast time.

Start with seasonal naive/cohort baselines, then a global count/quantile GBDT or temporal forecasting model shared across items. Pool sparse/new items by content/category; report uncertainty and insufficient-history flags. Evaluate WAPE/MAE, count deviance, quantile coverage and ranking NDCG/top-K recall for future best sellers, segmented by horizon/category/new items. MAPE breaks at zero sales. Compare against mature outcomes after the requested window closes; no offline metric proves that showing forecasts improves business decisions.

### Serving, cache and architectural choice

`GET /forecasts?category=&start=&end=&metric=` reads precomputed item-day predictions and aggregates the requested interval; constrain supported horizon/window granularity. The diagram's forecast branch is sales → aggregates/features → batch model → versioned forecast store → category/window top-K cache. A separate offer branch uses user eligibility/features and ranker. Store Forecast(item,date,as_of,model_version,mean,quantiles) and publish complete generations atomically; incomplete jobs leave the old generation available with freshness displayed.

An illustrative 200 ms interactive target is 10 ms auth/validation, 5 ms cache, 40 ms forecast-store/aggregation, 25 ms ranking/explanation lookup and 120 ms network/headroom. Cache keys include category, interval, metric, permissions, inventory/forecast generation; version keys avoid stale invalidation races. Popular windows precompute top lists, and late sales corrections trigger a new forecast generation rather than silently mutating an old as_of result. Assuming one million items×90 forecast days×4 bytes, means alone take 360 MB per generation, before keys/quantiles/replicas; size retention accordingly.

A traditional numerical service is the primary forecaster. An LLM may parse “best sellers next month” into validated parameters or explain retrieved numbers, but cannot invent sales predictions or bypass access. If an agent calls multiple tools, bound fanout/time and cache by data/spec/model versions; expensive generated explanations run offline or asynchronously. On forecast failure serve the last complete result with its timestamp or a seasonal baseline, never call stale numbers current. Test duplicate sales, late returns, stockout periods, repeated cached queries and a category permission change. A/B-test forecast-assisted workflows or premium offers separately, with trust guardrails and audit logs.

title: Property Rental Search System
question:
Redesign a property-rental website for global customers on cloud infrastructure. The prompt names payment, view, guest, search, and update services, with emphasis on fast, secure search and property browsing.

Requirements
Functional requirements:
Display property details including photos, location, and rent details.
Let international guests search across properties quickly and securely.
Support online payments.
Maintain guest state such as favorites and recently checked records.
Support property updates from the owner / dealer workflow.
Scale / constraints:
Global users need low-latency reads.
Photos and property metadata have different storage and caching needs.
Search should remain responsive as listings grow.
Design decisions to discuss:
split of payment, view, guest, search, and update services
search index freshness vs write complexity
CDN / object storage for photos
authentication and secure payment handoff
observability for failed searches, payment failures, and stale listings
Notes
Interviewer interest can center on search. Prepare filtering by location, rent, availability, and favorites, plus indexing and cache invalidation after listing updates.
Treat payments as a separate service boundary with idempotent payment attempts and clear failure states.
Do not leave a generic box named "process" in the workflow; replace it with concrete read, search, guest-state, update, and payment flows.

solution.contract_notes: For rentals, index location, date and occupancy filters; prevent ranking unavailable inventory and distinguish prospective search features from eventual booking outcomes.
solution.example: Scale is unspecified. Assume 20 million listings, 10 photos/listing at 200 KB: 40 TB photo storage before replicas; CDN hit rate dominates origin bandwidth. At assumed 10,000 search QPS and 100 IDs/page, avoid one database round trip per ID; shard indexes by geography and bulk hydrate/cache details. An illustrative 250 ms read budget reserves 70 ms index, 40 ms hydration, 20 ms guest-state join and 120 ms network/headroom. Regional read replicas/caches serve global users while property/payment writes have a clear home authority. On search outage offer cached results with freshness and rechecks; payment uncertainty remains pending. Monitor no-result/error rates, p99 by region, index lag, stale listing complaints, payment success/latency and webhook reconciliation age. Test update/index reordering, favorite races, concurrent booking, duplicate payment request and delayed provider success after a client timeout.
solution.trap: Payment timeout is PENDING uncertainty, not permission to charge again; stale search never reserves inventory.
solution.teaching_notes_markdown:
### Concrete service boundaries

The view service returns property details; search handles discovery; guest service owns favorites/recent history; update service validates owner/dealer mutations; payment service owns payment attempts and provider interaction. They can begin as modules sharing a database, but ownership and transactional boundaries remain explicit. Store Property(id,owner,location,capacity,rent,currency,availability,version), Photo(property,digest,object_key,order), Favorite(guest,property), RecentView(guest,property,last_seen), PaymentAttempt(id,booking_or_invoice,key,amount,currency,state,provider_id), and audit records. Clarify whether availability is long-term listing status or date inventory; assume date-range rentals if dates are requested, and never imply search alone reserves them.

`GET /properties/{id}` returns metadata and CDN photo URLs; `POST /search` takes location, rent range/currency, availability, guests and filters; `PUT/DELETE /guests/me/favorites/{property}` is idempotent. `PATCH /properties/{id}` requires owner/dealer authorization and If-Match version. `POST /payments` takes an idempotency key and a server-priced invoice reference, returning pending/succeeded/failed/requires_action. Never accept a client-supplied price as authority.

### Fast search and updates

The diagram's view/photo read path uses regional caches and a CDN over object storage; the search path uses a geo/text/filter index, and the guest path joins user-specific state after public candidate retrieval. Index location/geo cells, rent normalized for filtering with a stated FX timestamp, availability and listing attributes. Exact radius and requested date-range checks follow coarse index retrieval. Favorites-only search first obtains permitted favorite IDs, then intersects indexed candidates; don't cache one guest's favorites in a shared public response.

Owner changes commit property version and outbox in one transaction. Index/caches consume changes idempotently and reject older versions; deleted/unpublished properties get tombstones. Search may lag seconds, but detail and booking/payment revalidate authoritative status, current price/currency and availability. A read-your-write owner view can query the database while the index catches up. Cache immutable photo URLs by content digest; a photo replacement updates only metadata pointers. Purge/restrict unsafe/private media as necessary rather than assuming a long CDN TTL is always acceptable.

### Secure payment and global reliability

Use authenticated sessions, server-side RBAC, input validation, rate limits and scoped signed upload URLs; validate uploaded files before publication. Photos are separate from transactional metadata. Payment uses a hosted/tokenized provider handoff, signed verified webhooks and a state machine: CREATED→PENDING→SUCCEEDED/FAILED, with refund states separate. Unique idempotency keys and provider event IDs prevent duplicate charges/webhook application. Timeout leaves PENDING for reconciliation, not “failed, charge again.” A booking hold, if required, is an authoritative transaction with expiry and no-overlap constraints; a saga compensates a failed charge/expired hold. Never store raw card data in property services.

Scale is unspecified. Assume 20 million listings, 10 photos/listing at 200 KB: 40 TB photo storage before replicas; CDN hit rate dominates origin bandwidth. At assumed 10,000 search QPS and 100 IDs/page, avoid one database round trip per ID; shard indexes by geography and bulk hydrate/cache details. An illustrative 250 ms read budget reserves 70 ms index, 40 ms hydration, 20 ms guest-state join and 120 ms network/headroom. Regional read replicas/caches serve global users while property/payment writes have a clear home authority. On search outage offer cached results with freshness and rechecks; payment uncertainty remains pending. Monitor no-result/error rates, p99 by region, index lag, stale listing complaints, payment success/latency and webhook reconciliation age. Test update/index reordering, favorite races, concurrent booking, duplicate payment request and delayed provider success after a client timeout.

title: Real-Time Fraud Detection System
question:
Real-Time Fraud Detection System

Design a real-time fraud evaluation system for millions of daily transactions, 10,000+ requests per second, 50 ms decision latency, and zero-downtime ML model updates. Black Friday-style bursts and transaction success rate are explicit follow-ups.

Requirements

Design a service that evaluates every transaction in real time and returns one of:

Approve.
Flag for review.
Block.

Constraints:

Millions of transactions per day.
10,000+ requests per second.
50 ms latency budget for the decision path.
ML model updates must happen without downtime.
Promotional spikes such as Black Friday must preserve both throughput and transaction success rate.

Functional components:

Synchronous scoring API.
Feature lookup / feature computation.
Model inference service.
Rules / threshold layer for hard blocks and overrides.
Async logging and audit trail.
Model registry and rollout system.
Notes

A strong design keeps the critical path short:

client -> API gateway -> fraud scorer -> feature cache -> model server -> decision
|-> async event log / monitoring

Key design decisions:

Precompute hot features and store them in a low-latency feature cache; avoid joining large history in the 50 ms path.
Use model versioning with canary / shadow rollout. Keep old and new model versions loaded so rollback is instant.
Separate hard business rules from model score so compliance and risk teams can override safely.
Degrade gracefully under spikes: feature fallback, lower-cost model, queue only non-critical enrichment, fail-open or fail-review depending on risk policy.
Monitor p50 / p95 / p99 latency, approval rate, block rate, false-positive review rate, model drift, and feature freshness.

The trade-off is accuracy vs latency. A deep model with online feature joins may improve recall but break the 50 ms SLA; a two-stage design can use a fast model synchronously and a heavier async model for review routing.

solution.example: At 50,000 RPS and assumed 2 KB audit record, log ingress is 100 MB/s before replication. Review capacity is also finite: 0.1% routing at sustained peak is 50 reviews/s, infeasible for many teams; cap or prioritize according to explicit policy. Monitor p50/p95/p99, timeout/fallback, feature age, review backlog, approval/block, genuine false declines and mature fraud loss by segment. Tests cover duplicate requests/counters, cache loss, model warmup failure, rollback, audit lag and a fivefold burst with accepted-payment guardrails. The latency and fraud quality claims require those measurements, not merely this architecture.
solution.trap: Fraud API uptime is not legitimate payment approval rate; universal fail-open/closed policies fail differently.
solution.teaching_notes_markdown:
### Short critical path and throughput

`POST /fraud/evaluate` accepts transaction_id, amount/currency and authenticated account/device/payment context, returning APPROVE, REVIEW or BLOCK plus decision_id and policy/model versions. The 10,000+ RPS target is peak throughput; 10,000 sustained for a day is 864 million requests, much larger than “millions daily,” so distinguish peak from mean. Assume a fivefold Black Friday peak, 50,000 RPS, for a concrete capacity plan. At an assumed 20 ms end-to-end average service time, about 1,000 requests are in flight at that peak before headroom; use measured latency/utilization to size replicas.

The diagram's synchronous path is gateway → fraud scorer → parallel feature cache → in-process or nearby model → rules/decision. A proposed 50 ms budget is 5 ms gateway/auth, 10 ms parallel features, 10 ms inference, 5 ms rules/durable decision and 20 ms network/queue headroom. Specify whether this is p99; assume it is the strict target and measure each stage under peak. No warehouse join, remote LLM or heavy enrichment belongs here. Synchronous durable decision recording may use a low-latency replicated store/outbox; bulk audit analytics remains async.

### Features, policy and immutable decisions

Stream deduplicated events into keyed windows for transaction/device/account velocity, spending deviation, merchant history and known-risk signals. Cache aggregates and timestamps; compute only simple request-local features online. Training reconstructs point-in-time values and uses mature chargeback/investigation labels with forward splits; declined transactions have selective missing outcomes. A calibrated GBDT/small neural model plus a documented rules layer separates hard requirements from risk scores. Thresholds balance fraud dollars, genuine-payment acceptance and limited review capacity.

Store Decision(transaction_id,request_hash,action,score,feature_versions,model_version,rule_version,time) under a unique key. A retry returns that result and conflicting payload is rejected. Scoring does not capture funds: payment processing has its own idempotency/state machine. Velocity counters must deduplicate transaction events so a retry is not an extra attempted purchase. Publish an outbox to audit/review with idempotent consumers; reviewers claim once and overrides are appended, not silent edits to the historical decision.

### Zero-downtime updates and burst behavior

Register signed model artifacts with feature schema and calibration version. Load old/new models simultaneously, warm them, shadow on mirrored inputs, then canary by stable account/transaction assignment and monitor latency plus mature quality. Atomically move the routing pointer and retain the old compatible feature/model package for rollback. Schema changes need backward compatibility or dual feature production; reverting weights alone is insufficient.

Reserve/scale capacity before promotions, batch hot-feature reads, isolate review/enrichment from synchronous scoring and use bounded queues with admission control. On feature timeout use validated stale/missing-feature paths and a cheaper model. For low-risk known customers a documented fallback may approve; high-risk cases may review/block. A universal fail-open increases fraud and a universal fail-closed destroys transaction success. Report fraud-service availability separately from legitimate payment approval, checkout conversion and downstream payment success, which depend on more services. Bound retries with jitter and transaction IDs to prevent a retry storm.

At 50,000 RPS and assumed 2 KB audit record, log ingress is 100 MB/s before replication. Review capacity is also finite: 0.1% routing at sustained peak is 50 reviews/s, infeasible for many teams; cap or prioritize according to explicit policy. Monitor p50/p95/p99, timeout/fallback, feature age, review backlog, approval/block, genuine false declines and mature fraud loss by segment. Tests cover duplicate requests/counters, cache loss, model warmup failure, rollback, audit lag and a fivefold burst with accepted-payment guardrails. The latency and fraud quality claims require those measurements, not merely this architecture.

title: Ride Request Demand Prediction by Geohash and Premium Multiplier
question:
A ride-hailing platform prices each small area of a city separately. To choose a price it needs a forecast: how many riders will request a ride in the next minute in each area, and how that number would change under each price level it can apply. Design the machine learning system that produces this forecast, and tie every modelling choice to its effect on the marketplace: the balance between riders and drivers, driver supply, and how sensitive riders are to price.

What to deliver
Training input: a history of per-cell, per-minute sessions and requests, plus the price multiplier that was in effect in each cell and minute.
Prediction input: the same two counts for each cell over the last 5 minutes.
Output: for each cell, five numbers: the expected number of ride requests in the next minute under each of the five multipliers.
Design: a written answer to the six questions below.
Rules of the setting
1.
The service area is divided into geohash cells, each about 1.2 km by 600 m.
2.
For every cell there is a stream of rider-app data. For the most recent 5 minutes you receive two counts:
sessions: the number of app-open sessions in the cell.
requests: the number of ride requests made from the cell.
3.
The platform can apply one of five price multipliers to a cell: 0%, 15%, 50%, 70% or 100% extra.
Examples
A cell saw 40, 42, 51, 47 and 55 sessions and 9, 11, 12, 10 and 14 requests in the five minutes up to 18:04. The system returns five expected request counts for 18:05, one for each multiplier from 0% to 100% extra.
A quiet cell on the edge of the city had no request in the last 5 minutes. It still gets five forecasts, and the design must say where they come from.
Questions the design must answer
1.
Training rows and labels: define the prediction target and the training examples: what a row is, what its label is, and how the feature window and the label window line up in time.
2.
Features and sparse cells: describe the features, including how cells with little history are handled.
3.
Model and loss: choose a model family and a loss, and justify them for count data.
4.
Data splits: explain how you split data for training, validation and test without leaking the future.
5.
Meaning of the per-multiplier forecasts: explain what the predictions mean when the multiplier was chosen by the platform and not at random, and how you would make the per-multiplier numbers trustworthy.
6.
Metrics, serving and monitoring: define offline and online metrics, the serving path, and monitoring.
Constraints
Feature window: the last 5 minutes. Forecast horizon: the next 1 minute.
A fresh forecast for every cell and every multiplier is needed each minute.

steps: Conditional forecasts are not automatically causal
solution.contract_notes: Use historical pickup/order times and geography to define a future demand or duration target, with only features available at prediction time. Compare seasonal/time-of-day baselines and use forward time splits plus spatial holdouts. For duration, predict quantiles or calibrated intervals when late-delivery costs are asymmetric. For demand/premium effects, distinguish forecasting demand from estimating the causal response to a price multiplier; historic price is confounded by the platform’s own demand policy.
solution.example: For cell c and cutoff minute t, a feature row contains sessions and requests from t-4 through t inclusive. The label is R(c,t+1), requests in the next minute, and the treatment/input is the multiplier actually used during t+1. Thus the example ending at 18:04 predicts 18:05. Training must include the next-minute multiplier; using only the past multiplier and asking it to mean a future intervention changes the problem. At inference evaluate the same history under a∈{1.00,1.15,1.50,1.70,2.00}, returning five nonnegative expected counts, not five probabilities summing to one.
solution.trap: Historical platform-selected prices confound per-multiplier response; two count histories alone do not identify counterfactual demand.
solution.teaching_notes_markdown:
### Rows, alignment and output

For cell c and cutoff minute t, a feature row contains sessions and requests from t-4 through t inclusive. The label is R(c,t+1), requests in the next minute, and the treatment/input is the multiplier actually used during t+1. Thus the example ending at 18:04 predicts 18:05. Training must include the next-minute multiplier; using only the past multiplier and asking it to mean a future intervention changes the problem. At inference evaluate the same history under a∈{1.00,1.15,1.50,1.70,2.00}, returning five nonnegative expected counts, not five probabilities summing to one.

Features derived from the allowed window include five lag counts for each stream, sums, slopes, volatility, request/session ratios with safe zero denominators and recent conversion. Cell ID/embedding and deterministic time/calendar can be used if supplied/derivable; extra driver, weather or neighborhood counts are proposed extensions, not silently present inputs. A quiet cell is not necessarily zero demand: a global model shares patterns across cells, with shrunk cell effects/backoff to geography/time cohorts; a never-seen cell uses those priors and a wide uncertainty interval.

### Count model and forward validation

Start with last-minute/rolling-mean forecasts plus a pooled multiplier-conditioned Poisson regression or GBDT with Poisson loss. Let λ=exp(f(history,cell,time,a)); loss λ-y log λ plus a y-only constant gives a nonnegative expected count. If variance materially exceeds mean, use a negative-binomial head with learned dispersion. Zero inflation needs evidence; five zeros alone do not prove a structural-zero process. An optional exposure/conversion decomposition predicts next-minute sessions and requests per session, but the given inputs do not identify this independently without assumptions.

Split by increasing cutoff time, fit transforms only on training, and use an embargo where overlapping windows/labels would otherwise cross the split. Hold out whole cells/cities as a cold-geography test separately. Compare Poisson deviance, MAE/WAPE, aggregate count bias, interval coverage and calibration by cell activity/time/multiplier; avoid MAPE at zero. Every-minute serving updates the five-minute window in a keyed stream, then vectorizes five treatments per cell. With assumed 100,000 cells, 500,000 scores/minute is about 8,333/s; freshness and late-event correction matter as much as average throughput.

### Conditional forecasts are not automatically causal

Historical pricing responds to anticipated demand and scarce supply. Therefore E[R|history,A=a] generally differs from E[R(a)|history]; expensive-price periods may show high requests because they occurred during demand surges. The given logs cannot identify all five counterfactuals without exchangeability, consistency, positivity and treatment-interference assumptions. In particular, omitted supply/policy inputs confound pricing, and nearby cells interact through rider movement and driver relocation. Do not invent trustworthy response curves from the two-count history alone.

Run safe geo/time switchback randomized price experiments with logged propensities, supply and market context, washout and spillover-aware clusters. With defensible observed confounders and overlap, propensity weighting/doubly robust treatment models can supplement experimentation; they do not fix hidden confounding. Report unsupported multipliers as uncertain and constrain optimization rather than extrapolating confidently. Price response may reasonably be monotone for comparable demand, but observed conditional counts need not be; imposed monotonicity is an assumption to test.

Serve {cell,forecast_minute,as_of,model_version,λ[5],uncertainty,support_flags}; idempotent minute updates and event-time watermarks reject duplicate counts and expose stale data. Offline curves do not decide price alone: marketplace optimization must also forecast driver supply, matching and wait times, respecting rider elasticity, earnings and regulatory/product limits. Monitor requested/completed rides, rider conversion, wait/cancel, driver utilization/earnings and forecast calibration after labels arrive. Test zero sessions, quiet/new cells, late streams and treatment levels with no experimental support. No numeric five-count forecast can be derived from the example history without fitted parameters/data; any such numbers would be an explicitly labeled demo, not the answer's prediction.

title: Short Video Recommendation & Ranking
question:
Design a short-video recommendation or ranking system for Spotlight / Lens-style products, covering retrieval, ranking, short-term interest, cold start, delayed labels, and multimodal features.

Functional requirements
1.
Generate a personalized feed of fresh short videos or lenses per user.
2.
Capture short-term interest from recent watches, skips, likes, shares, hides, and follows.
3.
Support retrieval and ranking when only a minority of videos have text descriptions.
4.
Handle cold start for new users and new items.
5.
Train and serve models with enough observability to debug ranking regressions.
Scale / constraints
Large catalog, high request rate, strict latency budget for feed vending.
Most useful labels are delayed or biased.
Content is multimodal: frames, audio, captions, creator, engagement, safety.
Design decisions
Candidate generation: two-tower embedding retrieval, ANN index, graph/creator co-engagement, trending pools.
Ranking: lightweight online ranker vs heavier batch features; multi-task objectives.
Freshness and exploration; bias handling (popularity, position, delayed labels, feedback loops).

solution.example: Store versioned models, embedding/index manifests, feature schemas and audit lineage. Canary model/index pairs and retain compatible rollback. Monitor per-stage p99, feature age, retrieval-source yield, modality missingness, exposure completeness, maturity-adjusted quality and subgroup regressions. Debug a ranking change by replaying a request with frozen candidates/features to separate retrieval loss, feature drift, model score changes and re-ranking policy. Test delayed shares, missing text, sequence reordering, removed cached items and new-creator exposure rather than relying on one aggregate offline metric.
solution.trap: Missing captions do not imply missing content; visual/audio features are essential.
solution.teaching_notes_markdown:
### Short-term intent and multimodal discovery

Optimize satisfying watch/creation experiences and repeat use, using capped watch duration, duration-adjusted completion, shares and hides as training signals. Lens experiences may target meaningful lens use/creation instead of passive video watch; select the product contract before combining labels. Guard safety, reports, fatigue and creator diversity. A rapid skip is a prompt short-term signal; a share or later return can arrive much later, so use event-time sequence features and mature outcome windows.

Each impression logs actual visibility/playback, user/video/version, position, candidate source and model version. Features include the user's most recent watch/skip/like/share/hide/follow sequence, longer-term interests and recent repeat exposure. Encode video frames, audio/music, ASR/OCR where available, creator and quality/safety metadata. Most items lacking text remain retrievable through visual/audio embeddings; treating absent captions as empty semantic content would discard valuable items. Precompute item encoders offline and update new uploads incrementally.

### Candidate pools and ranker

The diagram's retrieval union includes two-tower ANN, co-watch/creator graph, followed creators, fresh/trending and bounded exploration. Deduplicate and apply region/age/safety eligibility, pre-rank thousands to hundreds, then a multi-task ranker combines candidate embeddings with the latest user sequence and context. Predict watch-time distribution, completion conditional on duration, share/follow and hide probabilities; mask unavailable delayed labels rather than treating them as zero. Re-rank to avoid duplicate creators/topics, maintain freshness and protect safety. A fixed global popularity list is a fallback, not personalization.

Cold users get declared preferences, language/context and diverse safe content; the first few skips/watches rapidly update session state. Cold videos/lenses use multimodal content, creator priors and controlled exposure, not imaginary engagement. Calibrate engagement heads on held-out natural-prevalence data, especially if training negatives are subsampled. Popularity and position bias need logged exposure/propensity and randomized slots; unseen items are not observed negatives.

### Serving, feedback and evidence

Assume a 150 ms p99 feed budget: 20 ms recent-history/features, 30 ms parallel retrieval, 15 ms filtering/pre-rank, 45 ms final rank and 40 ms re-rank/network. Scale is unspecified; with 20,000 QPS×200 final candidates, four million pair scores/s motivates item-feature caches, batch scoring and regional indexes. Cache a short continuation but refresh user intent and removals; cursor state includes feed/model version and seen IDs. On sequence-store failure use long-term content affinity; on ranker failure use safe fresh/popular pools, with fallback logging.

Use forward-time tests and duplicate-content/creator cold-start holdouts. Evaluate recall, NDCG on qualified watches, calibration, label maturity and negative-event/safety slices. User A/B tests track meaningful engagement and retention with predefined guardrails/duration; creator/social spillovers and novelty require extra analysis. Observe short-term utility separately from long-term health, since optimizing immediate duration can create feedback loops.

Store versioned models, embedding/index manifests, feature schemas and audit lineage. Canary model/index pairs and retain compatible rollback. Monitor per-stage p99, feature age, retrieval-source yield, modality missingness, exposure completeness, maturity-adjusted quality and subgroup regressions. title: Snap Ads Ranking
question:
Design an ads ranking system with feature construction, multi-task objectives, delayed labels, calibration, and business constraints.

Functional requirements
1.
Rank candidate ads for a user request using relevance, predicted engagement, advertiser objective, and policy/quality constraints.
2.
Build features from user history, ad creative, advertiser, context, and recent behavior.
3.
Train models for multiple engagement levels such as click, conversion, hide, long view, or downstream value.
4.
Handle delayed and sparse labels, especially conversions.
5.
Provide online metrics, offline metrics, and debugging tools for regressions.
Scale / constraints
Ranking happens under a tight online latency budget.
Labels are biased by position, auction exposure, targeting, and delayed conversion windows.
Business objectives combine user experience, advertiser ROI, revenue, and marketplace health.
Design decisions
Retrieval / candidate generation vs final ranking.
Single-task CTR vs multi-task model for several engagement levels.
Weighted logistic regression or deep ranking model; calibration and auction compatibility; exploration, cold-start ads, and budget pacing.

solution.contract_notes: Ads ranking must distinguish raw engagement from advertiser/user value. Exposure, conversion delay, spend pacing and calibration are evaluated under the stated policy, not a random row split.
solution.example: Assume 50,000 requests/s and 200 ranked ads: ten million pair scores/s. An illustrative 100 ms budget allocates 20 ms retrieval, 20 ms batch features, 30 ms model, 10 ms auction/budget and 20 ms network/headroom. Precompute creative features, version model/index, warm canaries and keep rollback compatible. Offline evaluate log loss, PR/AUC for diagnostics, calibration, expected-value ranking and mature conversion/ROI by slice. User-randomized tests assess revenue, advertiser outcomes and user retention/hide/complaint rates; auction/budget interference may require campaign/geo cluster or marketplace experiments. Predefine duration/guardrails, monitor sample-ratio mismatch, position/popularity feedback and advertiser concentration. Debug regressions using fixed-request replay plus budget/targeting/pacing traces, not model scores alone.
solution.trap: AUC alone cannot ensure auction-compatible calibrated probabilities or budget consistency.
solution.teaching_notes_markdown:
### Candidates, predictions and auction-compatible value

Retrieve ads eligible for the user/request from targeting indexes, embedding relevance and advertiser objective pools. Filter policy, age/region, campaign state, budget and creative quality before ranking. The output score must match the auction's payment objective: for a CPC bid b, expected revenue per impression is b·p(click); eCPM is 1,000 times that. A CPA bid requires p(conversion per impression), not raw pCTR. User harm/quality constraints and advertiser ROI limit revenue optimization; do not simply add CTR, hide probability and dollars on incompatible scales.

Features include recent/long-term user interests, creative image/video/text embeddings, landing page/product, advertiser historical quality, bid/objective, context/placement/device and recent ad frequency. Use smoothed historical aggregates with age/sample counts and point-in-time joins. New ads/advertisers use content and cohort priors plus limited exploration, with policy/quality screening before exposure.

### Multi-task model and labels

A shared feature encoder with separate calibrated heads predicts click, long view, hide and conversion/value. Use binary cross-entropy on observed task labels, masks for immature conversion windows and suitable regression/distribution loss for value. A click→conversion factorization can model pCVR conditional on click, but evaluation/selection effects matter; view-through conversions need a separate attribution contract. Baseline weighted logistic regression is interpretable and cheap; a deep cross/multi-task ranker captures creative-user interactions at more inference/training cost. Test negative transfer between tasks rather than assuming sharing helps.

Impression records include auction candidate/exposure/position, bid, model/feature versions, propensity and creative version. Join click and attributed conversion events after maturity; a day-old nonconversion may be censored under a seven-day window. Delayed-feedback/survival correction or mature-window training can handle this, while monitoring changing label delay. Correct negative subsampling/prior shift before probability calibration. Calibrate held-out predictions by objective/placement using Platt/isotonic or temperature methods with adequate support; bid×miscalibrated pCTR misallocates auctions even if AUC is high.

### Serving and marketplace state

The diagram is eligible retrieval → feature/model scoring → quality/auction/pacing → impression logging. Budget reservation and pacing are authoritative conditional updates, with unique auction/impression IDs; two serving replicas cannot overspend a campaign by independently trusting a cached budget. Exposure/click/billing events deduplicate separately. Idempotent retry returns the original auction result where possible, and unknown billing outcomes reconcile rather than charging twice. Keep budget/policy failures distinct from model failures; a validated simple scorer can replace an unavailable deep model while preserving eligibility and caps.

Assume 50,000 requests/s and 200 ranked ads: ten million pair scores/s. An illustrative 100 ms budget allocates 20 ms retrieval, 20 ms batch features, 30 ms model, 10 ms auction/budget and 20 ms network/headroom. Precompute creative features, version model/index, warm canaries and keep rollback compatible. Offline evaluate log loss, PR/AUC for diagnostics, calibration, expected-value ranking and mature conversion/ROI by slice. User-randomized tests assess revenue, advertiser outcomes and user retention/hide/complaint rates; auction/budget interference may require campaign/geo cluster or marketplace experiments. Predefine duration/guardrails, monitor sample-ratio mismatch, position/popularity feedback and advertiser concentration. Debug regressions using fixed-request replay plus budget/targeting/pacing traces, not model scores alone.

title: Spam Email Detection: Signals, Model, and Metrics
question:
Open-ended ML design plus light coding. Given a large corpus of past emails, design a system that identifies spam.

You are expected to:

1.
Ask clarifying questions to scope the problem.
2.
Propose spam signals/features and a classification approach.
3.
Define accuracy metrics — precision, recall, F1, false-positive rate — and reason explicitly about the trade-off between catching more spam vs. blocking real mail.
4.
Sketch class-level code for the system.

There is no single correct answer; the interviewer is evaluating how you decompose an ambiguous problem and handle trade-offs.

solution.contract_notes: Use sender/content/reputation signals available at receipt time, protect against adversarial manipulation, and prevent near-duplicate campaign leakage across splits. Evaluate precision at actionable recall and provide quarantine/recovery for false positives. Continuously monitor changed campaigns; a randomized static split can overstate future performance.
solution.example: Define undefined denominators explicitly in reporting. For an illustrative corpus of 10,000 emails with 1,000 spam, suppose TP=900, FP=90, FN=100, TN=8,910. Precision is 90.91%, recall 90%, F1≈90.45% and FPR=1%. Accuracy is 98.1%, but 90 real messages are still hidden. Lowering the threshold can catch more spam while increasing this harm; choose the operating point from review/recovery costs and precision/FPR targets, not accuracy alone. Calibrate scores on held-out natural-prevalence data after resampling.
solution.trap: High accuracy can still hide legitimate mail; headers alone cannot deduplicate trusted receipt events.
solution.teaching_notes_markdown:
### Clarify the spam decision

Ask whether the product tags, quarantines or rejects mail; whether phishing is a separate class; which languages/latency/volume matter; what labels exist; and how costly a missed real message is. Assume receipt-time spam quarantine, with user recovery, a 100 ms service budget and no permanent deletion. High precision is essential because false positives hide legitimate mail. A two-threshold design delivers low risk, quarantines high risk and flags intermediate risk without blocking delivery if policy allows.

Use sender/domain reputation, authentication results, sending-rate patterns, URL/domain reputation, subject/body text, HTML/link mismatch, attachment metadata and recipient-specific history available at receipt. Avoid executing attachments or fetching arbitrary links in the scoring request. Start with TF-IDF plus logistic regression/naive Bayes; a lightweight text encoder plus reputation features is a stronger option after a matched-latency comparison. Split by time and duplicate campaign/sender groups, not random nearly identical messages. Labels combine carefully audited user reports, recovered false positives and expert gold data, with provenance and safeguards against malicious reporting.

### Metrics and threshold example

With TP spam caught, FP legitimate quarantined, FN spam missed and TN legitimate delivered:

$$Precision=TP/(TP+FP),\quad Recall=TP/(TP+FN),$$
$$F1=2TP/(2TP+FP+FN),\quad FPR=FP/(FP+TN).$$

Define undefined denominators explicitly in reporting. For an illustrative corpus of 10,000 emails with 1,000 spam, suppose TP=900, FP=90, FN=100, TN=8,910. Precision is 90.91%, recall 90%, F1≈90.45% and FPR=1%. Accuracy is 98.1%, but 90 real messages are still hidden. Lowering the threshold can catch more spam while increasing this harm; choose the operating point from review/recovery costs and precision/FPR targets, not accuracy alone. Calibrate scores on held-out natural-prevalence data after resampling.

### Class-level implementation sketch

The following is executable without a model library. Its injected model must return a calibrated probability; the small demo model in the tests is a fixture, not a trained spam detector.

```python
from dataclasses import dataclass
from typing import Callable


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Email:
    message_id: str
    subject: str
    body: str
    sender_reputation: float
    authentication_failed: bool


class SpamDetector:
    def __init__(self, model: Callable[[dict], float], threshold=0.99):
        if not 0 <= threshold <= 1:
            raise ValueError("threshold must lie in [0,1]")
        self.model, self.threshold = model, threshold

    def features(self, email):
        return {
            "text": email.subject + "\n" + email.body,
            "sender_reputation": email.sender_reputation,
            "authentication_failed": email.authentication_failed,
        }

    def classify(self, email):
        p = float(self.model(self.features(email)))
        if not 0 <= p <= 1:
            raise ValueError("model must return a finite probability")
        return {
            "message_id": email.message_id,
            "spam_probability": p,
            "action": "QUARANTINE" if p >= self.threshold else "DELIVER",
        }
```

A production receipt service deduplicates by mailbox/message receipt ID, records model/feature/threshold versions and uses an outbox to apply the delivery action idempotently. Message-ID headers alone are attacker-controlled and not a sufficient receipt key. The diagram's classifier feeds a quarantine/recovery boundary; user corrections are reviewed label events, not immediate unrestricted model updates. Scale is missing: assuming 5,000 messages/s×20 ms average model time implies 100 concurrent inferences before headroom. Store encrypted raw mail with strict retention/access, cache reputations and use a validated fallback during model outages. Monitor precision/recall on mature audited samples, campaign/language drift, complaint/recovery rate and latency. Tests cover threshold equality, invalid probabilities and the metric example; real predictive accuracy requires the absent corpus and labels.

The dashed return is the feedback or reconciliation path described in the solution; durable state and authorization remain authoritative when work is retried.

title: Support Ticket Routing & Claiming System
question:
Design an internal support system where tickets can be submitted via email, a public API, and a web contact form; each agent sees and claims tickets matching routing rules (e.g. language, location); and managers can view metrics such as average first-response time and average close time over a chosen window. The graded decisions are normalizing multi-channel ingestion into one ticket model, a rules-based routing/claim path that avoids double-claim races, and a metrics pipeline that aggregates over rolling time windows without scanning full history.

Requirements
Functional
Accept ticket submission from three channels — email, public API, web contact form — and normalize into a single canonical ticket model.
Route tickets to agents by configurable rules (language, location, similar attributes); an agent views and claims eligible tickets.
A claimed ticket is owned by exactly one agent — no double-claim.
Managers query metrics over a time window: average first-response time and average close (resolution) time.
Non-functional / decisions to surface
Concurrency-safe claiming when multiple agents race for the same ticket.
A rules engine reconfigurable without redeploying.
Metric aggregation over arbitrary time ranges that does not scan full ticket history per query.

solution.contract_notes: For claiming tickets, atomically transition an unclaimed ticket to one agent with a lease/version, and record transfer/release events. The classification model may suggest a queue, but queue ownership and concurrent claims are enforced by the database state machine. Keep an audit trail and distinguish first-response time from final resolution quality.
solution.example: Example: one minute has two responses totaling 20 minutes and another has eight totaling 40. The combined mean is 60/10=6 minutes, not (10+5)/2=7.5. Late email events correct their event-time buckets; expose data_as_of so managers know freshness. Scale is unspecified: one million tickets/day is 11.6/s average; a tenfold burst is 116/s before replies. Index state/queue/time, partition event/bucket history and keep the claim database strongly consistent. An analytics outage delays metrics but never blocks intake/claims; an ownership-database outage blocks new claims safely. Test simultaneous claims, stale rules, duplicate intake, duplicate metric events, reopen correction, exact time boundaries and unequal bucket sizes. Monitor ingest lag, claim conflicts, unrouteable tickets, oldest unowned age and metric freshness.
solution.trap: Average bucket means is wrong; cohort definitions, contribution corrections and atomic claim eligibility are essential.
solution.teaching_notes_markdown:
### Canonical intake and configurable routing

Email adapters authenticate inbound webhooks, API clients authenticate requests and the web form uses abuse controls. All normalize to Ticket(id,external_source,external_id,requester,subject,body,language,location,created_at,state,owner,version,routing_version,first_response_at,closed_at). Unique (source,external_id) or a client idempotency key deduplicates intake; an email retry must not open another ticket. Thread replies use verified conversation tokens/provider thread mapping, not subject alone. Attachments go to scanned object storage with references in ticket metadata.

`POST /tickets`, `GET /tickets?eligible_for=me&cursor=...`, `POST /tickets/{id}:claim`, `/respond`, `/close`, and `GET /metrics?from=&to=&team=` form the API. Store versioned routing rules in a configuration database with validated predicates, precedence, destinations and effective time. An admin UI publishes a tested rule version without deployment; record which version made each assignment. Default/unmatched tickets go to triage. Listing eligible work can use a read model indexed by language/location/queue, but the claim operation must revalidate current rules, ticket state and agent skills/availability.

### Exactly one current owner

The diagram's routing queue proposes eligible tickets; only an atomic database claim establishes ownership. In one transaction lock the ticket, load authoritative eligibility and run the equivalent of:

```sql
UPDATE ticket SET owner = :agent, state = 'CLAIMED', version = version + 1
WHERE id = :ticket AND owner IS NULL AND state = 'OPEN' AND version = :seen_version
RETURNING id;
```

Return 409 if no row changes; the actual implementation includes authorization/rule checks in the same consistency boundary. A repeated claim by the same agent with the same request key returns the original result. Transfers/releases append events and use owner/version checks. A permanent owner assignment does not need an automatically expiring lease; if leases are chosen, expiry/renewal and takeover must fence the former owner's replies. Store response outbox and ticket timestamps transactionally so two channels cannot count/send the first response twice. Human replies, bot acknowledgments and internal notes are distinguished; assume first_response_at means the first public human response.

### Rolling metrics without history scans

Define both duration and cohort membership. Assume first-response metrics include tickets whose first response occurred in [from,to), and resolution metrics include final closes in that interval; creation-cohort metrics are a separate report because recent open tickets are censored. Duration is response/close timestamp minus created_at, measured in wall-clock seconds unless business-hours calendars are explicitly requested. Specify reopen policy; assume close metrics use final resolution after a defined reopen window and apply corrections if reopening invalidates it.

Emit idempotent metric-contribution records keyed by ticket,metric,event_version with event time, team, count=1 and duration_sum. Stream workers update minute buckets (team,metric,minute,sum_duration,count), maintaining a contribution ledger so duplicate/reordered events cannot double count and later corrections subtract the old contribution before adding the new one. Averages are total sum/total count, never an average of bucket averages. Query arbitrary ranges using preaggregated full buckets plus indexed raw contributions for the two partial boundary minutes; combine hourly/daily rollups for long windows. This scans at most bounded edge data plus rollups, not full ticket history. Report no completed observations separately from a zero duration.

Example: one minute has two responses totaling 20 minutes and another has eight totaling 40. The combined mean is 60/10=6 minutes, not (10+5)/2=7.5. Late email events correct their event-time buckets; expose data_as_of so managers know freshness. Scale is unspecified: one million tickets/day is 11.6/s average; a tenfold burst is 116/s before replies. Index state/queue/time, partition event/bucket history and keep the claim database strongly consistent. An analytics outage delays metrics but never blocks intake/claims; an ownership-database outage blocks new claims safely. Test simultaneous claims, stale rules, duplicate intake, duplicate metric events, reopen correction, exact time boundaries and unequal bucket sizes. Monitor ingest lag, claim conflicts, unrouteable tickets, oldest unowned age and metric freshness.

![W195 specific flow: Email / API / web intake → Canonical deduplicated ticket → Versioned eligibility rules → Atomic claim + reply state → Event ledger / time buckets → Manager window metrics.](../diagrams/W195_exact_review_151_200.svg)

Read the numbered path as Email / API / web intake → Canonical deduplicated ticket → Versioned eligibility rules → Atomic claim + reply state → Event ledger / time buckets → Manager window metrics. title: Analyzing Recent Machine Learning Paper Contributions and Applications
question: Share a machine learning paper you've read recently and discuss its main contributions and applications.

steps: A concrete paper discussion without invented reading history
solution.example: The user's recently read paper is not supplied. The following is an illustrative answer using an older paper as a study choice; it does not claim the user read it recently or conducted its experiments. Replace it with a paper you can actually defend, and date your reading honestly.
solution.trap: Do not imply reading history, benchmark gains or deployment experience absent from the user.
solution.teaching_notes_markdown:
### A concrete paper discussion without invented reading history

The user's recently read paper is not supplied. The following is an illustrative answer using an older paper as a study choice; it does not claim the user read it recently or conducted its experiments. Replace it with a paper you can actually defend, and date your reading honestly.

“The paper I would discuss is *LoRA: Low-Rank Adaptation of Large Language Models*. Its central contribution is to freeze a pretrained model and train a low-rank update rather than all weights. This is useful when one base model must support multiple task-specific adaptations under limited training/storage budgets.” The basic mechanism is documented in the [original paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2106.09685).

“For a frozen W₀∈R^(d_out×d_in), parameterize ΔW=(α/r)BA with B∈R^(d_out×r) and A∈R^(r×d_in). Train A and B on the downstream objective while freezing W₀. This uses r(d_in+d_out) trainable parameters instead of d_in·d_out. My own arithmetic example, not a reported benchmark, is a 4,096×4,096 layer with r=8: 65,536 trainable update parameters versus 16,777,216 full parameters, a 256-fold reduction for that layer.”

“An application would be adapting a support-answering model to a permitted domain corpus while keeping one base checkpoint. I would compare full fine-tuning, a frozen-model baseline and several LoRA ranks at equal data/selection budget. I would measure held-out answer quality, forgetting, training memory, update storage and serving latency. I would not infer whole-system memory savings directly from trainable parameter counts: frozen weights and activations still occupy memory.”

### Evidence and a defensible limitation

Explain which tasks/layers/ranks the paper evaluates before repeating benchmark claims; no benchmark numbers are asserted here. A discriminating experiment freezes data, prompt, optimizer budget and evaluation, then varies rank and adapted layers. This tests whether the low-rank constraint preserves useful adaptation and where it fails. A result could also reflect extra hyperparameter tuning, so match that budget and report seed variation.

The named cost is restricted update capacity and another rank/layer-selection choice; large domain shifts may need a larger rank or full adaptation. Multiple adapters also add versioning and base-checkpoint compatibility requirements. For deployment, approve data rights, retain base/adapter/tokenizer/prompt versions, canary against the existing system and keep rollback. A benchmark improvement does not establish better production reliability or lower end-to-end latency.

If asked “what would you do next?”, propose a controlled rank-versus-quality/storage curve on the actual application plus failure-slice analysis, rather than claiming your own successful deployment. This answer covers contribution, mechanism, application, evidence, limitation and next experiment while making its missing personal input explicit.

title: Applied Research Panel: Project Deep-Dive
question:
Applied Research opener. Present a project or paper of your choosing to a panel of three senior researchers. Roughly 5-10 minutes presenting, then 40-50 minutes of Q&A where each researcher follows up on a different axis. The depth probe is the entire round — high-level slide-walks fail. Coverage expectations:

Problem framing — why does this problem matter? What is the gap in prior work?
Method — derive the key equations or training objective on the spot.
Experiments — what were the ablations? What did not work? What is the minimal set of experiments that supports the claim?
Limitations — where does the method break? What failure mode did you observe?
Extensions — what would you do next with three more months?

steps: Derive the method at the board
Minimum experiments that could support the claim
solution.example: For the methods researcher, derive loss/gradients, dimensions, missing-modality behavior, threshold costs and why fusion should help. For the experimentalist, defend split leakage prevention, paired comparisons, prevalence, confidence intervals and matched-budget ablations. For the systems/product researcher, explain feature availability, bounded upload latency, review queue sizing, appeals, stale policy/model versions and rollback. Keep a concrete request/failure trace and error examples ready, rather than extra overview slides.
solution.trap: A fictional proposal does not support a completed result; defend ablations and missing evidence.
solution.teaching_notes_markdown:
### Prepare one deep technical story

No personal project/results are supplied. This is a **fictional research proposal and rehearsal**, not a claim about the user's experience: “Does multimodal intent fusion reduce false removal of legitimate historical/news weapon imagery while retaining prohibited-sale recall?” Use the problem to demonstrate depth rather than present invented metrics as completed research.

For a 7-minute opener, spend one minute on the policy/action and costly false positives, two on data and method, two on discriminating experiments, one on failure modes and one on the next study. State your own role only when adapting this to a real project. The gap/hypothesis is explicit: object recognition alone cannot distinguish depicted objects from prohibited commerce intent; textual/contextual fusion may help, but can fail with obfuscation or missing captions.

### Derive the method at the board

Let v be an image embedding, t a caption/OCR embedding and m modality masks. Define h=MLP([v;t;m]) and p=σ(wᵀh+b). For adjudicated binary policy label y, train

$$L=-\sum_i w_i\{y_i\log p_i+(1-y_i)\log(1-p_i)\},$$

with weights correcting documented sampling, not hiding label ambiguity. For multiple policies use independent sigmoid heads and a mask for unannotated policies. The logistic derivative at a head is ∂L/∂z=w(p-y); calibration and removal thresholds are separate held-out steps. At assumed calibrated probability p, false-removal cost C_FP and missed-violation cost C_FN yield the ideal binary action threshold C_FP/(C_FP+C_FN), while review adds a third action/capacity constraint. Explain all assumptions and why weighted training may require recalibration at production prevalence.

### Minimum experiments that could support the claim

Create train/validation/test splits by time and duplicate/campaign groups, plus expert-adjudicated contextual lookalikes and random production samples. Compare image-only, text-only and fused models with matched encoder/data/compute budgets; add shuffled-caption and removed-OCR ablations. Report action precision at fixed severe-violation recall, false removals per million, calibration, subgroup slices and latency with uncertainty clustered by campaign. A win on a handpicked difficult set alone does not establish production prevalence or aggregate impact.

Fictional outcomes should be phrased conditionally: “If fusion improves overall recall but fails on captionless news imagery, I would inspect whether text availability is a selection confound and test a stronger image-only branch.” Do not invent an observed 20% gain. Track failed runs, labeling disagreements, hyperparameter budget and whether gains survive a stronger baseline.

### Prepare the panel's three axes

For the methods researcher, derive loss/gradients, dimensions, missing-modality behavior, threshold costs and why fusion should help. For the experimentalist, defend split leakage prevention, paired comparisons, prevalence, confidence intervals and matched-budget ablations. For the systems/product researcher, explain feature availability, bounded upload latency, review queue sizing, appeals, stale policy/model versions and rollback. Keep a concrete request/failure trace and error examples ready, rather than extra overview slides.

Limitations include policy ambiguity, reviewer disagreement, multilingual OCR, adversarial text, distribution shift and correlated examples. In three more months: first audit labels and establish reproducible baselines; next collect targeted/random failure data and run the minimal ablations; finally calibrate, shadow and conduct a guarded online study. Freeze manifests/code/model/policy versions and predeclare success/guardrails. The defensible claim is the one these experiments support; a proposal is not a finished result and should be presented as such.

title: Applied Scientist: Solving an Ambiguous Business Problem
question:
Applied Scientist round built around an under-defined business problem. The interviewer states a vague, stripped-down prompt and waits; you must clarify goals, propose a plan, and reason through tradeoffs aloud.

From the official module: "A critical skill for this role is dealing with ambiguous and ill-defined problems... This module tests your ability to productively discuss a problem and walk through what you would do and why. The stated problem will be slightly understated / vague / undefined in the beginning."

Topic areas seen: search/ranking/experimentation, brand-safety scoring, generation-quality assessment.

steps: Turn an ambiguous request into a decision
solution.example: End with the next decision: “I would first validate whether retrieval is the bottleneck on a representative audit; if it is, I would run this bounded hybrid test. If it is not, I would revisit the funnel evidence.” This is a productive conditional answer with hypotheses, evidence, costs and alternatives. Replace assumptions as the interviewer supplies information; do not present the fictional diagnosis as known business data.
solution.trap: Do not select a model before diagnosing whether retrieval, inventory, instrumentation or checkout caused the business change.
solution.teaching_notes_markdown:
### Turn an ambiguous request into a decision

The actual business case is absent, so there is no unique numerical/model answer. Here is a **fictional worked dialogue** for “Improve search.” First ask who searches, what success means, which failure motivates the request, what can change and what latency/data/experiment constraints exist. Offer measurable alternatives: more satisfied purchases, less time to find a relevant result, or fewer zero-result queries. State a provisional assumption: a retail site wants more completed satisfactory orders per search with no worse returns, safety or p99 latency.

If the interviewer says “conversion is down,” do not assume the ranker is at fault. Check logging and sample mix, outages, inventory, price changes, query cohorts and label maturity. Decompose the funnel into search→eligible result→click→cart→paid→retained order. A checkout failure needs a different fix from poor retrieval. Propose a small diagnostic audit: replay representative failing queries, inspect candidate recall and human relevance, and compare recent periods by region/device/new users.

### A concrete conditional plan

Assume the audit finds exact-brand queries losing relevant in-stock products during retrieval. The baseline is lexical search plus current hard availability filters. Add a hybrid lexical/semantic candidate union, then a lightweight learning-to-rank model using query match, content similarity, price, user intent and quality. Do not add a large generator merely because the prompt is vague. Log candidate sets, displayed impressions, positions, assignment, feature/model versions and delayed order/return outcomes. Reconstruct training features as of request time and use forward-time/duplicate-product splits.

Offline require improved recall on brand queries and NDCG on judged relevance without safety/filter violations. Estimate serving cost: an assumed 10,000 QPS×200 ranked products is two million pair scores/s; if the available 100 ms budget has only 20 ms spare, precompute embeddings and bound candidate count or defer a heavier model. A small representative query set can falsify the approach cheaply before a full training project.

Online randomize persistently by user, define conversion/retained orders as primary and return rate, latency, zero results and marketplace concentration as guardrails. Predeclare power/duration and avoid repeatedly stopping at favorable significance. Exposure logging and limited exploration address position/popularity bias; observational increases after rollout cannot alone prove causation. Inventory spillovers may require geo/time switchbacks. Shadow/canary, keep the old retrieval/ranker available and define rollback conditions.

### Reason aloud about changing constraints

If labels are absent, use blinded human judgments and instrument feedback before claiming supervised uplift. If the deadline is one week, fix the demonstrated retrieval/filter defect and run a small safe test rather than propose a six-month platform. If brand safety dominates, define policy labels/action thresholds and review costs; if generation quality is the case, define a task-specific human rubric, factual/brand checks and a holdout, rather than reuse search NDCG blindly.

End with the next decision: “I would first validate whether retrieval is the bottleneck on a representative audit; if it is, I would run this bounded hybrid test. If it is not, I would revisit the funnel evidence.” This is a productive conditional answer with hypotheses, evidence, costs and alternatives. Replace assumptions as the interviewer supplies information; do not present the fictional diagnosis as known business data.
