title: Distributed Device Control
question:
Distributed Device Control

Design a distributed control system for a power-grid operator that manages tens of millions of internet-connected devices such as HVAC systems, EV chargers, and batteries.

The operator can issue commands such as:

“Reduce power consumption of eligible HVAC devices in the Northeast by 20% for the next 30 minutes.”

Devices have unreliable connectivity. A device may not receive the command, may reject it, may accept but fail to execute it, or may execute successfully but report telemetry late. Telemetry may also be duplicated, missing, or arrive out of order.

The system should support:

Targeting millions of devices by attributes such as region and device type
Reliable command distribution
Tracking delivery, acceptance, execution, and actual physical impact
High-volume telemetry ingestion and aggregation
Late/out-of-order telemetry and historical reconciliation
Determining whether the requested aggregate reduction has been achieved
Issuing additional commands when the system is under-delivering
Scalability, fault tolerance, and auditability

Assume:

~50M registered devices
Up to ~5M devices targeted by one command
Millions of telemetry events per second

Design the system end to end. Discuss APIs/data models, targeting, fan-out, delivery semantics, telemetry processing, reconciliation, closed-loop control, failure handling, and consistency trade-offs.

steps: Model intent separately from physical effect
solution.example: Five million targets at assumed 200 bytes/dispatch mean 1 GB logical fanout; over one minute that is about 83,333 commands/s. At an illustrative two million telemetry events/s×100 bytes, ingress is 200 MB/s or 17.28 TB/day before replication/indexes. Shard gateways/queues/aggregators by region/device and merge sums/counts hierarchically; hot regional summaries must not serialize each raw event. Long-term retention uses rollups with documented late corrections.
solution.trap: Delivered/accepted/executed/measured physical impact are distinct; delayed telemetry requires bounded control feedback and safe expiry.
solution.teaching_notes_markdown:
### Model intent separately from physical effect

`POST /commands` accepts an idempotency key, selector, requested aggregate reduction, start/end, safety constraints and control policy version; `GET /commands/{id}` returns delivery, acceptance, execution and measured-impact summaries separately. Store Device(id,region,type,capabilities,opt_in,connectivity,version), Command(id,target_snapshot,action,valid_from,expires_at,generation,state), DeviceCommand(command,device,state,ack_times,reason), and Telemetry(device,boot_id,seq,event_time,ingest_time,power,quality). Snapshot up to five million eligible device IDs/versions for audit; recheck safety/opt-out at actual dispatch/execution.

“Reduce consumption by 20%” needs a denominator and actuator semantics. Assume a 20% reduction from an estimated eligible-fleet baseline power for 30 minutes, translated into safe device-specific setpoints/duty schedules. Device capability, comfort, minimum charge and local override constrain allocation. A signed command includes command_id/generation, expiry and a bounded desired state, not “subtract another 20%” on every retry.

### Distribution and telemetry pipeline

The diagram is targeting registry → durable partitioned fanout → regional device gateways → signed device commands, with telemetry returning through a durable stream to state/impact aggregators and a closed-loop controller. Persistent outbound device connections tolerate NAT/offline behavior; per-device mailbox/desired-state state persists while disconnected. Device ACK means received, acceptance means locally feasible, execution reports actuator state, and telemetry measures watts. Retry unacknowledged valid commands with backoff; expired commands are never freshly executed. Device deduplication persists recent command IDs/generations across reconnect/reboot, and higher generations supersede old control intent.

Partition telemetry by device, deduplicate (device,boot_id,seq), retain event/ingest times and reject older state from replacing a newer live reading. Event-time windows with watermarks produce provisional aggregates; late data corrects historical windows through idempotent retractions/upserts. Keep raw immutable telemetry for reconciliation. Missing/stale devices are UNKNOWN, not zero consumption or confirmed success.

### Closed-loop control and scale

Estimate reduction as counterfactual baseline minus observed consumption, with baseline uncertainty and coverage reported. A pre-event matched weather/time model or randomized holdout can estimate baseline; naive pre/post comparison confounds weather and natural load. The controller compares confidence-bounded achieved kW to the target, accounts for command/telemetry delays and issues **new** bounded compensating command generations to spare eligible devices. Use hysteresis, rate limits, cooldowns and saturation/anti-windup; repeatedly commanding based on delayed telemetry can overcorrect. Local safety controllers always override remote optimization. At expiry restore safe prior/default policy with a watchdog even if the cloud is unreachable.

Five million targets at assumed 200 bytes/dispatch mean 1 GB logical fanout; over one minute that is about 83,333 commands/s. At an illustrative two million telemetry events/s×100 bytes, ingress is 200 MB/s or 17.28 TB/day before replication/indexes. Shard gateways/queues/aggregators by region/device and merge sums/counts hierarchically; hot regional summaries must not serialize each raw event. Long-term retention uses rollups with documented late corrections.

A gateway/region outage leaves device-local expiry/safety active; durable desired state replays after reconnect only if still valid. Controller leadership uses epochs and transactional generation changes; duplicate dispatch never implies another physical reduction. Restrict operator roles, sign commands, rotate device keys and audit selection, overrides and impact revisions. Test five-million fanout, disconnected targets, duplicate/out-of-order telemetry, accept-but-fail, late execution reports and underdelivery with delayed feedback. Monitor separate stage rates, measurement coverage/age, achieved kW uncertainty, command backlog and safety overrides rather than one “success” percentage.

title: Async Job Scheduler
question:
Async Job Scheduler

Design an asynchronous job scheduler supporting two job types: run-immediately jobs and delayed jobs that fire after a timer (e.g. one hour). The focus is fault tolerance — exactly-once execution and recovery when a worker dies mid-job.

Requirements

Design an async job scheduler:

Two job types: (1) jobs that should run as soon as possible, and (2) jobs submitted with a delay/timer (e.g. one hour) that should run as soon as possible after the timer elapses.
Primary emphasis is failure handling: how to achieve exactly-once execution and what happens when a worker crashes mid-execution.
Notes
The interviewer drives hard on correctness under failure: exactly-once semantics (visibility timeouts / leases + idempotency keys so a re-delivered job is not double-run), and worker-death recovery (lease expiry re-queues the job for another worker).
The delayed-job path is the design wrinkle: a durable timer/delay queue (or a time-bucketed store polled as timers come due) feeding the same ready queue as immediate jobs.
Difficulty is moderate; this maps closely to a standard job-scheduler design (queue + workers + durable store + retries), so a well-rehearsed template plus crisp exactly-once reasoning is enough.

steps: Durable timers feed one execution path
solution.example: Example: a one-hour delayed invoice job becomes due once, worker A charges then dies before success. B's retry sends the same payment idempotency key and records the existing charge; charging with a new key would duplicate money movement. A late success from A cannot replace B's token. Cancellation fences queued work and requests running interruption, but cannot undo an already committed external charge.
solution.trap: Leases do not ensure exactly-once physical execution or arbitrary external side effects.
solution.teaching_notes_markdown:
### Durable timers feed one execution path

`POST /jobs` accepts payload_ref, idempotency_key, run_at (now for immediate work), timeout and retry policy; `GET /jobs/{id}` returns state/attempts/result and cancel disables future starts. Store Job(id,tenant,key,request_hash,run_at,state,attempt_count,result_ref), Attempt(job,n,worker,token,lease_expiry,state) and Outbox. Unique (tenant,key) returns one logical job; binding the request hash rejects accidental key reuse.

Immediate jobs enter READY. Delayed jobs stay WAITING in an index on (state,run_at,id). Partitioned timer scanners use database time and lock/claim due batches, atomically change WAITING→READY and insert outbox events. Queue publication is retried after scanner crash, never the only timer record. Short-term timing wheels can accelerate due checks, but must rebuild from durable schedules after restart. At-least-once queue messages contain job_id/version, not authoritative ownership.

### Exactly-once effect versus execution

The diagram's workers atomically claim READY→RUNNING with a fencing token and renewable lease. They read payload, heartbeat, publish a complete output and conditionally commit SUCCEEDED for the current token; retryable failure/lease expiry creates another attempt with bounded backoff. Permanent failures enter FAILED/dead-letter state. Worker crash recovery can run the same code again. A lease does **not** guarantee exactly-once execution: the old worker may still run after a network partition, or may have performed an effect before its acknowledgment vanished.

Achieve one committed business effect by using job_id as a sink idempotency key, a transaction covering state+effect in one database, or an external system that durably deduplicates. An output object can be written per attempt then one manifest conditionally committed. If an external effect provides no idempotency/transaction/reconciliation, exactly-once effect is not generally achievable. Choosing strict at-most-once attempt launch instead means some crashed/uncertain jobs never retry; state the lost-work trade-off.

Example: a one-hour delayed invoice job becomes due once, worker A charges then dies before success. B's retry sends the same payment idempotency key and records the existing charge; charging with a new key would duplicate money movement. A late success from A cannot replace B's token. Cancellation fences queued work and requests running interruption, but cannot undo an already committed external charge.

Scale is unspecified. Assume one million live timers at 200 bytes each: 200 MB raw metadata plus indexes/replicas; if 100,000 expire at once, drain time depends on dispatch/worker capacity, not timer precision. Partition ready queues by job type/tenant, impose admission limits and monitor due-to-start delay, oldest timer, expired leases, retries and outbox lag. Test scanner failure after commit, lost queue ACK, duplicate timer delivery, worker crash around the effect and clock boundaries. The design promises durable scheduling and deduplicated effects under stated sink contracts, not physically once-only CPU execution.

title: Design a Distributed Job Scheduler with Cron, Pause, Resume
question:
Design a distributed job scheduler that supports cron-style recurring jobs, pause (allow in-flight jobs to complete, launch no new invocations), and resume. Workers are assumed effectively unlimited.

API surface:

submit(job, cron_expression)
pause(job_id) — already-running invocations finish; no new invocations launch.
resume(job_id) — re-enable future scheduled launches.
cancel(job_id)

Requirements: job definitions, schedules, and state must survive a scheduler restart (persistence); a launch must not be duplicated under failover (idempotency); observability of per-job last-run, next-run, status.

steps: Pause is checked at launch, not just timer creation
solution.example: Traffic is unspecified: assume one million minute schedules, about 16,667 invocations/s on average, with worse aligned bursts. Shard timers by job/time bucket, use bounded outbox batches and jitter only where the schedule contract permits. Multi-zone database replicas and leased scanner shards avoid a single scheduler failure point. Monitor schedule-to-start delay, paused-job launch violations, duplicate authorization, unresolved starts and last/next-run correctness. Test pause-versus-dispatch, resume retry, cancel-versus-success, scanner death and executor timeout. Recurrence must continue after one failed run; a failure does not silently disable the definition.
solution.trap: Pause must serialize with authoritative launch authorization; queued events cannot bypass paused state.
solution.teaching_notes_markdown:
### Pause is checked at launch, not just timer creation

Persist JobDefinition(id,payload_ref,cron,timezone,state,version,next_fire_at,last_run_id) and Invocation(job,scheduled_time,definition_version,state,token,result), unique by (job,scheduled_time). Assume UTC cron, no catch-up for occurrences while paused, and already-running work allowed to finish. State these choices because timezone/DST, overlap and missed schedules are otherwise ambiguous. Cancel is terminal: prevent new invocations and request cancellation of running ones; if a different cancellation contract is desired, define it separately from pause.

`submit(job,cron)` validates the expression and idempotency key, then stores ACTIVE and next_fire_at. `pause` changes ACTIVE→PAUSED and increments version in one transaction; `resume` changes to ACTIVE and computes the next future tick from database time. `GET /jobs/{id}` exposes state, last scheduled/start/end/result and next fire. A dashboard read may lag, but launch decisions use authoritative state.

### Failover-safe launches

The diagram's schedule scanner queries indexed due definitions and materializes logical invocation rows with an outbox. Dispatch locks the job definition and invocation, rechecks ACTIVE and the generation, and records one launch authorization before contacting the executor. Pause uses the same job lock. Thus a launch authorized before pause's linearization point is in flight and may finish; a later one is rejected, even if an old queue message exists. A queue merely waking workers cannot bypass that check. While paused, pending unlaunched ticks are marked skipped/suppressed according to the stated no-catch-up rule.

A failover scanner's duplicate insert hits the unique tick key, returning the original invocation. The executor needs a durable idempotent `start(invocation_id,payload)` API: a response timeout is reconciled by that ID rather than creating another launch. Without such an executor contract, conditional scheduler state alone cannot resolve a crash between sending the start and observing its result. Execution effects still require idempotency if worker retry is allowed. Unlimited workers remove a capacity bottleneck, not this ambiguity.

### Worked race and recovery

A minute job has tick 12:01 queued. Pause commits at 12:00:59; dispatch at 12:01 reads PAUSED and starts nothing. If dispatch authorization committed at 12:00:58 for already-due work, pause allows that invocation to finish. Resume at 12:05:20 schedules 12:06, not five unintended catch-up runs. Persisted timestamps let a restarted scheduler reconstruct this behavior.

Traffic is unspecified: assume one million minute schedules, about 16,667 invocations/s on average, with worse aligned bursts. Shard timers by job/time bucket, use bounded outbox batches and jitter only where the schedule contract permits. Multi-zone database replicas and leased scanner shards avoid a single scheduler failure point. Monitor schedule-to-start delay, paused-job launch violations, duplicate authorization, unresolved starts and last/next-run correctness. Test pause-versus-dispatch, resume retry, cancel-versus-success, scanner death and executor timeout. Recurrence must continue after one failed run; a failure does not silently disable the definition.

title: Design a Distributed Task Scheduler
question:
Design a distributed task scheduler.

Functional requirements:

1.
Submit tasks with metadata, priority, dependencies, and execution constraints.
2.
Store runnable and pending tasks durably.
3.
Assign work to workers while avoiding duplicate execution.
4.
Retry failed tasks with backoff and expose status.
5.
Scale the task queue and workers independently.

Scale / constraints:

Handle many tasks and workers without one queue becoming a bottleneck.
A task may fail, time out, or be picked by a worker that then dies.

Discuss: central vs sharded queues; lease/heartbeat semantics; priority and fairness; dependency resolution and idempotent retries.

steps: Sharded ready queues and dependency release
solution.example: Example: C depends on A and B. Two success messages for A count once; C remains blocked until B commits. If B's first worker returns after attempt 2 started, its old token is rejected. API/scheduler crash after database commit but before queue send is recovered by the outbox; a periodic reconciler finds ready tasks missing dispatch, expired leases and orphan workers.
solution.trap: Dependency eligibility, resource feasibility and fair selection are separate; stale owners require sink fencing.
solution.teaching_notes_markdown:
### Explicit scheduling objects

`POST /tasks` accepts tenant idempotency key, payload_ref, priority, dependencies, resource/capability constraints and retry limit; status/cancel/log APIs expose attempts and blocked reasons. Store Task(id,tenant,state,priority,ready_at,spec,attempt_count), Edge(parent,child), Attempt(task,n,token,worker,lease_expiry,result) and Outbox. Validate dependencies and reject cycles at admission. Persist pending and runnable tasks in SQL or a transactional key-value store; a queue message is not the only copy.

### Sharded ready queues and dependency release

The diagram's dispatcher routes READY tasks to resource-class/tenant shards; CPU-only work cannot block behind unavailable GPU work. Within a shard use weighted fair shares plus priority/aging, and backfill feasible small tasks while reserving progress for large jobs. Central queues are simpler for modest volume but can become hot locks; sharding improves throughput at the cost of approximate global priority and cross-shard balance. Work stealing moves eligible ownership through conditional state, not by duplicating claims.

A worker atomically changes READY→RUNNING, receives a generation token and heartbeat lease, and enforces resource/runtime limits. Completion requires current token, unexpired lease and active task/job state, and publishes a durable result manifest. In one transaction or through a deduplicated completion ledger, release a child only when all distinct predecessors succeeded. A duplicate parent completion cannot decrement remaining-dependency count twice. After retries exhaust, mark dependent tasks SKIPPED/FAILED_DEPENDENCY according to a declared fail-fast policy, while independent branches may continue if allowed.

### Failures and correctness example

On timeout or worker loss, fence the attempt, release confirmed resources and retry with capped exponential backoff/jitter. The lost worker can still run, so sinks need token fencing/idempotency by logical task ID; a lease only prevents two **valid owners**, not two physical processes. Deterministic invalid payloads fail fast rather than burn the retry fleet. Cancellation is an authoritative versioned transition and prevents late success from releasing dependents.

Example: C depends on A and B. Two success messages for A count once; C remains blocked until B commits. If B's first worker returns after attempt 2 started, its old token is rejected. API/scheduler crash after database commit but before queue send is recovered by the outbox; a periodic reconciler finds ready tasks missing dispatch, expired leases and orphan workers.

Scale is unspecified. Assume 100,000 tasks/s peak and 20 queue shards: 5,000 messages/s/shard before retries, subject to measured broker/DB capacity. One million active workers heartbeating every 30 seconds add 33,333 lease updates/s, needing sharded state or batched lease renewal. Autoscale workers from resource-feasible backlog/queue age, independently from queue partitions and API instances. Monitor tenant wait percentiles, fairness/starvation, dispatch lag, lease conflicts, retry causes and result completeness. Test duplicate delivery, partitioned worker, hot tenant and cross-shard dependency completion rather than treating queue acknowledgment as application success.

title: Design a Multi-Resource Loader/Scheduler
question:
Design a loader that schedules work across multiple constrained resources while respecting task dependencies, fairness across requesters, and failure handling.

Tasks may depend on other tasks. Resources have limited capacity. Discuss how you order and dispatch work, how you enforce fairness, and how you recover from failures.

solution.example: Suppose pool capacity is four CPU slots and 8 GB memory. Task A needs (2,6), B (2,4). They cannot run together even though CPUs fit; reserve the full vector and run one, then release its memory before admitting the other. Ten callers requesting the same 6 GB model version share one load and ten waiters, rather than allocate 60 GB. A changed version or incompatible environment is a different key.
solution.trap: Reserve full resource vectors only after dependencies; coalesce compatible loads without canceling other waiters.
solution.teaching_notes_markdown:
### Resource vectors and shared loads

Represent Task(id,requester,dependencies,required_resource_vector,state,attempt,token) and ResourcePool(id,total,reserved,health). The resource vector may include CPU, GPU, memory and I/O slots. A task is eligible only after all dependencies succeed; do not reserve its resources while it waits for a prerequisite that needs the same pool. Detect dependency cycles at submission and reject impossible resource requests. If this is a model/data loader, use ResourceVersion(id,version,state,waiters,refcount) and coalesce concurrent compatible load requests.

The diagram's dependency gate produces ready work; fair selection chooses a requester; an atomic reservation allocates the entire vector; a worker performs slow loading/execution outside central locks. Use weighted dominant-resource fairness or weighted deficit scheduling with per-requester concurrency limits and aging. A simple strict priority queue can starve small requesters; resource-aware backfill needs a reservation/aging policy so large tasks also progress. For one placement, reserve all required resources together transactionally or in a fixed global order with rollback to avoid partial-allocation deadlocks.

### State and API

`submit(spec,key)` returns a stable task ID; `status`, `cancel` and `acquire/release resource version` expose state. Store Task/Dependency/Attempt/Reservation and an outbox durably when restart recovery is required. States BLOCKED→READY→LOADING/RUNNING→READY_RESOURCE/SUCCEEDED, with RETRY_WAIT/FAILED/CANCELED alternatives. A generation token prevents a stale load of model v1 replacing current v2. Record one terminal notification per waiter and result; canceling one waiter does not cancel a shared load still needed by others. Evict only unreferenced resources, with memory pressure and reload cost considered.

### Failure example and sizing

Suppose pool capacity is four CPU slots and 8 GB memory. Task A needs (2,6), B (2,4). They cannot run together even though CPUs fit; reserve the full vector and run one, then release its memory before admitting the other. Ten callers requesting the same 6 GB model version share one load and ten waiters, rather than allocate 60 GB. A changed version or incompatible environment is a different key.

Workers heartbeat reservations/leases; failure fences the old attempt, retries transient I/O with bounded backoff and releases resources after reconciliation. Partial downloads write temporary objects and publish only after checksum validation. Persistent allocation records and observed process/memory state must be reconciled after restart; blindly resetting counters can overcommit live resources. On shutdown, stop admission, drain/cancel tasks and resolve waiters explicitly.

No arrival/resource distribution is given. Assume 100 new loads/s averaging 0.5 seconds and 200 MB transient memory: Little's law gives 50 in flight and about 10 GB transient memory before cache/headroom. Coalescing and retention change this substantially. Monitor queue age by requester, allocation fragmentation, resource leaks, cache hit/load reuse, stale completions and fairness. Test dependent-resource deadlock, one canceled waiter, simultaneous version requests, partial failure and eviction while referenced. This separates task ordering, resource feasibility and fairness instead of assuming one queue order solves all three.

![W271 flow: Requester dependency DAG → Shared resource versions → Fair feasible selection → Atomic full-vector reserve → Load outside locks → Fenced publish / waiters.](../diagrams/W271_exact_review_251_300.svg)

title: Design an Async Job / Task System
question:
First system-design round in the Salesforce LMTS onsite. Design a generic async job execution service — API surface, state machine, retry, idempotency, storage choice. Not asking for novel architecture, but for the candidate to explain a complete service cleanly end-to-end.

Requirements
Public API: submit(job_definition) -> job_id, status(job_id) -> state, cancel(job_id), optionally result(job_id) -> output.
Job lifecycle: submitted -> queued -> running -> (succeeded | failed | cancelled). Failed jobs may auto-retry per policy.
Worker pool consumes from the queue; jobs may take seconds to hours.
Retry semantics: exponential backoff with jitter; max attempt cap.
Idempotency: a duplicate submit (same client-side idempotency key) must not create a second job.
Persistence: jobs and their state survive worker / scheduler restarts.
Storage choice (RDBMS vs NoSQL) is an explicit discussion point.

steps: One logical job, several possible attempts
solution.example: Traffic is unspecified. Assume 100 jobs/s with five-minute mean runtime: about 30,000 simultaneous running jobs; 30-second heartbeat gives 1,000 updates/s before retries. Partition ready queues by type/tenant and add quotas/dead-letter inspection/log cursors. Job logs are append-only offset streams, not a large SQL field. Monitor time-to-start, attempts, lease loss, cancellation delay, outbox backlog and cost. Test duplicate submission, failed queue publish, worker crash after output, cancellation/commit races and result-read authorization. This delivers a complete service while keeping the storage and effect guarantees explicit.
solution.trap: A logical job and retry attempts differ; storage choice must implement idempotency/state consistency, not merely use a queue.
solution.teaching_notes_markdown:
### One logical job, several possible attempts

Expose `submit(job_definition,idempotency_key)→job_id`, `status(job_id)`, `cancel(job_id)` and `result(job_id)`. Bind a tenant-scoped unique key to a request hash; duplicate identical submits return the same job, while a different body under that key is a conflict. Define payload/image/resource/time limits and keep large payloads/results in object storage. A success response to submit follows durable metadata/outbox commit.

Choose an RDBMS initially because uniqueness, state/lease transactions, attempts and user queries are central. Job(id,tenant,key,hash,state,spec_ref,created_at,next_attempt_at,result_ref) and Attempt(job,n,worker,token,lease_expiry,error) use indexes on state/ready time and lease expiry. A queue wakes workers, and an outbox closes the database-to-broker atomicity gap. A partitioned conditional-write NoSQL store may fit much higher volume but requires deliberately implementing the same multi-record/index consistency; naming it does not remove those invariants.

### End-to-end state machine

SUBMITTED/QUEUED→RUNNING→SUCCEEDED or FAILED/CANCELED. Retryable attempt failure returns the logical job to QUEUED after RETRY_WAIT; preserve attempts rather than overwriting failure history. A worker claims queued state with a unique renewable lease/token, starts isolated work and heartbeats throughout seconds-to-hours execution. It uploads an output/checksum manifest before conditionally committing success. Retry transient infrastructure failures with exponential backoff and jitter up to a configured total-attempt cap; invalid definitions fail permanently. A reconciler expires stale leases and republishes ready outbox work after crashes.

Cancel atomically records cancellation intent, fences new claims and active completion, and asks the worker to stop cooperatively/forcefully after grace. Return CANCELING until durable finalization; don't claim an external side effect was undone. A late success from an old token cannot overwrite CANCELED. Repeated cancel is idempotent and a terminal success is not rewritten by a later request.

### Failure trace and estimate

The diagram's API/state/queue/worker/result path is a durable workflow, not an exactly-once CPU guarantee. If A performs an effect then dies before acknowledgment, B may retry. Use the same job/effect idempotency key at the sink, a shared transaction or a fenced conditional output commit; otherwise duplicate external effects remain possible. On a queue outage accepted jobs stay in SQL/outbox. On DB outage do not hand out unrecorded leases. On object-store failure leave output uncommitted and retry safely.

Traffic is unspecified. Assume 100 jobs/s with five-minute mean runtime: about 30,000 simultaneous running jobs; 30-second heartbeat gives 1,000 updates/s before retries. Partition ready queues by type/tenant and add quotas/dead-letter inspection/log cursors. Job logs are append-only offset streams, not a large SQL field. Monitor time-to-start, attempts, lease loss, cancellation delay, outbox backlog and cost. Test duplicate submission, failed queue publish, worker crash after output, cancellation/commit races and result-read authorization. This delivers a complete service while keeping the storage and effect guarantees explicit.

title: Distributed Job Scheduler / Calendar Service
question:
Design a distributed job scheduler / calendar service supporting millions of live scheduled tasks.

Functional: schedule(task_id, run_at_ts, payload), cancel(task_id), query(window_start, window_end) (powers a real-time dashboard). A worker pool executes tasks at their scheduled time with at-least-once semantics and idempotency hooks.

Variant: calendar service with timezones, recurrence rules (RRULE), and conflict detection.

Non-functional: millions of tasks live at once; sub-second worker pickup of due tasks; dashboard tolerates < 5s staleness, the schedule path tolerates none.

steps: Durable schedule path and due-time indexing
solution.example: Store Task(id,tenant,run_at,state,version,payload_ref), Attempt(task,n,token,lease_expiry), Outbox and a due index partitioned by time bucket plus hash shard. Millions of live future tasks remain in durable indexed storage; only a near-future horizon enters an in-memory timing wheel. On restart rebuild that wheel from SQL/conditional-write state. Shard leases distribute time buckets and fencing epochs prevent old scanners claiming after takeover. Poll near-due buckets at, for example, 100 ms, then atomically claim due tasks and enqueue dispatch through an outbox. Sub-second pickup also needs broker/worker capacity and clock synchronization; it is not achieved by polling alone.
solution.trap: Subsecond pickup cannot hold for arbitrarily aligned unbounded deadlines; strong schedule path and stale dashboard are separate.
solution.teaching_notes_markdown:
### Durable schedule path and due-time indexing

`schedule(task_id,run_at_ts,payload)` creates a caller-identified task with version and payload_ref; duplicate identical requests return the current record and differing reuse requires an explicit reschedule/version check. `cancel(task_id,expected_version)` conditionally marks CANCELED; `query(start,end,cursor)` returns scheduled records from a dashboard projection with data_as_of. Schedule/cancel acknowledgment follows a strongly consistent durable write, whereas the dashboard may lag under five seconds.

Store Task(id,tenant,run_at,state,version,payload_ref), Attempt(task,n,token,lease_expiry), Outbox and a due index partitioned by time bucket plus hash shard. Millions of live future tasks remain in durable indexed storage; only a near-future horizon enters an in-memory timing wheel. On restart rebuild that wheel from SQL/conditional-write state. Shard leases distribute time buckets and fencing epochs prevent old scanners claiming after takeover. Poll near-due buckets at, for example, 100 ms, then atomically claim due tasks and enqueue dispatch through an outbox. Sub-second pickup also needs broker/worker capacity and clock synchronization; it is not achieved by polling alone.

### Cancellation, execution and dashboard

The diagram separates authoritative scheduling from due dispatch, workers and an asynchronous query/read model. Workers validate current task state/version and attempt lease, run idempotently, heartbeat and conditionally commit the output. At-least-once delivery plus sink idempotency means duplicate dispatch cannot repeat a committed effect. Expired leases retry after fencing; timeout does not prove old work stopped. Cancellation wins against claims through a shared conditional transaction; after execution effects commit, cancellation cannot magically erase them. Log which race won.

Change events update a time-indexed dashboard projection idempotently using task version; cancel/reschedule removes the previous indexed time before adding the new one. An old delayed event cannot resurrect canceled entries. Expensive full-window scans need pagination and quotas. During projection outage schedule writes continue and the dashboard reports stale data; during schedule-store outage reject new acknowledged schedules rather than buffer them only in memory.

### Capacity and calendar variant

Assume ten million live tasks at 300 bytes: 3 GB raw metadata before indexes/replication. If one million are due at noon, a 10,000/s dispatch fleet takes at least 100 seconds; smooth admitted schedules, reserve capacity or report infeasible sub-second pickup instead of claiming unlimited timing precision. Monitor due lag, clock offset, hot buckets, expired leases and projection age; test reschedule/cancel against a due tick and region failover.

For calendars, retain timezone ID and RRULE/local start separately from UTC materialized occurrences. Define DST gaps/folds and bounded expansion horizon; edits have recurrence versions and occurrence exceptions. Conflict detection is an authoritative per-calendar/resource interval transaction with exclusion/no-overlap checks, not the stale dashboard. Adjacent half-open intervals [start,end) do not conflict. A recurrence update fences old generated occurrences, and cancellations preserve history. Calendar semantics add write coordination; they do not change at-least-once worker effect handling.

title: Job Scheduler System Design
question:
Job Scheduler System Design

Robinhood · System Design · 60 min · Free preview

Design a distributed job scheduler that runs typed jobs under an SLA, surfaces failures and logs, and guarantees each job runs at most once. The anchor Robinhood system-design prompt, especially for Senior+; often delivered nearly word-for-word and open-book.

Requirements
Schedule and run jobs of a given type. Each job has an SLA; if it exceeds the deadline, raise/record an error and let the user inspect logs.
Support recurring jobs (e.g. a job that runs every minute).
Guarantee at-most-once execution per scheduled run.
Handle a broad range of failure cases gracefully — this is where most of the follow-up time goes.

Deep-dive directions interviewers push on:

What happens when a worker or a component in the pipeline dies mid-execution? How do you still honor at-most-once and continue retrying?
A recurring job that fails must still send a notification — design how the failure path reliably triggers the notification even when parts of the system are down.
Retry strategy and backoff; how retries interact with the at-most-once guarantee.
Notes
The round is open-book and the prompt is stable, so the front half carries little differentiation. Proactively and thoroughly cover reliability and fault tolerance early; candidates who leave it thin get walked into follow-up traps and run out of time.
A common at-most-once implementation is conditional writes (compare-and-set on a claim/lease record) so two workers can't both execute the same run.
A frequently added constraint is that the scheduler only handles a single job *type* — don't over-generalize the model.

steps: Resolve the at-most-once versus retry contradiction
Reliable notifications and the retry alternative
solution.example: Under the alternative retry contract, lease/fence attempt IDs, cap attempts, checkpoint and use (run_id,effect_id) deduplication at sinks. A database transaction or idempotent payment endpoint can give one committed effect even with repeated code execution; arbitrary scripts cannot. Capacity is unspecified: with 100,000 minute definitions, average 1,667 runs/s and aligned-tick bursts need batch/scanner sharding, though worker availability still limits SLA. Monitor due/start delay, UNKNOWN runs, SLA misses, notification age and termination lag. Test every crash boundary around consume/send/ACK/effect/completion and demonstrate the corresponding availability-versus-once trade-off; do not claim a lease alone solves it.
solution.trap: Strict at-most-once launch and automatic retry after uncertain worker failure are incompatible; durable notification outbox is independent of worker survival.
solution.teaching_notes_markdown:
### Resolve the at-most-once versus retry contradiction

Strict “each scheduled run executes at most once” and automatic re-execution after an uncertain mid-run worker failure cannot both be guaranteed. A compare-and-set prevents two current claimants, but an expired lease does not stop the old worker, and a crash after an effect but before completion leaves an unknown outcome. State this before choosing the contract. For this answer preserve strict at-most-once **launch**: once dispatch intent is durably consumed, never automatically launch that run again. A failed/uncertain run can be inspected, and a user-requested rerun is a new run ID. If the interviewer instead wants retries, explicitly switch to at-least-once attempts with exactly-once committed effects using sink idempotency/fencing.

### Durable schedule and failure path

For the single-job-type variant store Definition(id,cron,timezone,enabled,SLA,payload_ref), Run(id,definition,scheduled_tick,state,dispatch_consumed,start,deadline,result_ref), LogRef and NotificationOutbox. Unique (definition,scheduled_tick) deduplicates recurring ticks under scanner failover. APIs create/update definitions, inspect runs/logs, cancel and explicitly rerun. Assume UTC/no overlapping same-definition runs unless specified. A recurring definition continues scheduling future ticks even if one invocation fails.

The diagram's scanner commits a logical tick and dispatch record. An idempotent executor start keyed by run_id is ideal; without it, mark consumed before sending. Crash before send can lose that execution, which is the honest cost of strict at-most-once. RPC timeout becomes UNKNOWN and is reconciled/queryable, not silently retried. Heartbeats are progress observations; expiration marks LOST/UNKNOWN and may request termination but never grants permission to relaunch the same strict run. Deadline violation records SLA_EXCEEDED and a failure notification even when the process keeps running; revoke/fence output authority and stop work where possible.

### Reliable notifications and the retry alternative

Record failure/SLA transition plus notification outbox in one transaction. A separate dispatcher retries the notification with exponential backoff and a stable event key, tracks provider acceptance and dead-letters persistent failure for operator attention. The worker itself is not responsible for being alive to send its own death notification. If the database is temporarily down, monitoring retains/reconciles observations and later records the durable failure; do not claim notification at the deadline under total control-plane outage. Deduplication makes one logical alert, while external message delivery can still be duplicate/uncertain without provider support.

Under the alternative retry contract, lease/fence attempt IDs, cap attempts, checkpoint and use (run_id,effect_id) deduplication at sinks. A database transaction or idempotent payment endpoint can give one committed effect even with repeated code execution; arbitrary scripts cannot. Capacity is unspecified: with 100,000 minute definitions, average 1,667 runs/s and aligned-tick bursts need batch/scanner sharding, though worker availability still limits SLA. Monitor due/start delay, UNKNOWN runs, SLA misses, notification age and termination lag. Test every crash boundary around consume/send/ACK/effect/completion and demonstrate the corresponding availability-versus-once trade-off; do not claim a lease alone solves it.

title: Job Scheduler with Task Dependencies (DAG Executor)
question:
Design a low-level scheduler where each job is a set of tasks with dependency relationships (a DAG). The scheduler must run a task only after all its prerequisites complete.

Requirements

Model the task graph and execution order (topological scheduling).
Track task states: pending, runnable, running, succeeded, failed, retrying.
Assign tasks to workers; define a retry policy, failure propagation (does a failed task cancel the whole job or allow downstream skip/retry?), and cycle detection.
Keep it concrete: tables, queues, worker lease/heartbeat, state transitions.

A common variant swaps the dependency DAG for a priority-based GPU scheduler: users submit high/low-priority ML training jobs onto a shared GPU pool — priority queue for selection, preemption (checkpoint first), aging to avoid starvation, checkpoint/resume for multi-day jobs, and GPU-crash/OOM/stuck-job recovery. Discuss the design.

solution.example: Example: decode→{augment,train}→evaluate. After decode commits, augment and train run concurrently; evaluate waits for both. A duplicate augment completion cannot release evaluate early. Worker loss retries train with a new token; its old worker cannot publish after successor ownership. Side-effecting task payloads need logical-task idempotency even if the queue/lease protocol is correct.
solution.trap: Duplicate parent completion cannot release a child twice; checkpointed GPU preemption requires full training state and fencing.
solution.teaching_notes_markdown:
### Graph and ready-state invariants

Store Job(id,tenant,state), Task(job,id,state,payload_ref,resource_spec,attempt_count,result_ref), Edge(job,parent,child), Attempt(task,n,token,worker,lease_expiry) and Outbox. `POST /jobs` validates unique IDs, existing dependencies and acyclicity with Kahn's algorithm/DFS in O(V+E). Roots enter RUNNABLE; others PENDING. `GET /jobs/{id}` exposes each task's state/attempt/error/output, and cancel records authoritative job intent.

The diagram's dependency gate feeds resource-class ready queues, then leased workers and conditional completion. On claim, transactionally check RUNNABLE and active job, set RUNNING and grant a unique token. Worker heartbeat renews only before lease expiry; late/stale completion is rejected. Successful completion first commits output, then one state transition releases children whose **all** distinct parents are SUCCEEDED. Use an edge-completion uniqueness key or an all-parent query; a repeated parent message must not decrement twice. Independent runnable tasks execute concurrently.

### Retry and failure policy

Transient failures move RUNNING→RETRYING with bounded exponential backoff, then RUNNABLE for a new attempt. Preserve the attempt/error history. Assume fail-fast jobs: exhausted retry marks the job FAILING, fences other attempts and marks blocked/runnable tasks canceled/skipped before publishing FAILED. An alternate continue-independent-branches policy must explicitly mark descendants SKIPPED and compute the final job result after those branches finish. Never leave a child waiting forever for an impossible parent. Cancel prevents new work and rejects late completion that would reopen dependencies.

Example: decode→{augment,train}→evaluate. After decode commits, augment and train run concurrently; evaluate waits for both. A duplicate augment completion cannot release evaluate early. Worker loss retries train with a new token; its old worker cannot publish after successor ownership. Side-effecting task payloads need logical-task idempotency even if the queue/lease protocol is correct.

### GPU variant and scale

For high/low-priority training, replace the DAG-ready selection policy with tenant-weighted GPU queues, aging and topology-aware gang reservations. Resource feasibility includes GPU model/count/memory and interconnect, not just priority. Preempt only allowed jobs: request checkpoint with model/optimizer/RNG/sampler state, validate durable manifest, revoke token and reclaim confirmed capacity. Non-checkpointable tasks lose work and need an explicit disruption policy. GPU crash may retry elsewhere; deterministic OOM calls for smaller batch/resource correction rather than infinite identical retries; stuck jobs need progress/watchdog thresholds separate from heartbeat liveness.

Scale is unspecified. Assume 100,000 jobs/day×10 tasks=one million task executions/day, about 11.6/s average; 20,000 live attempts heartbeating every 30 seconds add 667 updates/s. Separate CPU/GPU queues, batch outbox publication and partition task history while keeping each job's dependency transaction coherent. Reconciliation scans expired leases, unsent ready events and nonterminal job finalizers. Observe feasible queue delay, starvation, retry causes, checkpoint age, lost GPU-hours and output completeness. Test cycles, shared descendants, duplicate completion, failure during finalization and preemption/checkpoint races; queue delivery count is not a task success count.

title: Design a Distributed Metrics System
question: Design a distributed metrics / monitoring system. It must ingest high-volume metric data points (counters, gauges, timers) emitted by many services, store them efficiently as time series, and serve aggregation queries (dashboards, alerts) over time windows.

solution.example: Replicated logs/checkpoints replay after worker failure; atomic offset+aggregate commit or idempotent batch keys prevent duplicate counts. Late samples update event-time windows within a defined lateness horizon, with corrections retained for longer delays. On overload enforce per-tenant quotas and report dropped/rejected samples; query concurrency/cost budgets protect ingestion and other tenants. Use multi-zone replicas, backups and downsampling manifests. Test counter restart, duplicate batches, late samples, disappearing series, incompatible histogram buckets and high-cardinality abuse. Monitor ingest lag, dropped samples, active series/churn, query p99, alert freshness and rollup correctness.
solution.trap: Counter/gauge/histogram semantics differ and percentiles cannot be averaged.
solution.teaching_notes_markdown:
### Metric semantics and ingestion

Define samples as {tenant,metric_name,type,tags,event_time,ingest_time,value,source_id,sequence}. Counters are cumulative values or increments with an explicit mode/reset identity, gauges are point values, and timers are distributions represented by count/sum/compatible histogram buckets. Never average p99 values from separate hosts. Metric/tag cardinality is bounded by tenant budgets; request IDs belong in logs/traces, not metric labels.

The diagram's buffered agents batch over authenticated push endpoints or answer scrapes, ingestion validates type/schema/quota, a replicated partition log absorbs bursts and stream processors build time-series chunks/rollups. Partition by hash(tenant,series_id) with time chunking; series identity canonicalizes sorted tags and metric type. Deduplicate retried delta batches by source boot_id/sequence. Cumulative counters need monotonic/reset-aware rate computation instead of summing every observed reading. Client memory/disk buffers are bounded and expose drop/backpressure behavior; observing a service must not exhaust it.

### Storage, queries and alerts

Use a time-series engine for recent compressed append-oriented chunks and tag-to-series indexes, with object storage for older downsampled chunks. Store per-window sum/count/min/max and mergeable histogram state; gauges require declared last/average/min/max semantics. A query API accepts metric, authorized tag predicate, time range, step and aggregation. A planner prunes tenant/time/series shards, chooses a resolution no coarser than promised, merges states and returns data timestamps/completeness. Arbitrary historical resolution cannot reconstruct detail already downsampled away.

AlertRule(id,tenant,query,threshold,for_duration,evaluation_interval) drives sharded evaluators over recent aggregates. Persist pending/firing/resolved states, deduplicate incident keys and route notifications through an outbox with retries/suppression. An empty or stale series is UNKNOWN/no-data according to the rule, not automatically zero/healthy.

### Estimate and failure validation

Scale is unspecified. Assume one million samples/s×32 compressed-encoding bytes: 32 MB/s and 2.7648 TB/day before replication/indexes. Seven days raw is 19.35 TB logical, and three replicas about 58.1 TB excluding overhead. Actual compression/cardinality changes this; benchmark series churn. A fifteen-second batch plus fifteen-second rule interval and processing/headroom can target under one-minute alerts; a full one-minute batch cannot.

Replicated logs/checkpoints replay after worker failure; atomic offset+aggregate commit or idempotent batch keys prevent duplicate counts. Late samples update event-time windows within a defined lateness horizon, with corrections retained for longer delays. On overload enforce per-tenant quotas and report dropped/rejected samples; query concurrency/cost budgets protect ingestion and other tenants. Use multi-zone replicas, backups and downsampling manifests. Test counter restart, duplicate batches, late samples, disappearing series, incompatible histogram buckets and high-cardinality abuse. title: Design a Metric Counter Library

solution.example: Keep the requested overloads; canonicalize tags by sorted immutable key/value pairs. Specify that an omitted tag map queries the aggregate of all series for metricName, so the example tagged payment increment contributes to `getCount("api.requests", LAST_MINUTE)`. An exact supplied tag map matches that series; a separate filter API would be needed for partial tags. solution.trap: Omitted-tag query aggregates all metric series; bounded buckets imply explicit boundary precision; exact finite-buffer losslessness is impossible through arbitrary outage.
solution.teaching_notes_markdown:
### Public semantics before optimization

Keep the requested overloads; canonicalize tags by sorted immutable key/value pairs. Specify that an omitted tag map queries the aggregate of all series for metricName, so the example tagged payment increment contributes to `getCount("api.requests", LAST_MINUTE)`. An exact supplied tag map matches that series; a separate filter API would be needed for partial tags. Define windows as trailing [now-duration,now), using the library's monotonic receipt time locally. Negative increments are rejected for a counter; gauges are a separate metric type.

For bounded approximate time resolution, each series owns a ring of one-second buckets over a day plus sequence/generation metadata. `increment` finds the current slot, atomically resets it when its epoch differs, then adds value; lock reset+increment together or a rollover race loses counts. Query snapshots relevant buckets and sums by timestamp. A one-second bucket cannot answer an exact arbitrary subsecond boundary: either document at-most-one-second boundary approximation or keep timestamped events at much larger memory cost. Coarser minute/hour rollups reduce query work but have the same boundary rule. Probabilistic sketches are appropriate for distinct/count-min-style approximate questions, not silently substituted for required exact event counts.

### Threads, memory and flush

The diagram's hot path is local striped/per-thread counters → sealed immutable flush batches → central aggregate store. Avoid a single global mutex: a concurrent series registry plus per-series/stripe locks handles rotation, while summing/querying snapshots avoids calling network code under those locks. Background flush merges local stripes and exports delta batches with source_instance,boot_id,batch_seq. Retry the same immutable batch until ACK; the central sink deduplicates by that key. Clearing local buckets before durable handoff loses data; adding another cumulative snapshot as a delta double counts. Keep query-retention state separate from pending export state.

Bound series count/tag lengths and allowlist dimensions; on overflow use an explicit overflow series/rejection count rather than allocate one label per request. At an assumed 10,000 series×86,400 one-second 8-byte counts, naive retention alone is 6.912 GB before epochs/locks, so multi-resolution tiers or smaller series budgets matter. Thirty-second retention at full resolution plus minute/day rollups trades boundary precision for memory; advertise actual supported precision.

Flush failures use bounded disk spool, backoff and drop accounting when full. The host call remains nonblocking if that is the chosen contract, so arbitrary outage duration plus finite storage cannot guarantee lossless metrics. Local monotonic time avoids wall-clock jumps; exports include wall timestamps/offset quality for cross-host windows. Prometheus typically scrapes cumulative counters and handles rates/resets; StatsD-style increments are usually best-effort unless reliable transport/ACK/dedup is added. Test concurrent rollover/increment, tag-order equivalence, omitted-tag aggregation, ring expiry, duplicate flush and full spool. Measure hot-call overhead, active series, dropped increments and export lag separately from dashboard query speed.

title: Design a Real-Time Log Processing System
question:
Design a log processing system that ingests a continuous stream of application logs from a large service fleet and counts errors in real time. A dashboard and alerting layer sits on top, so error counts must be accurate and available with low latency.

Cover: ingest volume / retention / latency SLOs, a capacity calculation, the data model (LogEvent, time-bucketed ErrorCount, AlertRule), store choices with justification, an ingest and query API, the end-to-end pipeline with partitioning and windowing, and scaling trade-offs (latency vs. durability, freshness vs. state size, exactly-once cost). Address the follow-up: how do you reduce end-to-end latency?

steps: State an explicit workload and SLO
solution.example: To reduce end-to-end latency, shorten agent linger and microbatch intervals, use streaming rather than minute polling, increase balanced partitions/consumers, preaggregate hot counters and query cache/materialized windows. Keep durable group commit/replication; lowering fsync durability or skipping dedup changes correctness and must be an explicit trade-off. Smaller batches cost more network/CPU/state operations. Trace emit→agent→broker→processor→store→dashboard stages before optimizing the wrong link. Test duplicate replay, consumer crash at checkpoint, late/error-class corrections, hot-service flood and alert-provider outage; monitor lag/completeness, dedup expiry, p99 and reconciliation differences.
solution.trap: Accuracy requires idempotent offset/output handling and completeness watermarks, not simply low queue lag.
solution.teaching_notes_markdown:
### State an explicit workload and SLO

Assume one million LogEvents/s peak, 200 bytes/event, seven days raw hot retention and 90 days archived; target dashboard counts under one second fresh and p99 query under 500 ms for recent service windows. These are design assumptions because the prompt gives no numbers. Peak ingest is 200 MB/s; if sustained, 17.28 TB/day raw, 120.96 TB for seven days before replicas/index/compression. At assumed 10 MB/s safe ingest per queue partition, use at least 20 at peak and choose 40 for headroom/skew, validated by broker benchmarks.

Schema: LogEvent(event_id,tenant,service,host,boot_id,seq,event_time,ingest_time,level,error_class,message); ErrorCount(tenant,service,error_class,bucket_start,resolution,count,revision); AlertRule(id,query,threshold,for_duration,evaluation_interval,state). `POST /logs:batch` acknowledges the promised durable log boundary, and `GET /error-counts?service=&from=&to=&step=` queries materialized aggregates. Raw message/token search is a separate workload, not a reason to index every free-form label.

### Accurate pipeline and query path

The diagram's agents buffer/batch, ingest validates/authenticates, a replicated log partitions by tenant/service plus hash shard, and stream workers deduplicate event IDs before counting ERROR/FATAL in event-time windows. A service-level hot key uses partial counters by hash shard followed by sums. Commit input offsets, dedup state and aggregate revisions atomically through the stream engine or use idempotent batch contributions; replay after a crash must not add counts again. Late events update windows within a watermark policy and trigger explicit corrections; raw archive supports later reconciliation.

Store recent ErrorCount in a low-latency time-series/OLAP table keyed by tenant/service/time/error_class and raw logs in compressed time-partitioned object/columnar storage. Count queries scan bounded buckets and merge sum/count states. Alerts evaluate recent materialized windows, persist incident state and publish idempotent notification intents through an outbox; deduplicate repeated firings, suppress flapping and represent no-data as unknown.

### Failure and latency trade-offs

Client events need durable local spooling if full accuracy includes host crashes; otherwise document the loss boundary. Network retries preserve batch/event IDs. A lagging partition advances a completeness watermark, so the dashboard can show provisional counts instead of claiming complete zeros. A full backend/queue rejects/backpressures or uses bounded spool with explicit drops; unlimited losslessness and nonblocking finite buffers cannot both hold through an indefinite outage. Separate ingestion and query budgets to contain expensive scans/noisy services.

To reduce end-to-end latency, shorten agent linger and microbatch intervals, use streaming rather than minute polling, increase balanced partitions/consumers, preaggregate hot counters and query cache/materialized windows. Keep durable group commit/replication; lowering fsync durability or skipping dedup changes correctness and must be an explicit trade-off. Smaller batches cost more network/CPU/state operations. Trace emit→agent→broker→processor→store→dashboard stages before optimizing the wrong link. Test duplicate replay, consumer crash at checkpoint, late/error-class corrections, hot-service flood and alert-provider outage; monitor lag/completeness, dedup expiry, p99 and reconciliation differences.

title: Design a Real-Time Metrics Monitoring System
question:
Design a real-time monitoring system (Datadog / Prometheus style). Services emit metrics (counters, gauges, histograms, log lines) at high volume; the platform ingests them, supports fast dashboard queries, and fires alerts.

Functional

Services emit metrics at high volume.
Engineers / on-call query metrics for dashboards in seconds.
Alerts fire when a metric crosses a threshold or matches an anomaly rule.
Tiered retention: hot recent data queried often; cold long-term data queried rarely.

Non-functional

Ingest ~5M data points/sec at peak (~500k hosts x ~100 metrics, ~1GB/s raw).
Query p99 in the 1-2s range for dashboards spanning days to weeks.
Alert latency under 1 minute from emission to firing.
Cost-conscious storage: downsample aggressively for older data.

Discuss ingest, storage, query, downsampling, alerting, and cardinality control.

steps: Size and partition the stated workload
solution.example: Time-series identity includes tenant/name/type/sorted tags. Index tags to series, compress time/value chunks and retain full fidelity for a chosen recent window. For example retain ten-second samples seven days, one-minute rollups 30 days and hourly rollups one year; this is a proposed policy, and raw detail beyond it cannot be recovered from means. Keep counter deltas/reset markers and gauge min/max/last/sum/count; merge histogram counts before quantiles, never average p99. Logs use time/service indexes and object archive, not an unbounded label per line.
solution.trap: 5M points/s over50M base series implies10-second sampling; labels multiply cardinality.
solution.teaching_notes_markdown:
### Size and partition the stated workload

Five million points/s at about 1 GB/s raw implies roughly 200 bytes/point. Sustained peak is 86.4 TB/day raw; seven days is 604.8 TB before replication, indexes or compression. The 500,000 hosts×100 metrics give 50 million series before labels, so five million points/s corresponds to a ten-second average sampling interval, not one point/series/second. Tag expansion can multiply series enormously; restrict dimensions, enforce tenant budgets and expose rejected-series counts.

Agents collect counters/gauges/histograms and structured logs through separate schemas, batch with bounded local spooling and send to regional authenticated ingest. The diagram's durable partition log buffers bursts, keyed stream processors normalize/reset/deduplicate samples and write recent TSDB chunks plus immutable archival chunks. At an assumed safe 20 MB/s per log partition, 1 GB/s needs at least 50; choose 100+ for skew/headroom only after measurement. Hot tenants/series use subsharded partial aggregates where the metric is mergeable.

### Query and retention plan

Time-series identity includes tenant/name/type/sorted tags. Index tags to series, compress time/value chunks and retain full fidelity for a chosen recent window. For example retain ten-second samples seven days, one-minute rollups 30 days and hourly rollups one year; this is a proposed policy, and raw detail beyond it cannot be recovered from means. Keep counter deltas/reset markers and gauge min/max/last/sum/count; merge histogram counts before quantiles, never average p99. Logs use time/service indexes and object archive, not an unbounded label per line.

A query frontend checks tenant scope/cost, splits time/series shards, chooses the finest sufficient rollup, computes partial aggregations and streams/cache-merges results. Preaggregated common day/week views and bounded returned points make p99 1–2 seconds plausible. Arbitrary unbounded joins/cardinality scans cannot share the same guarantee; set query limits and asynchronous export. Rollup manifests make each published generation complete and replayable.

### Alerts and failure behavior

For under-one-minute alert latency, budget e.g. ten-second agent flush, ten-second ingest/processing, ten-second evaluator interval and twenty seconds notification/headroom. Rules define threshold/anomaly baseline, `for` duration, no-data behavior, suppression and routing. Persist pending/firing/resolved state and send idempotent outbox notifications with dedup/recovery. A two-minute `for` rule intentionally exceeds one minute; distinguish rule semantics from pipeline delay.

Replay durable logs/checkpoints after worker loss, deduplicate delta batches by source/boot/sequence and correct late windows with revisions. Cumulative counters require reset-aware rates. Ingest overload enforces per-tenant quotas and counts loss; collector-buffer overflow protects the host rather than crashing it. Region failover must avoid double ingest/counts and preserve tenant isolation. Monitor sample loss, active-series churn, queue lag, query p99, alert delay and storage cost; test counter restart, incompatible histogram buckets, backend outage, cardinality explosion and noisy-service load. Downsampling saves cost at a measurable resolution/extreme-detail price, which the dashboard must expose.

title: Design a User Behavior / Metrics Monitoring Aggregator
question:
Design an event monitoring and enrichment platform for product-behavior analytics.

Requirements:

Track user behavior across web and mobile (ad impressions, clicks, app installs, and other product events).
Provide SDKs and API endpoints for data collection.
Support real-time dashboard queries with low (sub-second) latency.
Support complex asynchronous warehouse queries for deeper analytics.
Keep raw events for offline jobs.
Enrich events with data such as reverse geolocation or compliance tags.
Discuss schemas, ingestion, aggregation, enrichment flow, dashboard storage, and efficient query tables.

Scale anchor: handle 100M+ events/day with sub-second dashboard query latency, and treat aggregate counts as requiring full accuracy (no dropped or double-counted events), pinning the design to exactly-once / idempotent semantics rather than best-effort.

Follow-up (ML loop): the same event pipeline becomes a feature source; be ready to design offline feature/label generation, a training pipeline, and a low-latency online serving path for a recommendation model.

solution.example: For recommendations, point-in-time joins produce user/item features and mature exposure→click/conversion labels; future events cannot leak into training. Shared transformations publish versioned online features, train a retrieval/ranker on forward-time splits, then canary a model/index package with exposure logging and controlled A/B tests. Online feature updates also deduplicate event IDs; a replay must not double user behavior. Monitor train/serve skew, feature age and eventual label quality separately from ingestion uptime. Validate duplicate mobile batches, out-of-order events, crash between checkpoint/write, enrichment correction, archive backfill and privacy deletion. A precise ledger and versioned corrections cost more than best-effort counters, which is the trade-off required by this prompt.
solution.trap: Exactly-once accepted-event aggregates need a contribution ledger/checkpoint boundary; offline devices prevent instantaneous completeness.
solution.teaching_notes_markdown:
### Define exactly what “full accuracy” covers

Acknowledge accepted events only after replicated durable append; SDKs retain a durable retry spool and stable event IDs until acknowledged. No finite mobile device can guarantee delivery after data is erased or never reconnects, so full accuracy means no dropped/double-counted **accepted** events and explicit reporting of collection gaps. A subsecond query can return a fast result with a completeness watermark; instantaneous globally complete counts are impossible when devices send late/offline.

At 100 million events/day the mean is 1,157/s. Assume tenfold peak and 500 bytes/event: about 11,574/s, 5.79 MB/s peak and 50 GB/day raw before compression/replicas. `POST /events:batch` accepts event_id,user pseudonym,device/session,tenant,event_type,event_time,schema_version and payload; return per-batch ACK/rejection. Store immutable raw events plus schema/consent metadata and a restricted identity mapping. Partition the durable log by user/device for local ordering; hot campaigns can use hash subshards.

### Enrichment and exact aggregates

The diagram's SDK→collector→durable log branches to raw archive, enrichment/stream aggregation and asynchronous warehouse. Reverse geolocation and compliance tags use versioned datasets, with address minimization/access controls; preserve original event and enrich_version so reprocessing is reproducible. Slow enrichment should not indefinitely block basic accepted-event counting: label pending/unknown dimensions and revise when enrichment arrives, rather than discard rows. Avoid raw IP in ordinary logs.

Deduplicate event_id with a retention horizon covering retries/replay, or retain a durable event/contribution ledger. Atomically checkpoint input offsets plus dedup/aggregate changes, or write idempotent per-batch contributions keyed by immutable batch ID. A retry cannot add another click. Event-time buckets keep sum/count by tenant/type/campaign/dimensions; late events or corrected enrichment retract the old contribution and add the new one. Materialized OLAP tables and preaggregated rollups serve subsecond dashboard queries; arbitrary deep joins go to asynchronous warehouse jobs. Raw object events enable backfill into a new aggregate generation, followed by validation and atomic pointer swap, not double addition to live counters.

### APIs, ML loop and operations

`GET /metrics` restricts dimensions/time/step and returns data_as_of/completeness. `POST /queries` creates a warehouse job with status/results APIs. Apply tenant query budgets, dimension cardinality limits, consent deletion and audit trails. SDK/schema versions, invalid records and dropped-spool counters remain observable. Region/consumer failure replays accepted log data; unresolved enrichment can delay dimensional completeness without falsely labeling it exact.

For recommendations, point-in-time joins produce user/item features and mature exposure→click/conversion labels; future events cannot leak into training. Shared transformations publish versioned online features, train a retrieval/ranker on forward-time splits, then canary a model/index package with exposure logging and controlled A/B tests. Online feature updates also deduplicate event IDs; a replay must not double user behavior. Monitor train/serve skew, feature age and eventual label quality separately from ingestion uptime. Validate duplicate mobile batches, out-of-order events, crash between checkpoint/write, enrichment correction, archive backfill and privacy deletion. A precise ledger and versioned corrections cost more than best-effort counters, which is the trade-off required by this prompt.

title: Design an Observability Logging System (Emit and Query)
question:
Design an observability logging system: services emit structured log events, and engineers query them during incidents and for audits.

Scale and requirements
1.
Fleet: 3,000 services. On average they emit 200,000 log events per second in total. Peak traffic is 5 times the average. One service can produce 10% of all traffic.
2.
Event: a timestamp, a service name, a host, a level (DEBUG to FATAL), a trace id, free-form key/value labels, and a message. The average encoded size is 400 bytes.
3.
Emit path: a client library inside each service sends events. Logging must never block a request or crash the service. Under normal operation, at most 0.1% of events may be lost. During an outage of the logging backend, the system may drop events, but it must count what it dropped.
4.
Query path:
Filter by time range, service, level and labels. Results come back newest first. For the last hour of one service, the p95 latency must be under 2 seconds.
Search for a substring or token in the message over the last 7 days, within 30 seconds.
Live tail of one service, with under 5 seconds from emit to display.
5.
Retention: 7 days searchable at full speed. 90 days in total for audit, where slower queries are acceptable.
6.
Multi-tenancy: one noisy service must not slow down ingestion or queries for the others.
Deliverables
1.
The architecture from the client library to storage. Name every component and what it buffers.
2.
The storage layout: how events are partitioned, indexed and compressed, and why that layout serves the queries in requirement 4.
3.
Capacity estimates for ingest bandwidth, daily storage, hot and cold storage, and the number of partitions in the ingest queue.
4.
The failure behaviour: the backend is down, a partition is lagging, a service floods the system, or a query is too expensive.
5.
Which requirement you would relax first if the cost had to fall by half, and what users would notice.

solution.example: If cost must halve, first propose reducing **seven-day full-speed arbitrary substring search** to shorter hot retention or slower archived substring scans, subject to owner agreement. Users notice slower older searches; preserve 90-day audit data and recent incident filters/live tail first. The savings need a measured breakdown—halving one tier does not guarantee halving total spend. Test backend outage, disk-full agent, 10% noisy service burst, lost ACK, stale cursors and multi-tenant queries; monitor normal/outage drop counts, queue lag, searchable freshness, query p95 and archive completeness.
solution.trap: Token index does not satisfy arbitrary substring search; nonblocking finite client buffers imply measured/countable loss.
solution.teaching_notes_markdown:
### Client-to-storage path and capacity

The client API enqueues structured events into a bounded lock-efficient RAM ring and returns without blocking the application. A background agent batches, compresses and optionally spools to bounded disk; failures increment drop counters by service/reason outside the overloaded logging path. Validate/redact secrets before export. Under normal operation measure loss≤0.1%; during prolonged backend outage explicitly drop lower-priority events when buffers fill, reserving capacity for ERROR/FATAL. “Never block/crash” and finite buffering preclude unconditional losslessness.

200,000 events/s×400 bytes is **80 MB/s**, **6.912 TB/day** raw average. Fivefold peak is **one million events/s and 400 MB/s**. Seven raw days are **48.384 TB**, and 90 total raw days **622.08 TB** before compression/replicas/indexes. Assuming 4:1 compression, seven hot days are 12.096 TB compressed logical and the remaining 83 days are 143.424 TB compressed logical; hot three-way replication is 36.288 TB, excluding search indexes and archive coding. Benchmark the compression/index multiplier; these are explicit sizing assumptions.

Assume an ingest partition sustains 10 MB/s at safe load: peak needs 40, choose 80 for headroom/skew. Partition by tenant/service plus hash(host/batch), not solely service, since one service is 10% of traffic (40 MB/s peak under proportional load). Replicated queue brokers buffer ingest batches; stream/index workers buffer bounded decode batches; hot columnar/search shards hold indexed chunks; object storage holds immutable compressed audit chunks. Each buffer has a quota, age metric and overflow behavior.

### Layout and query contracts

Event schema includes event_id,tenant,event/ingest times,service,host,level,trace_id,labels,message,source boot/sequence. Partition hot storage by tenant/service/time and hash within very large services; sort chunks by timestamp and build service/level/selected-label indexes. Token inverted indexes accelerate text search; arbitrary substring search needs n-gram indexes or bounded scans, with significantly higher index/storage cost. Specify both because token search alone does not meet substring requirements. Seven days stay on searchable hot shards; days 8–90 use compressed object partitions with catalog/min-max metadata for slower audits.

`POST /logs:batch` authenticates source and returns accepted/rejected IDs; `GET /logs` filters time/service/level/labels with newest-first (time,id) cursors pinned to a high-watermark; `POST /search` runs bounded seven-day message searches; `/tail` uses a reconnectable stream cursor. Last-hour single-service queries target p95<2 s by pruning chunks/indexes, and text search has a 30 s budget with cancellation/partial status. Live tail follows committed ingest offsets and batches under five seconds; slow clients get a gap/resync marker. Access control and redaction apply to live tail and archive as well as search.

### Faults, isolation and cost reduction

Backend down: agents spool then count/drop under policy, never block request threads. Lagging partition: autoscale/rebalance consumers, show completeness lag and retain durable batches. Flooding service: per-service ingest credits, isolated queues/shards and fair query concurrency prevent it consuming every partition. Expensive query: cost estimate, limits, timeout and async export protect other tenants. Duplicate batch IDs deduplicate retried accepted logs if the promised count requires it; diagnostic log loss is separately measured. Retain tombstones and versioned redaction/deletion policies for audits.

If cost must halve, first propose reducing **seven-day full-speed arbitrary substring search** to shorter hot retention or slower archived substring scans, subject to owner agreement. Users notice slower older searches; preserve 90-day audit data and recent incident filters/live tail first. The savings need a measured breakdown—halving one tier does not guarantee halving total spend. Test backend outage, disk-full agent, 10% noisy service burst, lost ACK, stale cursors and multi-tenant queries; monitor normal/outage drop counts, queue lag, searchable freshness, query p95 and archive completeness.
