### Architecture and request flow

![Design a Top-K trending items service: request, processing, state and result components.](../diagrams/W352_architecture.svg)

[Open the diagram at full size](../diagrams/W352_architecture.svg). This is a baseline component diagram for this question. The boxes describe responsibilities; they do not require a separate microservice for every box.

- **Request and state:** Timestamped events — object + event id → Stream ingress — deduplicate + partition. That component consults or updates **Durable event log — replay + retention** under the required access and consistency rules.
- **Work and result:** the work path passes through **Windowed aggregators — event-time + watermark** and **Merge top-K candidates — approximation + error**, producing **Ranked query result — window + freshness**. Bound waiting and retries where a slow dependency can stall this path.
- **Correctness point:** State the time window and approximation; expired events and late arrivals must have a defined correction rule.

When explaining the drawing, trace one normal request first, then a duplicate request, an unavailable dependency and recovery from saved state. If the question requires stricter guarantees or a different scope, state the change explicitly rather than treating this baseline as the only possible design.
<!-- architecture:W352:end -->

### Event and API contract

Accept batches of `{event_id,item_id,event_type,event_time,region}` into a replicated durable log only after validation; weights are view1, like3, comment4, share5. Reject unknown types/invalid future timestamps under a declared clock-skew policy. `GET /trending?scope=global|region&region=&window=10m|1h|24h&k=1..100` returns ordered `(item_id,score)` plus mode, snapshot timestamp, watermark, window bounds and staleness. Ties use item_id ascending. Serve immutable top100 snapshots from regional caches/edge caches; a request for smaller K slices the same version.

Use event-id partitioning first for authoritative dedup, then repartition accepted weighted events by item for full global totals and by `(region,item)` for regional totals. A duplicate id with conflicting payload is quarantined, not counted as a new event. Dedup persistence must cover replay/retry horizon; a short cache alone is not exact. Each processor atomically commits dedup/window state with input offsets or an equivalent idempotent transaction.

### Exact bucketed sliding windows and lateness

Define snapshot time T on its required bucket boundary and membership `[T-W,T)`. Maintain10-second buckets for 10m (60 active buckets) and 1-minute buckets for 1 h/24 h (60/1440). “Exact” means exact to these bucket boundaries, as permitted. Add accepted arrivals to their event-time bucket and corresponding rolling totals, expire whole old buckets by subtracting their stored per-item contributions, and update an ordered score index `(negative_score,item_id)` for each scope/window. Keep buckets through needed lateness/recovery horizon; do not expire history merely because processing wall time advanced.

Define a coordinated monotone watermark M from healthy source-partition progress with explicit idle-source handling. The question's lateness rule is **event_time<M-5min → drop from every window and increment late_dropped**, even if that event would fit 24 h. At exactly M-5min accept under this chosen inclusive allowance. Otherwise apply it only to windows containing event_time; old accepted events outside10m need not alter10m. An event7 minutes behind M is dropped; a share for c2 minutes late adds 5 and is reflected in the next≤10 s publish. Do not first apply24 h then discover it was too late. Revisions to already published snapshots carry a new version/as_of.

Key-owned items let each shard maintain its complete score; hot items can be salted into subshards with mini-batch `(item,bucket,region)` deltas, then a second keyed reducer reconstructs the **full item total before ranking**. Dedup remains global by event id. Partition timers expire buckets even during no new events, so quiet items leave rankings on time. For a 30, b17, c22 snapshot, K2 is[a, c]. Delete zero scores and never serve an expired heap entry as current.

### When local top-K merging is exact

If each item belongs wholly to exactly one ranking shard, any global topK item must be in that shard's topK under the same total order; otherwise K items on that shard already outrank it globally. Thus union/sort local top100 is exact for K≤100. If an item is split across shards, local topK can miss it: shard1 has a 60, x61, shard2 has a 60, y61; local top1 gives x/y but a's global120 wins. Aggregate split-item totals first, use provable candidate upper bounds/threshold algorithms, or label a heuristic merge approximate. The same warning applies when merging regional lists into a global ranking.

### Approximate/hybrid option with a real error contract

For nonnegative weighted events, Count-Min Sketch with width ceil(e/epsilon), depth ceil(log(1/delta)) gives for a fixed key $f\le\hat f\le f+\epsilon F$ with probability≥1-delta, F total weight, using O((1/epsilon)log(1/delta)) counters. It cannot enumerate keys: add a Space-Saving/Misra–Gries-style candidate tracker or exact candidate dictionary. Space-Saving with m counters has count error bounded by F/m and retains sufficiently heavy items; distinguish its overestimation from Misra–Gries undercounts. Keep per-time-bucket sketches/candidates and combine only live buckets; arbitrary expiration subtraction without preserving the required sketch/update guarantees is unsafe. Positive-only insert bucket sketches are simplest.

Use sketches to nominate candidates, then fetch exact bucket totals for the candidate union and sort, disclosing candidate-recall uncertainty. Exact candidate scores do not make topK exact if a missing candidate could beat them. When count intervals overlap the cutoff, expand candidates or return approximation/error bounds. Late accepted events update their bucket sketch; dropped events never enter any bucket. False-positive Bloom dedup would undercount and invalidates an exact claim, so use it only before an authoritative id check or label the approximation.

### Capacity and recovery

10B/day=115,741/s average; peak2M/s. At a chosen100 bytes/event, raw log ≈ 1 TB/day, average 11.6 MB/s and peak200 MB/s; replication3 is 3 TB/day before headers/indexes. Retain at least 24 h+5m plus operational replay margin; seven days chosen is 7 TB raw/21 TB replicated. Exact event-id dedup at 32 bytes/entry is 320 GB/day logical, or 2.24 TB for seven days before indexes/replication; compact durable id partitions or a bounded upstream retry contract is essential. Exactly-once guarantees beyond that retention horizon require an archival identity authority or a documented limit.

Window state depends on **nonempty item-region-bucket pairs**, not just event count. A pessimistic one-record/event representation at 24 bytes and 10B active-day events is 240 GB before extra10m/1 h indexes; millions of items/regions and repeated hot keys change sparse compression dramatically. Sum state, dedup and sorted indexes before sizing. A chosen100 GB checkpoint every 60 s needs1.67 GB/s aggregate write bandwidth plus replicas; incremental checkpoints reduce it, but measure actual state. Every10 s, P ranking shards publish 100 candidates per scope/window; at 100 shards, 3 windows, 101 scopes and 32 bytes/candidate this is ~97 MB/snapshot, 9.7 MB/s before regional fanout. Adjust region cardinality explicitly.

At 1M reads/s and an assumed 4 KB result, global response bandwidth is 4 GB/s; edge/regional caching amortizes origin reads but not client egress. Publish versioned snapshots atomically per window/scope, with short cache refresh and last-good fallback. Reads can survive a processor outage but must reveal stale timestamp/mode; never call it fresh after lag exceeds10 s.

Checkpoint processor state/offsets/watermark and immutable snapshot versions; recovery replays without duplicate application. On resharding move keyed state and offset ownership under a barrier/epoch so two reducers cannot publish competing totals. Backpressure buffers in the log, autoscale and throttle/quarantine bad sources; if capacity cannot catch up, disclose lag or switch to an explicit approximate mode, not silent event loss. Monitor accepted/duplicate/late_dropped, watermark/source skew, hot-key load, checkpoint duration, recovery and observed snapshot age/p99. title: Design a Trending-Hashtags Detection System
question:
Design a backend that detects and serves trending hashtags from posts. Requirements: surface trends while the real-world event is still happening (target ~1-minute end-to-end freshness), score posts from the last 24 hours with recency weighting, reflect broad community interest (not one small cluster spamming), require novelty (a new topic or a sharp spike vs its own baseline), and serve the ranked list with low read latency.

The hard part is combining recency, popularity, and novelty without letting stale evergreen tags dominate.

steps: Define a score that measures new broad interest
solution.example: Popularity is recency-weighted distinct contribution over 24 h: for tag h use $P_h(t)=\sum_{author\ a}\min(c,\sum_{posts\ p\in(a,h)}q_p e^{-(t-t_p)/\tau})$ with no contribution beyond24 h, chosen tau perhaps 2 h and author cap c. This reduces one author's spam but not an organized cluster; additionally require minimum independent authors and community spread (for example effective communities exp(entropy) or a maximum share from one trusted community cluster), plus platform-integrity filters. Community inference is noisy and must not suppress a real small-region event automatically; tune scope-specific thresholds with human audits.
solution.trap: Community inference is noisy and must not suppress a real small-region event automatically; tune scope-specific thresholds with human audits.

<!-- architecture:W353:start -->
### Architecture and request flow

![Design a Trending-Hashtags Detection System: request, processing, state and result components.](../diagrams/W353_architecture.svg)

[Open the diagram at full size](../diagrams/W353_architecture.svg). This is a baseline component diagram for this question. The boxes describe responsibilities; they do not require a separate microservice for every box.

- **Request and state:** Timestamped events — object + event id → Stream ingress — deduplicate + partition. That component consults or updates **Durable event log — replay + retention** under the required access and consistency rules.
- **Work and result:** the work path passes through **Windowed aggregators — event-time + watermark** and **Merge top-K candidates — approximation + error**, producing **Ranked query result — window + freshness**. Bound waiting and retries where a slow dependency can stall this path.
- **Correctness point:** State the time window and approximation; expired events and late arrivals must have a defined correction rule.

When explaining the drawing, trace one normal request first, then a duplicate request, an unavailable dependency and recovery from saved state. If the question requires stricter guarantees or a different scope, state the change explicitly rather than treating this baseline as the only possible design.
<!-- architecture:W353:end -->

### Define a score that measures new broad interest

Assume posts supply post_id, author_id, event_time, hashtags, language, region and an abuse-quality signal. Normalize hashtag case/Unicode under a versioned policy, resolve aliases cautiously and deduplicate a tag within a post. Use a durable post stream with update/delete corrections. `GET /trends?region=&language=&k=` returns rank, score components, topic label, as_of and freshness; a minute-level snapshot cache keeps reads cheap.

Popularity is recency-weighted distinct contribution over 24 h: for tag h use $P_h(t)=\sum_{author\ a}\min(c,\sum_{posts\ p\in(a,h)}q_p e^{-(t-t_p)/\tau})$ with no contribution beyond24 h, chosen tau perhaps 2 h and author cap c. This reduces one author's spam but not an organized cluster; additionally require minimum independent authors and community spread (for example effective communities exp(entropy) or a maximum share from one trusted community cluster), plus platform-integrity filters. Community inference is noisy and must not suppress a real small-region event automatically; tune scope-specific thresholds with human audits.

Estimate the tag's expected current rate from older same-hour/day-of-week data, excluding the current spike, using a smoothed robust baseline b_h. Novelty can be log((recent_rate+alpha)/(b_h+alpha)) with a minimum absolute-volume gate and uncertainty correction. A tag with 1 mention after 0 must not outrank a large real event merely due to an infinite ratio. Rank a bounded combination such as log1p(P)·max(0, novelty)·breadth after eligibility checks; coefficients/tau/gates are product hypotheses calibrated against editorial/user relevance labels, not universal constants.

### Stream computation and freshness

Partition by tag and maintain minute buckets for counts, capped author contributions and community distribution; decay aggregates incrementally and expire24 h-old state. Keep a separate longer-baseline history. Exact distinct authors need expiring per-author/tag state; sketches lower memory but cannot exactly undo arbitrary deletions/expiry, so use per-bucket sketches with disclosed error or exact candidate refinement. Extremely hot tags salt partial buckets, then merge full tag features before ranking; local fragment topK is insufficient.

Budget roughly 10 s intake/dedup, 20 s aggregation/feature update, 10 s rank/abuse checks and 10 s snapshot publication within a chosen60 s target, leaving10 s slack; measure the joint tail. Handle lateness with a stated watermark/correction horizon and versioned snapshots. Ranks refresh even when no posts arrive because recency decays. Persist state/offset checkpoints and raw permitted posts for replay; deletion/abuse decisions retract contributions and invalidate cached snapshots.

### Worked comparison and evaluation

An evergreen tag with 100k/day but stable recent activity has large P and near-zero novelty, so it can be in “popular” without being “trending.” A new regional earthquake tag with 10k recent independent authors across communities and a large baseline spike passes both novelty and breadth. Ten thousand repetitions by ten coordinated accounts fail cap/spread checks despite raw volume. Cold-start b uses a prior and absolute-volume threshold, not division by zero.

Evaluate event-detection delay, human-labeled trend precision/recall, novelty, community diversity, spam resistance and regional fairness, plus latency/cost/freshness. Compare to raw24 h count and recent-rate baselines with historical replay, using holdout events and attack simulations. Monitor stale evergreen leakage, bot share, accepted/retracted volume and model/score versions; canary rank changes and serve last-good snapshots labeled stale during outages. The diagram's bucket/merge path now computes these concrete recency/baseline/breadth features, rather than an unexplained generic count.

title: Design State-Wide Temperature Sensor Ingestion
question:
Design an ingestion pipeline for a temperature sensor every N square miles across a state. Serve three queries: the latest temperature per sensor, the global top-K hottest sensors, and a real-time heat map of the entire state.

Requirements
Functional: ingest sensor readings (sensor_id, lat, lon, temperature, timestamp); answer getLatest(sensor_id) -> reading; answer topK(K) -> list of (sensor_id, temperature); render a heat map over the state at a configurable spatial resolution.
Non-functional: ingestion sustained at thousands to tens of thousands of readings per second; queries served with sub-second latency; the heat map should be smoothly refreshable in a browser without re-ingesting raw points.
Data model: SensorRegistry (sensor_id, lat, lon, geohash, last_seen); hot store keyed by sensor_id (last reading); cold time-series store (sensor_id, ts) -> temperature; pre-aggregated heat-map tiles keyed by (zoom_level, tile_x, tile_y).
Notes
The three queries point at three different storage layouts; the right answer separates them explicitly rather than forcing one store to serve all three.

steps: Use three views for three different questions
Conditional latest, topK replacement and tiles
solution.example: Let state area be A square miles and density one sensor/N square miles: sensor count ≈ A/N, not a fixed number without A, N. As a chosen illustration100k sensors reporting every 10 s produce10k readings/s. Ingest `{sensor_id,sequence,event_time,lat,lon,temperature,unit}` through authenticated batched gateway → durable log partitioned by sensor. Validate registry location/calibration, plausible ranges, unit conversion, timestamp skew and duplicate sequence; quarantine suspect readings rather than silently distorting the heat map.
solution.trap: Validate registry location/calibration, plausible ranges, unit conversion, timestamp skew and duplicate sequence; quarantine suspect readings rather than silently distorting the heat map.

### Architecture and request flow

![Temperature readings and three serving views](../diagrams/W354_final_architecture.svg)

[Open the diagram](../diagrams/W354_final_architecture.svg). The ingestion stream feeds three access paths: latest-by-sensor, ranking over current sensor values, and spatial tiles. Replacing a reading removes its old contribution before applying the new value. The raw time-series archive supports replay; it is not scanned for every browser refresh.
<!-- architecture:W354:end -->

### Use three views for three different questions

Let state area be A square miles and density one sensor/N square miles: sensor count ≈ A/N, not a fixed number without A, N. As a chosen illustration100k sensors reporting every 10 s produce10k readings/s. Ingest `{sensor_id,sequence,event_time,lat,lon,temperature,unit}` through authenticated batched gateway → durable log partitioned by sensor. Validate registry location/calibration, plausible ranges, unit conversion, timestamp skew and duplicate sequence; quarantine suspect readings rather than silently distorting the heat map.

Persist `SensorRegistry(id,location,geohash,calibration,last_seen)`, append-only cold `(sensor,event_time,sequence)->reading`, hot `Latest(sensor)->(time,sequence,temp,quality,version)` and spatial `Tile(zoom,x,y,version)->cells(sum,count,min,max,freshness)`. APIs are `GET /sensors/{id}/latest`, `GET /hottest?k=&as_of=`, and `GET /tiles/{z}/{x}/{y}?version=` plus a lightweight tile-version update stream. Define topK as **latest valid nonstale temperature per sensor**, not all-time maximum; choose a stale threshold and deterministic sensor-id ties.

### Conditional latest, topK replacement and tiles

Compare `(event_time,sequence)` before overwriting Latest, so an older late arrival stays in cold history and cannot roll current temperature backward. For each accepted latest transition, update an ordered per-partition set by removing the old sensor score and inserting the new. Each sensor belongs to one owner shard, so union of local topK lists is sufficient for global topK under a consistent snapshot; asynchronously salt-free latest ownership avoids double membership. On stale timeout remove the sensor from active topK, label missing data and preserve last-observed time.

Heat-map materialization updates the sensor's spatial cell by **subtracting its previous current contribution then adding its new one**, not averaging every historical measurement and overweighting chatty sensors. Produce a zoom pyramid of cached raster/vector tiles; each cell stores sum/count and freshness, with interpolation only under a declared method/density/uncertainty mask. A cell with no fresh sensors is missing, not 0degrees. If sensor coordinates change, retract its old tile contribution before inserting the new. Publish tile versions/deltas so browser pan/zoom/refresh fetches changed tiles rather than every raw point.

### Size, failures and evidence

At 10k/s and 64B logical reading, raw volume ≈ 55.3 GB/day (before metadata/replicas); 100k latest rows at 64B are 6.4 MB logical. Tiles grow with chosen resolution/zoom, so cap zoom and cache hot views; point reads and small topK snapshots can stay subsecond independently of cold analytics. Do not send all sensor points to every browser just to redraw a heat map.

Commit state/offsets or idempotent transition versions so replay cannot double-add tile sums. Checkpoint latest/topK/tile views and rebuild from cold/log history; during failure serve last-good versions with explicit age. Degraded sensor health/clock skew/data gaps are separately monitored. Test late readings, equal timestamps, location changes, negative temperatures, stale expiry, no-data cells and a duplicate replay. The corrected diagram should branch one reading stream into latest KV, latest-temperature score index and spatial tile aggregation; a generic alerting chart does not answer these three APIs.

title: Near-Real-Time Friend-Played-Game Counter
question:
Design a service that, for a given (user, game) pair, surfaces near-real-time signals: how many of the user's friends have played the game, plus the total active-player count for the game.

Targets: ~10M users and ~100k games. The core challenge is the fan-out from a play event to every friend of the player without overwhelming the storage layer during peak hours.

steps: Avoid writing to every friend on every heartbeat
Total active users needs refcounts and expiry
solution.example: For example, 1k play events/s with mean 200 friends implies200k writes/s if naively fanned out; a 10k-friend user produces10k writes for one event, and heartbeat-driven repetition makes it worse. Coalescing to one first-play transition and computing high-degree/cold cases on read limits amplification. Cache common viewer/game queries, but authorize the viewer and include social/privacy/version changes so an unfriended/blocked player does not remain exposed. Edge add/remove events update cached intersections or invalidate/rebuild; do not assume the friend graph is static.
solution.trap: Cache common viewer/game queries, but authorize the viewer and include social/privacy/version changes so an unfriended/blocked player does not remain exposed.

<!-- architecture:W355:start -->
### Architecture and request flow

![Played-game relationships and active-session counts](../diagrams/W355_final_architecture.svg)

[Open the diagram](../diagrams/W355_final_architecture.svg). A permanent played relationship and a currently active session are different facts. Friend-played queries intersect friends with the game's played set, with selective cached/materialized results where needed. Session heartbeats refresh activity rather than repeatedly fan out a new friend counter increment.
<!-- architecture:W355:end -->

### Define “played” and “active” separately

Choose “friend has played” as a distinct user–game relation within a declared horizon (all-time by default), while “active player” means at least one live session/heartbeat in the last5 minutes, a chosen product definition. If product wants24 h players or simultaneous connections, change the state/expiry contract explicitly. 10M users and 100k games do not imply a 10¹²-cell dense matrix: store sparse `(player,game,last_played)` edges, social friend sets with versions/privacy, active session state and per-game active totals. APIs return `GET /users/me/games/{g}/signals` with friend_distinct_count, total_active, as_of and horizon.

### Avoid writing to every friend on every heartbeat

A raw session heartbeat updates only its player's session/expiry state. A player–game transition from never-played to played (or inactive to active if that is the desired friend metric) is the only potential fanout trigger; repeated plays do not increment a distinct count. For normal-degree users, fan out a deduplicated relation transition to friends' cached `(viewer,game)` materializations. Batch/coalesce updates by viewer/game and shard destination ownership. For high-degree/celebrity users or cold viewers, use read-time set intersection: current friend ids ∩ game player set, with compressed bitmaps/hash sets. Maintain a hybrid threshold based on measured degree, event rate and read heat, not a universal fixed degree.

For example, 1k play events/s with mean 200 friends implies200k writes/s if naively fanned out; a 10k-friend user produces10k writes for one event, and heartbeat-driven repetition makes it worse. Coalescing to one first-play transition and computing high-degree/cold cases on read limits amplification. Cache common viewer/game queries, but authorize the viewer and include social/privacy/version changes so an unfriended/blocked player does not remain exposed. Edge add/remove events update cached intersections or invalidate/rebuild; do not assume the friend graph is static.

### Total active users needs refcounts and expiry

Store per `(player,game)` active session refcount or latest accepted heartbeat expiry; multiple devices/sessions contribute **one** active player. On 0 → 1 increment a game counter shard, on 1 → 0 after the last session expires decrement. Timer/version checks prevent an old timeout expiring a newer heartbeat. Dedup session/event ids and use stable transitions; negative clamping does not repair replay. Shard hot game totals by player hash, periodically sum and publish cached near-real-time counts. Distinct all-time played edges do not expire merely because a current session ends.

Use durable logs/outbox plus versioned projection state/offsets and reconcile against canonical relations/session snapshots after failures. At a chosen average 20 games/user, sparse played edges are 200M; at 24B logical payload ≈ 4.8 GB before indexes/replicas, while graph/storage overhead can dominate. Friend count and total active may have different freshness; return timestamps rather than pretend one atomic global instant. Monitor fanout amplification, degree skew, projection lag, cache invalidation, active expiry and privacy failures. Test duplicate play, two sessions/one user, last-session expiry, friend removal and hot-user fallback. The diagram must show play/session and social relation sources, not like/unlike API labels.

title: Real-time status counting system design
question:
Real-time status counting system design

Assume there are one million devices that send a heartbeat and a status (out of 10 possible statuses) every minute. You need to design a system that can compute the count of devices for each status from the previous minute in real-time.

*A generic Python 3 code stub was provided in the editor (boilerplate def solution(): ... # Read data from standard input with an if __name__ == "__main__": block), but the task is an open-ended system design question rather than a testable coding exercise.*

solution.example: Ingest `{device_id,event_id|sequence,event_time,status}` via authenticated batches into a durable log, partition by hash(device_id), validate status/time skew and retain a declared lateness allowance (for example 10 s). Store `DeviceMinute(device_id,minute,latest_time,sequence,status)` plus partition-local ten-element count vectors. On the first accepted heartbeat for a device/minute increment its status; on a later status in the **same** minute decrement old and increment new; duplicate/stale sequence does nothing. This counts devices, not raw messages. Previous-minute counts remain provisional until watermark passes its end plus the chosen grace rule, then finalized/versioned.
solution.trap: Ten statuses are an enum, and missing devices appear in a separate missing/offline count rather than being assumed to have their last status.

### Architecture and request flow

![Real-time status counting system design: request, processing, state and result components.](../diagrams/W356_architecture.svg)

[Open the diagram at full size](../diagrams/W356_architecture.svg). This is a baseline component diagram for this question. The boxes describe responsibilities; they do not require a separate microservice for every box.

- **Request and state:** Entity state event — entity id + version → Event intake — deduplicate + order check. That component consults or updates **Latest entity state — authoritative version** under the required access and consistency rules.
- **Work and result:** the work path passes through **State transition stream — old group to new group** and **Count projection — idempotent delta + reconcile**, producing **Group status counts — freshness + rebuild path**. Bound waiting and retries where a slow dependency can stall this path.
- **Correctness point:** Count state transitions rather than raw messages; duplicates and out-of-order events must not inflate totals.

When explaining the drawing, trace one normal request first, then a duplicate request, an unavailable dependency and recovery from saved state. If the question requires stricter guarantees or a different scope, state the change explicitly rather than treating this baseline as the only possible design.
<!-- architecture:W356:end -->

### Define the minute before counting

There are 1M/60 ≈ 16,667 heartbeats/s average, potentially1M/s if devices synchronize at a minute boundary. Add randomized device jitter and provision for measured bursts. Choose a **tumbling previous calendar minute** `[floor(now/60)*60-60,floor(now/60)*60)` in UTC, counting each device once at its latest valid heartbeat/status in that minute. A rolling trailing 60 s or “current latest status with a 60 s TTL” answers different questions; expose those separately if needed. Ten statuses are an enum, and missing devices appear in a separate missing/offline count rather than being assumed to have their last status.

Ingest `{device_id,event_id|sequence,event_time,status}` via authenticated batches into a durable log, partition by hash(device_id), validate status/time skew and retain a declared lateness allowance (for example 10 s). Store `DeviceMinute(device_id,minute,latest_time,sequence,status)` plus partition-local ten-element count vectors. On the first accepted heartbeat for a device/minute increment its status; on a later status in the **same** minute decrement old and increment new; duplicate/stale sequence does nothing. This counts devices, not raw messages. Previous-minute counts remain provisional until watermark passes its end plus the chosen grace rule, then finalized/versioned.

### Query, recovery and checks

Reduce partition vectors under a common minute/snapshot boundary into a cached `MinuteCounts(minute,status_counts,seen_devices,missing,watermark,final)` record; `GET /status-counts?minute=previous` reads it, never scans1M device rows. Heartbeats that are late but within allowance revise that minute; beyond allowance are rejected/dropped with a metric and do not corrupt the current minute. Expire per-device/minute state only after lateness/replay safety; preserve id/sequence dedup long enough for retries.

At a chosen32B/device-minute entry, two active minutes are 64 MB logical state before database overhead; raw64B heartbeats are ~92 GB/day at 1M/min. Checkpoint state with offsets and replay idempotently; preserve last good snapshot with its age if aggregation is unavailable. question:
Design the last-minute like-count backend: exact count for one post, global top posts over the last minute, and region-based top posts over the same window. Peak ~1M likes/sec, average 100K-300K/sec.

One viable split
Exact point query: Redis hash buckets keyed by post and second; sum the latest 60 buckets at read time.

This differs from “relationships newly liked during the minute and still active”: that alternative must retract the original like's bucket when it is unliked. To avoid negative/unintuitive trending, a useful product choice is the latter active-recent-like metric: store each active `(user,post)` edge's like timestamp and region; unlike retracts that original live-window contribution, and unlike after it expired adds no negative current contribution. ### Architecture and request flow

![Recent Like Count and Top Posts in a Sliding Window: request, processing, state and result components.](../diagrams/W357_architecture.svg)

[Open the diagram at full size](../diagrams/W357_architecture.svg). This is a baseline component diagram for this question. The boxes describe responsibilities; they do not require a separate microservice for every box.

- **Request and state:** Timestamped events — object + event id → Stream ingress — deduplicate + partition. That component consults or updates **Durable event log — replay + retention** under the required access and consistency rules.
- **Work and result:** the work path passes through **Windowed aggregators — event-time + watermark** and **Merge top-K candidates — approximation + error**, producing **Ranked query result — window + freshness**. Bound waiting and retries where a slow dependency can stall this path.
- **Correctness point:** State the time window and approximation; expired events and late arrivals must have a defined correction rule.

When explaining the drawing, trace one normal request first, then a duplicate request, an unavailable dependency and recovery from saved state. If the question requires stricter guarantees or a different scope, state the change explicitly rather than treating this baseline as the only possible design.
<!-- architecture:W357:end -->

### Define what a “recent like” means

Choose accepted like-transition **events** in `[T-60s,T)`, with unlike as a signed reversal under a declared policy. This differs from “relationships newly liked during the minute and still active”: that alternative must retract the original like's bucket when it is unliked. To avoid negative/unintuitive trending, a useful product choice is the latter active-recent-like metric: store each active `(user,post)` edge's like timestamp and region; unlike retracts that original live-window contribution, and unlike after it expired adds no negative current contribution. State the choice in the response rather than quietly mixing event flow and state counts.

Mutation API uses desired state/idempotency/version and server-derived user/region; only false → true emits a counted edge event. `GET /posts/{id}/recent-likes?as_of=` returns count/window/watermark; `GET /trending?region=&k=` returns a snapshot with mode/as_of. Authoritative edge update plus outbox prevents retry overcount and allows unlike to name the matching version. Region is fixed at the original event under this chosen event-region metric, not retroactively moved when a user travels.

### Exact point path and ranked projection

Maintain per `(post,salt,second)` contributions and dedup/transition state, using atomic consumer state/offset commits. For second-aligned T, sum seconds T-60 through T-1 across salts; Redis Lua/transaction or a snapshot version makes the multi-bucket read consistent with concurrent expiration. A 60-second bucket design is exact only at **second boundaries**, not arbitrary subsecond cutoffs; if literal continuous-time exactness is required retain timestamped contributions for edge buckets. Include projection watermark: a fast Redis count is not instantly authoritative before its stream event arrives.

Kafka/Flink maintains identical event-time rules and per-post/global/region rolling totals, expiring original buckets and retracting only live contributions. Publish sorted-set or immutable top100 snapshots periodically (say1 s) to Redis and serve cached topK. Exact key-owned full-post totals permit merging local topK; if celebrity posts are salted, first recombine all salts for that post or mark candidate-only results approximate. A current topK-only heap is insufficient when top entries expire: retain all active counts/ordered candidates or rebuild from an authoritative count index.

### Capacity, failure and validation

At average 200k/s choose100B log events: 20 MB/s ≈ 1.73 TB/day raw; peak1M/s is 100 MB/s. A minute contains12M average or 60M peak contributions before aggregation/dedup, motivating sparse buckets, coalesced deltas and hot-post salting. Microbatch per-salt updates, bound late-event grace, preserve event/edge version identity and avoid one Redis increment for every raw request on a celebrity key. Durable logs/checkpoints rebuild both projections; cross-path watermarks explain temporary disagreement.

Test retry, unlike before/after expiration, like → unlike → like versions, second-boundary inclusion, out-of-order events, regional provenance and processor replay. Monitor count/rank path lag, stale snapshots, reconciliation differences, hot-shard load and dropped lateness. During overload preserve log events and disclose stale projections; do not call unprocessed likes exact-current. The given Redis/Flink split is viable only with these metric/consistency contracts.

title: Social Media Sentiment Tracking System
question:
Design a system that tracks public sentiment toward Netflix on social media over time: ingest posts, classify sentiment, aggregate, and surface trends so the team can see opinion shift around launches or price changes.

Requirements:

Collect posts from social platforms.
Classify sentiment as positive or negative.
Aggregate results and expose trends over time.
Structure the design into ingestion, aggregation, and offline ML.

steps: Ingestion: identify Netflix mentions and coverage
Aggregation: versioned binary predictions with uncertainty
Offline ML and a defensible trend
solution.example: A bounded inference queue batches a versioned classifier and writes `Prediction(post_version,entity,model_version,p_positive,label,confidence,status)`. Required labels are positive/negative; ambiguous/neutral/sarcastic/mixed examples are an audited uncertain bucket or are forced binary **with that limitation reported**, not silently discarded. An abstention policy should preserve denominator counts/coverage. Idempotent prediction keys ensure retries contribute once.
solution.trap: Match Netflix/company/product aliases with context so an incidental title or ambiguous word does not become a company opinion automatically.

### Architecture and request flow

[Open the diagram at full size](../diagrams/W358_architecture.svg). This is a baseline component diagram for this question. The boxes describe responsibilities; they do not require a separate microservice for every box.

- **Request and state:** Social post stream — post id + event time → Stream intake — deduplicate + access policy. That component consults or updates **Raw posts + model version — retention + corrections** under the required access and consistency rules.
- **Work and result:** the work path passes through **Bounded inference queue — rate + backpressure** and **Sentiment classifier — abstain + schema checks**, producing **Windowed sentiment view — confidence + sampling bias**. Bound waiting and retries where a slow dependency can stall this path.
- **Correctness point:** Do not confuse classifier accuracy with population sentiment; deletions, duplicate posts and sampling affect aggregates.

When explaining the drawing, trace one normal request first, then a duplicate request, an unavailable dependency and recovery from saved state. If the question requires stricter guarantees or a different scope, state the change explicitly rather than treating this baseline as the only possible design.
<!-- architecture:W358:end -->

### Ingestion: identify Netflix mentions and coverage

Collect permitted public posts through platform adapters with API quotas/cursors, retry/backoff and durable checkpointed log intake. Use canonical `(platform,post_id,version)` ids, author/time/language/source metadata and retention/deletion policies. Match Netflix/company/product aliases with context so an incidental title or ambiguous word does not become a company opinion automatically. Deduplicate transport retries; decide whether retweets/reposts represent reach or repeated content and report both views if useful.

Assume 100k posts/minute peak for planning: 1,667/s, not a scale supplied by the problem. A 256B normalized record is~.43 MB/s before text/media expansion; model throughput and source quotas determine actual capacity. Protect private identifiers and do not claim provider access is complete public opinion.

### Aggregation: versioned binary predictions with uncertainty

A bounded inference queue batches a versioned classifier and writes `Prediction(post_version,entity,model_version,p_positive,label,confidence,status)`. Required labels are positive/negative; ambiguous/neutral/sarcastic/mixed examples are an audited uncertain bucket or are forced binary **with that limitation reported**, not silently discarded. An abstention policy should preserve denominator counts/coverage. Idempotent prediction keys ensure retries contribute once.

Stream into minute/hour/day UTC counts by source/language/entity, with event-time lateness/correction rules. Store positive, negative, uncertain, error, total counts and optionally sums of calibrated p_positive, never average batch averages without weights. `GET /sentiment?start=&end=&grain=&source=` serves rollups and volume/coverage/freshness. An edit/reclassification retracts the prior contribution then adds the new one; deletion removes permitted derived content and adjusts counts under policy. A model release must recompute a comparison window or show a version discontinuity, not present an artificial opinion shift as news.

### Offline ML and a defensible trend

Build human-labeled samples stratified by source/language/topic/time, with guidelines for entity target, sarcasm and mixed sentiment; measure agreement and adjudicate. Use lexical/logistic or pretrained-text baselines and fine-tuned alternatives; time/source-family splits avoid duplicate leakage. Evaluate per-class precision/recall/F1, calibration, subgroup errors and drift; select threshold/abstention by validated product costs. Active review prioritizes uncertain/drifting and random audit cases, not only model-approved labels.

For a price change, compare a matched pre/post source/language mix, show post counts and confidence intervals clustered by author/day, annotate coverage/model changes and distinguish correlation from causation.100 positive/100 negative among200 posts is a 50% positive classified sample, not “half of customers approve.” Bots and engagement ranking can change sample composition. Use independent surveys/behavior when the decision needs customer population sentiment.

Monitor source outages, lag, classifier error/uncertainty, bot/duplicate share and per-model distribution; checkpoint state/offsets and replay without duplicate aggregates. During failures serve last-good time-stamped trends and explicit missing-source warnings. The requested architecture is intake → classification/aggregation plus an offline labeling/training/evaluation loop; generic rolling-topK mechanics alone do not solve sentiment quality.

<!-- architecture:W359:start -->
### Architecture and request flow

![Raw search, entity rollups and mention notifications](../diagrams/W359_final_architecture.svg)

[Open the diagram](../diagrams/W359_final_architecture.svg). Raw keyword search and entity-window counts have separate indexes. Entity extraction identifies mentions rather than sentiment. Window versions, late-event handling and rule-trigger deduplication keep chart corrections and notifications explainable; the answer's allowed analytics lag remains explicit.
<!-- architecture:W359:end -->

### Separate raw search from entity analytics and notifications

Choose a planning peak3M events/min=50k/s, 1 KB/event ≈ 50 MB/s or 4.32 TB/day if sustained; weeks of raw retention reaches tens ofTB before replication/indexing. Source-average traffic and compression must replace this peak-based upper planning rate.100k search QPS is a distinct serving workload, so do not send every keyword query to a stream processor or raw object store.

Ingest external article/post batches with source/event/version ids, timestamps, permitted text and checkpoints into a replicated log; archive immutable raw records to object storage. A full-text inverted index is partitioned by time/hash with replicas, analyzers and current-version/delete filtering, supporting boolean keyword combinations and paginated results. Query caches and hot time ranges reduce load, but cache keys include filters/permissions/index version. `GET /search?q=&start=&end=&cursor=` returns id/version snippets; rate-limit expensive wildcard/fuzzy queries rather than let them starve the cluster.

### Entity extraction and time-series state

An entity service resolves company names/tickers using a versioned alias/security master, contextual disambiguation, language and exchange/date metadata. “APPLE” can refer to a company or fruit; store confidence and evidence spans, with an uncertain path/manual audits. `Mention(event_version,entity_id,extraction_version)` is unique per entity/article under a **document-mention** metric; counting every repeated word is another explicit metric. Source edits/deletes retract prior mentions before replacement.

Aggregate event-time tumbling30min/hour/day/week buckets with UTC/market-calendar boundaries declared, lateness/watermark corrections and count/source coverage. Store mergeable counts (and distinct-author sketches only with error contracts) plus immutable historical snapshot versions. `GET /entities/{id}/series?grain=&start=&end=` reads analytical rollups; 10–30min lag allows cost-efficient microbatch extraction/indexing instead of demanding unnecessary millisecond state. Reprocess with new extraction versions without silently mixing series definitions.

### Subscription flow and reliability

`POST /subscriptions` records user, entity/filter, threshold, window, cooldown, destination and policy version. Evaluate subscriptions against closed/revised bucket transitions, e.g. mentions>N/hour with strict equality behavior, and emit a unique `Alert(subscription,bucket,threshold_version)` through an outbox. Notification workers retry under stable provider keys, track delivery and prevent every 1-minute reevaluation from resending the same alert. Hysteresis/cooldown and digest policies reduce spam; a correction dropping below threshold needs an explicit retraction policy.

Partition extraction/analytics by event/entity with hot-key salting followed by full-key aggregation. Independent consumer groups feed search, rollups and notifications; scaling one need not block the others. Raw log buffers breaking-news bursts, with enough retention/disk and backpressure before capacity is exhausted; “Kafka” is not infinite storage. Checkpoint offsets/state, replay idempotently and stage new index versions before alias swap. Preserve per-stage watermarks so a search result and time series can disclose different freshness.

Monitor feed gaps, event lag, extraction precision/recall, ambiguous aliases, search p99/cache/load, rollup reconciliation, notification duplicate/failure rate and storage growth. Failure examples: source retry counts once; updated article changes its company set once; notification timeout reconciles rather than creates a new logical alert; an index outage does not lose raw ingestion. title: System Design — Event Ingestion + Top-K Aggregation
question:
An originally-single-server event-reporting system must scale to a much higher request volume, and must additionally compute top-K aggregations across the event stream. OHAI onsite SD round with a heavy emphasis on the scale-up narrative.

Requirements
Original setup: a single server receiving event reports from clients.
New scale: request volume has grown sharply (orders of magnitude); the single-server bottleneck must be removed.
Additional capability: compute top-K aggregations over the event stream (e.g. top-K event types, top-K clients, top-K resources).
Round time: 45 minutes after a 10-minute behavioural opener.
Notes
Ingestion scale-out: front the system with a stateless load balancer; ingestion nodes are themselves stateless. Events land on a durable log (Kafka / Kinesis / OCI Streaming) keyed by a partition field (event type or client ID). Consumers downstream read the log for aggregation, storage, notification. Back-pressure: the log absorbs upstream bursts; consumers scale independently.
Top-K aggregation: exact top-K -> map-side per-partition counter heaps of size K, reduce-side merge of per-partition heaps for the global top-K. Approximate top-K (sub-linear memory) -> Count-Min Sketch for frequency estimation + a heap of candidates, or the Space-Saving (Misra-Gries / Metwally) algorithm keeping exactly K counters with bounded over-estimation.
Time-windowed top-K (last hour/day): tumbling or sliding-window aggregation (Flink / Spark Structured Streaming); each window emits its top-K snapshot.
Deep dives: exactly-once vs at-least-once delivery; late-arriving events and watermarks; storage of historical top-K snapshots; hot-key handling (one dominating event type forces a per-key partition scheme).

steps: Evolve the single-server design in stages
Count completely before selecting exact local leaders
solution.example: Begin by measuring whether the old server is CPU, network, database or disk-bound and preserving its event/ack contract. Choose illustrative new peak100k events/s at 500B=50 MB/s ingress (~4.32 TB/day sustained), then update with measured averages/retention. Add a load balancer and stateless authenticated ingestion replicas; require stable event ids, schema/version, key and event_time. Acknowledge only after durable replicated log acceptance, not merely after placing data in process memory. Migrate clients through the same API/version, compare old/new event accounting, canary and retain replay for rollback.
solution.trap: A sizeK heap alone cannot retain exact counts of arbitrary future heavy hitters or refill correctly after expiration.

- **Work and result:** the work path passes through **Windowed aggregators — event-time + watermark** and **Merge top-K candidates — approximation + error**, producing **Ranked query result — window + freshness**. Bound waiting and retries where a slow dependency can stall this path.

### Evolve the single-server design in stages

Begin by measuring whether the old server is CPU, network, database or disk-bound and preserving its event/ack contract. Choose illustrative new peak100k events/s at 500B=50 MB/s ingress (~4.32 TB/day sustained), then update with measured averages/retention. Add a load balancer and stateless authenticated ingestion replicas; require stable event ids, schema/version, key and event_time. Acknowledge only after durable replicated log acceptance, not merely after placing data in process memory. Migrate clients through the same API/version, compare old/new event accounting, canary and retain replay for rollback.

Partition the log to spread load while maintaining the required per-key order; consumers for raw archival, metrics and notifications scale independently. Queue lag/backpressure and bounded admission absorb bursts up to retained capacity. No finite queue can absorb sustained arrivals faster than processing indefinitely. `POST /events:batch` returns accepted/retryable ids; `GET /topk?dimension=&window=&k=` returns score/order, window, snapshot, exactness and freshness.

### Count completely before selecting exact local leaders

For exact counts, repartition by the **ranked key**, maintain every active key's count and expiration buckets, then a full ordered count index or sizeK selection over complete totals. Local topK merge is exact only when each key's entire score belongs to one shard (same deterministic score/id order). If partitioning by client while ranking event type, a type appears on many shards and can be missed: shard1 a 60/x61, shard2 a 60/y61 gives global a 120 but no local top1 a. Sum all per-type partials before local ranking, or use a candidate/error protocol and label approximation. A sizeK heap alone cannot retain exact counts of arbitrary future heavy hitters or refill correctly after expiration.

For approximate positive streams, Count-Min uses O((1/epsilon)log(1/delta)) counters and estimates fixed-key frequency between f and f+epsilon·total with high probability, but needs a separate candidate enumeration structure. Space-Saving keeps m counters with bounded overestimation and heavy-hitter recall; Misra–Gries is a related **different** undercounting algorithm, not the same update/error sign. Use more than K candidates when cutoff gaps are uncertain and exact-refine from bucket totals if possible. Exact candidate counts do not eliminate missing-candidate error.

### Windows, retries and scale-out failure

Define tumbling versus sliding and bucket precision, event-time watermark/allowed lateness and duplicate horizon. Store per-key bucket contributions, update rolling totals on arrival/expiry and publish immutable snapshots into a replicated cache plus historical store. Late accepted events revise affected snapshots; beyond policy are counted/dropped explicitly. Expiration timers run during idle periods. Salt hot keys into local subaggregates then combine full totals before ranking.

At-least-once delivery plus stable-id dedup/state-and-offset checkpointing yields exactly-once **effects** for the defined retained horizon; an unqualified end-to-end exactly-once promise across arbitrary external sinks is misleading. Recover from checkpoint+log, fence reshard epochs and atomically swap snapshot pointers. Reads use last-good snapshots with as_of during processor failures; ingestion can continue until durable backlog limits. Track end-to-end accepted → snapshot lag, duplicates/late drops, hot partitions, checkpoint/recovery, read p99 and cost. ### Fix the event, slice and window contract

Choose distinct accepted order events as the primary popularity score, with views/clicks a separate metric; do not add them without declared weights. Ingest `{event_id,item_id,restaurant_id,city,market,category,device,event_time,event_type}` with schema, authentication and stable-id dedup. Menu authorization/availability can filter a serving list without changing historical popularity definition.

Partition accepted events by ranked `(scope,key)` ownership and maintain sparse event-time buckets, per-window running totals and a deterministic `(score desc,item_id asc)` score index. Use seconds/minutes for 5min windows and coarser minute/hour/day layers for long history, while retaining fine buckets if the API requires exact endpoints. A 30-day exact arbitrary-second query cannot be answered by summing daily topK snapshots. Precompute popular5m/1 h/1d/30d windows for cache-hot endpoints; for arbitrary N either sum complete per-item bucket counts through a time-indexed store with a higher bounded latency, constrain allowed precision/windows, or use a disclosed approximation. Precomputing every market × category × device combination causes cardinality explosion, so materialize high-value slices and restrict/admit expensive combinations.

A restaurant has a bounded menu, making on-read sum/sort viable for cold restaurants; city/global need streaming full-key aggregation and cached top100. Hot items salt partial updates then recombine totals before ranking. Local topK union is exact only with complete nonoverlapping item ownership under the same scope; an item split by event/client shards can win globally without appearing locally. Retain all active count candidates so expiration can promote a previously lower-ranked item.

At 1M events/s and an assumed 100B/event, peak intake is 100 MB/s; sustained that rate would be 8.64 TB/day raw and 259 TB/30 days, before replicas. Use measured average, sparse bucket cardinality and retention/cold compaction to size state rather than dense items × all buckets. For offline-only delivery, batch the same deduped events into daily/hourly complete counts, then compute rankings with a documented refresh lag; near-real-time adds streaming deltas and periodic reconciliation to batch truth. Late events revise only within the allowed policy and label finalized/provisional results; refunds/cancellations require compensating the original order's live bucket if that is the chosen metric. title: Trending System / Top-K Hot Files
question:
Trending System / Top-K Hot Files

Design a real-time trending system: ingest a high-volume stream of impression/view events and serve a frequently-updated global top-K list of the hottest items (files, search terms, or articles). Discussion centers on dedup, windowed counting, approximate top-K, and a read path that stays available.

Requirements

Design a trending / top-K-hot-items service:

Ingest a stream of impression/view events; serve a global (non-personalized) top-K list of the hottest items.
The list refreshes on a short cadence (e.g. minute-level) over a rolling window (e.g. daily).
Discuss dedup (count distinct users per item within the window), high read availability for the list, and how to keep counting tractable at scale.
Notes
A canonical decomposition: serve the top-K list entirely from a distributed cache (no TTL) so reads survive backend hiccups; persist raw events append-only in NoSQL; shard counting via consistent hashing; have each shard report its local top-N each minute and an aggregator merge them into the global top-K.
Approximate-counting structures come up as natural follow-ups for memory bounds: Bloom filters for per-window distinct-user dedup, and Count-Min Sketch for heavy-hitter frequency (be ready to discuss over-estimation bias). Event-frequency-based sampling (sample hot items at a lower rate) is a good optimization to volunteer.
Real QPS for the Figma-specific framing can be low; calibrate to the stated scale and avoid reflexively designing for extreme throughput — over-engineering is penalized. Some interviewers want a particular answer and steer hard, while others reward any well-justified approach once you've hit the expected core.
Has appeared as "top-k hot file," "trending search," and "trending articles" across coding-adjacent and pure design rounds.

steps: Count distinct viewers, not repeated impressions
Approximation has several different error directions
solution.example: Assume a modest file-search deployment first (for example 10k events/s, 1k reads/s) and scale only when measurements require it. Event contract is `{event_id,file_id,user_id,event_time}`; filter unauthorized/deleted files at query time. Popularity is distinct users per file over `[T-24h,T)`, refreshed each minute with deterministic file-id ties. `GET /hot-files?k=` returns counts or estimates, window, as_of, mode. A million views from one user count once; transport dedup and user-distinct dedup are separate.
solution.trap: Bloom filters can suppress repeated users compactly, but false positives suppress genuine new viewers, biasing counts **down**, and ordinary filters cannot expire individual entries.
solution.teaching_notes_markdown:
<!-- architecture:W362:start -->
### Architecture and request flow

![Trending System / Top-K Hot Files: request, processing, state and result components.](../diagrams/W362_architecture.svg)

[Open the diagram at full size](../diagrams/W362_architecture.svg). This is a baseline component diagram for this question. The boxes describe responsibilities; they do not require a separate microservice for every box.

- **Request and state:** Timestamped events — object + event id → Stream ingress — deduplicate + partition. That component consults or updates **Durable event log — replay + retention** under the required access and consistency rules.
- **Work and result:** the work path passes through **Windowed aggregators — event-time + watermark** and **Merge top-K candidates — approximation + error**, producing **Ranked query result — window + freshness**. Bound waiting and retries where a slow dependency can stall this path.
- **Correctness point:** State the time window and approximation; expired events and late arrivals must have a defined correction rule.

When explaining the drawing, trace one normal request first, then a duplicate request, an unavailable dependency and recovery from saved state. If the question requires stricter guarantees or a different scope, state the change explicitly rather than treating this baseline as the only possible design.
<!-- architecture:W362:end -->

### Count distinct viewers, not repeated impressions

Assume a modest file-search deployment first (for example 10k events/s, 1k reads/s) and scale only when measurements require it. Event contract is `{event_id,file_id,user_id,event_time}`; filter unauthorized/deleted files at query time. Popularity is distinct users per file over `[T-24h,T)`, refreshed each minute with deterministic file-id ties. `GET /hot-files?k=` returns counts or estimates, window, as_of, mode. A million views from one user count once; transport dedup and user-distinct dedup are separate.

For exact rolling distinctness, keep `(file,user)->latest_view_time` plus an expiry heap/timing wheel/versioned timers; first live view increments, a repeat refreshes its expiry without increment, and a timeout decrements only if it still matches the latest timestamp. Keep late-event rules and enough previous view history if arbitrary historical queries/corrections are supported; latest-only state answers the current rolling view, not all past snapshots. Partition by file for complete counts, with salted `(file,user)` preprocessing for hot files followed by a full-file reducer. Cache periodic topN and merge only when each file's full count is owned by one shard.

### Approximation has several different error directions

Per-bucket HyperLogLog sketches offer mergeable distinct-user estimates (relative standard error about 1.04/sqrt(m) registers under usual assumptions), union live buckets and expose boundary precision; they do not support exact arbitrary deletions by subtraction. Bloom filters can suppress repeated users compactly, but false positives suppress genuine new viewers, biasing counts **down**, and ordinary filters cannot expire individual entries. Use rotating buckets/counting variants with their retention/error rules or exact checks behind positives. Count-Min estimates nonnegative event frequency **upward** within its epsilon·total bound and cannot by itself compute distinct users or enumerate heavy hitters. Candidate nomination plus exact/estimated distinct counts is a hybrid, not magically exact topK.

Sampling every view from hot files at a lower probability needs recorded inclusion probabilities and a distinct-user estimator consistent with that sampling; naively scaling sampled view counts estimates views, not distinct users. Prefer stable per-(file, user) hash sampling to keep repeat users consistent, then analyze variance/cutoff errors. Use rank stability and human/product validation rather than assuming any sketch's guarantee preserves the exact topK order.

### Read availability and durable recovery

Serve a small complete versioned snapshot from replicated cache, retaining last-good data without automatic TTL deletion to survive backend hiccups. “No TTL” does not mean infinitely fresh: include age, alert/staleness labels and explicitly remove deleted/forbidden files through a separate authoritative filter. Persist snapshots and raw permitted events in append-only durable storage; checkpoint distinct-count state/offsets and replay idempotently. If the cache fails, reload the last complete snapshot, not partially updated sorted-set members.

Example: userA views fileX ten times and userB once; exact score2, while 11 raw impressions is wrong. Refreshing A after 23 h should extend only A's live membership. Test repeated/late views, expiry after a refresh, file deletion, cache/processor outage and sketch-versus-exact sample error. Monitor distinct-state size, lag, estimated error, stale read age and hot-file skew. The performance trade-off is exact per-user state versus bounded sketches/approximate ranking, not whether to keep a blind cumulative counter.

title: L6 Staff System Design Loop
question: Google L6 (Staff) onsite includes two 60-min System Design rounds (one infra-leaning, one product-leaning). Common prompts: distributed rate limiter, global real-time notification system, anomaly detection service, Find-My-Device, dictionary range-query store, and global chain-restaurant menu sync. Walk through how you'd structure a Staff-level answer and where the L5→L6 bar actually is.

steps: Structure the hour around one selected problem
Adapt the deep dive to the actual prompt
Show staff scope through decisions, not more boxes
solution.example: An infra round needs an explicit authority/consistency boundary; a product round also needs user-visible behavior, rollout and product-error costs. For a distributed rate limiter, for example, define hard versus approximate limits, request/token cost, key/window and fail-open/closed behavior before choosing Redis. An atomic token-bucket decrement with idempotency handles same-key concurrency; regional leased budgets improve availability but bound overshoot differently from a global transaction. State those bounds and how degraded operation changes the contract.
solution.trap: Adjust to probes rather than recite a memorized schedule.
solution.teaching_notes_markdown:
<!-- architecture:W363:start -->
### Design scope and component flow

![L6 Staff System Design Loop: request, processing, state and result components.](../diagrams/W363_architecture.svg)

[Open the diagram at full size](../diagrams/W363_architecture.svg). This round does not specify one fixed product. The diagram makes the answer-planning steps explicit; choose the concrete scope before proposing production services.

- **Request and state:** Interview requirements — actor + requested action → Clarify constraints — scale + errors + latency. That component consults or updates **Explicit assumptions — domain not yet fixed** under the required access and consistency rules.
- **Work and result:** the work path passes through **Draw baseline components — ownership + request path** and **Analyze races + failures — verify invariants**, producing **Tradeoff summary — measurable validation**. Bound waiting and retries where a slow dependency can stall this path.
- **Correctness point:** No fixed product is specified in this round; this is an answer-planning diagram, not an invented production architecture.

When explaining the drawing, trace one normal request first, then a duplicate request, an unavailable dependency and recovery from saved state. If the question requires stricter guarantees or a different scope, state the change explicitly rather than treating this baseline as the only possible design.
<!-- architecture:W363:end -->

### Structure the hour around one selected problem

The prompt describes a loop, not a single system or an official published hiring rubric. A useful staff-level answer demonstrates decision quality and scope ownership; exact level assessment depends on interviewers and the actual role. In each 60-minute round spend roughly 0–7min agreeing users/actions/invariants and SLOs, 7–12 quantifying load/state/retention, 12–25 defining API/data/normal request path, 25–45 on the dominant correctness/scaling/failure trade-off, 45–55 on migration/operations/cost and 55–60 on unresolved assumptions and validation. Adjust to probes rather than recite a memorized schedule.

An infra round needs an explicit authority/consistency boundary; a product round also needs user-visible behavior, rollout and product-error costs. For a distributed rate limiter, for example, define hard versus approximate limits, request/token cost, key/window and fail-open/closed behavior before choosing Redis. An atomic token-bucket decrement with idempotency handles same-key concurrency; regional leased budgets improve availability but bound overshoot differently from a global transaction. State those bounds and how degraded operation changes the contract.

### Adapt the deep dive to the actual prompt

| Prompt | A substantive deep dive |
|---|---|
| Global notifications | Durable intent/outbox, subscription fanout, provider idempotency, retries/preferences and duplicates under timeout |
| Anomaly service | Event/feature freshness, seasonal baselines, precision/alert cost, backtesting and delayed labels; no model score equals an incident |
| Find-My-Device | Authenticated owner/device identity, location timestamp/accuracy, privacy/stalking controls, offline device and stale-position semantics |
| Dictionary range store | Ordered-key partitioning, range scans/merge/pagination, skew/splits, snapshot consistency and replication |
| Restaurant menu sync | Versioned menu entities/prices/availability, partial update conflict resolution, offline stores, atomic menu publication and rollback |

Each needs concrete API/schema and a failure trace once selected; this menu is a way to identify the hard subproblem, not a complete substitute design for every product simultaneously. Label assumed scale numbers and recompute when the interviewer changes them.

### Show staff scope through decisions, not more boxes

A solid senior answer often builds a correct service at the requested scale. A staff-strength answer also makes ambiguous cross-team constraints explicit, chooses what **not yet** to build, compares viable alternatives with costs, and owns migration, interfaces, operational risks and failure-domain effects. Explain a phased move from the existing system, compatibility/data backfill verification, canary gates, rollback and owner responsibilities; quantify a decisive trade-off such as global coordination latency versus bounded regional overshoot. Do not assert that all L5 or L6 interviews use one universal checklist.

Walk a normal request, duplicate request, partial failure and recovery against the same invariant. If the fleet/region is partitioned, state which user promise is weakened and why. End with how you would falsify the design using load tests, fault injection and rollout metrics. The retained planning diagram is appropriately an answer-structure diagram here; it must not be mistaken for a specific production architecture absent a selected product.

title: System Design for Full Stack Applications
question:
Design a full-stack application system that requires perfect collaboration between frontend and backend to support large-scale user and data operations. Detail how to handle high-volume data writes and how to optimize frontend performance in large-scale scenarios.

Requirements
Describe how to efficiently write large volumes of data into a database.
Identify methods to optimize Redis for supporting large-scale data writes.
Explain how the frontend can be optimized in such an environment, including rendering, data fetching, and user interaction.
Note

No specific coding implementation is required, just a comprehensive explanation of the system design strategies.

Example

Consider an e-commerce platform with millions of users purchasing and paying for items simultaneously.

steps: Ground the example in purchase correctness
Scale database and Redis writes deliberately
Make the frontend part of the data contract
solution.example: Use the supplied e-commerce example as a chosen scope: browse/catalog reads, checkout/order/payment writes and UI progress. Assume 100k write requests/s peak and 2 KB/order-intent payload ≈ 200 MB/s raw before indexes/replicas, then replace with measured traffic and average retention. APIs use stable client idempotency keys for checkout/payment, pagination for browsing and server-calculated prices/authorization. Store Order, OrderItem, InventoryReservation, PaymentAttempt and an outbox, with unique logical checkout/payment identities and versioned states. A Redis hit is not authority that a card was charged or inventory was reserved.
solution.trap: For payment provider timeout, reconcile the same operation id rather than create another charge.
solution.teaching_notes_markdown:
<!-- architecture:W364:start -->
### Architecture and request flow

![Ecommerce writes, derived cache and frontend state](../diagrams/W364_final_architecture.svg)

[Open the diagram](../diagrams/W364_final_architecture.svg). Authoritative purchase writes commit before derived Redis updates. Redis absorbs appropriate read/derived-state traffic, while batching and partitioning reduce database overhead without bypassing stock or payment correctness. The frontend consumes bounded versioned data and distinguishes optimistic local edits from a confirmed purchase.
<!-- architecture:W364:end -->

### Ground the example in purchase correctness

Use the supplied e-commerce example as a chosen scope: browse/catalog reads, checkout/order/payment writes and UI progress. Assume 100k write requests/s peak and 2 KB/order-intent payload ≈ 200 MB/s raw before indexes/replicas, then replace with measured traffic and average retention. APIs use stable client idempotency keys for checkout/payment, pagination for browsing and server-calculated prices/authorization. Store Order, OrderItem, InventoryReservation, PaymentAttempt and an outbox, with unique logical checkout/payment identities and versioned states. A Redis hit is not authority that a card was charged or inventory was reserved.

### Scale database and Redis writes deliberately

Partition orders by tenant/user/order hash and avoid a hot timestamp-only primary key. Batch independent inserts/events, use prepared statements/connection pools, narrow necessary indexes, append-oriented logs and asynchronous materialized views; WAL/group commit amortizes IO. Keep order creation/reservation invariants in transactions or a documented saga with reconciliation, not an asynchronous queue that claims success before acceptance. An outbox atomically records downstream work with the order. For payment provider timeout, reconcile the same operation id rather than create another charge.

Redis can absorb cache/session/cart/rate state with Cluster hash-slot distribution, hot-key sharding, compact hashes, bounded key sizes, pipelining and batched writes. Pipelining reduces round trips, not the work in one shard; avoid huge blocking commands/scripts and cross-slot multi-key “transactions” that cannot be atomic. Tune expiry with jitter to prevent simultaneous eviction/recompute, use replica/read policy and memory headroom, and measure AOF/replication/durability cost. Write-through preserves cache/DB ordering more simply; write-behind needs a durable queue and recovery because Redis loss must not erase paid orders. Backpressure/quotas and per-shard p99 are more informative than one aggregate ops/s number.

### Make the frontend part of the data contract

Virtualize long product/order lists, paginate/cursor-load server results, lazy-load/code-split routes and images, cache immutable assets via CDN and use appropriately sized images. Keep component state localized, stable row keys and memoization based on measured rerenders; avoid rendering thousands of DOM nodes on each stream event. Debounce search, cancel superseded requests, deduplicate/prefetch bounded requests and invalidate/revalidate caches by resource version. Optimistic cart/like updates can roll back on conflict; payment/order completion waits for authoritative confirmed state, with pending/unknown visibly distinct from success.

Use request ids/revisions to ignore stale out-of-order responses; reconnect progress via cursor rather than resubmit the purchase. Disable duplicate UI submissions as convenience, while server idempotency provides correctness. Show skeleton/progress/error/retry states without a main-thread blocking spinner loop; support accessible interaction and slow networks. Avoid polling every row individually; batch status endpoints or a bounded SSE/WebSocket feed updates only changed records.

### Validate the end-to-end system

Measure click-to-confirmed-order latency, Core Web Vitals/render/main-thread work, network request volume, backend queue/transaction p99, Redis hot-key/eviction/replication lag, payment unknown states and duplicate order/charge rate. Load-test purchase bursts and simulate DB/cache/provider failures. Roll out schema/cache/UI changes with compatibility, canary, reconciliation and rollback. If the cache fails, serve a bounded DB-backed degraded path or shed noncritical reads; never overload the DB with an unlimited cache stampede. The corrected diagram should be browser → API/transactional order DB/outbox with Redis/read views, not a generic interview-planning diagram.
