title: Embedded-Optimized Elevation Mapping
question:
Embedded-Optimized Elevation Mapping (45 minutes, whiteboard)

You need to maintain a local elevation map under embedded resource constraints while a robot moves and receives elevation observations.

Task

Design an algorithm/data structure to update a local elevation grid in real time, addressing:

Real-time updates: each observation frame must be processed within a fixed budget (justify via complexity).
Memory constraints: maintain only a fixed-size local window around the robot (sliding/local map).
Noise & outliers: fuse repeated observations to reduce noise and handle outliers.
Frame transforms: observations are in sensor/robot frame; fuse into the map frame given pose.
Output: per-cell elevation estimate (optionally with confidence/variance).
Abstract input
pose_t: robot pose at time t.
obs_t: a set of elevation observations (e.g., (x,y,z) points or scan-derived heights).
Map params: resolution r, window size W x H.
What to explain
Map representation (array, ring buffer, hashed grid, etc.) and how the sliding window works.
Fusion method (weighted average, recursive filter, variance update, time decay).
Complexity and embedded optimizations (precomputation, incremental update, SIMD/fixed-point, etc.).
Edge cases (window shifts, bounds, initialization/reset).

Discussion/whiteboard oriented; clear pseudocode or a step-by-step algorithm is expected.

Input:  (discussion) pose_t and obs_t stream; map size fixed
Output: Per-cell elevation estimate (and optional confidence) updated in real time

steps: A fixed local grid with world-cell identity
solution.example: This scalar Kalman/inverse-variance fusion assumes independent noise and a single local surface; correlated points from one frame should be downsampled/weighted so 100 adjacent hits do not imply100 independent measurements. A gate rejects outliers but can also freeze an old surface when a real object/terrain change occurs: track repeated consistent rejected observations, age confidence or reset under an explicit change policy. A 2.0m estimate with P=.04 and 2.2m observation withR=.04 givesK=.5, mean 2.1m, variance.02 before process noise/floors. A 10m residual is gated, not averaged blindly.
solution.trap: For map point(x, y), world cell is `(floor(x/r),floor(y/r))`; inside-window check occurs **before** modulo index mapping, so an outside point cannot wrap into a valid cell.
solution.teaching_notes_markdown:
### A fixed local grid with world-cell identity

Choose a locally fixed map frame, cell resolution r meters and W × H cells centered near the robot. Store dense arrays `mean_z`, `variance`, `last_seen`, `valid` plus integer world-cell origin and circular-buffer x/y offsets. For map point(x, y), world cell is `(floor(x/r),floor(y/r))`; inside-window check occurs **before** modulo index mapping, so an outside point cannot wrap into a valid cell. A sensor point becomes $p_M=T_{M,B}(pose_t)T_{B,S}p_S$ using calibrated extrinsics and synchronized pose; include pose uncertainty in observation variance.

When the robot crosses an integer cell, shift the origin/ring offset and clear only newly exposed rows/columns, keeping retained cells in their original world coordinates. For a teleport ≥W orH cells, clear the whole map. Never reuse an exposed slot's old height/confidence. Use generation tags or valid masks to avoid bulk writes if beneficial, but bound any deferred clearing work. Recenter only on cell boundaries to avoid interpolation/reblurring every frame.

### Per-point update pseudocode

```text
process_frame(pose, observations):
    shift_window_to_robot_cell(pose.xy)  # clear exposed strips or full reset
    T = map_from_body(pose) * body_from_sensor
    for p, sensor_variance in bounded_observations:
        q = T * p
        if nonfinite(q) or invalid_pose: reject/count
        cell = floor(q.xy / r)
        if cell not inside current window: continue
        i = circular_index(cell)
        R = max(R_min, sensor_variance + projected_pose_variance(q))
        if not valid[i]: mean[i]=q.z; variance[i]=R; valid[i]=true
        else:
            P = variance[i] + process_noise * elapsed_time(i)
            residual = q.z - mean[i]
            if residual^2 > gate^2 * (P + R): reject_or_pending_surface_change
            else:
                K = P / (P + R)
                mean[i] += K * residual
                variance[i] = max(P_min, (1-K)*P)
        last_seen[i] = frame_time only when accepted
```

This scalar Kalman/inverse-variance fusion assumes independent noise and a single local surface; correlated points from one frame should be downsampled/weighted so 100 adjacent hits do not imply100 independent measurements. A gate rejects outliers but can also freeze an old surface when a real object/terrain change occurs: track repeated consistent rejected observations, age confidence or reset under an explicit change policy. A 2.0m estimate with P=.04 and 2.2m observation withR=.04 givesK=.5, mean 2.1m, variance.02 before process noise/floors. A 10m residual is gated, not averaged blindly.

### Resource bound and edge cases

For M bounded points and shifts(dx, dy), transform/assign/fuse is O(M), exposed clearing O(min(WH, H|dx|+W|dy|)), worst O(WH); memory O(WH), independent of travel distance. Choose M_max/downsampling and fixed WH from measured worst-case time, not average throughput. A 250×250 map with four32-bit fields is about 1 MB plus masks/alignment; SIMD transforms, precomputed extrinsics, tile/block clears, bounded queues and fixed-point only with range/error analysis suit embedded hardware. Outputting the entire grid itself costs O(WH); publish changed tiles if the interface permits.

Handle negative coordinates with floor (not truncation), boundary clipping, empty frames, initial invalid cells, stale confidence, timestamp/pose interpolation, large recenter, nonfinite points and map-frame reset after localization jumps. Test a stationary plane with noisy repeats, a known rotated sensor transform and robot movement across a cell: the same world obstacle must remain in the same world cell while ring slots rotate. A 2.5D map cannot represent overhangs/multiple heights in one cell; flag that limitation rather than claim full3D mapping.

title: Mapping Celestial Coordinates for Sky Navigation
question:
Mapping Celestial Coordinates for Sky Navigation

How to map a plane in the sky?

def solution():
# Read data from standard input
# Write your code here
pass

if __name__ == "__main__":
solution()

steps: The supplied question does not identify one geometric problem
solution.example: For an **aircraft position**, if input is timestamped latitude/longitude/altitude and observer latitude/longitude/altitude, convert both geodetic positions to a consistent Earth-fixed Cartesian frame, subtract and rotate into local east/north/up. With relative vector(E, N, U), range=sqrt(E²+N²+U²), azimuth=atan2(E, N) and elevation=atan2(U, sqrt(E²+N²)). Earth ellipsoid/datum, altitude reference, units and synchronized times matter. A single image bearing cannot establish aircraft range/3D position without extra information; a stale exact GPS point does not locate a moving aircraft now.
solution.trap: A single image bearing cannot establish aircraft range/3D position without extra information; a stale exact GPS point does not locate a moving aircraft now.
solution.teaching_notes_markdown:
### The supplied question does not identify one geometric problem

“How to map a plane in the sky?” plus an empty stdin stub supplies no coordinate system, measurements, observer/time, projection or output format. “Plane” could mean an aircraft, a geometric plane or a sky-chart tangent plane. The title suggests celestial coordinates but the sentence suggests an aircraft. There is no honest unique judge-compatible implementation or numeric output until that ambiguity is resolved; do not replace it with an unrelated interval or elevation algorithm.

### Two concrete, explicitly conditional interpretations

For an **aircraft position**, if input is timestamped latitude/longitude/altitude and observer latitude/longitude/altitude, convert both geodetic positions to a consistent Earth-fixed Cartesian frame, subtract and rotate into local east/north/up. With relative vector(E, N, U), range=sqrt(E²+N²+U²), azimuth=atan2(E, N) and elevation=atan2(U, sqrt(E²+N²)). Earth ellipsoid/datum, altitude reference, units and synchronized times matter. A single image bearing cannot establish aircraft range/3D position without extra information; a stale exact GPS point does not locate a moving aircraft now.

For a **celestial direction** given right ascension alpha and declination delta in a named reference frame/epoch, the unit vector is `(cos(delta)cos(alpha), cos(delta)sin(alpha), sin(delta))`. Mapping it to an observer's altitude/azimuth additionally requires observation time, Earth orientation and observer location; mapping to pixels additionally requires projection, field of view and camera calibration. A tangent/gnomonic chart has a limited visible hemisphere and becomes singular90degrees from its center; no single flat projection preserves every spherical property.

A tiny runnable direction conversion for this chosen celestial-only contract is:

```python
import math


def radec_unit_vector(ra_degrees, dec_degrees):
    if not -90 <= dec_degrees <= 90:
        raise ValueError("declination outside sphere")
    a, d = map(math.radians, (ra_degrees, dec_degrees))
    return (math.cos(d) * math.cos(a), math.cos(d) * math.sin(a), math.sin(d))


assert all(abs(a - b) < 1e-12 for a, b in zip(radec_unit_vector(0, 0), (1, 0, 0)))
assert all(abs(a - b) < 1e-12 for a, b in zip(radec_unit_vector(90, 0), (0, 1, 0)))
assert abs(radec_unit_vector(0, 90)[2] - 1) < 1e-12
```

This O(1) function converts a direction only; it neither tracks aircraft nor implements a complete sky-navigation map. Once actual inputs/output are specified, test known cardinal directions, poles/wraparound, observer/time changes and projection boundaries against trusted reference transformations. State uncertainty/occlusion and missing-range behavior explicitly rather than infer unsupported coordinates.

For each integer or fraction sequence below, infer the generating rule and give the next term. Work by hand, without a calculator. A rule is only acceptable if it reproduces every given term.

-12 -11 -7 2 18 43 ?

### Compact rules that reproduce every given term

| Sequence | Next | One-sentence rule and verification |
|---|---:|---|
|1|48|Repeat operators −1,+2,×3,÷4:19 → 18 → 20 → 60 → 15 → 14 → 16 → 48.|
|2|25|Odd-position terms subtract the intervening even term (58−8=50, 50−10=40, 40−15=25); the even stream8,10, 15 has increments2,5,… increasing by3.|
|3|79|Add successive squares1,4, 9, 16, 25, 36:−12→−11→−7 → 2 → 18 → 43 → 79.|
|4|134|From the third term use a_n=2a_(n−1)+a_(n−2):4=2(3/2)+1, 19/2=2(4)+3/2, 23=2(19/2)+4,111/2=2(23)+19/2, then2(111/2)+23=134.|
|5|21|Repeat −1,+2,×3,÷4:7 → 6 → 8 → 24 → 6 → 5 → 7 → 21.|
|6|14|Odd positions5,8, 11, 14 add3; even positions3,9, 27 multiply by3.|
|7|10368|After seeds3,1, 2 each term is the product of the previous three: 6, 12, 144, then6·12·144=10368.|
|8|29|After seeds2,1 each term sums the previous two: 3, 4, 7, 11, 18, 29.|

Sequence2's even-stream rule can be made fully explicit as e_1=8, e_m=e_(m−1)+(3m−4) for m≥2; it produces every supplied even term without guessing an unstated future one. The next requested term is odd and already determined by40−15. Sequence4 uses exact halves, avoiding decimal calculator dependence; 6·12·144=72·144=10080+288=10368 by hand.

### A systematic search and the positional clues

First compute small integer differences and ratios and look for constant/higher differences or named simple lists (sequence3 exposes squares). Next test short repeating operator cycles and grouped blocks; sequence1's19/18/20/60 then15/14/16 suggests the same within-group−1,+2,×3 progression with÷4 between groups, and sequence5 confirms that cycle independently. Then split odd/even or mod-r positions: sequence6 immediately becomes arithmetic versus geometric streams. Try short additive/product recurrences (4, 7, 8), checking each eligible index from the start, and consider named sequences only if they explain all terms without extra exceptions.

Reject a candidate that fits only the final pair, changes operations ad hoc or fails one earlier value. A finite prefix has infinitely many continuations (one can interpolate a polynomial or append a special case), so these are simple consistent intended-style rules, not mathematically unique necessities. State the rule with the number; a bare list of guesses does not demonstrate it.

title: Python Data Structure Design for Game Metadata and Related Discord Servers
question:
Python Data Structure Design for Game Metadata and Related Discord Servers

Prompt

Design a data structure (e.g., dictionary/classes/tables) to store game metadata and the corresponding Discord servers relevant to each game.

Game metadata includes (extensible): name, genre, country, release date, platform(s), publisher. The source is external (Wikipedia, etc.).

Explain:

Your data model (keys, dedupe strategy, and how to support queries by name/genre/platform/publisher).
How to link games to Discord servers (many-to-many, primary keys, unique server identifiers).
How you would ingest and refresh from external sources (incremental vs full refresh, missing fields, conflict resolution).

No scraping code required; provide a clear example structure.

steps: Stable identities and a many-to-many relation
Refresh incrementally with provenance and atomic indexes
solution.example: A clear Python example (all data below is illustrative) is:
solution.trap: Names alone collide across remakes/platform editions; dedupe by reliable source ids and reviewed release/edition/publisher evidence rather than case-folding titles into one entity.
solution.teaching_notes_markdown:
<!-- architecture:W368:start -->
### Architecture and request flow

![Python Data Structure Design for Game Metadata and Related Discord Servers: request, processing, state and result components.](../diagrams/W368_architecture.svg)

[Open the diagram at full size](../diagrams/W368_architecture.svg). This is a baseline component diagram for this question. The boxes describe responsibilities; they do not require a separate microservice for every box.

- **Request and state:** Metadata input or query — stable game and server ids → Catalog interface — normalize + validate. That component consults or updates **Game and server indexes — many-to-many links** under the required access and consistency rules.
- **Work and result:** the work path passes through **Ingest and refresh — version + deduplication** and **Query and link logic — genre, platform, publisher**, producing **Consistent metadata result — refresh diagnostics**. Bound waiting and retries where a slow dependency can stall this path.
- **Correctness point:** Use stable game/server identities and maintain many-to-many links; names alone are not reliable unique identifiers.

When explaining the drawing, trace one normal request first, then a duplicate request, an unavailable dependency and recovery from saved state. If the question requires stricter guarantees or a different scope, state the change explicitly rather than treating this baseline as the only possible design.
<!-- architecture:W368:end -->

### Stable identities and a many-to-many relation

Use internal game_id independent of display name and `SourceIdentity(source,external_id)->game_id` for Wikipedia/source ids, with aliases/localizations separated from canonical names. Names alone collide across remakes/platform editions; dedupe by reliable source ids and reviewed release/edition/publisher evidence rather than case-folding titles into one entity. Store unknown country/date as null with source/provenance, not invented defaults. Country may mean development/publisher/release market and needs a declared field meaning.

A clear Python example (all data below is illustrative) is:

```python
games = {
    "g1": {
        "name": "Example Quest",
        "aliases": ["EQ"],
        "genres": {"rpg"},
        "country": None,
        "release_date": "2025-02-03",
        "platform_ids": {"pc", "console-x"},
        "publisher_id": "pub1",
        "metadata_version": 3,
        "sources": {
            "name": ("wiki", "page123", 17),
            "release_date": ("publisher", "release7", 4),
        },
    }
}
servers = {
    "123456789012345678": {
        "name": "Quest Community",
        "invite_url": None,
        "verified_at": None,
    },
    "987654321098765432": {"name": "All RPGs", "invite_url": None, "verified_at": None},
}
# Discord guild snowflake is a stable string id, not an expiring invite URL.
game_servers = {("g1", "123456789012345678"), ("g1", "987654321098765432")}
name_index = {"example quest": {"g1"}, "eq": {"g1"}}
genre_index = {"rpg": {"g1"}}
platform_index = {"pc": {"g1"}, "console-x": {"g1"}}
publisher_index = {"pub1": {"g1"}}
assert name_index["eq"] & platform_index["pc"] == {"g1"}
assert {s for g, s in game_servers if g == "g1"} == set(servers)
```

For a database normalize Game, GameAlias, Genre, Platform, Publisher, GameGenre, GamePlatform, DiscordServer and `GameServer(game_id,guild_id PRIMARY KEY)` with indexed join columns. Reverse guild → games supports a server covering many games; one game can have many language/regional communities. In memory maintain both link-direction sets for O(degree) queries rather than scanning every relation. Name search uses normalized exact alias index plus optional full-text matching; filter queries intersect indexed id sets and return canonical records.

### Refresh incrementally with provenance and atomic indexes

Fetch permitted source change feeds/revisions/ETags where available; otherwise periodic scheduled full comparison. Persist source cursor, revision, content hash, fetch time, parser version and field-level provenance. Upsert by stable external identity, ignore duplicate/older revisions and rederive secondary indexes atomically from the old/new record. A platform change must remove obsolete index membership as well as add new membership. Reconcile periodic full manifests to catch missed deletes; an absent optional field is not necessarily an instruction to erase a more authoritative value.

Choose per-field source precedence/effective dates (for example publisher announcement for date, curated moderation for official guild status), retain conflicting candidates and route consequential identity conflicts for review. Never merge guilds because names match or delete all links merely because an invite expired. Model tombstone/delist and manual overrides separately; rechecks flag inaccessible/mismatched guilds. APIs list/search games, read linked servers and authorized admin refresh/link changes with versions. Test duplicate titles across editions, many-to-many links, missing fields, stale revisions, source deletion and index removal. No scraping implementation or live-source result is required by this prompt.

title: Simulation-style coding problem with scaling follow-up (mini system design)
question:
Simulation-style coding problem with scaling follow-up (mini system design)

Implement a simulation-style program: given an initial state and a sequence of events/operations, update the system state in order and output the final result and/or per-step outputs.

Requirements:

First, state and justify your assumed input format (initial parameters, event list, fields per event).
Clearly define the output.
Provide time/space complexity.

Follow-up (scale up): if the number of events and data size grow significantly, or the system must support high concurrency/distributed processing, describe how you would evolve the design:

Algorithm/data-structure optimizations;
Batch vs streaming;
Concurrency control and consistency;
Sharding, queues, caching, fault tolerance, and observability.

Note: since the original prompt is missing, present your solution as a reusable simulation framework with pluggable rule interfaces.

steps: A reusable executable contract, with rules injected
solution.example: The original simulation domain is explicitly missing. Define input as initial JSON-like state plus an already ordered event iterator of dictionaries with string id; the injected pure rule `transition(state,event)->(new_state,output)` defines domain legality. Preserve list order as authoritative; if timestamps are used, require a documented tie order before calling this framework. Return the final state and one result per input occurrence, labeling duplicate replay. A duplicate id with different payload is a conflict. The example rule below is a declared inventory fixture, not an invented original exercise.
solution.trap: For large data use immutable/persistent structures or transactional write sets, compact state-specific indexes and optional streamed output rather than deep-copying everything.
solution.teaching_notes_markdown:
<!-- architecture:W369:start -->
### Architecture and request flow

![Pluggable ordered-event simulation](../diagrams/W369_final_architecture.svg)

[Open the diagram](../diagrams/W369_final_architecture.svg). The unspecified game/domain rules stay in an injected transition function. The executable inventory fixture is one labeled demonstration, not a guessed hidden original problem. Sharding is safe only across independent state owners; events touching shared state still need an explicit common order/transaction.
<!-- architecture:W369:end -->

### A reusable executable contract, with rules injected

The original simulation domain is explicitly missing. Define input as initial JSON-like state plus an already ordered event iterator of dictionaries with string id; the injected pure rule `transition(state,event)->(new_state,output)` defines domain legality. Preserve list order as authoritative; if timestamps are used, require a documented tie order before calling this framework. Return the final state and one result per input occurrence, labeling duplicate replay. A duplicate id with different payload is a conflict. The example rule below is a declared inventory fixture, not an invented original exercise.

```python
from copy import deepcopy


def simulate(initial_state, events, transition):
    """Input events are ordered dicts with unique string id; rules are injected.
    transition(state,event) -> (new_state,output). A duplicate id/payload reuses
    the original output without applying the transition twice.
    """
    state = deepcopy(initial_state)
    seen = {}
    outputs = []
    for index, event in enumerate(events):
        if not isinstance(event, dict) or not isinstance(event.get("id"), str):
            raise ValueError(f"event {index}: string id required")
        identity = event["id"]
        if identity in seen:
            previous, result = seen[identity]
            if event != previous:
                raise ValueError("conflicting duplicate event id")
            outputs.append(
                {"id": identity, "duplicate": True, "result": deepcopy(result)}
            )
            continue
        # Isolated candidate prevents a failing rule from partially mutating state.
        candidate, result = transition(deepcopy(state), deepcopy(event))
        state = candidate
        seen[identity] = (deepcopy(event), deepcopy(result))
        outputs.append({"id": identity, "duplicate": False, "result": deepcopy(result)})
    return {"state": state, "outputs": outputs}


def inventory_rule(state, event):
    # Chosen demonstration only; original domain rules are not supplied.
    item = event["item"]
    quantity = event["quantity"]
    if type(quantity) is not int or quantity <= 0:
        raise ValueError("positive integer quantity required")
    if event["type"] == "receive":
        state[item] = state.get(item, 0) + quantity
    elif event["type"] == "ship":
        if state.get(item, 0) < quantity:
            return state, {"accepted": False, "reason": "insufficient"}
        state[item] -= quantity
    else:
        raise ValueError("unknown event type")
    return state, {"accepted": True, "remaining": state[item]}


if __name__ == "__main__":
    start = {"book": 2}
    events = [
        {"id": "a", "type": "receive", "item": "book", "quantity": 3},
        {"id": "b", "type": "ship", "item": "book", "quantity": 4},
        {"id": "c", "type": "ship", "item": "book", "quantity": 2},
    ]
    result = simulate(start, events + [events[1]], inventory_rule)
    assert (
        result["state"] == {"book": 1}
        and result["outputs"][2]["result"]["accepted"] is False
    )
    assert result["outputs"][3]["duplicate"] and start == {"book": 2}
    assert simulate(start, [], inventory_rule) == {"state": start, "outputs": []}
    try:
        simulate(start, [events[0], dict(events[0], quantity=8)], inventory_rule)
    except ValueError:
        pass
    else:
        raise AssertionError("conflicting id reuse accepted")
    print(
        "W369: final state book=1; rejected shipment, duplicate replay, empty and conflict checks passed"
    )
```

### Example and complexity

Starting book stock2, receive3 gives 5, ship4 gives 1, ship2 is rejected, then a duplicate ship4 reuses its prior result and leaves stock1. Invalid syntax/rule exceptions abort the run; a valid but infeasible business operation can return a rejected output without mutation. Copies isolate caller input and protect current state from a partially mutating failed rule. Tests cover the final result, rejection, exact duplicate, conflict and empty stream.

Let E events, S state size, P event/output payload and R rule cost. This safe generic copy-based reference costs O(E(S+P+R)) time, O(S+E·P) retained state/output/dedup storage, not a falsely claimed O(E) independent of state size. For large data use immutable/persistent structures or transactional write sets, compact state-specific indexes and optional streamed output rather than deep-copying everything. A domain rule that schedules future work uses a priority queue with `(time,tie_id)`; an already ordered input stream needs no heap.

At scale partition by independent entity key and preserve per-key ordering through a durable log. A single-threaded owner or versioned DB transaction linearizes updates; cross-entity invariants need transactions/coordinated saga, not arbitrary partitioning. Atomically checkpoint state+cursor+dedup or replay idempotently; use outbox/stable operation ids for external effects, fencing for stale workers and snapshots to bound recovery. Batch reduces overhead; streaming reduces latency, with backpressure and bounded buffers. Cache only versioned query views, and monitor rejected/duplicate/conflict counts, lag, state size and deterministic replay hashes. Without actual original rules no framework can claim original hidden tests passed.

title: Design a Food Review System with Reward Bonus
question:
Design a food-review system on top of DoorDash orders. A user who completed an order submits one review per item (text, 1-5 star rating, optional photos/video). The system aggregates per-item ratings as a 5-point average + count, lists reviews with like counts (like/unlike), and rewards reviews reaching 100+ likes with DoorDash credit. A variant pairs this with a monthly driver-payout subsystem.

Non-functional: read-heavy (per-item rating reads dominate — cache aggressively); bursty writes (a viral item attracts thousands of reviews); reward credit must be idempotent (rewarded exactly once at the 100-like crossing); multimedia served via CDN with size/type validation and moderation.

steps: Validate purchase eligibility before accepting a review
Exactly one reward at the qualifying crossing
Scale, failure and optional payout variant
solution.example: `POST /orders/{id}/items/{line_id}/review` accepts rating1..5, text, uploaded-media refs and client idempotency key. Check authenticated ownership and completed order/line server-side; choose one review per **order line** with unique(order_id, line_id, author), clarifying whether repeat purchases allow another item review. Store Review(id, order, line, item, author, rating, version, moderation, status), Media(asset, type, size, scan_status), LikeEdge(review, user, liked, version), RatingAggregate(item, sum, count, version), RewardGrant(review UNIQUE, threshold_policy, grant_id, status, credit_ref) and outbox. Read APIs return rating average+count and paginated approved reviews/like state; creator reward status is separate.
solution.trap: Average is total_sum/total_count, never average of per-shard averages; zero reviews returns no rating.
solution.teaching_notes_markdown:
<!-- architecture:W370:start -->
### Architecture and request flow

![Design a Food Review System with Reward Bonus: request, processing, state and result components.](../diagrams/W370_architecture.svg)

[Open the diagram at full size](../diagrams/W370_architecture.svg). This is a baseline component diagram for this question. The boxes describe responsibilities; they do not require a separate microservice for every box.

- **Request and state:** Review submission — user + purchase evidence → Review service — eligibility + moderation. That component consults or updates **Review and reward ledger — unique qualifying action** under the required access and consistency rules.
- **Work and result:** the work path passes through **Validated reward event — outbox** and **Reward worker — idempotent credit**, producing **Published review — reward status + audit**. Bound waiting and retries where a slow dependency can stall this path.
- **Correctness point:** One qualifying review earns one reward; retries and moderation changes need explicit ledger transitions.

When explaining the drawing, trace one normal request first, then a duplicate request, an unavailable dependency and recovery from saved state. If the question requires stricter guarantees or a different scope, state the change explicitly rather than treating this baseline as the only possible design.
<!-- architecture:W370:end -->

### Validate purchase eligibility before accepting a review

`POST /orders/{id}/items/{line_id}/review` accepts rating1..5, text, uploaded-media refs and client idempotency key. Check authenticated ownership and completed order/line server-side; choose one review per **order line** with unique(order_id, line_id, author), clarifying whether repeat purchases allow another item review. Store Review(id, order, line, item, author, rating, version, moderation, status), Media(asset, type, size, scan_status), LikeEdge(review, user, liked, version), RatingAggregate(item, sum, count, version), RewardGrant(review UNIQUE, threshold_policy, grant_id, status, credit_ref) and outbox. Read APIs return rating average+count and paginated approved reviews/like state; creator reward status is separate.

Media uploads use scoped signed URLs with declared size/type checks, malware/content moderation and CDN delivery only after approval; untrusted client MIME is insufficient. Review text/rating is pending until moderation passes. An edit/rejection/deletion retracts the old approved rating contribution and adds the new approved one under versioned events. Average is total_sum/total_count, never average of per-shard averages; zero reviews returns no rating. Cache per-item sum/count/average and invalidate/version on changes, with hot-item sharded/coalesced projection updates. Writes remain durable before cached success is advertised.

### Exactly one reward at the qualifying crossing

A review like is desired state with unique(review, user), so duplicates don't increment. Define reward eligibility as first **accepted canonical like-count transition old<100≤new** while review is approved and anti-abuse eligibility holds. In one serialized per-review transaction/CAS, apply the edge transition/count and insert RewardGrant plus outbox under unique(review, policy). A retry or 101 → 99 → 100 re-crossing cannot create a second grant. An eventually consistent display counter is not the sole authority for a monetary threshold; use a correct per-review transition owner or reconcile it against unique accepted edges.

Credit worker sends stable grant_id to the credit ledger's idempotent posting API, records pending/granted/unknown and reconciles timeout with the same id. A local DB row alone cannot guarantee no duplicate external credit if the ledger lacks idempotency/status query. Choose that downstream contract; a crash after credit-before-ack must not retry under a new grant id. At 99 likes two concurrent valid likes lead to count 101 but one grant. Like removal/moderation after a grant needs an explicit versioned reversal/abuse policy, not silently issuing another credit when eligibility returns. Reward amount was not supplied, so configure/report it rather than invent currency values.

### Scale, failure and optional payout variant

Assume 1M reviews/day and 50M review reads/day ≈ 579 reads/s average with large hot-item skew; size caches/CDN and peak rates from measured bursts, not only averages. Partition reviews by item for reads with author/order eligibility indexes; likes by review/user and notification/reward workers have bounded queues/retries. Monitor rating drift, duplicate grants, threshold reconciliation, media backlog, review abuse and cache freshness. Test duplicate review/like, concurrent99 → 100, credit timeout, edited ratings, rejected media and aggregate rebuild from canonical reviews.

A monthly driver payout subsystem is a distinct ledger workflow: freeze eligible completed-delivery/adjustment line items by driver/month, calculate minor-unit amounts using versioned rules, create one payout id, reconcile provider settlement and support audited adjustments. Do not reuse a review-like counter as payable balance. The prompt gives no driver compensation formula, so the architecture can share idempotency/outbox/ledger discipline but cannot compute payouts without those inputs.

title: DS Business Case: Credit Lending P&L Decomposition
question:
DS Power Day case round. The interviewer presents a concrete credit/lending business scenario and asks you to frame the analysis, decompose the P&L, and propose levers. Mental math is part of the round. Examples reported:

Should we offer line-of-credit increases to a specific customer segment? Forecast revenue and default impact.
A new credit product is launching in a new geography — analyse expected profitability.
A risk-model change has been proposed — what is the P&L sensitivity?

Walk through: (1) clarify the goal (revenue uplift vs default reduction vs combined profit), (2) decompose into a P&L equation, (3) identify levers, (4) do an approximate mental-math sensitivity check on the dominant lever. Do not jump to modelling — the graded signal is business decomposition first.

steps: Decide what evidence would change the recommendation
solution.example: With 10,000 customers, 200 USD incremental balance each and an 8% net spread yield, spread income is 160,000 USD. Subtract 40,000 servicing and 80,000 expected loss to obtain 40,000 USD profit. A one-percentage-point PD increase at EAD 200 USD and LGD 50% costs 10,000 USD.
solution.trap: A credit limit is not EAD; a policy can change risk on existing balances, and interest/loss accounting must avoid double-counting defaults.
solution.teaching_notes_markdown:
### Frame an incremental lending decision

For a credit-line increase, compare expected risk-adjusted profit under the new policy with profit under the no-change policy. The actual cohort and financial inputs are not supplied, so the calculation below is an explicitly hypothetical example. Clarify the horizon, eligible customers, expected usage, interest/fee recognition, default definition, recoveries, funding, servicing and any capital requirement before choosing a model.

A one-period approximation for a roughly homogeneous cohort is

$$
\Delta\Pi=N\left[\Delta B(y-c_f)-\Delta(PD\cdot EAD\cdot LGD)
+\Delta\mathrm{fees}-\Delta\mathrm{servicing}\right]
-\Delta\mathrm{fixed\ costs}-\Delta\mathrm{capital\ charge}.
$$

Here N is customer count, $\Delta B$ is incremental average drawn balance per customer, y is interest yield before credit losses, and $c_f$ is funding rate. PD is default probability over the same horizon, EAD is exposure at default and LGD is the loss fraction after recoveries. The bracketed amounts are per-customer currency; fixed costs and capital charge are cohort totals. The change in expected loss is the new-policy loss minus the old-policy loss, not automatically a change in PD alone. Use a discounted monthly cash-flow model when timing, repayments, delinquency or recoveries materially affect value.

### Work a mental-math example

Assume 10,000 customers receive 1,000 USD of additional limit and draw an average of 20%, giving 200 USD incremental balance each. Let annual interest yield be 12%, funding cost 4%, extra servicing 4 USD/customer, and additional fixed/capital costs zero for this illustration.

| Component | Per customer | Cohort total |
|---|---:|---:|
| Net interest spread: $200(0.12-0.04)$ | 16 USD | 160,000 USD |
| Additional servicing | −4 USD | −40,000 USD |
| Amount available before credit losses | 12 USD | 120,000 USD |
| Assumed incremental expected loss | −8 USD | −80,000 USD |
| Incremental annual profit | 4 USD | 40,000 USD |

Break-even incremental loss is therefore 12 USD/customer. For sensitivity, additionally assume incremental EAD is 200 USD and LGD is 50%. A one-percentage-point PD increase adds

$$200\times0.5\times0.01=1\ \text{USD/customer},$$

or 10,000 USD across the cohort. Four percentage points would erase the illustrated 40,000 USD profit. A credit limit is not EAD, however, and a policy-induced PD change can affect existing balances too. Recalculate the complete affected book when that is true. Keep interest recognition consistent with expected-loss accounting so the same default loss is not charged twice.

### Identify coupled levers before modeling

Revenue levers include take-up, utilization, pricing, fees and retention. Risk levers include eligibility, limit size, PD/EAD/LGD calibration and collections. Costs include funding, servicing, acquisition, fraud, launch work and capital. These interact: increasing price can reduce take-up or change borrower selection, so do not optimize each spreadsheet cell independently.

For a new geography, add local demand, distribution, payment operations, currency exposure and launch costs; determine the relevant local requirements rather than inventing current rules. For a proposed model change, translate score/threshold changes into actual approvals, balances and losses. A 1% AUC gain does not imply a 1% profit gain.

### Decide what evidence would change the recommendation

Use mature, time-valid cohorts and compare against the no-change policy. Check segment calibration, selection effects and uncertainty in the dominant driver. A controlled eligible-cohort rollout or credible causal design is needed before attributing retention/default changes to an offer. Set loss, customer-outcome and operational guardrails, and specify a rollback threshold. Present a sensitivity range and the missing evidence that would reverse the decision rather than an unsupported precise forecast.

### Further study

- [F140: Design a credit-model business evaluation without confusing accuracy and profit.](../14_regression_and_experiment_depth.md#f140)

title: Design a Polling Schedule with a Boot State and a Live State
question:
A live feed produces one record every 30 seconds. The records pass through two stores before they reach a database you control, and the second hop is slow and of unknown shape. Design the procedure that reads them with a fixed schedule, so that every scheduled read returns exactly one new record and the copy in your database stays as fresh as possible.

Setting
1.
The feed writes record k (k = 0, 1, 2, ...) into store A at time 30k seconds. Every record has an integer id equal to k and a data field.
2.
A is a black box: it cannot be read or changed.
3.
A is copied into database B. Record k becomes readable in B at time b_k = 30k + d_k, where the lag satisfies 0 <= d_k <= 300 seconds. Records reach B in id order (b_k never decreases with k) and none is lost. Nothing else is promised about the pattern of the lags: they may be constant, jittery, or arrive in batches.
4.
B can be read but not changed. B stores no timestamps. A read can ask for all records with id greater than a given id, or for one record by id.
5.
You fully control database C and the process that fills it. A poll reads B once, instantly and at no cost. C keeps a cursor, the highest id it has stored. A poll at time T returns every record with id above the cursor that is readable in B at T; C stores them and moves the cursor. C only knows its own clock, not A's.
6.
The copy behaviour of B is the same in the test environment and in production. In the test environment C runs the same polling code against a copy of the feed.
States
1.
Boot state (test environment): the polling rate may change freely and polls that return the wrong number of records are ignored. It exists to learn about B.
2.
Live state (production): polls run on a fixed schedule with interval x seconds. A poll fails when it returns 0 records or 2 or more records. No failure is acceptable.
3.
Freshness: the staleness of a record is the time from b_k until the first poll that returns it. In the live state the worst-case staleness should be as small as possible.
What to decide
1.
What C does in the boot state, and what it measures.
2.
The exact condition under which C moves from boot to live.
3.
The live poll interval x and the times at which live polls run, with a justification that no poll fails and that staleness is as small as that allows.
4.
What C does when the boot state shows that no live schedule can avoid failures.

The phase of a live schedule is the time of its first poll, taken modulo the interval x. Two schedules with the same interval and the same phase poll at the same moments of every cycle.

Examples
1.
Every record reaches B exactly 47 seconds after it was written (d_k = 47). Any interval of 30 seconds is failure free at every phase, because each 30 second window then holds exactly one arrival. Polling at 30j + 48 seconds keeps each record 1 second stale.
2.
Even records reach B 10 seconds after they were written and odd records 25 seconds after. A 30 second schedule is failure free only for phases in [25, 40) seconds modulo 30. Starting at phase 25 seconds leaves the earliest-arriving record 15 seconds stale.
3.
Records reach B in pairs, records 2m and 2m+1 together at time 60m + 50 (record 2m has a lag of 50 seconds and record 2m+1 a lag of 20). Every poll that sees one record of a pair sees both, so no interval and no phase avoids failures.
Constraints
The feed rate is exactly 1 record per 30 seconds and the lag bound is 300 seconds.
The boot state may run for several minutes but not for ever. Polls need not be rate limited in the boot state.
Clocks on the machines running C run at a rate within 50 parts per million of the feed's clock.
Follow-up 1: arrivals that no schedule can poll cleanly

Take the case of example 3, or any pattern whose arrivals are spread over 30 seconds or more. Define a read contract and a schedule for which no poll ever fails, say what it costs in staleness, and say what C can do if boot never gets to observe the pattern at all.

Follow-up 2: staying failure free for weeks

The live schedule must keep working while the clocks drift. State how long a schedule lasts without correction, how to schedule the polls so that errors do not add up, and what the live process does when its own assumptions stop holding.

<!-- architecture:W372:start -->
### Architecture and request flow

![Arrival observations, feasibility and fixed polling](../diagrams/W372_final_architecture.svg)

[Open the diagram](../diagrams/W372_final_architecture.svg). Boot can estimate observed arrival phases, but finite observations cannot prove a forever-correct schedule under the original arbitrary-lag assumptions. With an additional valid arrival envelope, choose a feasible phase and account for drift. Otherwise change the read contract, rather than claim adaptive backoff guarantees exactly one result.
<!-- architecture:W372:end -->

### Under the stated assumptions, finite boot cannot certify a failure-free live mode

Write arrivals in one idealized clock as $b_k=a+30k+d_k$, with unknown feed epoch a and 0≤d_k≤300. If a fixed live interval x returns exactly one new record forever, cumulative arrivals and polls differ only by a bounded startup amount. Bounded lag gives arrival rate1/30, while the polls consume1/x, so **x=30 seconds** is necessary in feed-clock time. A different interval eventually runs out or accumulates records.

Let its poll assigned to record k be $p_k=a+30k+\theta$. Because a poll includes records readable at that instant, exactly one requires $p_{k-1}<b_k\le p_k$, equivalent to $d_k\le\theta<d_k+30$ for every k. Hence a known entire pattern permits a phase iff

$$\boxed{\sup_k d_k\le\theta<\inf_k d_k+30},\qquad \boxed{\sup d-\inf d<30}.$$

For an infinite pattern where sup/inf endpoints are not attained, write the individual strict inequalities rather than carelessly discard endpoint subtleties; the robust positive-slack condition above is the useful operational one. Worst staleness is sup(θ-d_k). With a known attained max and no drift, choose θ=max d and achieve range(max d−min d); any earlier phase misses that max-lag arrival, and a later phase only increases every staleness.

### What boot actually measures, and why the transition condition is missing

Poll frequently and track id-specific last-absent/first-present times, giving intervals for each b_k, then subtract30k (in calibrated clock units) to estimate aligned arrival offsets without reading A. Detect duplicates/batches and maintain an uncertainty-aware feasible phase intersection. A finite observed range≥30 or a simultaneous pair proves no phase fits those observations. An observed range<30 only shows a phase fits **the past**: any finite fixed-lag boot prefix can be followed by the allowed batch pattern, with the same copying behavior in test and production interpreted as one unknown process. “Same behavior” does not promise a known finite period, stationarity envelope or that rare failures have already appeared.

Thus there is **no exact finite-data-only boot → live condition guaranteeing the original no-failure requirement**. Remain in boot/reject that strict mode unless an independently justified future arrival envelope/periodic contract and clock-phase bound are supplied. A finite boot timeout returns “uncertifiable/unsupported,” not a guessed safe phase. Transfer from a test clock to production also needs a production epoch/rate calibration; shared lag behavior alone does not transfer absolute clock phase.

The helper below computes only the **observed** feasible interval and demonstrates the counterexample; it must not be called a future guarantee.

```python
def feasible_phase(arrivals, period=30.0):
    """Observed indexed arrivals only; cannot certify unobserved future lags."""
    if not arrivals:
        raise ValueError("observations required")
    aligned = [time - period * index for index, time in arrivals]
    lower = max(aligned)
    upper = min(aligned) + period
    return (lower, upper) if lower < upper else None


def poll_counts(arrivals, first, period, polls, cursor=-1):
    counts = []
    for j in range(polls):
        now = first + j * period
        ready = [i for i, t in arrivals if i > cursor and t <= now]
        counts.append(len(ready))
        if ready:
            cursor = max(ready)
    return counts


if __name__ == "__main__":
    fixed = [(k, 30 * k + 47) for k in range(100)]
    assert feasible_phase(fixed) == (47, 77)
    assert poll_counts(fixed, 47, 30, 100) == [1] * 100
    jitter = [(k, 30 * k + (10 if k % 2 == 0 else 25)) for k in range(100)]
    assert feasible_phase(jitter) == (25, 40)
    assert poll_counts(jitter, 25, 30, 100) == [1] * 100
    pairs = [(k, 60 * (k // 2) + 50) for k in range(100)]
    assert feasible_phase(pairs) is None
    assert poll_counts(pairs, 50, 30, 4) == [2, 0, 2, 0]
    # Same finite boot prefix, incompatible future: an allowed batching suffix.
    boot = [(k, 30 * k + 10) for k in range(10)]
    assert feasible_phase(boot) == (10, 40)
    future = boot + [(10, 350), (11, 350)]
    assert feasible_phase(future) is None
    print(
        "W372: phase intervals, exact boundaries, batched impossibility and finite-boot counterexample passed"
    )
```

### Apply the examples and relax the contract when necessary

Constant d47 yields θ∈[47, 77), all phases modulo30, and θ47 gives zero ideal staleness (θ48 gives the example's1 s). Alternating10/25 yields θ∈[25, 40), modulo30 the union[25, 30)∪[0, 10), with θ25 worst15 s. Paired arrivals yield no phase: any poll sees either0 or 2 from a pair, and changing x cannot separate simultaneous arrivals.

The freshest robust alternative is to allow a poll to return **zero or more** new records and store the batch idempotently. Poll every chosenδ (e.g.1 s), so staleness after availability is at mostδ plus scheduling/clock error, and batches are not failures. It works even if boot never observes the rare pattern. If exactly one returned record is indispensable, change B's read contract to `get(cursor+1)` and deliberately delay to the latest guaranteed availability: with known feed epoch, poll record k at a+30k+300, giving staleness300−d_k≤300 s. With only arrival-derived epoch interval[a_low, a_high], schedule at a_high+30k+300, yielding bound300+(a_high−a_low), up to 600 s before better calibration. Buffering a batch in C and releasing one record/30 s also changes “scheduled read of B” into a different contract and must be named as such.

### Clock drift and weeks of operation

At 50ppm, phase error can grow4.32 s/day against the feed; two independently bounded C clocks can differ by up to 100ppm when transferring calibration. Schedule absolute deadlines t0+n·30 on a monotonic clock, not `sleep(30)` after work, to avoid extra accumulated execution-time error. Absolute scheduling does not remove oscillator-rate drift.

For a certified envelope with spread R<30 choose θ=max d+g, 0<g<30−R. Initial phase slack is min(g, 30−R−g); with drift bound ρ and initial calibration uncertainty e, guaranteed horizon is at most(slack−e)/ρ. Centering maximizes slack; constant lag permits15 s ideal slack and at 50ppm about 3.47 days without resynchronization. Freshness-optimal θ=max d has zero slack on one boundary and is not robust for weeks. Bound residual clock discipline/resync often enough, preserve cursor across correction and avoid double/skip polls. If the envelope/clock certificate expires or health checks detect violation, leave strict-live mode **before** its guarantee is lost or use the relaxed batch contract; observing a failed poll and retrying cannot retroactively satisfy “no failure.”

title: Cross-Domain SSO After an Acquisition, and OIDC Across Sites
question:
Design single sign-on across two unrelated domains, then generalise it to OpenID Connect (OIDC) across several sites with delegated access to third-party tools.

Part 1 — Cross-domain single sign-on

A business owns foo.com and has just acquired bar.com. A user who signs in on either domain must be signed in on the other domain automatically, with no second password prompt.

1.
Explain why one session cookie cannot cover both domains.
2.
Design the sign-in flow. Give every redirect, the request parameters, and where each session is stored.
3.
Design sign-out so that signing out on one domain ends the session on both.
4.
List the attacks the flow must resist (for example open redirects, token replay and CSRF) and how the design prevents each one.
Part 2 — OIDC across multiple sites

The company now runs several sites that must share one login.

1.
Design the architecture: the identity provider, the relying parties and the tokens each one holds.
2.
Give the OIDC flow that each site uses, and explain the purpose of the ID token, the access token and the refresh token.
3.
Inside the app, a signed-in user must be able to grant the app access to certain third-party tools. Design the authorisation flow, the scopes, and how the app stores and refreshes the third-party tokens.
Output

Sequence diagrams (or numbered message lists) for each flow, and the reason for each security-relevant choice.

steps: Cross-domain login uses a common identity authority
Logout is server invalidation, not cookie magic
Delegated third-party tools are a separate authorization grant
solution.example: A cookie for foo.com cannot be scoped to unrelated bar.com; Domain cookies cover an allowed domain suffix, not arbitrary owners. Put a shared identity provider at `login.company.example` and register foo/bar as separate relying-party clients with exact HTTPS callbacks. Each app stores its own server session and host-only Secure, HttpOnly cookie; IdP has its own login cookie. The browser establishes bar's local session when it visits bar and follows an IdP redirect without another password. Foo cannot directly set bar's cookie, and cross-site iframes/third-party cookies are not a reliable prerequisite.
solution.trap: Foo cannot directly set bar's cookie, and cross-site iframes/third-party cookies are not a reliable prerequisite.
solution.teaching_notes_markdown:
<!-- architecture:W373:start -->
### Architecture and request flow

![Cross-Domain SSO After an Acquisition, and OIDC Across Sites: request, processing, state and result components.](../diagrams/W373_architecture.svg)

[Open the diagram at full size](../diagrams/W373_architecture.svg). This is a baseline component diagram for this question. The boxes describe responsibilities; they do not require a separate microservice for every box.

- **Request and state:** Browser — target application → Identity redirect — state + nonce + PKCE. That component consults or updates **Identity provider — sessions + registered clients** under the required access and consistency rules.
- **Work and result:** the work path passes through **Code exchange — validate redirect and issuer** and **Application session — token validation**, producing **Scoped application access — logout + expiration**. Bound waiting and retries where a slow dependency can stall this path.
- **Correctness point:** Do not share raw session cookies across unrelated domains; validate issuer, audience, nonce and redirect binding.

When explaining the drawing, trace one normal request first, then a duplicate request, an unavailable dependency and recovery from saved state. If the question requires stricter guarantees or a different scope, state the change explicitly rather than treating this baseline as the only possible design.
<!-- architecture:W373:end -->

### Cross-domain login uses a common identity authority

A cookie for foo.com cannot be scoped to unrelated bar.com; Domain cookies cover an allowed domain suffix, not arbitrary owners. Put a shared identity provider at `login.company.example` and register foo/bar as separate relying-party clients with exact HTTPS callbacks. Each app stores its own server session and host-only Secure, HttpOnly cookie; IdP has its own login cookie. The browser establishes bar's local session when it visits bar and follows an IdP redirect without another password. Foo cannot directly set bar's cookie, and cross-site iframes/third-party cookies are not a reliable prerequisite.

Numbered authorization-code flow for **each** app:

1. Browser → foo `/login`; foo creates a short-lived login transaction with random state, nonce, PKCE verifier and intended local return path.
2. Foo → browser302 to IdP `/authorize?response_type=code&client_id=foo&redirect_uri=https%3A...foo...callback&scope=openid%20profile&state=S&nonce=N&code_challenge=C&code_challenge_method=S256`.
3. IdP authenticates once (or reuses its existing SSO session), obtains required consent and 302 redirects to foo callback with single-use code and matching state.
4. Foo checks the browser-bound state, then server → IdP token endpoint exchanges code, exact redirect_uri, client authentication and code_verifier overTLS.
5. Foo verifies ID-token signature/trusted issuer, audience/azp, expiry and nonce, maps `(issuer,subject)` to its account, rotates/creates local session and redirects only to an allowlisted local return path.
6. Visiting bar repeats its own transaction/client/callback; IdP's session avoids a second password, and bar receives its own tokens/session, never foo's raw cookie.

ID token is an identity assertion to that relying party; access token authorizes its audience's API; a refresh token, if issued, obtains new tokens and stays server-side. Do not send an ID token as a generic API bearer credential or merge accounts merely by unverified matching email. These distinctions follow [OIDC Core](https://openid.net/specs/openid-connect-core-1_0.html).

### Logout is server invalidation, not cookie magic

A CSRF-protected logout on either app invalidates its local session and initiates IdP end-session. IdP marks the shared session revoked and sends signed back-channel logout tokens to registered apps; each validates issuer, audience, event/subject-or-sid and replay identity, then invalidates matching local sessions. Browser cookies on other domains may remain physically present but no longer map to valid sessions. Use a durable delivery/retry ledger and idempotent logout consumers. The mechanism is defined by [OIDC Back-Channel Logout](https://openid.net/specs/openid-connect-backchannel-1_0.html).

Instant cross-site logout during a partition cannot be guaranteed by asynchronous notifications alone. To require immediate enforcement, apps check a central session/revocation epoch on protected requests and fail closed if it is unavailable; otherwise state the bounded session-cache/token lifetime during which revocation may lag. A self-contained unexpired access token may remain usable unless the resource checks revocation or its short expiry ends; logout does not universally revoke every third-party grant.

### Delegated third-party tools are a separate authorization grant

When a signed-in user selects “connect tool,” create a browser/user-bound OAuth transaction with state, PKCE and exact registered callback to that tool provider. Redirect for consent to only required scopes (read versus send/delete separately); exchange returned code server-side and bind the grant to local user, provider account, scope and token audience. Encrypt refresh/access tokens in a secrets store, keep them out of browser/logs, refresh with concurrency control and rotation/reuse detection where supported, and provide disconnect/revocation. An app SSO session is not consent to every tool. Verify current local permissions before each delegated action and handle expired/revoked grants with reconnection rather than silently widen scopes.

Use short-lived single-use codes, exact redirect matching, state/nonce/PKCE, HTTPS, issuer/key/audience validation and allowlisted local return paths against CSRF, code interception, mix-up, open redirects and replay. Protect sessions from fixation/XSS with rotation/cookie controls; keep user-controlled claims out of authorization decisions. Use least privilege and sender-constrained/rotating tokens when supported, consistent with [OAuth Security BCP](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9700.html).

- [F170: Design a cache without serving incorrect data.](../17_distributed_systems_depth.md#f170)

title: Deep Dive — What Happens When You Access a URL
question:
Deep Dive — What Happens When You Access a URL

Open-ended deep-dive round: explain everything that happens when you enter a URL in a browser. The interviewer probes wherever you go — DNS, CDN, service discovery, authentication, inter-service communication protocols — so steer toward areas you can defend in depth.

Requirements

Open discussion: when you access a URL (e.g. www.example.com) in a browser, what happens end to end? Expect drill-downs into:

DNS resolution and how it works in detail.
CDN / edge caching behavior.
Service discovery and how services locate one another.
Authentication.
Communication protocols between services/components.
Notes
It is a genuinely open round with no fixed script — questions can feel random, and the interviewer will keep digging into whatever you raise. Candidates who opened broad got pulled into details they couldn't answer.
The winning strategy is to deliberately drive the conversation toward subsystems you know cold and go deep there, rather than spreading thin across the whole stack.

steps: Walk one URL all the way to a page
Go deep on DNS without conflating caches and truth
solution.example: Parse scheme, hostname, port, path, query and fragment; the fragment stays client-side. A bare name needs browser policy to choose a scheme/search; assume `https://www.example.com/`. Browser may upgrade viaHSTS and satisfy the request from a valid cache/service-worker response. Otherwise it reuses a suitable existing connection or resolves the hostname using browser/OS caches and a configured recursive DNS resolver. The resolver follows root → TLD → authoritative delegation on cache misses, obtains A/AAAA (possibly via CNAME/HTTPS records) and caches withTTL. The browser typically races usableIPv6/IPv4 paths; DNS routing can select a CDN edge rather than the origin.
solution.trap: The browser typically races usableIPv6/IPv4 paths; DNS routing can select a CDN edge rather than the origin.

<!-- architecture:W374:start -->
### Architecture and request flow

![Deep Dive — What Happens When You Access a URL: request, processing, state and result components.](../diagrams/W374_architecture.svg)

[Open the diagram at full size](../diagrams/W374_architecture.svg). This is a baseline component diagram for this question. The boxes describe responsibilities; they do not require a separate microservice for every box.

- **Request and state:** Browser — requested origin → DNS + edge routing — TLS + connection. That component consults or updates **Origin and session state — identity + cache rules** under the required access and consistency rules.
- **Work and result:** the work path passes through **Authenticated request — route + service lookup** and **Application handler — access + response policy**, producing **Browser rendering — cache + origin enforcement**. Bound waiting and retries where a slow dependency can stall this path.
- **Correctness point:** DNS, TLS, authentication and browser-origin policy solve different problems; trace their separate failure points.

When explaining the drawing, trace one normal request first, then a duplicate request, an unavailable dependency and recovery from saved state. If the question requires stricter guarantees or a different scope, state the change explicitly rather than treating this baseline as the only possible design.
<!-- architecture:W374:end -->

### Walk one URL all the way to a page

Parse scheme, hostname, port, path, query and fragment; the fragment stays client-side. A bare name needs browser policy to choose a scheme/search; assume `https://www.example.com/`. Browser may upgrade viaHSTS and satisfy the request from a valid cache/service-worker response. Otherwise it reuses a suitable existing connection or resolves the hostname using browser/OS caches and a configured recursive DNS resolver. The resolver follows root → TLD → authoritative delegation on cache misses, obtains A/AAAA (possibly via CNAME/HTTPS records) and caches withTTL. The browser typically races usableIPv6/IPv4 paths; DNS routing can select a CDN edge rather than the origin.

For HTTP/1.1 orHTTP/2 HTTPS, establish TCP thenTLS (or resume), validate certificate chain/hostname/time and negotiate protocol viaALPN; HTTP/3 usesQUIC overUDP withTLS1.3 integrated. TLS protects transport and authenticates the server; it does not prove the application user may access an order. A CDN terminates a declaredTLS boundary, checks cache key/method/headers/freshness and either returns a hit or forwards a miss to the origin/load balancer. Private/personalized responses must not enter a public cache under an incomplete key; respect Cache-Control, Vary and authorization/cookie policy.

The load balancer selects a healthy eligible backend with deadlines/connection limits. The handler authenticates session/token, authorizes the resource, validates input and calls downstream services/data stores. Service discovery maps a logical name to changing endpoints viaDNS, registry or proxy/service mesh; it is not the same as the public domain'sDNS authority. HTTP/JSON, gRPC overHTTP/2 or durable asynchronous messages fit different synchronous/stream/retry needs. Propagate trace/deadline/verified identity, not arbitrary spoofable headers, and retry only safe/idempotent operations.

The response returns status, headers and bytes, possibly compressed/streamed. Browser follows redirects under origin policy, parsesHTML intoDOM andCSS intoCSSOM, executes/defer-loads scripts, fetches subresources, computes layout, paints and composites. Script/layout work can delay interactivity after network completion. Cookies, CORS/CSP and same-origin restrictions govern browser behavior separately from server authorization. Rendering repeats incrementally as resources/scripts arrive.

### Go deep on DNS without conflating caches and truth

A recursive resolver performs recursion for the client; root/TLD/authoritative servers usually give referrals/authoritative records. NS records delegate, MX serves mail, TXT can carry verification, CAA constrains certificate issuance and A/AAAA supply addresses. TTL limits ordinary cache freshness but is not an immediate invalidation broadcast. Negative answers also cache under their rules. DNSSEC authenticates DNS data when correctly validated, not encryption orHTTP user identity; encrypted DNS protects the resolver path under its trust model.

ShortTTLs speed endpoint changes but increase lookup load and do not guarantee every client honors instant failover; longerTTLs improve cache hit/availability but prolong stale routing. GeoDNS can choose based on resolver/client-location hints yet suffers cache granularity, while anycast announces the same IP from many edges and lets routing choose a path that is not necessarily lowest application latency. A failedDNS lookup, TLS validation, erroring origin and blocked browser cross-origin read are different incidents. Instrument DNS/connect/TLS/TTFB/render timings and trace one cache hit, one miss and one authentication failure before expanding the design.

title: Design a Feature Flag System
question:
Build a feature-flag platform that lets engineers roll out flags by percentage or user attribute, evaluated cheaply at scale on the server-side request path.

Functional requirements:

API for defining/updating flag rules (boolean, percentage rollout, attribute-based targeting).
A flag-evaluation API on the hot request path that is sub-millisecond at high QPS — evaluation cannot become a request-path bottleneck.
Consistent percentage rollouts (same user → same answer across requests).
Runtime rule updates that propagate in seconds without rebooting client services.
Audit logs and an emergency kill-switch.

Scale targets: tens of thousands of evaluations/sec per cluster; update fan-out to many services; eventual consistency on the order of seconds is acceptable.

Key decisions to surface: push vs. pull vs. hybrid rule delivery; centralized eval service vs. in-process SDK with cached rules; how percentage rollouts stay stable (hashing strategy and salt); how to bound the blast radius of a bad rule (staging, canary, kill-switch).

steps: Put evaluation in the process, distribution off the hot path
solution.example: At tens of thousands evaluations/s, sub-millisecond target favors an in-process SDK reading an immutable compiled rule snapshot, not a network RPC for each flag. Control APIs create/update/publish/rollback flags with expected revision; store `Flag(id,environment,type,default,ordered_rules,rollout_salt,owner,revision,status)` plus audit and immutable snapshot hashes. Validate types, operator/regex cost, bounds, missing-attribute behavior and rule precedence (for example emergency disabled → explicit deny/allow → ordered attribute rules → percentage → default). Keep arbitrary user code out of rules and authorization/security invariants outside optional product flags.
solution.trap: Specify user/account/session unit; missing identity needs an explicit default rather than randomizing each request.

<!-- architecture:W375:start -->
### Architecture and request flow

![Design a Feature Flag System: request, processing, state and result components.](../diagrams/W375_architecture.svg)

[Open the diagram at full size](../diagrams/W375_architecture.svg). This is a baseline component diagram for this question. The boxes describe responsibilities; they do not require a separate microservice for every box.

- **Request and state:** Operator change — config generation → Configuration service — validate + approve. That component consults or updates **Versioned config store — prior rollback version** under the required access and consistency rules.
- **Work and result:** the work path passes through **Distribution stream — snapshot + deltas** and **Local SDK evaluation — deterministic bucketing**, producing **Application behavior — freshness + exposure logs**. Bound waiting and retries where a slow dependency can stall this path.
- **Correctness point:** Version every update and keep a safe fallback; eventual delivery alone does not establish current configuration.

When explaining the drawing, trace one normal request first, then a duplicate request, an unavailable dependency and recovery from saved state. If the question requires stricter guarantees or a different scope, state the change explicitly rather than treating this baseline as the only possible design.
<!-- architecture:W375:end -->

### Put evaluation in the process, distribution off the hot path

At tens of thousands evaluations/s, sub-millisecond target favors an in-process SDK reading an immutable compiled rule snapshot, not a network RPC for each flag. Control APIs create/update/publish/rollback flags with expected revision; store `Flag(id,environment,type,default,ordered_rules,rollout_salt,owner,revision,status)` plus audit and immutable snapshot hashes. Validate types, operator/regex cost, bounds, missing-attribute behavior and rule precedence (for example emergency disabled → explicit deny/allow → ordered attribute rules → percentage → default). Keep arbitrary user code out of rules and authorization/security invariants outside optional product flags.

For percentage rollout compute a specified cross-language hash of `(environment,flag_id,stable_salt,unit_id)` mapped to[0, 1), then enable when h<p. Keep the salt stable across **rule revision/percentage** changes; including every new revision in the hash would reshuffle cohorts.20%→30% monotonically adds users whose h is in [.2, .3), with existing cohorts stable. Specify user/account/session unit; missing identity needs an explicit default rather than randomizing each request. Attribute targeting can override percentage under the declared rule order, and changing attributes can legitimately change a result.

### Push notifications plus authoritative pull

SDK starts from a verified snapshot/local last-known-good file, fetches current environment generation, and subscribes to an ordered change/version stream. Push a small generation/digest hint, then pull signed/hashed immutable snapshot/delta; a missed event triggers periodic poll/version-gap recovery. Apply a whole compatible snapshot atomically so one request cannot observe half of two revisions. SDKs report generation/lag/health; rollout stages can canary rule evaluation and shadow comparisons before broad publish. If offline, continue the documented safe default/last-known-good policy, mark stale and reconnect with backoff/jitter.

An emergency kill switch is a high-priority versioned override bypassing normal bake stages, with reserved distribution capacity and short reconciliation polls. It still takes network/SDK propagation time; it cannot instantly alter an isolated process. Critical unsafe actions may need independent fail-closed server authorization rather than a stale local flag. Rollback publishes a **new generation pointing to old immutable rules**, so clients do not reject it as an out-of-order lower generation.

### Scale and verify

Assume 100kSDK instances and 50 KB snapshots: one full fanout is 5 GB; small version hints/deltas and regional cache tiers reduce origin pressure. Evaluation O(number_of_rules_checked) stays bounded through compiled indexes, limited rule count and no per-eval synchronous logs; asynchronously sample exposures/decision reasons by flag/generation while preserving needed experiment semantics. Reject concurrent stale edits with 409, keep actor/reason/audit and test compatibility across SDK versions.

Measure local evalp99, CPU/allocation cost, rule-count worst case, distributionp95/max lag, stale SDKs, kill-switch convergence and error/default rates. Test hash parity across languages, percentage boundaries, missing attributes, invalid rules, lost/duplicate/out-of-order updates, offline bootstrap and rollback. The diagram's config store → distribution → local evaluator expresses this exact separation; eventual notifications alone are not configuration authority.

### Further study
