title: Wikipedia Internet Archive / Web Crawler
question:
Design a crawler/archive system that starts from a primary VM and roughly 1000 small bot VMs, creates an initial copy of Wikipedia-like content, and keeps the archive updated over time.

Requirements
Start from a primary VM and around 1000 small bot VMs.
Create an initial copy of Wikipedia-like web content.
Keep the copied content updated over time.
Fetch web pages at large scale; one prompt note mentions roughly 100m pages.
Bots must parse fetched pages and discover new URLs.
Handle scheduling, deduplication, frontier management, retry, and politeness/rate control.
Store page content and metadata so updates can be detected.
Notes
Split the design into frontier service, crawler workers, parser/extractor, content store, metadata/index store, and scheduler.
A clean data flow is: pop URL from frontier, resolve/fetch, parse content, store page/blob plus metadata, extract links, normalize/dedup links, enqueue new or recrawl candidates.
The strongest design decision is how to partition URLs across 1000 bots while avoiding duplicate fetches. Consistent hashing or URL-host partitioning are natural options.
Per-host politeness belongs near scheduling, not inside ad hoc worker sleeps. Use host-level rate limits and queues so one large domain cannot starve the rest of the crawl.
Update handling can use periodic recrawl, content hashes, ETag/Last-Modified when available, and priority queues for frequently changing pages.
Candidate failures tend to come from shallow follow-up handling: bottleneck ownership, worker failure, duplicate URL explosions, and how to recover progress after a bot dies.

steps: The primary coordinates; it must not own all progress in RAM
Failures, bottlenecks and proof of progress
solution.example: Start with one primary scheduler/control VM and about 1,000 bots, but put frontier/seen/fetch metadata in durable replicated storage and content blobs in object storage. A standby/reconciling replacement can resume primary duties from versioned leases; one primary failure must not erase 100M page progress. Store URL, host, next_fetch, priority, state, lease_epoch, attempt, ETag, LastModified, content hash, current blob ref and immutable FetchVersion/links. Admin create/status/pause APIs freeze crawl scope and agent identity.
solution.trap: A standby/reconciling replacement can resume primary duties from versioned leases; one primary failure must not erase 100M page progress.
solution.teaching_notes_markdown:
<!-- architecture:W387:start -->
### Architecture and request flow

![Wikipedia Internet Archive / Web Crawler: request, processing, state and result components.](../diagrams/W387_architecture.svg)

[Open the diagram at full size](../diagrams/W387_architecture.svg). This is a baseline component diagram for this question. The boxes describe responsibilities; they do not require a separate microservice for every box.

- **Request and state:** Seed URLs — crawl scope → URL frontier — normalize + deduplicate. That component consults or updates **Seen URL and crawl state — fetch history** under the required access and consistency rules.
- **Work and result:** the work path passes through **Host-aware scheduler — robots + rate limits** and **Fetch and parse workers — bounded bytes + retries**, producing **Content and discovered URLs — indexed crawl results**. Bound waiting and retries where a slow dependency can stall this path.
- **Correctness point:** Bound per-host load and total fan-out; cycles, duplicate URLs and failed fetches must not grow the crawl forever.

When explaining the drawing, trace one normal request first, then a duplicate request, an unavailable dependency and recovery from saved state. If the question requires stricter guarantees or a different scope, state the change explicitly rather than treating this baseline as the only possible design.
<!-- architecture:W387:end -->

### The primary coordinates; it must not own all progress in RAM

Start with one primary scheduler/control VM and about 1,000 bots, but put frontier/seen/fetch metadata in durable replicated storage and content blobs in object storage. A standby/reconciling replacement can resume primary duties from versioned leases; one primary failure must not erase 100M page progress. Store URL, host, next_fetch, priority, state, lease_epoch, attempt, ETag, LastModified, content hash, current blob ref and immutable FetchVersion/links. Admin create/status/pause APIs freeze crawl scope and agent identity.

Partition host queues into sufficient virtual shards by consistent hash; assign shard leases to bots/scheduler groups with fencing. This keeps one host's politeness budget coordinated even when many bots fetch different URLs. Within a shard, ready-time/priority queues avoid one huge host blocking others; bots can request batched leases from ready hosts. Atomic unique URL insert plus lease claim deduplicates discovery and worker retries. URL hash alone without shared host rate coordination can overwhelm one popular origin.

### Initial copy versus incremental archive

Initial crawl seeds allowed URLs/sitemaps (or permitted bulk export for Wikipedia-like sources), fetches with DNS/TLS/size/redirect/time bounds, parses HTML, archives body+metadata and normalizes/enqueues links. Preserve URL → content hash/version; identical bodies can reuse blob storage without merging distinct URL history. Respect source access/politeness; adding bots does not increase allowed rate against a single domain. For a chosen 100M pages at 50 KB, initial content is 5 TB raw; at 1,000 bots each averaging 1 eligible fetch/s it needs 100,000 s ≈ 27.8 h, **only if** host diversity/network/policy allow 1000/s. A single host limited to 1/s cannot be done faster than ~3.17 years without a bulk/negotiated source feed.

Incremental recrawl priority uses observed change rate, importance/expiry and max staleness, with per-host quotas. Conditional GET with ETag/If-Modified-Since can avoid unchanged body transfer; 304 updates fetch metadata without creating duplicate content. Hash 200 responses to detect changes, preserve timestamped versions, update link graph, and handle deletes/redirects/tombstones under archive policy. Don't assume Last-Modified is always present or trustworthy. Frequently changing pages get more budget but aging ensures tail coverage.

### Failures, bottlenecks and proof of progress

After fetch/upload, before completion commit, worker loss can leave refetchable leased work/orphan blob; unique version/outbox commits avoid duplicate index effects. Expired leases recover with fencing, transient DNS/5xx/429 retry backoff, permanent failures get diagnostics, and poison pages do not crash the bot fleet. Primary restart rebuilds ready queues from durable state; rebalancing shards must not create concurrent host owners. Protect public crawl workers from private-network redirects/SSRF and unbounded decompression/JS execution.

Separate fetch, parse and storage queues with backpressure so the network cannot outpace object store/parser memory forever. Monitor pages/s by host, raw and changed bytes, frontier size/oldest age, recrawl staleness, duplicate/trap rate, politeness violations, bot leases and content hash coverage. Test bot loss, primary loss, duplicate URL explosion, 304/change/delete and one hot domain. An archive is complete only for the chosen finite observed scope; an updating web requires ongoing versioned coverage, not a static visited flag forever.

title: Design a Read-Once Password Sharing Service
question:
Design a service that lets a signed-in user hand a password to another person through a link that works only once. The user creates the secret, receives a URL, and sends the URL to someone else. The first time the recipient opens it they see the password; every later attempt must fail.

Requirements
1.
Create: a signed-in user submits a secret (a short text of up to 4,096 bytes) and gets back a URL. The user can add a label such as the recipient's name.
2.
Read once: the URL reveals the secret to exactly one successful reader. Two people opening it at the same moment must not both succeed. After a successful read the stored secret is gone.
3.
Many users: any number of users can create secrets independently. A user sees only their own secrets and their status.
4.
Same password, many creators: two users may share the same password text. Their secrets must stay separate, and nothing in storage may reveal that the two texts are equal.
5.
Same password, many recipients: one user may share the same password with several people. Each recipient has their own URL, reading one URL does not use up the others, and the user can see which recipient has read it.
6.
Confirm the read: the creator can ask whether a URL has been read, and when. Say precisely what the system can and cannot confirm.
7.
Expiry and revoke: a secret expires after a time the creator picks, at most 7 days. The creator can revoke an unread secret early. An expired, revoked or already read URL gives the same answer as an unknown one.
8.
Recipients are anonymous: a recipient does not need an account.
Scale
2,000,000 secrets are created per day, spread over the day, with a peak of 10 times the average.
On average each URL receives 3 page loads, because chat tools and mail scanners fetch links to preview them, and 90% of URLs are eventually read by a person.
Metadata (not the secret) is kept for 90 days for audit.
Deliverables
1.
The API: endpoints, request and response fields, and status codes.
2.
The data model and what is stored in plain, hashed and encrypted form.
3.
The URL: what it contains and why it cannot be guessed.
4.
How the read-once rule holds when two requests race, when the server crashes mid-request, and when a link-preview bot opens the URL first.
5.
Capacity estimates for request rates and storage.
6.
The corner cases from requirements 4 to 7, each with the behavior you choose.
Examples
Alice creates one secret and sends the URL to Bob. Bob opens it and sees the text. Bob opens it again and gets the same "not found" answer a random URL would give. Alice sees the status change from pending to read, with the time.
Alice and Carol both choose the password hunter2. Alice shares it with Bob and Dave using two URLs. Bob reads his; Dave's URL still works; Carol's secret is unaffected, and the stored data for the three secrets looks unrelated.

solution.example: `POST /v1/secrets` requires the creator's session and CSRF protection; body `{text, label, expires_at}` is validated as UTF-8 text of at most 4096 bytes and an expiry in the next seven days. Return 201 `{id, url, expires_at, status:"pending"}`; invalid input is 400 and unauthenticated creation 401. `GET /v1/secrets?cursor=…` and `GET /v1/secrets/{id}` require ownership and return label, creation/expiry times, status and consumed_at, never plaintext or the capability URL again. Wrong owner and unknown IDs both return 404. `DELETE /v1/secrets/{id}` revokes pending data atomically; return 204 for an owned existing record, including an already terminal record.
solution.trap: `GET /v1/secrets?cursor=…` and `GET /v1/secrets/{id}` require ownership and return label, creation/expiry times, status and consumed_at, never plaintext or the capability URL again.
solution.teaching_notes_markdown:
<!-- architecture:W388:start -->
### Architecture and request flow

![Design a Read-Once Password Sharing Service: request, processing, state and result components.](../diagrams/W388_architecture.svg)

[Open the diagram at full size](../diagrams/W388_architecture.svg). This is a baseline component diagram for this question. The boxes describe responsibilities; they do not require a separate microservice for every box.

- **Request and state:** Sender or recipient — unguessable capability → Secret service — hash token + authenticate. That component consults or updates **Encrypted secret record — expiry + consumed state** under the required access and consistency rules.
- **Work and result:** the work path passes through **Atomic consume operation — one successful claim** and **Decrypt and return once — avoid plaintext logging**, producing **Deleted or consumed result — clear expired state**. Bound waiting and retries where a slow dependency can stall this path.
- **Correctness point:** The database atomically consumes the secret; a read followed by delete can allow two readers.

When explaining the drawing, trace one normal request first, then a duplicate request, an unavailable dependency and recovery from saved state. If the question requires stricter guarantees or a different scope, state the change explicitly rather than treating this baseline as the only possible design.
<!-- architecture:W388:end -->

### Contract and API

There is a fundamental delivery boundary: the service can guarantee **at most one successful consume transaction**, but cannot guarantee exactly one human receives the plaintext. A server can commit consumption and crash before returning bytes; a recipient can receive bytes and lose the response acknowledgment. This design burns the secret on a committed consume, favoring confidentiality over retryable delivery. The creator's status means “consumed by the service”, not proof that Bob read or understood it.

`POST /v1/secrets` requires the creator's session and CSRF protection; body `{text, label, expires_at}` is validated as UTF-8 text of at most 4096 bytes and an expiry in the next seven days. Return 201 `{id, url, expires_at, status:"pending"}`; invalid input is 400 and unauthenticated creation 401. `GET /v1/secrets?cursor=…` and `GET /v1/secrets/{id}` require ownership and return label, creation/expiry times, status and consumed_at, never plaintext or the capability URL again. Wrong owner and unknown IDs both return 404. `DELETE /v1/secrets/{id}` revokes pending data atomically; return 204 for an owned existing record, including an already terminal record.

`GET /s/{token}` returns a generic landing page with a Reveal button and does **not** consume. `POST /s/{token}/reveal` returns 200 `{text}` only for the consume winner; unknown, expired, revoked and consumed capabilities all return the same 404 body. Rate limiting can return 429 independently of token validity. Responses use TLS, `Cache-Control: no-store`, no third-party scripts/analytics, a restrictive CSP and `Referrer-Policy: no-referrer`.

This deliberately interprets “opens” as an explicit reveal action: ordinary preview GETs must not consume. If the literal first HTTP GET must reveal, a preview bot may be the one reader; that requirement cannot simultaneously guarantee the intended person wins. A button reduces accidental consumption but is not proof of humanity; a bot can also POST.

### Records, encryption and independent links

Store `Secret(id, owner_id, token_lookup, label, created_at, expires_at, state, consumed_at, ciphertext, nonce, wrapped_dek)`. Generate an independent 256-bit cryptographically random token for every link; the URL contains that capability alone. Store HMAC(server_lookup_key, token), indexed uniquely, rather than the token itself; protect and rotate the lookup key. A random ID is an owner-facing identifier, not a substitute for authorization.

Encrypt each secret using an independent random data key and authenticated encryption with a fresh nonce. Authenticate immutable record identity as associated data; wrap the data key using a managed encryption key. Plain metadata includes owner, dates and state; labels may themselves be sensitive and can be encrypted separately. Never store deterministic ciphertext, plaintext hashes, content-deduplication keys, plaintext secrets or full capability URLs in logs. Identical text consequently produces unrelated stored ciphertext. A compromised encryption service is outside this storage-only secrecy guarantee.

### Atomic consume, revoke and cleanup

Route each token to one authoritative database partition. Within a transaction lock its record, test `state=pending AND expires_at>database_now`, retrieve encrypted material, clear ciphertext/nonce/wrapped key, and mark consumed with a database timestamp. Commit before decrypting and returning the winning in-memory material. A competing consume or revoke serializes on the same row; only one state transition wins. Crash before commit rolls back; crash after commit can permanently burn the secret. Never automatically retry an ambiguous consume in a way that returns plaintext twice. If commit acknowledgment is lost, resolve transaction status where possible, but return the same unavailable result once consumed. A read replica must not authorize reveal.

A cleanup job erases unread expired payloads, while the transaction's time predicate enforces expiry even if cleanup lags. Keep terminal audit metadata for 90 days, then delete it. Backups and database history need bounded retention and encrypted key lifecycle: clearing a live column alone does not erase historical copies. Decryption rights must reject consumed/expired records and expired per-record keys must become unrecoverable according to the stated backup policy.

### Worked example and capacity

Alice creates two independent links labeled Bob and Dave, and Carol creates a third, all for `hunter2`. Each has a distinct random token, key and ciphertext. Bob's consume changes only Bob's row; Dave and Carol remain pending. Alice sees Bob's consumed_at, not Bob's identity, since anonymous recipients can forward URLs. Revocation racing Bob is decided by transaction order; no later caller can distinguish revoked from unknown.

Two million creates/day average 23.15/s, peak about 232/s. Six million landing GETs/day average 69.44/s, peak about 695/s; 1.8 million eventual human reveals/day average 20.83/s, peak about 209/s, before malicious traffic or retries. These are separate request classes; a landing GET plus reveal is two requests. At most 14 million seven-day pending records require 57.344 GB at the 4096-byte maximum payload, or 14.336 GB at an assumed 1 KB average, before encryption/index/replication overhead. Ninety-day metadata holds about 180 million records; at an explicitly assumed 200 bytes each, 36 GB logical, plus indexes and replicas. Deletes reduce ordinary live payload below the all-unread upper bound. Test simultaneous reveals, consume/revoke races, expiry exactly at the boundary, crash after commit, duplicate plaintext across creators, independent recipient links and preview-only GETs.

title: Design a Notification / Alert Fan-Out System
question:
Design a notification system that receives alerts from upstream services and fans out to all subscribers across multiple channels — email, SMS, push, in-app.

Functional

Upstream services publish alerts (order ready, dasher arrived, promo, system incident).
Subscriber model: per user, per alert type, per channel.
Alerts fan out to all matching subscribers via their preferred channels.
Users can mute / opt out per alert type and per channel.
Throttle: a user never receives more than N notifications/minute regardless of upstream volume.

Non-functional

High fan-out: one system-incident alert can target millions of subscribers.
Per-channel SLAs differ: push near-real-time; email/SMS tolerate 1-2 min; in-app eventually consistent.
Email/SMS have hard provider rate limits; backpressure must propagate, not drop.
At-least-once delivery; dedupe by (user_id, alert_id, channel).

solution.example: For example, with N=3, email+push for alert A reserve two units, SMS for B reserves the third, and email for C waits until a reservation ages out. Two workers racing for the last unit cannot both reserve. Use a monotonic authority clock and retain reservation IDs long enough to distinguish retry attempts. Whether retries consume another unit must be defined: to enforce a hard bound on **send attempts**, every new provider request consumes one, even if the previous result was unknown.
solution.trap: Repeating the same reservation must not spend a second unit.
solution.teaching_notes_markdown:
<!-- architecture:W389:start -->
### Architecture and request flow

![Design a Notification / Alert Fan-Out System: request, processing, state and result components.](../diagrams/W389_architecture.svg)

[Open the diagram at full size](../diagrams/W389_architecture.svg). This is a baseline component diagram for this question. The boxes describe responsibilities; they do not require a separate microservice for every box.

- **Request and state:** Domain event — stable event id → Notification coordinator — recipients + preferences. That component consults or updates **Preference and delivery state — opt-outs + attempts** under the required access and consistency rules.
- **Work and result:** the work path passes through **Per-channel queues — rate + quiet hours** and **Email, push or SMS — retry + deduplication**, producing **Delivery status — suppression + audit**. Bound waiting and retries where a slow dependency can stall this path.
- **Correctness point:** Recheck eligibility at delivery; duplicate events and provider retries must not ignore opt-outs or resend indefinitely.

When explaining the drawing, trace one normal request first, then a duplicate request, an unavailable dependency and recovery from saved state. If the question requires stricter guarantees or a different scope, state the change explicitly rather than treating this baseline as the only possible design.
<!-- architecture:W389:end -->

### Delivery unit and API

Create an alert once with `POST /alerts {idempotency_key, type, audience_ref, template_version, variables, expires_at}`. Expand a versioned audience snapshot into recipients using checkpointed chunks, then select each user's enabled channels from `Preference(user,type,channel,enabled,quiet_hours,timezone,version)`. Store `Delivery(alert,user,channel,status,next_attempt,attempt_count,provider_id)` with a unique `(alert,user,channel)` key. The producer's outbox makes event creation durable; an accepted alert returns 202 and a status URL, not a promise of immediate receipt.

Define N as the maximum **channel dispatches** per user in any rolling 60 seconds across all alert types and channels. Sending one alert by email and push consumes two units. This is an explicit interpretation of the cross-channel limit; if the product means N logical alerts, reserve one alert unit and separately bound its channel fanout.

### Shared rate authority and queues

Before dispatch, all channel workers reserve from the same per-user atomic limiter. Under a lock or a single-key transaction, remove reservations at or before `now−60s`, check the remaining count, and insert a unique delivery reservation if below N. Repeating the same reservation must not spend a second unit. If full, return the oldest reservation's expiry as next eligibility and move the delivery to a delayed queue. A fixed calendar-minute counter permits 2N requests around a boundary and does not satisfy a rolling limit. Rate-authority failure defers sends; disconnected workers cannot spend independent copies of the budget.

Use separate durable priority queues and worker pools for push, in-app, email and SMS, with provider-wide quotas and per-user serialization. Push can normally start within seconds while email/SMS drain within one or two minutes. Large audiences are partitioned by recipient, never processed as one transaction. Recheck preferences and quiet hours immediately before dispatch. A high-priority lane can reserve infrastructure capacity but cannot silently bypass the hard N limit. Provider errors use exponential backoff with jitter, retry deadlines and a dead-letter queue; invalid tokens and permanent addresses terminate their delivery.

### Correctness, overload and example

There is an unavoidable overload constraint: if a user generates more than N channel deliveries/minute indefinitely, “all within two minutes” and the hard cap cannot both hold. Choose durable deferral with a maximum age, then explicit expiration or a permitted digest; expose backlog age and suppressed/expired totals. Do not discard unexpired work silently.

For example, with N=3, email+push for alert A reserve two units, SMS for B reserves the third, and email for C waits until a reservation ages out. Two workers racing for the last unit cannot both reserve. Use a monotonic authority clock and retain reservation IDs long enough to distinguish retry attempts. Whether retries consume another unit must be defined: to enforce a hard bound on **send attempts**, every new provider request consumes one, even if the previous result was unknown.

A provider timeout may have delivered the message. A durable logical-delivery key plus a provider idempotency key prevents duplicates only to the extent the provider honors it; otherwise choosing retry trades possible duplicates against possible loss. Arrival times and duplicate deliveries inside an external provider cannot be bounded by this limiter. Report separately durable creation, accepted dispatch and user interaction. Size from audience deliveries rather than alert count: an assumed one-million-recipient alert on two channels creates two million tasks; with a 100k-task/s expansion budget that takes at least 20 seconds, excluding provider quotas. Monitor queue age, limiter delays, provider acceptance/error rates, duplicate keys and end-user latency by channel.

- [F162: Design a durable work queue with retries and leases.](../17_distributed_systems_depth.md#f162)

title: Design a Notification System with Preferences and Fan-out
question:
Design a notification system with user preferences, fan-out, multiple delivery channels, retries, and observability.

Requirements surfaced in the round: distinguish read vs resolved state (unresolved action items must persist until completed); group/dedupe related events (e.g. 12 friend-activity events → one grouped row); expose a stable notification_id and dedupe_key; cross-device consistency for unread counts and resolution; a compact count endpoint for the badge; polling vs SSE; and accessibility.

steps: Read and resolved are different states
solution.example: For example, twelve comments on one document produce twelve durable child events but one group row, “12 new comments on Plan”. The unread badge counts groups containing at least one visible child newer than read_through_seq. An unresolved approvals list uses domain resolution and can still contain a read group. A thirteenth comment makes a previously read group unread again. Define whether a new task reopens a resolved group; preferably use a new action ID when it is a different obligation.
solution.trap: Only the authoritative action service—such as an approval or payment service—can emit resolution; opening a panel or clicking “mark read” cannot prove the task completed.
solution.teaching_notes_markdown:
<!-- architecture:W390:start -->
### Architecture and request flow

![Grouped notifications, read state and resolution](../diagrams/W390_final_architecture.svg)

[Open the diagram](../diagrams/W390_final_architecture.svg). Reading and resolving are independent. A read-through sequence updates unread state consistently across devices, while unresolved action items remain visible until the relevant business action resolves them. Grouped children retain provenance and a stable group identity; retries and duplicate events do not inflate the badge.
<!-- architecture:W390:end -->

### Read and resolved are different states

Model `Notification(id,user,group_key,type,created_at,version,payload,action_ref)`, `Group(user,group_key,last_activity,child_count,latest_child_seq)` and `UserGroupState(user,group_key,read_through_seq,resolved_at,resolution_version)`. A notification can be read while its required task remains unresolved. Only the authoritative action service—such as an approval or payment service—can emit resolution; opening a panel or clicking “mark read” cannot prove the task completed.

For example, twelve comments on one document produce twelve durable child events but one group row, “12 new comments on Plan”. The unread badge counts groups containing at least one visible child newer than read_through_seq. An unresolved approvals list uses domain resolution and can still contain a read group. A thirteenth comment makes a previously read group unread again. Define whether a new task reopens a resolved group; preferably use a new action ID when it is a different obligation.

### APIs and synchronization

`GET /notifications?cursor=…&filter=unread|unresolved|all` returns stable group IDs, summary, latest sequence, read/resolution state, actions and an opaque pagination cursor ordered by `(last_activity,id)`. `PUT /groups/{id}/read {through_seq}` atomically advances a per-user maximum; it cannot mark concurrently arriving later children read. `POST /actions/{action_id}/complete` goes to the domain service with an idempotency key and authorization. Its transactional outbox publishes the resolution, which the notification projection applies idempotently by version. `GET /notification-summary` returns unread-group count and a state version.

Use WebSocket/SSE updates containing group changes and count/version, with polling and cursor-based catch-up after reconnect. Canonical read state belongs to the user, so a phone read propagates to the laptop; a per-device delivery receipt only describes transport. Out-of-order events cannot lower read_through_seq or overwrite newer resolution. On a sequence gap or expired cursor, fetch a fresh snapshot. Projection lag is visible through versions; completion may return a pending indicator until the group projection catches up.

### Storage and usability

Partition by user for list, state and badge transactions, and deduplicate source events by `(source,event_id,user)`. Atomically update the group and its unread-count contribution so replay cannot inflate badges. Keep payloads minimal and check current document permissions when rendering; deleted or inaccessible content is redacted. A group key must include tenant and resource identity to prevent accidental merging.

Make the badge a navigation aid with accessible text, keyboard actions, clear read styling and a separate “needs action” filter. Avoid twelve interrupting toasts for the grouped example; collapse updates without losing the underlying events. Bound retained history, group sizes and payload size, and paginate the children. Test new child versus mark-read races, simultaneous reads on two devices, duplicate resolution events, completion failures, reconnect gaps and permission revocation. These checks verify the two state machines independently rather than equating dismissal with completion.

### Further study

- [F090: Design a rate-limited LLM classification pipeline.](../09_ml_system_design.md#f090)
- [F162: Design a durable work queue with retries and leases.](../17_distributed_systems_depth.md#f162)

title: Notification System
question:
Design Reddit's notification system: deliver in-app, push (APNs/FCM), and email notifications for events (reply, mention, mod action, trending post). Supports per-channel preferences, bundling/digesting, and throttling. Scale: hundreds of millions of users, tens of millions of notifications per minute.

Interviewer drives at
Event trigger pipeline (transactional outbox -> Kafka, partitioned by user, idempotency via request id).
Preference resolution (inline vs cached vs Bloom pre-filter; the high-fanout celebrity-post collapse).
Channel selection and dispatcher topology (per-provider DLQ, backoff, webhook status updates).
Bundling / sliding-window aggregation into digests; throttling against APNs/FCM hard quotas.
Deduplication via dedup_key.
Delivery-semantics triad: exactly-once logical creation, at-least-once dispatch, best-effort user-visible delivery.

solution.example: For example, a reply event replayed three times creates one inbox row and one push task; a phone reconnecting after missing its socket update reads that row by cursor. A million-follower event is drained in bounded chunks so direct replies do not wait behind it. Reserve capacity for actionable notifications, collapse lower-value bursts only under an explicit policy, and monitor end-to-end age by type, lag, dedup hits, dropped/expired work, preference lookup failures and token rejection. On a settings-service outage, use a versioned last-known setting with a defined maximum age or defer sensitive sends; do not indiscriminately push blocked content.
solution.trap: Never create an unbounded in-memory follower list.
solution.teaching_notes_markdown:
<!-- architecture:W391:start -->
### Architecture and request flow

![Notification System: request, processing, state and result components.](../diagrams/W391_architecture.svg)

[Open the diagram at full size](../diagrams/W391_architecture.svg). This is a baseline component diagram for this question. The boxes describe responsibilities; they do not require a separate microservice for every box.

- **Request and state:** Domain event — stable event id → Notification coordinator — recipients + preferences. That component consults or updates **Preference and delivery state — opt-outs + attempts** under the required access and consistency rules.
- **Work and result:** the work path passes through **Per-channel queues — rate + quiet hours** and **Email, push or SMS — retry + deduplication**, producing **Delivery status — suppression + audit**. Bound waiting and retries where a slow dependency can stall this path.
- **Correctness point:** Recheck eligibility at delivery; duplicate events and provider retries must not ignore opt-outs or resend indefinitely.

When explaining the drawing, trace one normal request first, then a duplicate request, an unavailable dependency and recovery from saved state. If the question requires stricter guarantees or a different scope, state the change explicitly rather than treating this baseline as the only possible design.
<!-- architecture:W391:end -->

### Durable creation and recipient fanout

Reddit-style notifications start from committed domain events: a reply, mention, vote milestone or followed-post update is written with a transactional outbox. Publish immutable IDs and minimal references to a durable log, then recipient workers apply blocking, notification settings, mute and current authorization. Store one inbox item under a unique `(recipient,source_event,type)` key. A Bloom filter can accelerate a negative membership check only when its false positives cause an authoritative lookup; treating “possibly muted” as definitely muted would lose valid notifications.

Use user-keyed partitions for ordering and idempotency. Ordinary events fan out into inbox writes; celebrity subscriptions require chunked, checkpointed campaigns, throttling and optional aggregation. A digest groups events by a defined user/resource/time window, retains the source IDs and emits one logical item per digest generation. Never create an unbounded in-memory follower list. Fanout-on-read helps in-app history, but proactive mobile pushes still require recipient work.

### Channel dispatch and receipts

After durable inbox creation, enqueue channel tasks with a unique `(inbox_item,channel)` key. Provider adapters for APNs/FCM and email enforce quotas, per-user rate limits, localization and quiet hours; use bounded exponential retries with jitter, TTLs and a dead-letter workflow. Invalidate permanently rejected device tokens and maintain tokens per installation, not just per user. An ephemeral socket or Redis Pub/Sub route can wake an online device, but the inbox/log remains the recovery source.

Provider acceptance is not a human read. Track `created`, `queued`, `provider_accepted`, `failed/expired`, and an authenticated client `opened` event separately. Replays must not create duplicate logical inbox items. Where the provider supports idempotency use the same key for retries; otherwise an ambiguous timeout entails a possible duplicate or loss. Client deduplication by inbox ID improves visible behavior but cannot recall an already displayed OS notification.

### Sizing and overload example

At an assumed 20 million recipient notifications/minute, the average is about 333k/s. A 250-byte compact logical item is 5 GB/minute or 300 GB/hour before indexes, replication and channel tasks. This is a recipient-expanded rate, not a source-event rate; multiplying again by follower count would double-count. Partition throughput and storage from measured per-shard limits and leave room for bursty famous accounts.

For example, a reply event replayed three times creates one inbox row and one push task; a phone reconnecting after missing its socket update reads that row by cursor. A million-follower event is drained in bounded chunks so direct replies do not wait behind it. Reserve capacity for actionable notifications, collapse lower-value bursts only under an explicit policy, and monitor end-to-end age by type, lag, dedup hits, dropped/expired work, preference lookup failures and token rejection. On a settings-service outage, use a versioned last-known setting with a defined maximum age or defer sensitive sends; do not indiscriminately push blocked content.

- [F162: Design a durable work queue with retries and leases.](../17_distributed_systems_depth.md#f162)

title: Notification System (Event + Batch)
question:
Design Airbnb's notification system. Supports two pipelines: event-triggered single notifications (booking confirmation, check-in lock code) and bulk batch sends (promotional pushes to host cohorts). Delivery channels include email, SMS, push, and X / Twitter.

Requirements
Functional
Event pipeline: subscribe to upstream events (booking placed, check-in date reached) and emit a notification to the affected user.
Batch pipeline: scheduled or on-demand mass sends to a cohort (e.g. promotional push to potential hosts).
Multi-channel: email, SMS, mobile push, third-party social.
Per-user channel preferences and global quiet hours.
Templating with localization.
Non-functional
Tens of millions of notifications per day, with bursty event traffic.
At-least-once delivery with idempotency; user must not receive the same booking confirmation twice.
Configurable per-channel retry and backoff.

steps: Event and campaign paths share delivery, not priority
solution.example: Choose per-channel deadlines/rate limits: for example, a configured exponential retry base of one second, full jitter, one-minute cap and maximum useful age; honor bounded Retry-After and stop on permanent invalid-address/token errors. Circuit breakers and fair tenant/campaign queues prevent a failed promotional provider from exhausting transactional workers. An outbox preserves committed intents through broker failure; campaign progress advances only after a page's deduplicated intents commit, so a restarted expander neither skips nor duplicates recipients.
solution.trap: Durable queue/idempotency gives one logical notification, but duplicate-free external email/SMS after unknown sends needs provider/status/client support. Isolates event urgency from paced batch campaigns, validates booking/timer versions and defers quiet hours.
solution.teaching_notes_markdown:
### Event and campaign paths share delivery, not priority

A booking confirmation and a host-marketing campaign must not compete equally for an SMS/provider quota. Subscribe to booking/check-in events through transactional upstream outboxes or an equivalent durable event source. Check-in-time notifications additionally use durable timers keyed by booking, scheduled instant and event version; a canceled or rescheduled booking invalidates the old timer. The batch API creates a Campaign(id,template_version,cohort_snapshot,scheduled_at,expiry,state), then expands its immutable cohort through checkpointed pages. Both paths create the same recipient/channel delivery intent, but use separate priority queues, concurrency budgets and provider-rate allocations, reserving capacity for time-critical transactional events.

`POST /campaigns` supports scheduled/on-demand campaigns and idempotency; `/campaigns/{id}:pause|cancel` stops undispatched work. `GET /notifications/{id}` returns intent/attempt status, and preference APIs version the user's opt-ins, channel order, language, timezone and quiet hours. Events/timers carry booking_id and version so a stale check-in code is not sent after cancellation. Never send a private booking code through a public social post: a social connector is only for explicitly authorized, appropriate content and only where the provider supports the chosen authenticated operation.

### Data, template and policy boundary

```text
Notification(id, source_event_or_campaign, recipient, kind, template_version,
             locale, payload_ref, business_version, expires_at, state)
Delivery(id, notification_id, channel, destination_version, scheduled_for,
         state, provider_key, provider_message_id, next_retry_at, lease)
Preference(user, version, allowed_channels, quiet_hours, timezone, locale)
CampaignShard(campaign, shard_id, cursor, state, emitted_count)
Template(id, version, locale, channel, body, approved_variables)
Attempt(delivery_id, number, request_time, response, error)
Inbox/Outbox(source,event_id UNIQUE,payload_hash,processing_state)
```

Deduplicate intents by (business event/version,recipient,notification kind) and deliveries by (notification,channel,destination). Do not generate a new confirmation because an upstream booking event was replayed. Version templates, localize with explicit fallback, validate variables and escape per channel. Sensitive booking data belongs behind restricted references or an authenticated deep link; ordinary logs contain IDs/reason codes, not lock codes. Channels are chosen by a documented rule: promotional opt-outs are binding, quiet hours defer to the next valid local instant, and any emergency/transactional exception must be explicitly configured rather than silently bypass global policy. Recheck consent, booking state, token validity and expiry immediately before dispatch; campaign-start eligibility can be stale by send time.

### Delivery guarantees and retry states

The diagram follows durable source/timer or cohort expansion → shared intent store/policy → priority channel queues → adapters → result/reconciliation. A worker leases a Delivery, renders a deterministic payload/version, and calls its provider using the same stable provider_key on retry. States SCHEDULED→QUEUED→SENDING→ACCEPTED/DELIVERED where observable, with UNKNOWN, RETRY_WAIT, SUPPRESSED, EXPIRED and EXHAUSTED alternatives. Provider acceptance is not user receipt/read. Repeated callbacks deduplicate by provider event ID and cannot regress a terminal result. Expired check-in/promotional messages are suppressed; a quiet-hours delay past useful expiry becomes an explicit expired outcome.

At-least-once queue processing can give one durable logical confirmation, but **no duplicate external delivery** also requires provider-side idempotency/status lookup or client presentation dedup. A send accepted externally followed by a lost response is ambiguous. Do not switch providers/channels and blindly resend it as a new confirmation. Query the original identity where supported; otherwise retain UNKNOWN and choose an explicit manual/at-most-once-versus-retry policy. An unconditional once-only email/SMS promise is impossible across a non-idempotent provider timeout. Treat alternate channels as independently intended deliveries only if product policy authorizes them, not as an accidental duplicate workaround.

Choose per-channel deadlines/rate limits: for example, a configured exponential retry base of one second, full jitter, one-minute cap and maximum useful age; honor bounded Retry-After and stop on permanent invalid-address/token errors. Circuit breakers and fair tenant/campaign queues prevent a failed promotional provider from exhausting transactional workers. An outbox preserves committed intents through broker failure; campaign progress advances only after a page's deduplicated intents commit, so a restarted expander neither skips nor duplicates recipients.

### Capacity, failure walkthrough and validation

For a concrete assumption use 50 million intended notifications/day: about 579/s average, or 5,787/s at a chosen tenfold peak. If 1.4 channels/intent are actually selected, mean dispatch is 810/s and peak 8,102/s. At an assumed 300-byte intent plus 200-byte delivery, logical metadata is roughly 29 GB/day before attempts/indexes/replicas. Campaigns can exceed that peak: ten million recipients in ten minutes require 16,667 expansions/s, constrained by provider quotas and consent/quiet-hours scheduling. A bounded queue absorbs temporary throttling, but cannot guarantee unbounded backlog storage or deadlines above sustained provider capacity; pause campaigns/admit slower and expose delayed status.

Example: booking event E is delivered twice. The first transaction creates one confirmation; the second resolves to it. A provider accepts its send then times out: the delivery stays UNKNOWN under the same key, and a late success closes it without another send. A campaign recipient opts out after expansion: dispatch recheck marks it SUPPRESSED. Test these, booking cancellation against a timer, cohort-page crash, timezone/DST quiet hours and template version replay. Monitor event-to-intent/dispatch/delivery percentiles, oldest urgent work, campaign completion, provider throttle, expired/suppressed/UNKNOWN rates and visible duplicate reports; availability includes preserving durable pending work, not inventing successful delivery.

<!-- architecture:W392:start -->
![W392 exact flow: Durable event / check-in timer → Cohort snapshot / paced pages → Intent + consent / localization → Priority per-channel queues → Stable-key provider adapters → Status / UNKNOWN reconciliation.](../diagrams/W392_exact_review_392_396.svg)

Read the numbered path as Durable event / check-in timer → Cohort snapshot / paced pages → Intent + consent / localization → Priority per-channel queues → Stable-key provider adapters → Status / UNKNOWN reconciliation. The dashed return represents replay/reconciliation under the stated version, deduplication and authority rules; the slow delivery/read side does not own the accepted input.
<!-- architecture:W392:end -->

[Batch behavioral checks](../test_review_392_396.py) validate the explicit notification, crossing, uniqueness and ranking fixtures. The capacity/SLO numbers are calculations and targets, not production measurements.

title: Notification System — Push to Followers on New Post
question:
Notification System — Push to Followers on New Post

Onsite SD round. Design a push-notification service: when a user creates a new post, every follower receives a notification. The interviewer treats it as a product-flavored design (not pure infra), so weighting is on data model + fanout strategy + delivery guarantees rather than on cluster topology.

Requirements

Functional:

A user creates a post → every follower of that user gets a notification.
Notifications must be deliverable to multiple device types (mobile push via APNs / FCM, web push, in-app inbox).
Support read / unread state, mark-as-read, and delete from inbox.
Tolerate offline followers — notifications queue until the device reconnects.

Scale (rough working numbers for the discussion):

100M users, average 300 followers, peak post rate ~10K/s.
Latency target: p50 < 5s, p99 < 30s for normal authors (first-batch delivery should feel real-time); availability 99.9%+; durability is the hard requirement — a lost post event is unrecoverable.

Decision points the interviewer probes:

Fanout-on-write vs fanout-on-read — when does each break down (celebrity users with millions of followers)?
Hybrid fanout: write for normal users, read for celebrities. Where do you draw the line?
Idempotency and deduplication when a worker retries.
Backpressure when a downstream provider (APNs) throttles.
Notes
The round is in-person on a laptop — type your reasoning into the shared doc rather than relying on a whiteboard photo.
The product-design angle matters: define the notification payload schema, the inbox API, and how it interacts with feed ranking.
Cover the celebrity problem explicitly. Pure fanout-on-write with a 50M-follower account writes 50M rows per post; degrade to fanout-on-read for that segment and merge at fetch time.
Discuss exactly-once vs at-least-once delivery — push providers are at-least-once; the inbox layer must dedupe by (post_id, user_id).
Mention metrics: delivery latency p50/p99, fanout queue depth, provider throttle rate.
The standard hybrid threshold in production designs is on the order of ~10K followers: under it, fan-out-on-write into a per-user precomputed-feed table (≤200 recent × ~2KB per row); over it, store the post once and merge at read time. Celebrities are flagged in the Follow table so the post-create worker can skip their write-fanout.
Two *different* thresholds are in play: the fan-out-on-write-vs-read line (~10K) above, and a separate *paced-campaign* trigger for true hot authors — below ~100K opted-in followers enqueue all shards at high priority; above it, create a campaign that splits followers into ~50K-follower shards and *paces* shard dispatch so provider quotas are respected and progress is checkpointed (never scan all of a celebrity's followers in one query).
Use a pub/sub bus (Kafka / Redis pub-sub) keyed on user_id for the delivery side: each post-create publishes a fanout job, sharded workers consume and route to the per-device WebSocket or push provider. This is the same shape WhatsApp-style designs use to scale a single chat-server farm — any worker can serve any user because routing is decoupled from connection ownership.
Track delivery per (user_id, client_id) not per user_id — a user with phone + tablet + web has three rows in the Inbox table and three independent ack states.
Behind the fanout bus, a bounded queue is doing two jobs that often get conflated: (1) decoupling post-create latency from delivery latency, and (2) backpressure when APNs/FCM throttle — the queue absorbs the slowdown without spilling 429s back to the author. Surface both in the design.
Cache hot-key reads (viral post inbox entries) in a non-sharded Redis replica set to avoid a single shard's CPU melting.
Provider failures & token hygiene: retry *temporary* provider errors with exponential backoff + jitter; on a *permanent* error mark the device token invalid and stop sending, emitting an invalid-token event back to the Device service for cleanup. Cap retry age so a stale "new post" push is never delivered hours late, and batch sends by provider + platform. Provider acceptance ≠ user-visible delivery — an APNs/FCM success only means the message was accepted, not seen.
Multi-region: run stateless API / orchestration / dispatch workers in several regions with region-local, mirrored-failover queues; the follower graph and notification store tolerate eventual consistency across regions — only the initial post write needs strong consistency, so keep it off the cross-region synchronous path.
Canonical data model & write-path details
Transactional outbox between POST /posts and the post_created event: write the post row and an outbox row in the *same* transaction, then a relay publishes to the bus. Publishing separately is the classic lost-notification bug — the post commits but the trigger is dropped if the process crashes.
Model the follower edge as (author_id, shard_id, follower_id) so a celebrity never collapses to one partition; carry per-edge notify_on_post / muted / blocked on the edge, but keep user-global quiet_hours + timezone in a separate preference so a timezone change does not rewrite every follow edge.
Split the record in two: a follower-level Notification (canonical, with a UNIQUE dedupe_key on (post_id, follower_id, channel)) and per-device NotificationReceipt rows. The parent status aggregates from children — dispatched = ≥1 device accepted, opened = any device opened, exhausted = all devices permanently failed or retry budget spent. The full Notification.status lifecycle is scheduled → queued → dispatched → opened, with terminal suppressed (filtered out before send), expired, and exhausted.
Quiet hours = defer, not drop. Create the notification, compute the next valid send time in the user's timezone, set scheduled_for, and release it from a delayed queue later.
Filter as late as possible (during shard expansion / just before dispatch), not at event-creation time — otherwise a user who mutes or unfollows seconds after the post still gets pushed.
Working capacity numbers for the estimate: ~30M DAU, ~15M posts/day, ~200 opted-in followers/post → ~3B candidate notifications/day (~35K/s avg, 350K/s peak), celebrity fanout up to ~20M recipients per post; store ~250 bytes of compact metadata per recipient (template id, actor, post id, state) and render the provider payload at dispatch time. At ~250 bytes × ~3B/day that is ~750 GB/day of hot notification state, ~5.25 TB at 7-day retention before replication.

steps: Resolve the two workloads and two thresholds
solution.example: Three billion×250 bytes is **750 GB/day**, **5.25 TB/seven days** compact recipient metadata before replication. At an assumed 1.5 devices and 64-byte receipt, another 288 GB/day precedes indexes/attempts. The rough graph is 100 million×300=30 billion edges; at assumed 24 bytes/edge, 720 GB logical before adjacency indexes/replicas. Shared post payloads belong in read replicas/CDN caches; a replicated hot-object cache can relieve a viral key, but a single nonsharded cache is not a universal scaling cure. Inbox writes still shard by recipient. Test outbox crash, fanout-page replay, celebrity pacing, duplicate per-device ACK, quiet hours, mute/delete/token rotation during queueing and regional replay. Track p50/p99 separately by author class, fanout/dispatch age, throttle/token failures, duplicate rendering and completeness of campaign shard coverage.
solution.trap: Separates10K inbox-materialization threshold from100K campaign pacing; hybrid inbox pull cannot erase celebrity push fanout. Corrects2M/s rough-peak versus350K/s alternate assumptions, canonical parent/per-device receipts and late preference/token checks.
solution.teaching_notes_markdown:
### Resolve the two workloads and two thresholds

For the rough peak, 10,000 posts/s×an assumed 200 opted-in recipients/post is **two million candidate notifications/s**; using all 300 average followers gives three million/s. The later daily scenario is 15 million posts/day×200=three billion/day≈34,722/s, with its separately assumed tenfold peak≈347,222/s. These are different peak assumptions. Design for the two-million/s envelope if that post rate and fanout coincide, or explicitly bound/admit workload; do not quote 350,000/s as the consequence of 10,000 posts/s.

Use the supplied ~10,000-follower line as an initial **inbox materialization** threshold, tuned by posting frequency/active-reader ratio. Ordinary authors fan out compact inbox references; high-follower authors retain one author stream and merge candidates at inbox fetch. A separate ~100,000 opted-in-recipient trigger creates a **paced delivery campaign** with roughly 50,000-recipient pages/shards; below it, enqueue expansion shards promptly under the normal budget. Neither threshold removes the work of sending a push to every opted-in recipient: a 20-million-recipient celebrity still needs O(20 million) delivery decisions, 400 such expansion shards and enough provider quota. Lazy celebrity inbox reads save inbox writes, not the outbound pushes or required delivery receipts. If all followers demand pushes, that write/fanout cost remains.

### Canonical model and APIs

```text
Post(id,author,version,state,created_at), PostOutbox(event_id UNIQUE,post_id,...)
Follow(author_id,shard_id,follower_id,notify_on_post,muted,blocked,version)
Preference(user_id,timezone,quiet_hours,channel_optins,version)
Device(user_id,client_id,platform,token,token_version,valid)
Notification(id,post_id,follower_id,channel,dedupe_key UNIQUE,
             scheduled_for,expires_at,state,template_id)
NotificationReceipt(notification_id,client_id,token_version,
                    state,provider_id,attempt_count,ack_cursor)
InboxEntry(user_id,notification_id,created_at,read_at,deleted_at,version)
FanoutCampaign(post_id,policy_version,state), FanoutShard(campaign,shard,cursor,state)
```

`POST /posts` atomically commits the post and outbox, then ACKs; a relay may replay. `GET /notifications?cursor=`, `PUT /notifications/{id}/read`, `DELETE /notifications/{id}`, `/devices` and `/preferences` support inbox/devices. Parent Notification deduplicates (post,follower,channel); receipts track phone/tablet/web independently. Read/open state may synchronize across devices at user level while transport ACK remains per device. Delete writes a tombstone/read-model version so replayed fanout cannot reinsert a removed inbox entry. Return compact payloads with notification/post/actor/template IDs and deep link; render channel/localized content near dispatch.

### Fanout, live routing and semantics

The diagram is post outbox → author/shard fanout → preference/dedup intents → user-keyed durable delivery partitions → connection directory/gateways or APNs/FCM/web push. Author follow lists partition by (author,shard), avoiding one huge celebrity query. A follower snapshot/cursor defines eligibility as of the post; recheck current follow/mute/block/consent at expansion and dispatch so a later removal can suppress a pending push. An eventually consistent remote graph can violate immediate mute/block expectations: route dispatch checks to an authoritative preference version or state the permitted propagation delay. Post/notification recovery requires durable replicated state; asynchronous regional mirrors alone cannot promise zero acknowledged-event loss through a whole-region disaster.

Normal-author inbox notifications are materialized idempotently. Celebrity candidates merge from author streams at fetch, then acquire stable virtual notification IDs and per-user read/delete exceptions; outbound push workers upsert the same canonical identity when needed. Feed ranking may order candidates, but cannot silently discard a required inbox notification. Use snapshot/high-watermark cursors and dedup push/pull overlap. New devices fetch canonical unread history; provider queues/TTL are only wakeups, not the sole offline store. At-least-once retries may repeat transport; clients render notification_id once. Provider acceptance means dispatched on at least one device, opened means any device opened; exhausted means every intended valid device failed permanently or spent its retry/age budget. No devices is an explicit no-destination/pending-inbox state, not a fake successful push.

### Backpressure, quiet hours and capacity

Bounded queues both detach post-create latency from expansion and buffer temporary provider throttling. They do not create unlimited rate: pause paced campaigns, isolate provider/tenant quotas and reserve normal-author capacity for the stated p50<5 s/p99<30 s target. Celebrity full completion is separately estimated; first-batch speed is not all-recipient speed. Quiet hours create SCHEDULED until the next local valid time, then consent/expiry is checked again. Retry transient errors with capped backoff+jitter, bounded Retry-After and useful-age TTL; permanent bad tokens are invalidated by token version and reported to Device service, avoiding deletion of a newly rotated token. Ambiguous provider sends retain the same identity where supported; externally exactly-once notification display needs provider/client dedup, not just a worker ACK.

Three billion×250 bytes is **750 GB/day**, **5.25 TB/seven days** compact recipient metadata before replication. At an assumed 1.5 devices and 64-byte receipt, another 288 GB/day precedes indexes/attempts. The rough graph is 100 million×300=30 billion edges; at assumed 24 bytes/edge, 720 GB logical before adjacency indexes/replicas. Shared post payloads belong in read replicas/CDN caches; a replicated hot-object cache can relieve a viral key, but a single nonsharded cache is not a universal scaling cure. Inbox writes still shard by recipient. Test outbox crash, fanout-page replay, celebrity pacing, duplicate per-device ACK, quiet hours, mute/delete/token rotation during queueing and regional replay. Track p50/p99 separately by author class, fanout/dispatch age, throttle/token failures, duplicate rendering and completeness of campaign shard coverage.

title: Stock Price Alert Notification System
question:
Design a stock price alert notification system similar to a Robinhood-style watchlist alert feature. Users create threshold alerts; the system ingests real-time quotes, detects threshold crossings, and delivers notifications via push, email, or SMS.

The core challenge is indexing millions of alerts so each quote update does not scan everything, and decoupling fast threshold matching from slower notification delivery.

steps: Define a crossing, then index that predicate
Ordered evaluator, durable trigger, slow channel pipeline
solution.example: A worker crash replays the last in-progress quote using unique Trigger keys. A provider outage grows an isolated bounded backlog; alert messages include observed price/time and expire rather than arrive hours later pretending current price. Corporate actions/symbol changes require versioned threshold adjustment or user reconfirmation, not silent unit changes. Monitor quote age/gaps, match/trigger lag, hot shard pressure, trigger dedup, delivery latency and stale/expired alerts. Tests cover equal endpoints, price jumps, reverse movement, duplicate/out-of-order quotes, cancel race and recurring rearm. Freshness/coverage metadata is essential when upstream data is incomplete.
solution.trap: Exact up(old,new] and down[new,old) threshold ranges avoid scanning all alerts; sequenced quote/config state, gap recovery, armed transitions and trigger outbox commit preserve crossings across retry.
solution.teaching_notes_markdown:
### Define a crossing, then index that predicate

Assume one-shot alerts by default; recurring alerts need an explicit rearm/hysteresis/cooldown policy. Choose an authoritative quote type (e.g. consolidated last trade) and market session, currency/price precision, adjusted-versus-raw treatment and how an alert behaves when created while already above its threshold. For this answer creation records the latest valid price and waits for a future crossing; it does not retroactively trigger from an old quote. Prices/thresholds use fixed-point integer ticks. This is an alert service, not trade execution.

`POST /alerts` takes instrument, direction ABOVE/BELOW, threshold, channels, recurrence and idempotency key; update/cancel uses alert version, and reads expose active/triggered/expired/delivery status. Store Alert(id,user,instrument,direction,threshold,version,armed,state,created_at), SymbolState(instrument,feed_epoch,last_seq,last_price), Trigger(alert,alert_version,quote_event_id,cycle UNIQUE,observed_price,time), Delivery and Outbox. Instrument identity includes market/currency, not just a text ticker.

For consecutive valid prices p_old,p_new, an upward crossing satisfies **p_old<T≤p_new**, so query an ordered threshold index in (p_old,p_new]. A downward crossing satisfies **p_new≤T<p_old**, querying [p_new,p_old). Keep separate ABOVE/BELOW ordered indexes per instrument, each threshold mapping to alert IDs. Unchanged prices trigger nothing; a jump can match many thresholds. Work is O(log A_symbol+M) per quote/shard, where M is actual matches, rather than scanning every alert. For an instrument with a million alerts, a small price move that crosses ten thresholds need not inspect a million rows. A simultaneous jump crossing 100,000 alerts still has unavoidable O(100,000) intent work.

### Ordered evaluator, durable trigger, slow channel pipeline

The diagram is sequenced quote intake → instrument-partitioned threshold match/state → atomic trigger/outbox → independent notification queues/workers. A single fenced owner per instrument shard applies quote and alert-config changes in order. Many quiet symbols share workers; very hot symbols can split their alert sets by alert-ID hash and broadcast each quote to those shards, which each maintain ordered price/config state and threshold indexes. This trades repeated small quote processing for parallel match fanout, without losing any alert subset.

Reject duplicate/old source sequence numbers within a feed epoch; detect gaps and obtain replay before claiming all crossings were observed. Epoch resets require a trusted recovery snapshot/replay boundary, not comparing unrelated sequences. If only a last-price snapshot is available after a gap, a transient threshold crossing may be unrecoverable: mark the gap/degraded coverage rather than invent complete detection. A replayed old quote must not rearm or retrigger an already processed alert.

Commit last applied quote cursor, armed-state transition and Trigger/Outbox identity together within each shard. Huge match sets can be checkpointed as a durable in-progress quote job with paged matches; finish/resume its ordered state transitions before applying later quotes for that shard. Never advance the only durable quote cursor beyond work that can no longer be reconstructed. Config edits/cancel carry versions; a queued old-version trigger is suppressed according to the documented cancel boundary. Notification delivery does not block the quote matcher; retries use trigger/delivery IDs and provider rate limits.

### Recurrence, example and operations

An ABOVE=100 alert seeing 99→100 fires once; 100→101 does not fire again. A recurring variant might rearm only below 99 (chosen one-unit hysteresis), then require another below-to-at/above100 crossing after cooldown. Store this state and, at scale, index rearm boundaries too; scanning every disabled alert on every tick defeats the index. BELOW alerts mirror the inequality. A quote 100→99 crosses BELOW=99, whereas 99→99 does not.

Scale is unspecified. Assume ten million alerts, 10,000 instruments, 100,000 quotes/s peak and 200 bytes/alert: 2 GB logical alert metadata before indexes/replicas. Mean 1,000 alerts/instrument conceals hot-symbol skew. If 1% of quotes generate fifty triggers, output is 50,000 delivery intents/s, sized independently of ingestion. At assumed 200 bytes/intent, ten MB/s is the triggered-path metadata rate before replication. Snapshot indexes, replay configuration/quote logs, enforce per-user alert limits and expire obsolete alerts.

A worker crash replays the last in-progress quote using unique Trigger keys. A provider outage grows an isolated bounded backlog; alert messages include observed price/time and expire rather than arrive hours later pretending current price. Corporate actions/symbol changes require versioned threshold adjustment or user reconfirmation, not silent unit changes. Monitor quote age/gaps, match/trigger lag, hot shard pressure, trigger dedup, delivery latency and stale/expired alerts. Tests cover equal endpoints, price jumps, reverse movement, duplicate/out-of-order quotes, cancel race and recurring rearm. Freshness/coverage metadata is essential when upstream data is incomplete.

title: Daily Puzzle Submission and Leaderboard System
question:
Design a daily-puzzle product where users submit one answer per day, see their score, and view a leaderboard; the system also schedules puzzles.

Functional: schedule one puzzle per day per locale; accept a single submission per user per puzzle, score it server-side, return the score and current rank; serve a leaderboard (per locale/day and all-time).

Scale: 10M+ users, ~1M DAU; heavy leaderboard reads; submission burst at midnight local time; single-region or active-active. Design decisions: where to score, idempotent submission, leaderboard storage (Redis sorted-set vs columnar batch).

steps: Puzzle identity and one durable submission
Scoring, rank and the transactional boundary
solution.example: Example: user U submits answer A at midnight from phone and answer B from browser. One unique insert wins; both operations resolve to that one attempt or the conflicting request is rejected. Two correct users receive 100 each and rank by accepted server time/ID. Broker outage does not lose accepted scores; it delays materialization and the API either waits/reads authority or reports rank temporarily unavailable. Monitor publish coverage, midnight p99, duplicate/conflict rates, score/rank watermark lag, all-time drift and abuse. Test timezone/DST day boundaries, simultaneous submissions, duplicate score events, correction/rebuild and pagination pinned to a rank snapshot. No all-time ranking should average daily ranks or blindly add the same daily score twice.
solution.trap: Unique(user,puzzle) rather than client key prevents two-device double attempts; immutable round/locale assignment, versioned server scoring, deduplicated additive all-time contributions and rank containing own submission are explicit.
solution.teaching_notes_markdown:
### Puzzle identity and one durable submission

A locale/day puzzle uses an explicit IANA timezone and local calendar date; it is not a rolling UTC24-hour bucket. Store Puzzle(id,locale,local_date,publish_at_utc,close_at_utc,state,content_ref,checker_version,answer_ref), unique (locale,local_date). Prepublish content/version in advance, then a durable scheduler atomically activates the due row with an outbox; duplicate timers cannot create a second daily puzzle. Define DST boundaries and locale switching: assume each user selects one competition locale per competition round, recorded in UserRound(user_id,round_id,locale) with a unique (user_id,round_id) key. Puzzle records map to that round. Submission checks this immutable assignment, preventing several all-time contributions by changing timezone.

`GET /puzzles/today?locale=`, `POST /puzzles/{id}/submissions`, `GET /leaderboards?locale=&day=&cursor=`, `/leaderboards/all-time` and `/me/rank` form the API. Submission(user,puzzle,answer_hash,received_at,score,checker_version,submission_id,board_version) has **UNIQUE(user,puzzle)** independently of the client idempotency key. Two devices with different keys still get one attempt. Matching retry returns the original score/result; a different answer conflicts and cannot replace a low score. The server validates trusted receive/close time, authorizes locale and scores with the pinned checker, never trusts a client score. Answers/checkers are restricted so ordinary puzzle delivery does not reveal them.

### Scoring, rank and the transactional boundary

Choose a concrete illustrative rule: 100 points for a correct answer, zero otherwise, with earlier valid server submission time then submission ID breaking ties. Actual puzzle scoring can replace this versioned checker. CPU-cheap deterministic checking can occur inside the submission flow; expensive untrusted checks run in isolated workers with PENDING status and one immutable submission claim. If product demands an immediate scored response, admission/checker latency must meet that contract; a queued check cannot honestly return a final score yet.

Commit accepted submission/score and an outbox in one database transaction. The diagram's leaderboard materializer applies a uniquely keyed score contribution once to a per-locale/day ordered board and an all-time total. All-time is additive across **distinct** accepted puzzles, so outbox replay must not increment twice. For corrections, retain a score/version ledger and replace its contribution by the difference with version checks. Submission receipt returns score plus a rank from a leaderboard snapshot that includes that submission; wait for its board watermark or query the authoritative index. Do not return an absent rank as “current” merely because the cache has not caught up. Return rank_as_of/version, because subsequent submissions can change it immediately.

Use Redis sorted sets/order-statistic indexes for hot top-N and personal rank; a relational score table remains canonical. A plain score-only ZSET tie order is insufficient for time/ID ties. Encode a collision-free ordered composite in a lexicographic index with constant numeric scores, or use a ranked index with comparator (−score,received_at,submission_id); do not pack unbounded timestamp fields into a floating score and lose precision. Rebuild cache from accepted scores if lost, then replay after a coherent snapshot watermark. A columnar warehouse is useful for long-term analytics/rebuilds, not the sole low-latency mutable rank path.

### Midnight, replication and example

One million DAU submitting once/day means about 11.6 submissions/s average. If a chosen 30% arrive within the first minute of the busiest locale's day, that is 5,000/s before retries; real locale distribution determines the burst. At ten million accounts, an assumed 64-byte all-time index row is 640 MB logical before index overhead/replicas. One million 200-byte submissions/day add 200 MB/day plus answer/history storage. Cache puzzle content/top pages, reserve submission/checker capacity and stagger **publishing work**, never move the official puzzle opening just to hide overload.

Single-region multi-zone storage is simplest for the stated scale. If active-active ingress is required, route a (user,puzzle) claim to one authority or use global conditional uniqueness; asynchronous independent writes in two regions can accept two answers. Losing a region may sacrifice new-submission availability unless the uniqueness authority fails over safely. Leaderboards can be stale with disclosed rank_as_of, but the one-attempt rule cannot be eventually reconciled after awarding two attempts.

Example: user U submits answer A at midnight from phone and answer B from browser. One unique insert wins; both operations resolve to that one attempt or the conflicting request is rejected. Two correct users receive 100 each and rank by accepted server time/ID. Broker outage does not lose accepted scores; it delays materialization and the API either waits/reads authority or reports rank temporarily unavailable. Monitor publish coverage, midnight p99, duplicate/conflict rates, score/rank watermark lag, all-time drift and abuse. Test timezone/DST day boundaries, simultaneous submissions, duplicate score events, correction/rebuild and pagination pinned to a rank snapshot. No all-time ranking should average daily ranks or blindly add the same daily score twice.

![W395 exact flow: Locale/day scheduled puzzle → Unique user/puzzle submission → Pinned server checker / score → Durable contribution + outbox → Day/all-time ranked projection → Versioned rank + top-page reads.](../diagrams/W395_exact_review_392_396.svg)

Read the numbered path as Locale/day scheduled puzzle → Unique user/puzzle submission → Pinned server checker / score → Durable contribution + outbox → Day/all-time ranked projection → Versioned rank + top-page reads. The dashed return represents replay/reconciliation under the stated version, deduplication and authority rules; the slow delivery/read side does not own the accepted input.
