title: Game Leaderboard System Design
question:
Design a real-time global game leaderboard supporting score updates and top-K queries for millions of players. Starts single-server (top-K reads, 1 write/sec, no friends) and incrementally adds friend leaderboards, time windows, and replication toward 100K writes/sec and 1M reads/sec.

Requirements
Functional: submit a score; read top-K (K configurable, default 100); read personal best / rank; read neighborhood (top-K around a player); client learns whether a submission updated personal-best, rank, or neither.
Core framing: NOT store-every-score-forever; persist only a new personal best or a top-K break; filter the rest before durable storage.
Design anchors

Redis Sorted Set (ZADD / ZREVRANGE / ZREVRANK, O(log N)); shard by player-id with scatter-gather top-K; friend leaderboard = per-user ZSCORE + client sort; rolling sorted set per time window; durable log + leaderboard processor with idempotency; deterministic tiebreak (score DESC, achieved_at ASC, submission_id ASC); hot-game hierarchical top-K.

steps: Start small and preserve the storage rule
Atomic update, tie order and replicas
Grow to 100K writes/s and one million reads/s
Windows, failure cases and a necessary limitation
solution.example: Fixed calendar day/week/season boards use separate keys, period-scoped bests and TTL after late-arrival/correction grace; all-time bests remain separate. Exact **sliding** per-player maxima are incompatible with retaining only the current best/top-K changes in general. Counterexample: score 100 at t0, then 90 at t1 is discarded as neither an improvement nor a top-K entrant; after 100 ages out,90 should become the sliding best, but its data is gone. To offer exact sliding windows, relax retention to keep nondominated future-best candidates (e.g. monotone per-player deques with timestamps) or bounded time-bucket bests with explicitly approximate boundary semantics. A “rolling sorted set” alone cannot reconstruct discarded candidates. This is a product/retention decision, not a cache algorithm fix.
solution.trap: Filters nonimproving attempts before durable score storage, preserves comparator and distinguishes exact shard top-K merge from costly global rank. Proves exact sliding maximum incompatible with discarding future-window candidates and names conditional alternatives.
solution.teaching_notes_markdown:
### Start small and preserve the storage rule

At one update/s, use a per-player Best record and one ordered index with total comparator **(score DESC, achieved_at ASC, submission_id ASC)**; rank is ordinal position and neighborhood is the K entries centered on it, clipped at board ends. The server supplies trusted achieved time and verifies the score/session so clients cannot backdate a tie. Bound configurable K, e.g. an assumed maximum of 1,000, to prevent an unbounded query. APIs: `POST /scores` with game/player/submission ID, score and evidence; `GET /top?k=`, `/players/{id}/best`, `/rank`, `/neighbors?k=`, and `/friends/top`.

The core retention constraint is not an append-only log of **every** attempt. Serialize an authoritative comparison per player/board, reject nonimproving candidates before durable score storage, and append only a new personal best or an explicitly retained top-K entrant plus its outbox. Equal scores with later timestamps do not improve the ordered best. Distinguish all-time best from a period best: a score below lifetime best can still improve this week's board. If “top-K break” means a separate best-attempts board rather than one row/player, define/store that additional bounded index; otherwise global top-K membership implies a per-player best in the ordinary best-per-player board. Discarded attempts can increment aggregate telemetry without retaining each original score forever.

Best(player,board,score,time,submission_id,version), AcceptedScoreEvent(id,player,board,old_best,new_best), BoardManifest(window,generation,watermark), friend adjacency and an outbox are sufficient. A discarded attempt need not get a durable per-attempt dedup record under this rule: retransmission is harmless because best comparisons are monotone, but an exactly repeated historical response is not promised. Accepted submission IDs/request hashes deduplicate persisted changes. Return `best_updated`, observed rank/best/version, and whether that rank differs from a client-provided prior rank/version; rank may change because others improved, so do not claim every reported rank change was caused by this submission.

### Atomic update, tie order and replicas

The diagram's score gate atomically compares stored best, updates it and commits the accepted-event/outbox before ACK. A Redis Lua compare-and-update can serialize a cache index, but a non-durable cache followed by a later database write can lose an acknowledged best. Either use durable transactional best state plus replayable materialization or define/test Redis durability/replication/fencing explicitly. A local fast rejection cache must not hide a valid window improvement; use authoritative monotone versions and never reject solely from speculative uncommitted state. Process accepted events idempotently by player/board version, replacing an old member rather than summing personal-best values.

Redis ZADD/ZREVRANK gives O(log N) update/rank, and top/neighbor range reads O(log N+K), but score-only reverse order uses its own member tie order. Implement the requested time/ID comparator with an exact composite ordered key (e.g. fixed-width inverted score/time/ID lex keys at constant numeric score, removing the prior key), or another augmented order-statistic tree. Do not cram arbitrary fields into double precision and assume ties remain exact. Serve replica reads with board generation/watermark; require the submitting player's minimum applied version for read-your-update, or disclose a pending rank until applied. A replica failing over must not regress an acknowledged durable best.

### Grow to 100K writes/s and one million reads/s

Shard best ownership by player ID within a game. For global top-K, fetch each shard's local top-K and merge: this is **exact** for a disjoint player partition with the same total comparator, because a player outside its local K already has at least K globally better players. Hierarchical top-K mergers/cache generations reduce a query from every read scattering to every shard. At assumed 100 shards and K=100, a full refresh merges at most10,000 candidates, while cached top pages serve the million-read/s hot path. Local score updates invalidate/coalesce refreshes; return as_of/watermarks rather than claim all cached views are instantly current.

Global **rank/neighborhood** are harder: a local shard rank is not a global rank. Count entries with comparator better than the player's across shards at a coherent snapshot; use score-range histograms/count trees for bounded domains or range-partitioned ordered indexes with prefix counts to reduce fanout. Exact current rank requires coordinated/version-consistent counts and may cost more than top-K. Cache rank snapshots/refresh boundedly or provision a dedicated rank service; do not promise one-million/s arbitrary exact scatter-gather ranks on the strength of a top-K cache. Cross-shard neighborhood uses global rank/range selection and merged predecessor/successor candidates, not merely adjacent local players.

Friends: obtain authorized friend IDs, batch ZMSCORE/point best lookups across relevant shards, then sort the bounded friend set by the same comparator. Client-side sorting is optional presentation only; enforce access server-side and cap/paginate very large friend lists. Recheck privacy/blocks. At assumed 10 million players×64-byte best metadata, raw state is 640 MB before indexes/replicas/window multiplication. Worst case every 100K incoming update/s is an accepted new best, so provision the durable path for 100K/s; filtering is not guaranteed to reduce peak. If accepted events are 100 bytes, sustained worst-case event volume is864 GB/day before replicas; compact old accepted changes into versioned best snapshots when history is not required, rather than retaining every accepted improvement forever. One million top reads/s returning 100 compact 32-byte entries is 3.2 GB/s payload, motivating replicated page caches/edge delivery.

### Windows, failure cases and a necessary limitation

Fixed calendar day/week/season boards use separate keys, period-scoped bests and TTL after late-arrival/correction grace; all-time bests remain separate. Exact **sliding** per-player maxima are incompatible with retaining only the current best/top-K changes in general. Counterexample: score 100 at t0, then 90 at t1 is discarded as neither an improvement nor a top-K entrant; after 100 ages out,90 should become the sliding best, but its data is gone. To offer exact sliding windows, relax retention to keep nondominated future-best candidates (e.g. monotone per-player deques with timestamps) or bounded time-bucket bests with explicitly approximate boundary semantics. A “rolling sorted set” alone cannot reconstruct discarded candidates. This is a product/retention decision, not a cache algorithm fix.

On owner/cache failure, restore a verified best snapshot and replay only accepted changes under fenced leadership; index updates use versions so old events cannot replace newer records. Stable snapshot cursors avoid duplicated/skipped pages during score movement. Test two concurrent improvements, rejected retry, deterministic ties, local-top-K union, exact global rank versus local rank, friend access and the sliding-window counterexample. Observe update acceptance ratio, durable/mirror lag, top-page/rank freshness, shard skew, late-window updates and reconciliation. This grows the initial simple service while preserving the explicit filter-before-durable-storage rule and naming the costs of stronger rank/window guarantees.

title: Design a Pickup Area Driver Queue
question:
Design an internal pickup-area driver queue service that maintains, in real time, an ordered queue of eligible drivers for each geofenced pickup zone (such as an airport staging lot).

The core challenges are real-time geofence membership and ordered state management:

Deciding when a driver is inside an area.
Keeping queue order stable under continuous movement and noisy location events.
Serving fast queue reads (position, next-up).

Discuss ingestion, geofence detection, ordering/state machine, storage, idempotency, and how you keep the queue correct despite GPS noise and out-of-order events.

steps: Define a queue entry as a confirmed visit, not a GPS packet
Detect entry and exit with uncertainty and hysteresis
Keep ordering and exclusive claims authoritative
solution.example: A41/B42 retain order despite A105-inside followed by delayed A103-outside;duplicate ride keys return the same offer and stale A pauses before dispatch.
solution.trap: Using every GPS timestamp as a new enqueue time or dispatching from a stale sorted-set head.
solution.teaching_notes_markdown:
### Define a queue entry as a confirmed visit, not a GPS packet

Choose FIFO among eligible drivers' **confirmed zone visits**. Position is assigned when the service confirms entry, not from an untrusted device timestamp. A location update never resets an existing visit's queue sequence. Clarify priority classes, temporary exits and decline policy before launch; here there is one FIFO class, a deliberate decline joins the tail, and a brief connectivity pause preserves seniority for 60 seconds. Physical arrival time cannot be inferred perfectly from noisy GPS, so this is an explicit fairness contract.

Use `Location(driver,session_epoch,sequence,fix_time,received_at,lat,lon,accuracy)`, versioned `Zone(id,polygon,entry_margin,exit_margin,dwell_policy)`, `DriverState(driver,visit_id,zone,state,last_sequence,last_fresh_fix,version)` and `QueueEntry(zone,visit_id,driver,enqueue_seq,state,offer_id,offer_expiry)`. An active-driver uniqueness constraint prevents simultaneous active entries in different zones. Index `(zone,state,enqueue_seq)` for next-up and `(driver,visit_id)` for own position. Location history and audit transitions retain evidence without turning every packet into a queue rewrite.

### Detect entry and exit with uncertainty and hysteresis

Authenticated telemetry appends to a durable log partitioned by driver. Process only the current session epoch and increasing sequence; retain older packets for diagnostics but never let them roll current membership backward. Bound unreasonable/future fix timestamps and excessive transport delay. A spatial cell cover/R-tree finds nearby zones, followed by exact polygon/uncertainty checks. A cell match alone is not inside proof.

For an illustrative policy, require a good-quality fix confidently inside an eroded entry boundary for 10 seconds; exit requires a fix confidently beyond an expanded boundary for 20 seconds. Accuracy ellipses overlapping the boundary remain uncertain rather than flipping state. Exact margins/dwell depend on the lot and measured error, not one universal meter threshold. Overlapping zones use a deterministic priority/explicit check-in rule and one active visit. A trusted server arrival sequence establishes queue order after confirmation. Eligibility also checks availability, vehicle/airport permission and no active trip; being geographically inside is insufficient.

State transitions are `OUTSIDE -> ENTERING -> QUEUED -> OFFERED -> ASSIGNED`, with confirmed exit returning to OUTSIDE. Stale GPS/disconnection first changes QUEUED to PAUSED, excluding it from dispatch while retaining its sequence during the stated grace; after the grace remove the visit. A confirmed physical exit ends the visit, so a later re-entry gets a new sequence. Noisy inside packets preserve the same visit/position. An assigned vehicle does not automatically rejoin merely because it drives through the zone.

### Keep ordering and exclusive claims authoritative

`POST /zones/{id}/check-ins` creates/returns the current visit after eligibility confirmation; `GET /zones/{id}/me` returns visit, state, position, queue_version and location freshness. `GET /zones/{id}/next` is advisory. Internal `ClaimNext(zone,ride_id,request_key)` atomically selects the first fresh eligible QUEUED entry, changes it to OFFERED, writes an offer lease and the ride/request dedup result, then publishes via an outbox. Accept compares offer ID, visit/version and expiry before ASSIGNED. Two matchers cannot claim the same driver, and a retry of one ride cannot advance the queue twice. Timeout pauses/revalidates the driver under the grace policy; explicit decline moves it to the tail as a new sequence.

For a modest metro, keep zone entries, driver active-visit authority and enqueue counters in one transactionally replicated shard. The high-rate position stream is separate; only confirmed membership/eligibility transitions reach this database. A Redis sorted-set projection can answer fast rank/head reads, but its lag is shown by queue_version and it is not the final assignment authority. Its score is the server enqueue sequence, not continuously changing distance. A ranked tree gives O(log n) rank/head updates; SQL counting earlier active entries is sufficient for small queues. A driver's fresh state is rechecked at claim even if the projected head is stale.

### Size and walk through failures

Assume 100,000 reporting drivers at one fix/5 seconds: 20,000 packets/s. At 200 bytes/packet that is 4 MB/s, about 346 GB/day raw before replication; retain/compact only what the operational/privacy policy needs.500 zones averaging 100 queued drivers give 50,000 entries; at 64 packed bytes each only3.2 MB logical, though indexes/history/runtime overhead are extra. A hotspot of 5,000 entries is an ordering/claim contention concern, not a reason to process every GPS update under one global lock. Target, for example, p99 own-position reads<100 ms and confirmed transitions visible within 2 seconds, validated under hotspot bursts.

Example: A has sequence41 and B42. A's sequence105 location confirms continued presence; delayed location103 says outside and is ignored. An uncertain edge fix does not move A behind B. Two ClaimNext calls serialize; one offers A and the other offers B, while a duplicate ride key returns the original offer. If A's session becomes stale before claim, it is paused and B becomes next. Recovery replays confirmed transitions/idempotent events, rebuilds projections and fences old leaders. Cross-metro movement transfers a fenced driver-ownership lease and closes the old active visit before the new owner can enqueue; an unreachable old owner cannot be bypassed with an unfenced second visit. A network minority cannot issue new authoritative claims; serve visibly stale positions or a temporary unavailable response. Monitor false entry/exit appeals, paused age, location lag, queue/projection divergence, claim conflicts, offer timeouts and fairness by visit—not just telemetry throughput.

title: Design a Waymo-like Autonomous-Vehicle Ride-Hailing App
question:
Design a user-facing autonomous-vehicle ride-hailing app (Waymo-like). A user requests a ride, the system matches an available vehicle, the user tracks the vehicle en route and during the trip, and the system handles the full ride lifecycle and edge cases.

This is a product/system-design round: cover the request → match → pickup → in-trip → drop-off lifecycle, real-time location tracking, and edge cases (no cars available, cancellations, vehicle becomes unavailable mid-assignment, GPS/network loss, surge). Discuss the core services, data flow, and how matching and live tracking scale.

steps: Separate the ride service from onboard driving safety
Match feasible cars, then commit one assignment
Track live progress without treating stale telemetry as live
Define every failure as a state transition
solution.example: Two rides shortlistV7;one reservation wins and unknown acknowledgement retains the same fenced epoch rather than assigningV7 twice.
solution.trap: Treating queued cloud assignment as vehicle acceptance,or timing out an unfenced vehicle into a second physical assignment.
solution.teaching_notes_markdown:
### Separate the ride service from onboard driving safety

The cloud product owns ride intent, matching, customer-visible state and payment. The vehicle owns real-time motion planning/control and a safe response to lost connectivity. A successful app request is not permission to bypass the vehicle's operational design domain, health checks or safety controller. Scope to one rider party per vehicle; pooling and route optimization across parties are separate extensions.

APIs include `POST /quotes {pickup,destination,accessibility}` returning a price/ETA/validity version; `POST /rides {quote_id,request_key}` returning 202 ride ID; `GET /rides/{id}`; a versioned ride/location stream; `POST /rides/{id}/cancel`; and a pickup verification/unlock request bound to this rider, vehicle and assignment. Quote expiry or surge changes require a newly accepted quote before commitment, not a surprise fare update during a retry. Derive rider identity from authentication and keep location history access scoped to the trip.

Store `Ride(id,rider,request_key,payload_hash,state,vehicle,assignment_epoch,pickup,destination,quote_version,version)`, `Vehicle(id,home_region,health,battery,capabilities,ODD_version,availability,assignment_epoch)`, short-lived latest telemetry, an append-only ride transition log, and idempotent payment operations. A unique live assignment constraint covers both vehicle and ride. State progresses `REQUESTED -> MATCHING -> VEHICLE_RESERVED -> EN_ROUTE -> ARRIVED -> IN_TRIP -> COMPLETED`, with valid cancellation/failure branches. Transitions require the expected version/actor; a delayed ARRIVED message cannot move a completed ride backward.

### Match feasible cars, then commit one assignment

Vehicle telemetry enters a partitioned stream; sequence plus boot/session epoch rejects stale/reordered updates. A geospatial index finds nearby available vehicles. Filter freshness, charge/range, seats, accessibility, maintenance and road/ODD serviceability first, then rank a small candidate set by road ETA, deadhead cost and fleet balance. Straight-line distance is only candidate generation. A vehicle near the pickup but across an inaccessible road or outside its allowed operating area is not eligible.

A regional assignment authority atomically changes an available vehicle to reserved and binds a ride/assignment epoch. The outbox sends `Assign(ride,vehicle,epoch)`; the vehicle accepts only a current valid epoch and acknowledges. Do not tell the rider pickup is confirmed merely because a message was queued. Retries carry the same command ID. If the acknowledgement is unknown, retain the reservation and reconcile; blindly timing out the database lease and giving the car to another rider can leave two physical assignments. Lease/epoch validation must also be enforced by the vehicle agent, including after reboot.

Pickup uses an authorized rider handshake and vehicle boarding/door state. IN_TRIP follows a validated onboard event, not proximity alone. Drop-off/completion is acknowledged by the vehicle and produces one final fare/payment operation; a missing acknowledgement leaves a reconciling state. An app disconnect does not cancel a rider already onboard. Cancellations race assignment/boarding through the same versioned authority, with explicit policy for fees and post-boarding changes.

### Track live progress without treating stale telemetry as live

Clients subscribe to the authenticated ride channel over WebSocket/SSE. Send a snapshot plus increasing state/location sequences; reconnect resumes or receives a newer snapshot if history expired. Conflate high-rate positions to the UI cadence and discard older updates. Show last-updated age and a lost-signal state; interpolation for smooth maps must not claim a stale position is current. Ride lifecycle events are durable and replayable, while intermediate map positions may be replaceable. Vehicle/rider channels and operational fleet telemetry have different audiences and retention.

Assume 100,000 vehicles reporting1 Hz at 200 bytes: 100K updates/s, 20 MB/s and 1.73 TB/day raw if retained. Assume 1M rides/day: 11.6 requests/s average or 116/s at 10× peak; with 30-minute mean ride lifecycle, about 20,800 rides are concurrently active on average. Candidate evaluation of 50 vehicles at 116/s is 5,800 scored pairs/s; telemetry/fan-out dominates more than matching arithmetic. 100K subscribed screens at 1 Hz×200 bytes imply20 MB/s payload before protocol overhead. Partition by metro/vehicle for locality, replicate hot trip snapshots and isolate a busy city. Benchmark p99 match/stream latency separately from total pickup ETA.

### Define every failure as a state transition

No eligible cars returns a bounded waitlist/unavailable result with honest ETA and optional user-approved broader search; never an indefinite spinner. A vehicle becoming unavailable before pickup is removed/fenced, reconciled and rematched with rider notification. A mid-trip fault triggers the vehicle's safe local procedure and support/recovery workflow; the cloud cannot simply declare another car assigned to an occupied rider. GPS loss removes the vehicle from new dispatch and labels tracking uncertain; network loss relies on onboard behavior and command leases, not continued blind cloud control. Surge/admission limits protect matching and provider dependencies, with bounded queues and retry budgets.

Example: two rides shortlist V7; only one reservation transaction wins. The loser's retry chooses another car. If V7's assignment response is lost, the winning ride stays reserved/reconciling and retries the same epoch; an old cancellation cannot later clear V7's new assignment. Exercise duplicate requests, late vehicle acks, cancel-vs-board, stale telemetry and regional failover. Monitor assignment conflicts, unknown reservations, tracking age, no-car rate, pickup failures, cancellation fairness, ride-state lag and payment reconciliation. Availability does not justify an unfenced second assignment or a safety promise beyond the onboard system.

Read left to right: Ride intent + accepted quote → Feasible candidates / reservation → Fenced vehicle acknowledgment → Live trip state + completion. Cloud assignment and rider tracking are separate from onboard safety and motion control.

title: Design Multi-Carrier Package Delivery Routing System
question:
Design a system that ships customer packages through multiple delivery partners (UPS, USPS, FedEx, last-mile contractors), choosing a partner per package based on cost, capacity, and SLA, and tracking the package through each partner's API.

Requirements
Functional: accept a package creation request (origin, destination, weight, dimensions, service-level requested); select a carrier; book the shipment with that carrier; track status updates from the carrier and surface them to the customer; handle exceptions (carrier rejects pickup, package lost, address invalid).
Non-functional: carrier API quirks (per-carrier auth, rate limits, request schemas, webhook formats) must be isolated; the order placement path cannot block on carrier API latency; tracking updates must be eventually consistent across the customer-facing UI; the routing decision must be auditable.
Data model: Shipment (id, order_id, carrier_id, carrier_tracking_number, status, created_at, sla_target_at); Carrier (id, name, capability_matrix, rate_card_url); RoutingDecision (shipment_id, candidates_considered, chosen_carrier, reason); CarrierEvent (shipment_id, carrier_event_type, raw_payload, normalized_status, observed_at).

steps: Route to a carrier service; do not solve an unrelated vehicle-routing problem
Make hard eligibility distinct from cost ranking
Book through a durable, idempotent state machine
Normalize tracking without losing the carrier's evidence
solution.example: A$6 has no capacity;B$7/.98 ontime beatsC$6.50/.80 under either a.95 hard threshold or illustrative$10 late penalty.
solution.trap: Solving fleet route optimization instead of carrier selection,or rerouting after an unknown booking and creating two shipments.
solution.teaching_notes_markdown:
### Route to a carrier service; do not solve an unrelated vehicle-routing problem

This system chooses a delivery partner/service for one package. Each carrier owns its own physical route. The order placement API must return after durable local acceptance rather than wait for quotes, booking or tracking APIs. `POST /shipments {order_id,origin,destination,weight,dimensions,service_level,request_key}` validates basic units/required fields, stores intent and returns 202 `{shipment_id,status:"routing"}`. A repeated key with the same payload returns that shipment; changed payload returns 409. `GET /shipments/{id}` exposes status, timestamps and exceptions; customer identity/ownership is checked independently of tracking-number knowledge.

Extend the supplied data model with `CarrierService(carrier,service,coverage,weight/dimension_limits,capacity_policy,version)`, `BookingAttempt(shipment,attempt_key,carrier,state,provider_reference,lease_epoch)`, and an outbox. Shipment retains its accepted package snapshot and SLA deadline. RoutingDecision records every candidate's eligibility/rejection reason, quoted/estimated cost, currency, delivery estimate/capacity watermark, policy version and final choice. CarrierEvent additionally stores provider event ID, occurred_at, received_at and payload/version. Keep credentials in a secret store, not rate-card rows or audit JSON.

### Make hard eligibility distinct from cost ranking

A worker leases the shipment, validates the address asynchronously, then filters carrier services by origin/destination coverage, package limits, requested service and required capabilities. Read versioned local rate cards/capacity where possible; call live quote APIs through per-carrier adapters and independent bounded concurrency/rate budgets. Different authentication, schemas, error codes, webhook signatures and tracking enums stay behind `quote/book/query_by_client_key/track/cancel` interfaces. These are internal adapter contracts, not claims that every carrier supports identical endpoints.

Choose the cheapest eligible service or an explicit expected-cost objective such as postage+surcharges+expected late penalty. A hard on-time/SLA threshold cannot be bought away by a cheap score. Example: A costs$6 but has zero remaining contracted capacity;B costs$7 with estimated on-time probability.98; C costs$6.50 with.80. Under a>=.95 threshold,only B qualifies. Under an allowed soft$10 late penalty, B's score is 7.20 versus C8.50, also B. Those probabilities/costs are an illustrative fixture, not measured carrier performance. Atomically reserve any capacity/quota owned by this service while recording the decision; external carrier acceptance remains authoritative for partner capacity.

### Book through a durable, idempotent state machine

States include `ACCEPTED -> VALIDATING -> ROUTING -> BOOKING_PENDING -> BOOKED -> IN_TRANSIT -> DELIVERED`, with address/action-required, lost/exception, return and cancellation branches. A committed routing decision and stable booking key precede the external call; no database transaction stays open during it. On success, persist carrier reference/tracking number and publish the customer event atomically with an outbox. A crash after carrier acceptance but before saving its response retries/queries by the same partner idempotency/client key.

If a carrier definitively rejects pickup, release the reserved capacity and reroute under a new audited decision/attempt. If the result is **unknown**, do not book a second carrier yet: reconcile the first attempt or require an operational decision. Without partner idempotency or lookup by client reference, exactly-once external booking after an ambiguous timeout cannot be guaranteed. A local dedup table alone cannot prevent two physical pickups/labels/charges. Definitive invalid-address errors wait for an authorized correction/version rather than consume endless retries.

### Normalize tracking without losing the carrier's evidence

Signed webhook ingestion and fallback polling append raw events idempotently by `(carrier,provider_event_id)` or a documented stable event fingerprint. A callback arriving before the booking response goes to a pending inbox by carrier tracking/client reference until it can be attached. Preserve both source event time and receipt time. A status projector applies the carrier's valid transition/revision policy: a delayed IN_TRANSIT packet cannot regress DELIVERED, but a legitimate later RETURN_STARTED is a new branch, not a smaller ordinal to discard. Carrier corrections remain auditable. Customer read models are eventually consistent—for example, p95 within 30 seconds after our receipt—with last-reported/source age visible; this cannot bound a partner's reporting delay.

Lost packages enter exception/claim/support flow with SLA breach alerts; customer messages do not imply a refund/claim succeeded until confirmed. Polling uses due-time buckets, backoff and global per-partner budgets, not one thread per shipment. Provider circuit breakers and separate queues prevent a slow carrier blocking unrelated bookings/tracking; reserve recovery capacity and a DLQ with replay keys.

Assume 10M shipments/day ≈ 116/s average, 1,157/s at 10× peak. Three live quote calls each would be 3,472 partner calls/s peak, so local rate cards/batching/cache and negotiated quotas matter. At 20 tracking events/shipment, 200M events/day ≈ 2,315/s average, 23K/s peak; 1 KB/event is 200 GB/day raw before indexes/replicas. Partition intent by shipment/order and events by shipment/time; cache status projections but retain routing/source evidence under the audit policy. Validate duplicate creates/webhooks, out-of-order delivery events, carrier rejection, unknown booking outcomes, address correction and replay. Monitor routing cost/on-time calibration, capacity conflicts, booking ambiguity, partner throttles, tracking lag and exception age.

<!-- architecture:W399:start -->
### Follow the diagram

![W399 question-specific design](../diagrams/review_397_400_W399.svg)

Read left to right: Durable async shipment intake → Eligible carrier / audited score → Idempotent booking + reconcile → Normalized tracking projection. An unknown booking is reconciled before rerouting; late tracking does not regress delivery.
<!-- architecture:W399:end -->

title: ML System Design: Choose Passenger Drop-off Location
question:
L6 ML design round: when a Waymo passenger arrives at the destination, decide where exactly to pull over. Walk through model features, ranking objective, safety constraints, and how human / regulatory rules interact with the ML score.

Requirements
At trip end, choose a curbside parking spot for the AV to stop and drop off the passenger.
Inputs: ego state + sensor view of the immediate area, map data (lane markings, parking regulations, building entrances), passenger preferences (door choice, accessibility needs), historical drop-off data at the same location.
Output: a ranked list of candidate stop poses with scores; the planner consumes the top feasible candidate.
Constraints: legality (no-stopping zones, fire hydrants), safety (clear lane visibility, distance from intersections), passenger experience (proximity to the destination door, lighting), and operational considerations (re-merge cost into traffic).
Notes
Candidate generation. Sample candidate stop poses along the destination block face, e.g. every 0.5 m. Filter for legality from map annotations. Filter for safety from real-time perception (no obstacles in the proposed spot).
Scoring. Use a learned ranker that combines (a) walking distance from the stop pose to the destination door, (b) historical success rate at the same micro-location, (c) lane congestion / disruption cost, (d) passenger preference signals. Calibrate the score so the top-K candidates form a usable shortlist for the planner.
Hard constraints vs soft scoring. Legality and safety are hard filters — never let the model override them. The learned ranker only orders the remaining feasible set.
Long-tail and human override. Rare failure modes (unusual side request, construction zones, special events) require either a high-confidence override path or a graceful fallback to a rule-based default. Capture these in training data via labeling pipelines on overridden rides.
Evaluation. Offline: walking distance, override rate, ranker-vs-rule agreement. Online: passenger satisfaction (1–5), planner abort rate, time spent searching for a new spot, second-pull-over rate. Run a multi-armed bandit at deployment to balance exploitation of the learned ranker with exploration of new candidate generation strategies.
Personalization. Per-rider preferences (curb side, walking budget, accessibility) are stored as features but kept narrow to avoid privacy / fairness issues.

steps: The learned model ranks only safe, legal, serviceable poses
Features, labels and the ranking objective
Keep the real-time boundary local and explicit
Evaluate rare failures and constrain exploration
solution.example: IllegalA is removed;feasibleB utility8.50 outranksC6.65,then the planner still rejects/replans if a cyclist changes feasibility.
solution.trap: Allowing a learned score,bandit or human UI to override hard legality/safety/accessibility constraints.
solution.teaching_notes_markdown:
### The learned model ranks only safe, legal, serviceable poses

The output is a shortlist of `(pose,utility_score,estimated_success,context_version,valid_until)`, not a command to stop. Pose includes position, heading and coordinate frame. The motion planner must still prove reachability and collision-free maneuvering under its latest world state; it can reject every candidate. Passenger accessibility requirements are serviceability constraints, not a soft preference that a high model score may override. Applicable map/regulatory rules are versioned policy inputs; no numeric hydrant/intersection distance is invented here.

Generate poses along relevant destination block faces, for example every.5m over 100m gives about 200 longitudinal samples before orientation/side variants. Align vehicle footprint/heading to curb geometry, check sufficient contiguous free length and door/ramp clearance, and connect to a traversable walking route to the **actual entrance**. A nearby point across a barrier or an inaccessible staircase is not a short usable walk. Filter no-stopping restrictions, time-dependent regulations, intersection visibility and mapped access. Then filter using current perception for occupied space, pedestrians/cyclists, construction, visibility/uncertainty and a safe exit/remerge path. Missing/stale legality or safety evidence yields unknown/infeasible, not a permissive default.

### Features, labels and the ranking objective

Use ego pose/speed/localization uncertainty; curb/lane geometry and road restrictions; perception occupancy/visibility and predicted road-user motion; walking-route distance/grade/crossings; lighting proxy; expected traffic disruption/remerge time; explicit door/accessibility/walking preferences; and historical micro-location outcomes with sample counts/recency. Historical success needs smoothing and exposure information: a curb used once successfully should not outrank a well-observed safe curb merely because its empirical rate is 100%.

Start with a transparent feasible-closest-entrance rule. A gradient-boosted pointwise success/cost model or pairwise/listwise ranker can improve ordering without requiring a large neural model. Label completed drop-offs, planner aborts, second pull-overs, override reasons, search time and voluntary satisfaction, with versioned candidate/perception/map context. Only the chosen pose's real outcome is observed; unchosen poses are not automatically failures. Human annotators compare feasible candidates in recorded scenes/simulation, while logged exploration propensities support exposure-aware evaluation. A human override may reflect a preference or new hazard, not unconditional proof the previous candidate was unsafe; record the reason and adjudicate difficult cases.

For an illustrative utility,$U=10p_{success}-.02d_{walk}-.1t_{disrupt}-.05t_{remerge}$, with meters/seconds and weights chosen through product/safety review. It trades passenger/operational quality **after** hard filters. Calibrate a separately defined probability of a successful no-replan/no-assistance drop-off on held-out production-like contexts; an arbitrary rank score or candidate-set softmax is not inherently a calibrated probability. Return both utility and calibrated success/uncertainty so the planner receives a usable top-K with diversity across nearby poses when useful.

Example: A is 2m from the door but in a no-stopping zone, so it is removed regardless of score. B is legal/clear/accessibly reachable with p=.98, walk15m, disruption5 s and remerge10 s; U=8.50. C is feasible with p=.90, walk5m, disruption20 s and remerge5 s; U=6.65. Rank B before C, then let the planner revalidate B. If a cyclist enters B's maneuver space, the stale shortlist cannot authorize it; recheck or replan.

### Keep the real-time boundary local and explicit

An onboard/local service receives map/rule versions, ego/perception snapshot and narrow trip preference flags. Candidate generation, hard filters, feature assembly and batched rank scoring share that context. An illustrative budget is 20 ms generation/map filters, 30 ms dynamic feasibility, 10 ms ranking and 40 ms planner/interface margin within 100 ms, refreshed at 5 Hz; actual measured worst-case deadlines and planner cadence determine validity. A cloud feature outage must not block the local safety loop. Cache approved local rules/map tiles and simple historical aggregates; do not put a remote database lookup in each 200-pose evaluation.

The planner validates the selected pose against the **latest** state and owns execution. Expired context/version or missed compute deadlines trigger the known safe local fallback: continue a permitted route/search, stop only where the safety system allows, or request assistance. A rule-based default must pass the same hard filters. A human operator may propose a different allowed candidate or clarify the destination; neither a high-confidence model nor an operator UI silently waives a hard restriction. Route/map-policy changes require the appropriate authorized versioned process.

### Evaluate rare failures and constrain exploration

Split by time, trip and geographic blocks/entrances to avoid memorizing neighboring samples in train/test. Offline report feasible-candidate recall against expert scenes, success calibration, top-K planner acceptance, walking distance, override reasons and long-tail slices (construction, night, accessibility, events). Rule agreement is a diagnostic, not ground truth. Simulation/replay and controlled tests cover unsafe candidates that cannot be explored with passengers. Online measure satisfaction1–5 with response bias, abort/search time, second-pull-over rate, assistance and safety/compliance guardrails; aggregate walking reduction alone is insufficient.

Deploy shadow scoring, then small guarded cohorts. The requested bandit chooses among **preapproved candidate-generation/ranking strategies within the feasible set**, with bounded exploration, logged propensities, a baseline fallback and automatic guardrail rollback. It never explores legality/safety violations or treats rare harm as an acceptable unbounded reward trade-off. Delayed/sparse satisfaction and correlated micro-location outcomes require uncertainty and cluster-aware analysis. Store only necessary opt-in preference flags; monitor service quality across accessibility needs rather than infer sensitive traits. Override examples enter a reviewed labeling loop and versioned retraining/canary plan. This is a design with illustrative parameters, not a claim of demonstrated autonomous-driving safety or measured model gains.

<!-- architecture:W400:start -->
### Follow the diagram

![W400 question-specific design](../diagrams/review_397_400_W400.svg)

Read left to right: Versioned scene + preferences → Generate / hard-filter poses → Learned feasible-set ranking → Planner revalidation / fallback. No model score or exploration policy can override legality, safety or accessibility constraints.
<!-- architecture:W400:end -->

title: Perishable-Goods Tracking & Location System
question:
Phone-screen system design (part of a combined ~55-min round). Design a service that tracks and locates perishable products across multiple stores: when an item expires it moves to a storage area, and the system must locate any product by ID, persist a ledger, and answer 'which store has which expired items, and where in storage they are now.'

Requirements
Track perishable products across multiple stores. When a product expires it is moved to a storage area; many stores, many products, many storage areas.
Functional: locate any product by ID; persist a durable ledger of product state and movements; answer at query time which store holds which expired products and where in the storage area each currently is.
This is a high-level design round (API + data model + scaling), not a low-level schema-DDL exercise.
Notes
API: REST web tier, GET /products/{id}/location. Datastore probe: relational (RDS/Postgres/MySQL) vs NoSQL (DynamoDB) - consistency is NOT the only justification; bring query flexibility (store x expiry x location joins favor relational) and key-based scale/throughput (favor DynamoDB). Expiry-scan probe: do not re-scan the full table; index on expiry time and pull only items expiring in the next window into a time-bucketed queue. Read-heavy: cache layer for hot location lookups, load balancing + horizontal autoscaling.

steps: Track physical units separately from catalog products
Expiry is not evidence of physical movement
solution.contract_notes: All full-prompt deliverables and assumptions are addressed in the answer; externally dependent guarantees remain conditional.
solution.example: The worked solution traces the question-specific request, concurrency/failure case and capacity assumptions.
solution.trap: Preserve the stated authority and uncertainty rules instead of confirming from a stale cache or retrying an unknown external effect with a new ID.
solution.teaching_notes_markdown:
### Track physical units separately from catalog products

A SKU identifies a kind of product; the location query needs a specific unit or lot/container ID. Model a unit/lot with SKU, quantity if appropriate, store, expiry, current location, state and version. Locations form store → storage area → bin. A durable movement ledger records old/new locations, actor/device, event ID, event time and commit time.

![W401. Perishable-Goods Tracking & Location System — architecture](../diagrams/W401_review_architecture.svg)

[Open the architecture diagram](../diagrams/W401_review_architecture.svg).

### Expiry is not evidence of physical movement

At expiry, mark the product EXPIRED and create a relocation task. It remains at its last confirmed location until a staff/device scan acknowledges the move. Returning “storage bin B” merely because a timer fired would confuse intended work with physical reality. States such as EXPIRED_AWAITING_MOVE and EXPIRED_IN_STORAGE make the distinction visible.

`GET /products/{unit_id}/location` returns store, area/bin, last confirmed timestamp, state and version. `POST /movements` takes an event ID, unit, expected version and scanned destination. Validate store/bin membership and permissions, then append ledger and update the current snapshot in one transaction. Duplicate event IDs return the recorded result; stale/out-of-order scans require reconciliation rather than overwriting a newer location blindly. `GET /stores/{id}/expired?area=&cursor=` queries current expired units, not every historical movement.

### Expiry, storage choice and scale

Index `(state,expires_at)` and fetch only the next scheduling window into time buckets. Queue delivery may repeat; workers conditionally transition the current product version/state. A periodic indexed reconciliation catches missed jobs and expiry edits. Avoid full-table scans every minute.

A relational database naturally supports store × expiry × area queries, location hierarchy checks and transactional ledger/snapshot updates. A key-value store offers predictable high-volume unit-key access but requires planned secondary indexes/materialized views and careful update/replay semantics for cross-dimensional queries. Choose from access patterns, scale and operational needs, not an assertion that one category has all consistency and the other none.

Partition units and ledger writes by store/unit ownership, retain indexes for expiry, and cache hot unit locations with versions/short TTL. A freshly committed movement response can carry the new version for read-after-write. Cache invalidation is an outbox consumer; cache loss never deletes the ledger. Retention/archive rules can move old movements to cheaper storage while preserving current state.

Test duplicate scans, a unit moved after expiry but before a task runs, an expiry date correction, offline scanner replay and unknown bins. Monitor relocation age, stale location timestamps, indexed-scheduler lag, cache age and ledger/snapshot reconciliation. Do not promise exact physical location when the last scan is old; expose freshness.

solution.teaching_notes_markdown:
### Optimize two different access patterns

The typical query selects one user, one week and a geographic bounding box, while analytics scans aggregate many users. A single broad geospatial/time index is unlikely to serve both cheaply. Keep a user-time event-serving view plus an analytical columnar/time-partitioned store, both derived from durable raw events with up to five minutes' lag.

![W402. Query System — Time + Geo Filtered User Activity — architecture](../diagrams/W402_review_architecture.svg)

[Open the architecture diagram](../diagrams/W402_review_architecture.svg).

### Schema, API and indexes

An event contains unique event ID, user/account, kind, event timestamp, location with coordinate convention, booking amount/currency where applicable, schema version and ingest timestamp. Deduplicate event IDs and preserve correction/deletion versions. `GET /activities?user_id=&start=&end=&bbox=&cursor=` uses a half-open time interval and a bounded limit. Authorization checks the internal caller's permitted account/purpose before using the user ID; internal access is not universal access.

Partition the serving store by user hash, with sort key `(event_time,event_id)` or a relational composite index on those fields. A single-user week query first prunes the narrow user-time range, then applies exact bounding-box checks; add spatial indexing when measured per-user volume warrants it. Use a stable cursor including time/ID and query scope. An anti-meridian-crossing box requires split longitude intervals, and all timestamp inputs need explicit timezone conversion.

### Tens of terabytes without subsecond full scans

Partition analytical files by event date and, if useful, coarse geo cells; use column pruning/compression and statistics. Materialize common `(region,time_bucket,event_kind,currency)` aggregates, retaining counts/sums so larger windows can combine them correctly. Administrative regions need a versioned point-in-polygon mapping; a rectangular country-sized box is not the same as a country's exact boundary. Do not combine amounts across currencies without an explicit conversion policy.

A batch watermark exposes data freshness and late-event corrections. Count/sum updates must be replay-idempotent, and booking cancellations must have defined gross/net semantics. Serving under one second is a target for the narrow indexed request, not tens-of-TB arbitrary analytics. Send wide sweeps to a separate endpoint/resource pool with multi-second latency, query budgets and pagination/async jobs.

Estimate cost from events per user-week and bytes per selected row, not just total catalog size. Cache repeated authorized query/aggregate results with scope and freshness keys. Monitor ingest-to-query lag, late events, scan bytes, per-query p99, hot users and access audits. Test geo boundaries, duplicated/corrected events, daylight-saving inputs, stale materialized views and cursor retries under new arrivals.

title: Ride-Hailing System Design (Uber)
question:
Design an Uber-style ride-hailing service. The interviewer drives on high-frequency driver GPS writes (dedup/throttle), geospatial indexing (Quadtree vs H3), and Redis GEO caching.

Design a ride-hailing service (Uber/Lyft-style): riders request rides and the system matches them to nearby drivers.

Geospatial indexing is the central trade-off - Quadtree vs H3 (hex grid): cell uniformity, neighbor lookup, hot-cell handling, rebalancing cost. Use Redis GEO (sorted-set / geohash backed) as the hot cache for 'drivers near a point'; discuss GEOSEARCH mechanics and TTL/eviction for stale locations. solution.teaching_notes_markdown:
### Make the location index fast without making it the assignment authority

Drivers send frequent coordinates; dispatch needs the latest sufficiently fresh available locations. A raw location history and a live geo index have different purposes. Authenticate the driver/session, sequence updates and coalesce redundant pings rather than persisting every one-second sample synchronously.

![W403. Ride-Hailing System Design (Uber) — architecture](../diagrams/W403_review_architecture.svg)

[Open the architecture diagram](../diagrams/W403_review_architecture.svg).

### Handle out-of-order writes and staleness

Each ping carries driver/session epoch, sequence, coordinate and observation time. Reject old epochs/sequences, validate implausible movement and record receive time. Update the live index only with a newer accepted ping. Persist compact trajectories asynchronously at a product-defined sampling/movement threshold, retaining more detail where safety/legal requirements demand it. A coalescer must not erase important trip events.

Quadtree cells adapt to spatial density but require split/merge/rebalance logic. H3 gives hierarchical hexagonal cells, easy neighbor expansion and convenient partition keys, though cell areas/distortion and pentagons still matter. With either, query nearby cells then compute true distance/ETA and apply freshness/eligibility filters; a cell match is only a candidate test. Redis GEO can serve a hot radius/box query using geohash-backed sorted sets. **Individual GEO members do not have independent key TTLs**: maintain last-seen timestamps, filter results and remove stale members explicitly (or rotate bucketed keys). A whole-key expiry cannot safely expire one stale driver among active ones.

### Reserve the driver once

A rider request has an idempotent trip/request ID. After candidate retrieval, conditionally transition a driver from AVAILABLE to OFFERED/RESERVED under one trip ID in the authoritative store. An accepted offer confirms the trip; rejected/expired offers release only if the reservation generation still matches. Two dispatchers can see the same cached driver, but only one reservation succeeds. Do not rely on removing a GEO member as the entire consistency mechanism.

Partition by city/region and subdivide hot cells while querying neighbors to avoid boundary blind spots. Match fairness can account for wait time, idle time, ETA and prior offers; nearest straight-line distance alone is not a complete policy. Surge/hot areas need admission, supply-aware routing and retry caps rather than unlimited expanding searches.

Monitor GPS age, discarded old updates, per-cell load, candidate recall, reservation conflicts, offer timeout and pickup ETA. Test stale/out-of-order pings, driver movement across cells, duplicate rider requests and two riders competing for one driver. No QPS is supplied: derive location input as active drivers divided by ping interval and benchmark geo update/query capacity at the expected hot-city peak.

solution.teaching_notes_markdown:
### Give locations and matches different consistency contracts

Locations can be slightly stale and still produce a useful candidate list. A match cannot assign one driver to two riders. Use a fast derived geospatial index for search and a strongly coordinated reservation record for assignment.

![W404. Rider-Driver Matching System — architecture](../diagrams/W404_review_architecture.svg)

[Open the architecture diagram](../diagrams/W404_review_architecture.svg).

### Requests, stores and lifecycle

`POST /rides` validates pickup/dropoff and returns one request ID under a client idempotency key. Store the request, rider and current state durably. Location pings have driver/session sequence and freshness; index by city plus H3/geohash cells and expand into neighboring cells before computing travel-time estimates. Keep only eligible, fresh candidates and cap the search radius/deadline.

Driver state follows AVAILABLE → RESERVED_FOR_OFFER → ASSIGNED → ON_TRIP → AVAILABLE, with explicit offline/reject/expiry paths. Each reservation contains ride ID, lease/generation and expiry. Atomic compare-and-set from AVAILABLE prevents competing matchers from winning the same driver. Accepting an offer verifies both driver and ride state under a coordinated transaction/owner; unique active driver and active rider-request constraints provide protection against duplicate assignments. A stale expiry worker can release only its own reservation generation.

A relational transactional store works well for ride/reservation constraints. A partitioned key-value system can work with conditional writes and a deliberate cross-record transaction/owner model; “eventual consistency everywhere” cannot enforce the no-double-assignment rule. The geo index remains derived, so a stale candidate can lose reservation and the matcher tries another within a bounded budget.

### Regional scale and recovery

Route each ride and driver to one city/region authority and define transfer when a driver crosses ownership boundaries. Do not let two regions concurrently consider the same driver available. Partition large cities by cells or driver hash, querying adjacent cells while preserving per-driver reservation ownership. Candidate scoring can use ETA, rider waiting and driver fairness; monitor the trade-off instead of always favoring the newest nearest driver.

Persist transition and outbox notification together, deduplicate events and let clients reconnect by ride ID/cursor. If a matcher crashes after reserving but before sending, a reconciler can resend the same offer or safely expire it. A declined/expired offer releases capacity, while an uncertain acceptance must be reconciled before reassignment. If the index fails, use a bounded fallback or report matching delay; never fabricate an assignment from unavailable state.

Size location writes as drivers × ping frequency and matching QPS as ride arrival/retry rate, with hot-city skew separately. Monitor request-to-match latency, GPS/index age, reservation conflicts, unaccepted lease age, double-assignment invariant and regional failover. Test concurrent matching, duplicate acceptance, lost notification, cancellation/accept races and a driver crossing a partition boundary.

Search listings by date range, location, guest count.

Confirm the booking once payment succeeds; release the hold otherwise.

solution.teaching_notes_markdown:
### Search can be stale; booking ownership cannot

Search returns likely available listings filtered by geography, capacity and dates. Checkout acquires a short authoritative hold for **every night** in the requested half-open stay `[check_in,check_out)`. The checkout date is not an occupied night. Concurrent overlapping requests must compete at the listing-night authority rather than trust search results.

![W405. Airbnb Booking System Design — architecture](../diagrams/W405_review_architecture.svg)

[Open the architecture diagram](../diagrams/W405_review_architecture.svg).

### Data and atomic hold

Use Listing, ListingNight `(listing_id,date,state,hold_id,version)`, Hold `(id,user,expiry,state)`, Reservation and PaymentAttempt. Pre-create or transactionally create unique night rows for the bookable horizon. To hold a range, lock its night rows in date order, clear only provably expired ordinary holds, require all nights free, then write one hold and update every night in a transaction. If any night is unavailable, roll back the entire range. A PostgreSQL exclusion constraint over date ranges is another valid model, with careful state/expiry handling.

`POST /holds` takes listing/dates/guest count and a client key; repeat requests return the same hold, while changed payload under the same key conflicts. `POST /reservations` starts payment against the accepted price snapshot. Return `409` with conflicting dates when a stale search result loses the hold race.

### Expiry must not race an uncertain payment

Before calling the provider, conditionally change HELD to PAYMENT_PENDING while still unexpired. An expiry worker and this transition serialize on the hold; only one wins. During payment pending, retain night allocation until the external outcome is resolved, or use a verified void/refund compensation before release. A timeout is not evidence of failure. Use stable provider operation keys and query status after a lost response; provider idempotency/lookup is a required dependency for duplicate-charge protection.

Verified success atomically marks nights BOOKED, confirms the reservation and creates an outbox event. Idempotent completion cannot book the range twice. Failed/voided payment releases only that hold's nights. Cancellation applies policy, records an idempotent refund job and updates availability under explicit timing rules; a stale retry cannot free nights now owned by another reservation.

### Geography, capacity and failure

Serve search near users with caches/index replicas, but route a listing's booking writes to one home shard/region. Multi-night transactions remain within that listing's authority. An outage can delay checkout for affected listings while search stays available; confirming from a stale replica would sacrifice the central invariant. Hot listings need rate limits and bounded lock waits, not just more stateless workers.

Monitor hold/lock conflicts, expiry lag, payment-pending age, confirmed reservations versus allocated nights and search-to-hold failure rate. Test overlapping/adjacent date ranges, double-submit, payment success after timeout, expiry/start-payment races and concurrent cancellation/new holds. Exactly one confirmation follows from authoritative atomic allocation plus guarded finalization, not from caching or a distributed lock that expires without fencing.

solution.teaching_notes_markdown:
### The hotel provider owns the final inventory decision

Search can use our cached room offers, but other sellers can consume the same rooms. A fresh availability check followed by a separate create call is still a race unless the provider offers an atomic hold/confirm operation or an exclusive inventory allotment. Our local database lock cannot lock the hotel's external inventory.

![W407. Design a Hotel Booking System with External Inventory — architecture](../diagrams/W407_review_architecture.svg)

[Open the architecture diagram](../diagrams/W407_review_architecture.svg).

### Model and query

Store Hotel with latitude/longitude and attributes; RoomType with capacity/features; ProviderOffer with provider/hotel/room-type IDs, stay dates, cancellation terms, currency, price and freshness/version; and Booking with immutable selected offer, provider reservation/hold reference, status and payment operation. Room-type nightly quantity is different from an individually assigned physical room—confirm the provider's model.

`GET /hotels?lat=&lon=&radius=&check_in=&check_out=&rooms=&filters=` first applies geo/catalog constraints and then date/quantity offer availability. Use a spatial index or coarse geo cells plus exact distance filtering, along with indexes for provider/hotel/date/room type. Multiple requested rooms must be confirmed together under the provider's atomic quantity semantics, not merely because each of several independent checks once returned one room.

### Booking sequence and consistency

Create an idempotent booking intent. Revalidate the selected rate, restrictions and availability with the provider and obtain an atomic hold where available. Present changed price/terms before charging. Store provider hold and deadline, then use an idempotent payment authorization/capture flow consistent with the supplier's contract. Confirm the supplier reservation and local status through durable pending states and reconciliation. No local transaction spans the payment provider and supplier.

If one external step succeeds and another fails, follow the defined compensation: void/refund payment or cancel supplier inventory as policy permits. A timeout is UNKNOWN, so query by stable client/provider IDs before making another reservation or charge. Require provider idempotency/status lookup for safe retries; if absent, the exact guarantee is limited and manual reconciliation may be necessary.

### Cache and failures

Cache search offers with freshness metadata and update them through feeds/webhooks/polling. A short TTL reduces expected stale failures but cannot eliminate out-of-band sales. At final confirmation, the provider's atomic outcome wins. If sold out, report the conflict, refresh alternatives and preserve the user's search; do not silently substitute a different price/room. If the provider is slow, show pending/timeout status rather than a false confirmation.

Bulkhead/rate-limit each provider and serve partial search results with explicit freshness. A provider outage should not block all hotel groups. Monitor search latency, cache age, reprice/sold-out rate, unknown booking age, duplicate-provider operations and payment/supplier reconciliation. Test two sellers racing for the last room, multi-room partial failure, lost confirmation response and a provider hold expiring during payment.

Cart operations: a shopper can add an item, remove an item, change a quantity and view the cart. Reads are far more frequent than writes, and every operation must feel instant.
