solution.example: The worked solution traces the question-specific request, concurrency/failure case and capacity assumptions.
solution.trap: Preserve the stated authority and uncertainty rules instead of confirming from a stale cache or retrying an unknown external effect with a new ID.
solution.teaching_notes_markdown:
### Keep large binaries out of the metadata database

An agent detects a crash, captures a bounded artifact and uploads it durably. The backend records service/build/host/time/signal, extracts stack signatures and lets authorized engineers search and download. Core dumps can contain credentials and user memory, so access, isolation and retention are part of the core design.

![W421. Core Dump Collection System Design — architecture](../diagrams/W421_review_architecture.svg)

[Open the architecture diagram](../diagrams/W421_review_architecture.svg).

### Upload and processing contracts

`POST /dumps` accepts service/build, size/checksum and an idempotency key, validates tenant/quota and issues a short-lived upload token scoped to one object. Multipart/resumable uploads avoid restarting multi-GB artifacts after a network interruption. Finalization verifies size/checksum/object completion before marking the dump AVAILABLE and creating an extraction job. Incomplete multipart uploads have lifecycle cleanup; they must not appear as downloadable complete dumps.

The agent uses a disk quota, bandwidth limit and priority/sampling policy. A bad deployment causing thousands of crashes must not fill every host disk or saturate production networks. Record dropped/sampled counts and retain useful first examples plus representative build/signature samples. A backend acknowledgement follows durable object/manifest acceptance, not just receipt by one API process.

### Metadata, grouping and query

Store dump ID, tenant/service, build ID, host, event/ingest time, signal, object/version/checksum, size, extraction state, signature and retention deadline. Index service/build/time/signature; group by normalized stack frames/build rather than raw ASLR addresses. Preserve original extraction versions so re-symbolication with corrected symbols is reproducible. Match symbols to the exact trusted build, and run parsers in a resource-limited sandbox because malformed binaries can exploit or exhaust them.

Search uses bounded pagination and account/service authorization. Download requires a fresh authorization check and short-lived signed object access, with an access audit. Broad “all engineers” access is inappropriate when dumps contain sensitive memory. Redaction/minidumps reduce exposure but cannot guarantee every secret was removed; encryption, least privilege and retention remain necessary.

### Size bursts and enforce deletion

For an illustrative one thousand one-GB dumps in a bad-deploy hour, ingest is one TB/hour, about 278 MB/s payload before replication/retries. Thirty days at ten TB/day means 300 TB primary storage, so size caps, dedup/group-aware sampling, compression and lifecycle tiering have substantial impact. These are assumptions; obtain actual crash/dump size distributions.

Retention deletes the object, metadata/search references and derived symbolication artifacts under a recorded tombstone/workflow; retries cannot resurrect an expired dump. Keep legally/operationally required audit metadata separately from raw memory retention. Reconcile orphan objects and missing index records. Test partial uploads, duplicate finalization, checksum mismatch, symbol mismatch, extractor crash, unauthorized download and burst quota behavior. Monitor spool age, dropped captures, upload completion, extraction lag, storage growth, deletion completion and access anomalies.

title: Cross-Platform Client Logging Library
question:
Design a logging library that runs on both web (browser SPA) and mobile (iOS/Android) clients and ships logs to a backend collector without degrading client-side performance.

Logs are emitted by application code and must reach a backend collector.
Hard constraint: emitting a log must never block the calling thread or noticeably degrade UX.
The backend has a single ingest API; throughput from any client is variable and can spike.
Drive hard on backpressure: what happens when call volume grows and the in-flight batch gets too large to send.

steps: Bound the work done by the logging call
One ingest API under variable throughput
solution.contract_notes: All full-prompt deliverables and assumptions are addressed in the answer; externally dependent guarantees remain conditional.
solution.example: The worked solution traces the question-specific request, concurrency/failure case and capacity assumptions.
solution.trap: Preserve the stated authority and uncertainty rules instead of confirming from a stale cache or retrying an unknown external effect with a new ID.
solution.teaching_notes_markdown:
### Bound the work done by the logging call

The application thread should enqueue a small immutable event and return; it must not wait for disk, network, batching or retries. Set a maximum event size/field budget and avoid expensive recursive serialization/stack capture on every call. A literal zero-pause guarantee is impossible in ordinary browser/mobile runtimes because scheduling and GC can pause execution, so the implementable contract is bounded application work with no deliberate blocking, validated against UX/frame-time budgets.

![W422. Cross-Platform Client Logging Library — architecture](../diagrams/W422_review_architecture.svg)

[Open the architecture diagram](../diagrams/W422_review_architecture.svg).

### Queue and batch policy

Define event ID, session sequence, severity, event/monotonic time, schema and approved fields. Copy only bounded primitive data or require immutable event input; otherwise a caller can mutate the log after enqueue. In multithreaded mobile code, use an appropriate bounded concurrent queue or a try-lock/drop policy—waiting on a contested mutex violates the stated emission contract. Browser serialization can run in a Web Worker; native apps use a dedicated executor.

For example, cap queued encoded data at one MB, one event at eight KB, batches at64 KB or one second, and two in-flight requests. These are chosen limits to benchmark. A full queue drops/samples low-priority records with counters, reserves bounded space for higher severity and eventually drops even high severity rather than exhausting memory. A larger batch is not an unbounded escape hatch. Split oversized batches at event boundaries after a413; drop/quarantine a single over-limit event.

### One ingest API under variable throughput

The collector accepts a batch ID plus unique event IDs, enforces tenant/device quotas and returns per-batch/per-event acknowledgement as its contract requires. Retry transient failures with capped exponential jitter, honor429/Retry-After, and stop retrying permanent validation/auth errors until corrected. A timed-out request may already have arrived, so backend deduplication is necessary. Preserve queue ordering where useful but allow controlled sampling; do not let a poison record block every later event.

Offline buffering has byte/age quotas and backpressure too. Disk writes happen in the worker, and storage can be evicted or unavailable. On browser page hide, `sendBeacon`/keepalive may improve delivery but does not prove durable collector receipt. Mobile background execution is OS-limited. The combination of never-waiting emission, finite memory/storage and arbitrary outages cannot promise lossless delivery; state the bounded-loss policy and expose counters.

### Privacy, lifecycle and tests

Filter sensitive fields by an allowlisted schema before transmission, partition data by account, expire it and avoid placing secrets in logs. Configuration changes can adjust levels/sampling without application logic branches. Avoid sending logs about transport failure recursively through the same failing queue.

Test sudden producer spikes, queue overflow, slow collectors,413/429, duplicate ACK loss, offline/online transitions, app suspension and logout/account change. Measure log-call p99, frame drops, battery/CPU, memory, spool size and end-to-end loss. A transport worker that is reliable but drains the battery still fails the client-library requirement.

title: Design an Audit Logs Service
question:
Design an audit-log service where users can query audit events belonging to their own account.

Audit events are generated from account activity and retained as an append-only transaction log.
The query path must support low-latency, account-scoped lookups.
Design the storage model for the transaction logs and the query indexes.
Discuss scaling as log volume and account count grow.
Authorization is part of the read path: a user must never query another account's audit log.

solution.contract_notes: All full-prompt deliverables and assumptions are addressed in the answer; externally dependent guarantees remain conditional.
solution.example: The worked solution traces the question-specific request, concurrency/failure case and capacity assumptions.
solution.trap: Preserve the stated authority and uncertainty rules instead of confirming from a stale cache or retrying an unknown external effect with a new ID.
solution.teaching_notes_markdown:
### Enforce account scope before querying

Audit events describe actions and must remain append-only under the retention policy. Each event contains event ID, account, actor, action/resource, outcome, trusted event/ingest time, schema/version and correlation ID. Actor identity is not necessarily the owning account; an administrator's action may affect another account and needs explicit attribution.

![W423. Design an Audit Logs Service — architecture](../diagrams/W423_review_architecture.svg)

[Open the architecture diagram](../diagrams/W423_review_architecture.svg).

### Capture without a lost-write window

When a business operation commits in its own database, write an audit outbox event in the same transaction. A relay may retry, so the audit sink has a unique event ID and idempotent insert. This avoids a successful account change followed by a lost best-effort logging RPC. It is not a distributed transaction across every business service; each producer must define its own capture boundary. Sensitive rejected attempts may need a separate durable security-event path.

Store immutable canonical events durably, then build query indexes by `(account_id,event_time,event_id)`, partitioning large histories by account hash and time. An analytical search index can add action/resource filters, but the original record remains the source of truth. Use stable pagination cursors including query scope and `(time,id)` tie-break; timestamps alone can collide. State ingestion freshness and handle late events/corrections with appended follow-up records rather than editing history invisibly.

### Authorization, scale and retention

Derive allowed accounts from the authenticated principal and account membership/role checks. Never trust a request's account ID merely because it appears in a filter. Apply the same account predicate to storage, cache keys, exports, cursor validation and object downloads; recheck permissions on each page. Service-to-service calls use scoped workload identity. Cross-account administrator access is separately authorized and audited.

Use immutable/WORM storage where the threat/compliance model requires it, integrity checks and separated write/read/admin privileges. Hash chains can help detect some changes but need trusted anchoring and do not replace access control. Redact/minimize sensitive payload fields before capture; append-only storage is a poor place to retain unnecessary secrets forever. Define retention/deletion/legal-hold policy and make it auditable rather than claiming immutable means no lifecycle management.

Partition/index by measured hot-account volume and archive old segments to cheaper object storage. Common recent-account reads can use a scoped cache with freshness; wide exports become bounded asynchronous jobs. Monitor producer/outbox lag, duplicate/missing events, query p99, per-account skew, retention completion and denied access. Test forged account IDs/cursors, stale membership, retries, late events, index outage and a cache key missing tenant scope.

title: Environment-specific Logging Without Code Modifications
question:
Given two environments (prod and deployment) with identical codebases, accomplish the following: Record logs only in the deployment environment and not in the prod environment without changing the code logic. All logs should be written to the same file.

Constraints

Do not add any environment-check logic in the code.
Do not use a load balancer.
Do not utilize multiple servers.
It is a monolithic environment setup.

How can this be achieved?

Example
Input
logging environment settings in the configuration file

solution.contract_notes: All full-prompt deliverables and assumptions are addressed in the answer; externally dependent guarantees remain conditional.
solution.example: The worked solution traces the question-specific request, concurrency/failure case and capacity assumptions.
solution.trap: Preserve the stated authority and uncertainty rules instead of confirming from a stale cache or retrying an unknown external effect with a new ID.
solution.teaching_notes_markdown:
### Configure the logger externally

Use the same application binary and logging calls in both environments, but supply different logging configuration at the same external path. The deployment configuration routes the root logger to one file; the production configuration turns logging off. No load balancer, second server or application `if environment` branch is needed.

This assumes the monolith already uses a configurable logging framework. If it writes directly with `print`, raw file calls or a native library that ignores that framework, a logger configuration cannot magically suppress every output without changing its capture/runtime setup. State that limitation rather than claiming an arbitrary program obeys an unrelated config file.

![W424. Environment-specific Logging Without Code Modifications — architecture](../diagrams/W424_review_architecture.svg)

[Open the architecture diagram](../diagrams/W424_review_architecture.svg).

### Concrete Logback example

For an application already using SLF4J/Logback, start the unchanged process with the standard external configuration property:

```sh
java -Dlogback.configurationFile=/etc/myapp/logback.xml -jar myapp.jar
```

In the deployment environment, `/etc/myapp/logback.xml` contains:

```xml
<configuration>
  <appender name="ONE_FILE" class="ch.qos.logback.core.FileAppender">
    <file>/var/log/myapp/application.log</file>
    <append>true</append>
    <encoder>
      <pattern>%date %-5level [%thread] %logger - %msg%n</pattern>
    </encoder>
  </appender>
  <root level="INFO">
    <appender-ref ref="ONE_FILE"/>
  </root>
</configuration>
```

In production, the file instead contains:

```xml
<configuration>
  <root level="OFF"/>
</configuration>
```

Only framework-managed application logs at configured deployment levels go to that single file; set DEBUG if lower-severity messages are required. Audit any package-specific logger/appender configuration so it does not bypass or duplicate the root route. Deployment creates/permissions the directory and chooses file ownership; the application does not infer its environment.

### Explain the operational boundary

“All logs in the same file” means one configured destination for the monolith's governed loggers, not multiple files per module. Add rotation/retention with a rolling appender if required, defining whether rotated segments still satisfy the intent. If two independent processes actually write one path, safe concurrent rotation needs a separate plan; the stated single-monolith setup avoids that complication.

Validate with the same startup binary in each environment: emit representative framework logs, confirm the deployment file receives them once, and confirm production emits none through the governed framework. Inspect stdout/access/native logs separately if “all logs” literally includes them. Disabling production logs also removes diagnostic evidence, so confirm that this is the intended operational requirement; the technical mechanism remains configuration, not environment checks added to business code.

title: Event Logger with batching, fsync, and group commit follow-ups
question:
Problem: Event Logger

Design and implement an event logger that appends events to a durable log.

Requirements
Support appending events to the log.
Support writing in-memory events to the underlying storage in batches.
Consider durability semantics: when to call fsync (or an equivalent forced flush).
Follow-up directions (conceptual)
How to do batching to improve throughput.
Trade-offs for fsync frequency (latency vs durability).
How group commit works in real databases: merging concurrent commits and notifying multiple waiters after a single flush.

Note: The original description does not specify exact I/O formats or constraints; this is commonly treated as a systems/design + implementable component question where you define interfaces, concurrency model, and durability guarantees.

# Write your code here

solution.contract_notes: All full-prompt deliverables and assumptions are addressed in the answer; externally dependent guarantees remain conditional.
solution.example: Ten accepted append Futures share one fsync, become durable together, and recovery discards an incomplete trailing record.
solution.trap: Preserve the stated authority and uncertainty rules instead of confirming from a stale cache or retrying an unknown external effect with a new ID.
solution.teaching_notes_markdown:
### Define what append success means

`append(event)` returns a Future after bounded-queue acceptance. The event becomes **durably acknowledged only when that Future completes**, after the writer has written, flushed the language buffer and called fsync. Waiting for acceptance alone does not establish durability. This interface lets several concurrent callers share one physical flush.

![W425. Event Logger with batching, fsync, and group commit follow-ups — architecture](../diagrams/W425_review_architecture.svg)

[Open the architecture diagram](../diagrams/W425_review_architecture.svg).

### Runnable batched logger

[Download the implementation](../event_logger_425.py) and [behavior checks](../test_booking_logging_401_425.py). Create an existing durable parent directory, instantiate the logger and call `future.result()` when the caller needs a durability barrier. `close()` drains accepted work and reports failure; use it during orderly shutdown.

```python
"""W425: bounded asynchronous appends; Futures acknowledge fsync group commit."""

from concurrent.futures import Future
import json
import os
from pathlib import Path
import queue
import threading
import time


class EventLogger:
    def __init__(
        self, path, max_batch=100, flush_seconds=0.01, queue_size=10000, sync=os.fsync
    ):
        if max_batch < 1 or flush_seconds < 0 or queue_size < 1:
            raise ValueError("Invalid batching limits")
        self.path = Path(path)
        self.max_batch = max_batch
        self.delay = flush_seconds
        self.sync = sync
        self.queue = queue.Queue(queue_size)
        self.lock = threading.Lock()
        self.closed = False
        self.error = None
        if not self.path.parent.is_dir():
            raise ValueError("Create the durable parent directory first")
        self.file = open(self.path, "a+b")
        # Recovery accepts only a complete JSONL prefix, truncating a torn final line.
        self.file.seek(0)
        valid_end = 0
        self.next_sequence = 1
        while True:
            line = self.file.readline()
            if not line:
                break
            if not line.endswith(b"\n"):
                break
            record = json.loads(line)
            if record["sequence"] != self.next_sequence:
                raise ValueError("Corrupt sequence")
            self.next_sequence += 1
            valid_end = self.file.tell()
        self.file.truncate(valid_end)
        self.file.flush()
        os.fsync(self.file.fileno())
        directory = os.open(self.path.parent, os.O_RDONLY)
        try:
            os.fsync(directory)  # make a newly created log's directory entry durable
        finally:
            os.close(directory)
        self.worker = threading.Thread(target=self._run, daemon=True)
        self.worker.start()

    def append(self, event):
        # Snapshot/validate JSON at the API boundary; do not retain mutable caller objects.
        payload = json.loads(json.dumps(event, allow_nan=False))
        future = Future()
        future.set_running_or_notify_cancel()  # accepting an append is not cancellable
        with self.lock:
            if self.closed or self.error:
                raise RuntimeError("Logger unavailable") from self.error
            try:
                self.queue.put_nowait((payload, future))
            except queue.Full:
                raise BufferError("Log queue full; event not accepted")
        return future

    def _run(self):
        batch = []
        try:
            stop = False
            while not stop:
                item = self.queue.get()
                if item is None:
                    break
                batch = [item]
                deadline = time.monotonic() + self.delay
                while len(batch) < self.max_batch:
                    try:
                        item = self.queue.get(
                            timeout=max(0, deadline - time.monotonic())
                        )
                    except queue.Empty:
                        break
                    if item is None:
                        stop = True
                        break
                    batch.append(item)
                records = []
                sequences = []
                for payload, future in batch:
                    sequence = self.next_sequence
                    self.next_sequence += 1
                    sequences.append(sequence)
                    records.append(
                        json.dumps(
                            dict(sequence=sequence, event=payload), allow_nan=False
                        ).encode()
                        + b"\n"
                    )
                self.file.write(b"".join(records))
                self.file.flush()
                self.sync(self.file.fileno())
                for (_, future), sequence in zip(batch, sequences):
                    if not future.cancelled():
                        future.set_result(sequence)
                batch = []
        except BaseException as error:
            with self.lock:
                self.error = error
            for _, future in batch:
                if not future.done():
                    future.set_exception(error)
            while True:
                try:
                    item = self.queue.get_nowait()
                except queue.Empty:
                    break
                if item is not None and not item[1].done():
                    item[1].set_exception(error)
        finally:
            self.file.close()

    def close(self):
        with self.lock:
            first = not self.closed
            self.closed = True
        if first:
            while self.worker.is_alive():
                try:
                    self.queue.put(None, timeout=0.05)
                    break
                except queue.Full:
                    pass
        self.worker.join()
        if self.error:
            raise RuntimeError("Durable log write failed") from self.error
```

The writer owns file order and sequence numbers. It snapshots JSON input before enqueue so later caller mutation cannot change the stored event. A full queue rejects the new event explicitly instead of consuming unbounded memory. Accepted appends cannot be cancelled by cancelling their Future. Keep Future callbacks short because completion callbacks may execute on the writer thread.

### Why group commit helps

One fsync per event provides low batching delay but makes throughput depend heavily on sync latency. If fsync takes three milliseconds, a serialized one-event scheme tops out near333 syncs/s before other work. A100-event group could amortize that cost toward33,333 events/s, subject to encoding/write/device limits. Group members wait for batch accumulation plus write/sync; this is a throughput/latency trade-off, not free speed.

`flush()` moves Python-buffered bytes to the operating system; fsync requests persistence to the storage device under the filesystem/hardware contract. A background sync every interval can lose the unsynced suffix after a crash if callers were acknowledged earlier. The implementation avoids that particular lie by acknowledging only after the shared fsync. It also syncs the containing directory for the log's creation; rotating/renaming files requires its own file/directory durability steps. Host/device destruction still needs replication/backups—fsync is not geographic durability.

### Recovery and failure semantics

On startup, accept a contiguous complete JSONL prefix, truncate an incomplete final line, and reject complete malformed/corrupt sequence records. For stronger bit-corruption detection, add length/checksum framing and checkpoints/segments; JSON parsing alone is not a cryptographic integrity guarantee. A sync/write failure fails affected and queued Futures, stops accepting new events and surfaces on close. It must not return success then quietly discard a batch.

An unacknowledged event can nevertheless survive a crash if bytes reached storage before the process died. Callers retrying after an uncertain acknowledgement need stable event IDs and deduplication if exactly one logical record matters. A Future timeout does not remove the accepted event. Multiple processes must not append through separate copies of this in-memory sequencer; route to one writer/partition or add a proper cross-process protocol.

The tests verify ten waiters sharing one sync, sequence/order and torn-tail recovery, payload snapshotting, close draining and explicit fsync failure. They exercise local behavior, not physical power-loss reliability or production throughput. The generic `solution()` stub defines no stdin format, so the component API above is an explicit, testable interpretation of the task.

title: HFT Onsite Round 3 — Sort Complexity + Linux Fundamentals + tail(n) Design
question:
A fully verbal / whiteboard Citsec HFT (Singapore) onsite round — no live coding submission, a wide-ranging interrogation across three areas:

1.
Sort-algorithm complexity, especially quicksort worst case: average vs worst, pivot-selection strategies, when quicksort beats/loses to heapsort and mergesort.
2.
Linux fundamentals: shared memory (shm, mmap), interrupt handling, context switching, system calls.
3.
Design tail -n on a very large file: backward seeking, chunked reads, mmap, and what to do when n is itself large.

Reported as a high-pressure round with rapid cross-examination — treat that as calibration, not a personal signal.

steps: Sorting: bounds and the mechanism behind them
Linux primitives in the relevant execution path
tail -n without reading a huge file unnecessarily
solution.example:
Example: `a
b
` with n=1 skips the final delimiter and finds the preceding one, outputting `b
`; `a
b` outputs `b`. A one-line file without newline returns all bytes. The scan costs O(bytes inspected in the suffix), at worst O(file size), plus unavoidable output cost. n huge approaches a full forward output but need not allocate n lines. `mmap` can simplify indexed backward access, but ordinary seek/read avoids giant mappings and concurrent-truncation fault risks. Define concurrent-file behavior: use an initial-size snapshot, cap reads at it, and report shrink/read errors; `tail -f` is a separate rotation-following feature. For a pipe, consume forward into a deque of n lines or a disk spool; memory is proportional to retained **bytes**, not a constant merely because line count is capped.
solution.trap: Quicksort expected and worst bounds differ; tail must skip terminal delimiter and stream output with bounded bytes even for huge n; syscalls and context switches differ.
solution.teaching_notes_markdown:
### Sorting: bounds and the mechanism behind them

Quicksort partitions around a pivot. Balanced partitions give T(n)=2T(n/2)+Θ(n)=Θ(n log n); repeatedly choosing an extreme gives T(n)=T(n−1)+Θ(n)=Θ(n²). Random pivoting yields expected O(n log n) for any fixed input independent of the randomness, not a deterministic worst-case bound. First/last pivots fail on sorted data; median-of-three helps common patterns but adversarial input still exists. Three-way partition avoids wasting recursion on many equal keys. Recurse on the smaller partition and iterate the larger to bound stack O(log n); naive recursion can reach O(n).

Heapsort gives deterministic O(n log n) and O(1) auxiliary array space but worse locality/branch behavior than quicksort in many workloads. Mergesort gives O(n log n), is naturally stable and sequential-I/O friendly, but conventional array merging needs O(n) scratch space. Introsort starts with quicksort and switches to heapsort at a depth limit, combining common-case locality and worst-case protection. Stability, element move cost, cache behavior, data distribution and external storage decide the winner; comparison-sort Ω(n log n) does not constrain radix/counting methods under bounded-key assumptions.

### Linux primitives in the relevant execution path

A syscall crosses from user mode into the kernel to request an operation; it need not switch to another process. A context switch saves/restores execution context and may change address space/TLB state; switching threads in one process can avoid an address-space change but still has scheduling/cache costs. An interrupt notifies the CPU of an asynchronous device/timer event; the handler does bounded work and often defers heavier processing. An exception/page fault is synchronous to an instruction and may trigger disk I/O; do not call every kernel entry an interrupt.

Shared memory maps the same physical pages into multiple processes, avoiding repeated payload copies but requiring synchronization and a clear lifetime/ownership protocol. `mmap` maps file-backed or anonymous memory; access faults pages in lazily and uses page cache. `MAP_SHARED` exposes shared updates under synchronization/persistence rules, while `MAP_PRIVATE` is copy-on-write. Mapping a terabyte does not instantly load a terabyte, but touches, page tables, address space and truncation hazards still matter. Shared visibility is not equivalent to crash-durable fsync/msync semantics.

### tail -n without reading a huge file unnecessarily

For n≤0 output nothing. Open the regular file in binary mode, capture its size and examine the last byte. A final newline terminates the last line; it does not create an extra empty line. Starting at EOF, read fixed-size blocks backward (e.g. an assumed 64 KiB), scan each block from right to left and count newline delimiters. Skip the one exactly at EOF; after the nth earlier delimiter, the output begins immediately after it. If fewer than n lines exist, start at zero. Then stream bytes **forward** from that offset to the captured EOF, so memory is O(block size), even when n or an individual line is enormous. UTF-8 multibyte boundaries do not affect newline-byte discovery; decode only at a complete line boundary or emit bytes directly.

Example: `a\nb\n` with n=1 skips the final delimiter and finds the preceding one, outputting `b\n`; `a\nb` outputs `b`. A one-line file without newline returns all bytes. The scan costs O(bytes inspected in the suffix), at worst O(file size), plus unavoidable output cost. n huge approaches a full forward output but need not allocate n lines. `mmap` can simplify indexed backward access, but ordinary seek/read avoids giant mappings and concurrent-truncation fault risks. Define concurrent-file behavior: use an initial-size snapshot, cap reads at it, and report shrink/read errors; `tail -f` is a separate rotation-following feature. For a pipe, consume forward into a deque of n lines or a disk spool; memory is proportional to retained **bytes**, not a constant merely because line count is capped.

title: Build a Discord-like TCP Chat Server with Slash Commands, Rooms, Reconnection, and Persistence

Build a runnable multi-client TCP chat server with slash commands, chat rooms, per-room history, reconnection, and persistence across restarts.

Requirements
1.
Multi-client TCP server: listen on a configurable port, serve many clients at once, and read line-based input terminated by
. Each line is either a command (starts with /) or a chat message.
2.
Slash commands, at least:
/help: list the available commands.
/nick <name>: set or change this user's nickname.

/quit: disconnect gracefully.
3.
Rooms: create a room (for example /create <room>), join a room (/join <room>), and list rooms (/rooms). A message sent to a room is broadcast to every user in it. A plain message from a user who is in no room gets a helpful error.
4.
History: when a user joins a room, show that room's last 10 messages.
5.
Reconnection: define a user identity (for example user id plus token). A user who disconnects can reconnect later, restore their identity, and rejoin the rooms they were in.
6.
Persistence: users and nicknames, rooms, memberships and room history (at least a retained window) survive a server restart. Any storage is fine (SQLite, files, a key-value store); describe your data model.
7.
Scalability: the server need not be distributed, but explain how the design would scale: the concurrency model for many connections, the storage bottleneck, broadcasting across several server instances, and slow clients.
Input
A port number on the command line.
Lines typed by clients connected with telnet, nc, or PuTTY.
Output / deliverable
A runnable server, a short description of the protocol and data model, and a manual test script showing two clients chatting in a room, history on join, and state restored after a server restart.
Example
client A: /nick alice        -> id=<id> token=<token> nick=alice
client A: /create general
client A: /join general
client B: /nick bob
client B: /join general
client A: hello              -> client B sees "[general] alice: hello"
(restart the server)
client A: /login <id> <token> -> welcome back alice, rooms and last 10 messages restored

solution.example: SQLite work is synchronous and serialized here, appropriate for a local exercise but a measured event-loop/storage bottleneck. Offload a serialized database writer or use async database access, batch inserts and partition rooms at higher volume. Multiple gateway instances need shared durable history, a room-owner/sequence service and broker fanout to gateways holding members; the token/membership database cannot remain an uncoordinated local file. At an assumed 1,000 messages/s×200 bytes and 100 recipients/message, output is roughly 20 MB/s before protocol overhead. Restrict line length/names and parameterize SQL. Tests cover command errors, history limit, login/restart and broadcast; no internet-scale or encrypted transport claim is made.
solution.trap: A socket is not persistent state; identity/membership/history commit before broadcasts. Bounded slow-client output, explicit1000-message retention and real restart recovery implemented.

title: Design a 1:1 Chat System (Pub/Sub, Partitioning, Multi-Region)
question:
Design a one-on-one (1:1) chat system: two users exchange text messages in real time from phones, laptops and browsers, and each user may be logged in on several devices at once.

Scale and assumptions
1.
Users: 100 million daily active users. Each sends about 50 messages per day. Peak traffic is 3 times the average.
2.
Message: a sender, a recipient, a client-generated message id, a timestamp and a text body of up to 4 KB. The average encoded size is 300 bytes.
3.
Presence: at peak, about 20% of daily active users hold an open connection.
4.
Regions: users are spread over three geographic regions (for example US, EU and Asia-Pacific). Two users in a conversation may live in different regions.
5.
History: messages are kept indefinitely, and a user can scroll back through any conversation.
Functional requirements
1.
Send a message to one other user. When the recipient is online, every one of their connected devices receives it within about 500 ms in the same region.
2.
When the recipient is offline, the message is stored and delivered when a device reconnects. Nothing is lost and nothing is shown twice, even when a client retries a send.
3.
Messages within one conversation appear in the same order on every device of both users.
4.
Delivery and read receipts are sent back to the sender.
5.
Load the most recent page of a conversation's history, and page backwards.
Parts to address
1.
Pub/sub and fan-out: how a message travels from the sender's connection to each of the recipient's live connections. Cover which component holds connections, how the system knows where a user is connected, and what happens when a device is offline or reconnects.
2.
Partition key: how messages are partitioned in the message store and in any queue or topic. State the key, why it serves the read and write paths, and what alternatives you rejected.
3.
Cross-region: what happens when sender and recipient are in different regions. Cover where the conversation's data lives, the latency a cross-region message pays, and what happens when a region fails.
4.
Database scaling: how the message store grows to years of history, including sharding, replication, hot conversations and the split between recent and old data.
Deliverables
1.
An architecture diagram (in words is fine) naming each component on the send and receive paths.
2.
The data model for messages and conversations.
3.
Capacity estimates: write rate, storage per day and per year, number of connection gateways, and number of storage shards.
4.
The failure behaviour for a lost acknowledgement, a dropped connection, a gateway crash and a region outage.
Constraints
Group chats, media attachments and end-to-end encryption are out of scope, but the design should not prevent adding them.
State every assumption you add beyond the numbers above.

solution.example: Lost ACK returns the same committed seq on resend. Dropped socket/gateway crash leaves history intact and reconnect replays after cursor; duplicate pushes are suppressed by seq. A region outage reroutes connections, recovers consensus authority/directory and replays outbox/history; directory loss does not lose messages. Keep encryption/access checks, quotas and retention indexes ready for future media/groups/E2EE without claiming those features now. Monitor write/read tail latency, replication/delivery lag, cursor gaps, duplicate suppression and gateway pressure; test concurrent sends, ACK loss, device offline for years, gateway death and region failover with committed-prefix verification.
solution.trap: Same conversation needs one sequence authority; user/time-only partitioning and asynchronous DR cannot meet consistent order/no acknowledged loss. All supplied capacity figures computed.
solution.teaching_notes_markdown:
### Capacity and records

100 million DAU×50 messages gives **five billion messages/day**, about **57,870 writes/s average**, **173,611/s peak**. At 300 bytes average, content is **1.5 TB/day** and **547.5 TB/year** logical; three replicas are about 1.6425 PB/year before indexes/receipts/backups. Indefinite history is continuing growth, not one year's provision. Peak open users are 20 million. Assuming one connection/user and 20,000 connections/gateway, need 1,000 gateways before headroom; at an assumed 1.5 devices/connected user, 1,500. Real device count and tested per-gateway memory/output rate determine sizing.

Conversation(id,participants,home_region,next_seq,epoch), Message(conversation_id,seq,sender,client_msg_id,body,time), Dedup(sender,client_msg_id,request_hash,conversation,seq), DeviceCursor(user,device,conversation,delivered_seq,read_seq) and membership records define the model. Unique client identity binds sender/body/conversation and returns the original seq on retry. An ACK follows atomic dedup+sequence+message+outbox commit; timestamps are display metadata, not ordering authority.

### Send, fanout and partition key

The diagram is device→authenticated connection gateway→conversation owner/shard→replicated message log/outbox→regional pub/sub routers→all live recipient devices (and sender's other devices). A TTL session directory maps user to region/gateway/connection IDs; gateways own sockets and heartbeat directory entries. Offline users need no permanent socket/pubsub consumer because history persists. On reconnect a device fetches messages after its durable delivered cursor, deduplicates by conversation/seq and acknowledges only after local persistence; read receipts advance monotonically by max sequence and are distinct from gateway delivery.

Partition queue/message writes by conversation_id for one ordered stream and efficient history pages. Partition old storage by (conversation_id,time/sequence bucket) so one long conversation is not an unbounded physical partition. User partitioning would scatter one conversation across sender/recipient copies and complicate ordering; timestamp-only partitioning makes history fan out and creates hot time buckets. A conversation sequencer orders concurrent opposite-direction sends; idempotent retry never allocates another message. History pages use exclusive before_seq cursors. Pub/sub is a delivery hint/replay trigger, not the only durable copy.

### Regions, shards and failure behavior

Give each conversation one home ordering authority; gateways forward cross-region sends there, then deliver from nearby recipient gateways. Both parties pay the relevant WAN path and durability quorum latency; the same-region 500 ms target is not automatically a worldwide bound. Use three-region consensus replication if no acknowledged message may be lost through region failure, and fence the old leader before promoting a quorum survivor. During loss of quorum stop acknowledging new messages, while clients retain pending sends under the same ID. Async remote replication would lower latency but cannot promise RPO zero, so make that trade-off explicit.

For shard sizing, assume 2,000 safe writes/s per logical shard: peak needs at least 87, choose 128 for throughput headroom. Storage dominates yearly growth: at an assumed 2 TB usable logical recent data/shard, one year alone would need 274 shard-equivalents before replication, so tier old immutable buckets to object storage with indexed manifests and warm read caches. These are assumptions, not product facts. Hot 1:1 conversations get dedicated ownership/caches or rate limits; a globally ordered conversation cannot be parallelized arbitrarily without a sequencer.

Lost ACK returns the same committed seq on resend. Dropped socket/gateway crash leaves history intact and reconnect replays after cursor; duplicate pushes are suppressed by seq. A region outage reroutes connections, recovers consensus authority/directory and replays outbox/history; directory loss does not lose messages. Keep encryption/access checks, quotas and retention indexes ready for future media/groups/E2EE without claiming those features now. Monitor write/read tail latency, replication/delivery lag, cursor gaps, duplicate suppression and gateway pressure; test concurrent sends, ACK loss, device offline for years, gateway death and region failover with committed-prefix verification.

title: Design a Chat Application with Group and Offline Support
question: Design a chat application that supports one-on-one and group messaging with user registration, real-time message delivery, and offline support (messages delivered when a recipient reconnects).

steps: Durable conversations, not just open sockets
solution.example: Lost ACK/dropped gateway is recovered by client key/cursor; an outbox crash replays without creating another message. Message-store outage leaves sends pending/failed explicitly, not socket-ACKed as saved. Region failover chooses quorum/fenced authority if acknowledged-message loss is forbidden; async replicas have a disclosed RPO trade-off. Partition by conversation for ordering/history and time-bucket long histories; cache recent pages. Test repeated sends, concurrent group membership removal, reconnect gap, slow consumer and receipt reordering. Monitor durable-ACK latency, commit-to-device delay, backlog age, unauthorized reads and duplicate-render rate. This covers registration, groups and offline recovery without mistaking presence for membership or delivery for read status.
solution.trap: Presence/online push differs from durable membership/history; per-device cursors and client keys prevent displayed replay duplicates.
solution.teaching_notes_markdown:
### Durable conversations, not just open sockets

Assume text 1:1/groups, registration/login, near-realtime delivery and offline history; clarify group limits/retention because they drive fanout cost. Registration stores salted password hashes or uses an identity provider, sessions are short-lived/refreshable and every send/history request checks current conversation membership. `POST /conversations`, `/conversations/{id}/messages` with client message key, `GET /messages?after|before_seq=`, and receipt APIs form the contract.

Store User, Conversation(id,type,next_seq,epoch), Membership(conversation,user,role,joined_seq,left_seq), Message(conversation,seq,sender,client_id,body,time) and DeviceCursor(user,device,conversation,delivered,read). Decide whether new members see prejoin history; assume only from joined_seq unless a policy grants more. An owner/leader per conversation commits sequence+message+dedup+outbox atomically before ACK. Sender retries return the same seq; sequence, not device clock, orders messages across devices.

### Online and offline flow

The diagram's connection gateways authenticate sockets and publish TTL session mappings. Conversation outbox events flow through pub/sub to gateways serving online members, with per-device acknowledgments and UI deduplication. Offline members do not require one giant queue per device: durable conversation history plus membership/cursor supplies backlog on reconnect. Push notifications wake the app and carry minimal metadata, not authoritative delivery/read state. Read receipts advance by max seq and remain eventually consistent.

Groups multiply delivery work; push to each gateway once with its local recipient set, and bound per-group/member rates. Large groups can pull history from shared conversation storage rather than materialize message bodies per recipient. A removal/deletion event invalidates current access and stale queued delivery; cached media/extensions need the same policy. Use bounded socket queues, slow-client disconnect and after_seq replay rather than letting one stalled user block fanout.

### Estimate and failures

No scale is provided. Assume one million daily users×20 sends/day=20 million/day (~231/s average); if mean group delivery fanout is 15, output is ~3,472 deliveries/s before peak/device multiplication. At assumed 300 bytes/message, content storage is 6 GB/day logical. Separate connection count, storage writes and fanout throughput when sizing shards/gateways.

Lost ACK/dropped gateway is recovered by client key/cursor; an outbox crash replays without creating another message. Message-store outage leaves sends pending/failed explicitly, not socket-ACKed as saved. Region failover chooses quorum/fenced authority if acknowledged-message loss is forbidden; async replicas have a disclosed RPO trade-off. Partition by conversation for ordering/history and time-bucket long histories; cache recent pages. Test repeated sends, concurrent group membership removal, reconnect gap, slow consumer and receipt reordering. Monitor durable-ACK latency, commit-to-device delay, backlog age, unauthorized reads and duplicate-render rate. This covers registration, groups and offline recovery without mistaking presence for membership or delivery for read status.

![W429 flow: Registration / chat sessions → Conversation membership → Ordered durable message log → Gateway pub/sub fanout → Device ACK / read cursors → Offline history replay.](../diagrams/W429_exact_review_426_450.svg)

title: Design a Collaborative Spreadsheet (Google Sheets)
question:
Salesforce AI Engineer onsite system-design round. Design a web service like Google Sheets, with the interviewer steering focus onto the backend and data model — concurrency control for simultaneous editors, storage of large sheets, snapshot / version backup.

Requirements
Web-based spreadsheet: rows x columns of cells, each cell holds a value or a formula referencing other cells.
Multi-user collaboration: many editors on the same sheet concurrently; edits propagate to all viewers in near-real-time.
Persistence: a sheet survives server restarts; full history accessible (versioning / snapshots).
Scale: very large sheets (millions of cells); some sheets are tiny.
Interviewer explicitly emphasises backend + data models — frontend rendering and offline sync are out of scope.

solution.example: Assume one million nonempty cells at 100 encoded bytes: 100 MB logical/snapshot, excluding formulas/dependencies/history. A 1,000-cell edit should append a delta and rewrite affected chunks, not a 100 MB full file. At an assumed 1,000 edits/s×200 bytes, log growth is 17.28 GB/day for one very hot sheet; enforce limits and retention/cost policy while preserving the promised history. Multi-zone replicas, sequencer epochs and conditional writes prevent split-brain owners. Test two simultaneous same-cell writes, row insertion against formula references, duplicate op, cycle creation, stale recalculation and crash during snapshot publication. Monitor append lag, formula fanout/cost, snapshot age and replay time; no text-collaboration algorithm is necessary to define this centralized cell-operation contract.
solution.trap: Same-cell conflict, structural row IDs, formula dependencies/recalc versions and snapshot/log cutover require explicit semantics; generic text-OT answer was removed.
solution.teaching_notes_markdown:
### Backend model and concurrency rule

Store Workbook/Sheet(id,owner,ACL,head_version), RowID/ColumnID(order_key,deleted), Cell(sheet,row_id,col_id,raw_value_or_formula,last_version), Dependency(sheet,source_cell,target_cell), Operation(sheet,seq,op_id,actor,base_version,payload), Snapshot(sheet,version,manifest) and partitioned cell chunks. Use stable row/column IDs rather than physical offsets so inserting a row does not force rewriting every stored coordinate. Formula references retain stable identity plus relative/absolute semantics; structural edits define how display addresses and range expansion change. Sparse chunks avoid storing empty millions of cells, while range tiles support large scans.

Choose one fenced authoritative sequencer per sheet and online editing, since offline sync/frontend are out of scope. Operations include set-cell, batch/paste, insert/delete row/column and ACL changes. Each op_id is unique, and the server assigns an increasing seq in a durable transaction before broadcast. Concurrent writes to the same cell use declared **server-order last-write-wins**, retaining both in history; clients can optionally send expected_cell_version for conflict rejection instead of silent overwrite. Batch paste is atomic at an agreed size limit. Stable-ID structural operations against deleted rows/cells are rejected or reported as no-op according to a documented rule, not misapplied to a shifted neighbor.

### Formulas and coherent versions

The diagram's ordered edit service updates cells and dependency indexes, then a recalculation scheduler invalidates reachable dependents and evaluates a topological order. Cycles produce a deterministic cycle error (or a separately scoped iterative-calculation policy). Version volatile functions/time/random seeds per calculation epoch and restrict external-data functions so two replicas do not compute incompatible values. Derived values carry input sheet_version and are published as a calculation batch; a late calculation for v10 cannot overwrite v11. For expensive sheets expose CALCULATING/version lag rather than mix values from inconsistent inputs and claim a current snapshot.

`POST /sheets/{id}/operations`, `GET /cells?range=&version=`, `/changes?after_seq=`, `/history` and `/restore` provide backend APIs. Restore creates a new version from an old snapshot, preserving history, and needs authorization/version preconditions. Viewers receive a snapshot at v plus replay v+1 onward; register a replay boundary before switching to live events to avoid the snapshot/broadcast gap.

### Persistence, scale and failures

Append operations and outbox durably; periodically materialize immutable chunk snapshots with a complete manifest/checksum and version. Recovery loads a verified snapshot and replays the tail. Keep full history through logs+snapshots, compacting storage without deleting the only reconstructible prior version. Hot sheets may have dedicated owners; tiny sheets share workers. One globally ordered sheet has a per-sheet throughput ceiling, so chunk storage/parallel recalculation improves capacity without pretending arbitrary concurrent sequencing is free.

Assume one million nonempty cells at 100 encoded bytes: 100 MB logical/snapshot, excluding formulas/dependencies/history. A 1,000-cell edit should append a delta and rewrite affected chunks, not a 100 MB full file. At an assumed 1,000 edits/s×200 bytes, log growth is 17.28 GB/day for one very hot sheet; enforce limits and retention/cost policy while preserving the promised history. Multi-zone replicas, sequencer epochs and conditional writes prevent split-brain owners. Test two simultaneous same-cell writes, row insertion against formula references, duplicate op, cycle creation, stale recalculation and crash during snapshot publication. Monitor append lag, formula fanout/cost, snapshot age and replay time; no text-collaboration algorithm is necessary to define this centralized cell-operation contract.

title: Design a Real-Time Instant Messaging Application with Media Support

steps: A modest service with explicit media state
solution.example: At the example 1,000 users and 500 messages/s, use a few WebSocket/API instances, a replicated SQL message store, a small durable event broker and object storage/CDN; the stated message rate matters more than user count alone. Assume 300 bytes/text message for illustration: 150 KB/s, 12.96 GB/day logical text if sustained, before replicas/indexes. Media bytes may dominate and need separate size/rate limits.
solution.trap: Unverified attachments cannot be messaged as ready, and private blob delivery uses current conversation access; small supplied scale does not need invented global architecture.
solution.teaching_notes_markdown:
### A modest service with explicit media state

At the example 1,000 users and 500 messages/s, use a few WebSocket/API instances, a replicated SQL message store, a small durable event broker and object storage/CDN; the stated message rate matters more than user count alone. Assume 300 bytes/text message for illustration: 150 KB/s, 12.96 GB/day logical text if sustained, before replicas/indexes. Media bytes may dominate and need separate size/rate limits.

User/Session stores authenticated identity; Conversation/Membership owns 1:1/group access; Message(conversation,seq,sender,client_id,kind,body_or_attachment,time) and DeviceCursor support ordered history/reconnect. Attachment(id,owner,object_ref,size,digest,mime,state) is UPLOADING→SCANNING→READY/REJECTED. `POST /attachments` returns resumable signed upload URLs; finalize verifies content and scans before a message can reference READY media. Files are never streamed through every chat database write, and private download URLs are scoped/short-lived with current membership checks.

### Send and receive paths

`POST /conversations/{id}/messages` or an authenticated socket command includes a client ID; a transaction validates current membership, allocates conversation seq, writes message/dedup/outbox and then ACKs. Per-conversation order is consistent on all devices; unique (sender,client_id) prevents retries duplicating the message. The diagram's outbox→broker→gateway fanout reaches all online member devices. Presence directory entries expire; durable cursors/history deliver missed messages when a gateway dies or a user reconnects. Clients deduplicate by conversation/seq and page backwards with before_seq.

Group membership changes have versions and ordered authorization boundaries; removal prevents future sends/downloads and queued delivery. Clarify whether prejoin history is visible; assume membership-scoped history. Delivery means device ACK; read is a later monotonic cursor, neither equivalent to a successful socket write. Push notifications are wakeups, not the only retained message copy.

### Failures and evolution

A failed media upload remains private and can resume missing parts; unused uploads expire through a safe sweeper. A message commit followed by broker failure is repaired by outbox replay. A lost ACK returns the same message on resend; a storage outage produces pending/retry rather than false save. Slow clients have bounded queues and reconnect/replay, preventing one file/message recipient exhausting memory. File links are validated and downloads limited/scanned; enforce rate limits, encryption, tenant access and audit without storing credentials in message logs.

For an assumed 500 ms online latency target, reserve 100 ms durable write, 100 ms broker/gateway and 300 ms network/device headroom; test actual p99 and fanout distribution. Partition later by conversation and time bucket, with stateless gateways and shared connection directory; don't add global multi-region consensus solely because the product resembles a large messenger. Monitor ACK/delivery delay, attachment processing, cursor lag and access errors. Test corrupt uploads, duplicate finalize/message, group removal during download, offline reconnect and gateway failover.

title: Design a Slack-like Chat System with Deletion Semantics
question:
Design a Slack-like chat system supporting messages within conversations and channels. Users can send and receive messages, delete specific messages, and delete whole conversations.

The main focus is correct deletion semantics:

Deleting a conversation must make it disappear for everyone — both online and offline users.
The system must work for users currently online and users who are offline (possibly for a long time).

Clarify early: latency needs (real-time vs. eventual consistency → WebSockets vs. polling), scale (users, messages/sec), whether deletion is a hard delete or keeps an audit log, how long deletion data is retained for offline users, and delivery guarantees.

steps: Define global deletion and the offline limit
solution.example: Scale is unspecified. Assume one million messages/day and 100 members/conversation: deletion may invalidate 100 membership views but a single durable conversation tombstone can gate all reads immediately. Large deletions enqueue partitioned cleanup, with per-user change streams and bounded gateway buffers. On notification outage reads still deny from authoritative state; when authority is unavailable do not serve uncertain cached deleted/private data as current. Monitor delete-to-client propagation, stale-epoch rejections, purge backlog and resync frequency. Test send/delete races, offline for longer than tombstone TTL, replayed create, cached history/search/media and backup restoration. Availability is deliberately constrained where it would defeat the global deletion contract.
solution.trap: Arbitrarily offline clients cannot be instantly erased; global server tombstone/epoch and mandatory old-cursor resync prevent resurrection while physical purge/audit policy is explicit.
solution.teaching_notes_markdown:
### Define global deletion and the offline limit

Clarify latency, group/channel size, retention/audit and hard versus logical deletion. Assume a global conversation delete becomes unavailable on server reads immediately after authoritative commit, online clients receive a deletion event within a proposed second, and reconnecting clients purge it before ordinary sync. No server can erase bytes from a permanently offline/untrusted device or someone's screenshot; if immediate offline disappearance is required, restrict cache lifetime/require online decryption authorization and state that even this cannot revoke already captured plaintext.

Store Conversation(id,state,epoch,deleted_at,delete_seq), Membership, Message(conversation,seq,id,body,deleted_at,version), UserConversation(user,conversation,visibility), and ChangeLog(user_or_conversation,seq,type,target,epoch). Message delete creates a tombstone/redaction; whole-conversation delete atomically sets DELETED/increments epoch and emits durable deletion events. All sends/reads/search/export/media checks reject that conversation epoch; physically deleting every message synchronously is unnecessary and would be expensive. Old retries/broker messages cannot recreate it; IDs are never reused.

### Online and reconnect protocol

The diagram's deletion transaction writes the authoritative state plus outbox. Pub/sub routes tombstones to every subscribed gateway; online clients remove the conversation and local search/cache immediately upon applying delete_seq. An ACK cursor records change progress. At reconnect, authenticate, sync authoritative membership/conversation manifests and tombstones **before** replaying old messages; a stale cached chat cannot render first and disappear later as an afterthought. If a client's cursor is older than retained change history, require full resync and clear local conversation state absent from the server manifest.

Arbitrarily long offline clients make finite tombstone-only retention insufficient. Keep a compact durable deleted-ID/epoch record indefinitely, or force full authoritative resync beyond a retention cutoff; message-body retention may be much shorter. Deleting offline users' materialized inbox copies is derived cleanup, not the source of truth. Search indexes, notifications, attachments and CDN authorization receive delete events and also enforce current conversation access, preventing delayed indexes from leaking content.

### Races, storage and scale

Serialize send/delete through the conversation authority. If send commits first, deletion hides it; if delete commits first, send fails. Late old-epoch delivery/ACK cannot reopen state. Audit requirements may retain encrypted restricted records separate from user-visible data; declare whether actual hard erasure/purge has a completion SLA and how backups age out. Do not promise both indefinite full audit plaintext and immediate physical erasure without a policy decision.

Scale is unspecified. Assume one million messages/day and 100 members/conversation: deletion may invalidate 100 membership views but a single durable conversation tombstone can gate all reads immediately. Large deletions enqueue partitioned cleanup, with per-user change streams and bounded gateway buffers. On notification outage reads still deny from authoritative state; when authority is unavailable do not serve uncertain cached deleted/private data as current. Monitor delete-to-client propagation, stale-epoch rejections, purge backlog and resync frequency. Test send/delete races, offline for longer than tombstone TTL, replayed create, cached history/search/media and backup restoration. Availability is deliberately constrained where it would defeat the global deletion contract.

<!-- architecture:W432:start -->
![W432 flow: Delete message/conversation → Atomic tombstone + epoch → Durable deletion outbox → Current read/access gate → Online invalidation fanout → Offline manifest resync.](../diagrams/W432_exact_review_426_450.svg)

Read the numbered path as Delete message/conversation → Atomic tombstone + epoch → Durable deletion outbox → Current read/access gate → Online invalidation fanout → Offline manifest resync. title: Group Chat / Messaging System Design
question:
Design a group-chat / messaging product that supports 1:1 and group conversations, real-time delivery, offline message retention, and read receipts. Asked at both the phone-screen-SD slot and onsite system-design slot; the deep-dive direction shifts toward top-N hottest groups, fan-out trade-offs, and message storage schema.

Requirements
Functional
Send/receive text in 1:1 and group conversations (group size up to ~100 members).
Real-time delivery for online recipients, durable delivery for offline recipients.
Persist messages for ~30 days (clarify retention).
Read receipts and online / last-seen presence.
Optional: media attachments via blob storage.
Non-functional
Hundreds of millions of active users, tens of thousands of messages/sec at peak.
Sub-second end-to-end latency for online recipients.
High availability; eventual consistency acceptable for read receipts and presence.
Scoped out (confirm)
Voice/video calls, payments, business-account features, E2E encryption (some interviewers probe E2EE).

solution.example: At tens of thousands of sends/s, choose an illustrative 50,000/s and mean twenty recipients: one million recipient deliveries/s, multiplied by active devices. At assumed 300 bytes/message, raw history is 15 MB/s, 1.296 TB/day and 38.88 TB/30 days before replicas/indexes. A hottest group can saturate its sequencer/fanout despite modest total load; dedicate capacity, batch gateways, rate-limit senders and use pull/replay when socket queues overflow. Push reduces online latency; pulling shared history reduces write amplification and supplies offline recovery.
solution.trap: Thirty-day retention implies reconnect gaps after expiry; group receipts use per-user sequence cursors and top-N local merge has exactness caveats.
solution.teaching_notes_markdown:
### Ordered history and bounded groups

Assume text/groups≤100, thirty-day message retention, subsecond online delivery; exclude voice/video/payments/business features/E2EE, with media optional. Store Conversation(id,epoch,next_seq), Membership(conversation,user,role,joined_seq,left_seq), Message(conversation,seq,sender,client_id,body,time), DeviceCursor and Receipt(user,conversation,last_read_seq). Unique sender/client ID deduplicates send retries, and one conversation owner commits sequence+message+outbox before ACK. Partition by conversation plus sequence/time bucket; TTL/archive policy removes bodies after thirty days while cursors/tombstones retain enough context for explicit history-gap responses.

The diagram's durable stream fans once to each gateway with online group members, which sends to all their devices. Offline users read shared history from cursor, avoiding body copies per recipient. `POST /messages`, `GET /history?before_seq=`, and monotonic delivered/read updates make transport and receipt semantics explicit. For group receipts, per-user read_seq suffices; compute “seen by” as read_seq≥message_seq instead of storing 100 rows/message unnecessarily. Presence/last-seen comes from permissioned heartbeat+TTL and can lag without changing membership.

### Top-N hot groups and fanout

Count activity in an explicit rolling window, e.g. accepted messages or active participants, with idempotent event updates. Shard counters by group/time/hash and sum for ranking; merging only local top-N lists can miss a globally heavy distributed key unless candidate bounds or a validated heavy-hitter approximation are used. For a small group-cardinality set, merge exact counts and maintain a bounded global heap. Define the metric before claiming “hottest.”

At tens of thousands of sends/s, choose an illustrative 50,000/s and mean twenty recipients: one million recipient deliveries/s, multiplied by active devices. At assumed 300 bytes/message, raw history is 15 MB/s, 1.296 TB/day and 38.88 TB/30 days before replicas/indexes. A hottest group can saturate its sequencer/fanout despite modest total load; dedicate capacity, batch gateways, rate-limit senders and use pull/replay when socket queues overflow. Push reduces online latency; pulling shared history reduces write amplification and supplies offline recovery.

### Failure and correctness

A lost ACK returns the existing seq; duplicate fanout is suppressed by clients. A gateway crash rebuilds connections/cursors from durable history; pub/sub loss prompts replay. Membership/ban/deletion is rechecked at send/read and invalidates queued delivery. An offline user returning after thirty days gets a documented retention gap, not a fictional complete backlog. Optional attachments use private object storage with the same access/retention gates.

Use multi-zone replicated conversation storage and fenced owner failover; cross-region order would add WAN coordination and should be scoped separately. Monitor commit-to-device p99, outbox age, hot-group queue pressure, retention gaps and receipt freshness. Test two simultaneous sends, group removal during fanout, stale read receipts, day-thirty expiry and top-N skew. Delivery/read/presence can converge eventually where allowed; acknowledged message durability and conversation order have a stronger boundary.

![W433 flow: Up-to-100-member group → Conversation owner / sequence → Thirty-day durable history → Gateway-local fanout → Read receipt / presence TTL → Replay + hot-group metrics.](../diagrams/W433_exact_review_426_450.svg)

title: Real-Time Collaborative Code Editor
question:
Design a CoderPad-like session: one admin can edit, all viewers see real-time updates, new joiners catch up immediately, optional code execution. The interviewer explicitly forbids referring to operational-transform algorithms — derive the propagation model from scratch.

Requirements

Functional:

Create a session; one user is admin (editor), others are viewers.
All viewers see admin edits in real time.
New users joining mid-session see the current state immediately.
Optional code execution (do not over-design — the interviewer signals this is not the focus).

Non-functional:

Latency for viewer-side update: tens of ms.
Session-level scale (10s of concurrent viewers); deployment-level scale (10k concurrent sessions).
Tolerate brief network blips on the viewer side.
Notes
The expected propagation model:
Admin client emits delta events (insert/delete with (position, length, payload)).
Server stages deltas in an append-only per-session log and broadcasts to subscribed viewers over WebSocket.
Viewers apply deltas locally.
New joiners receive a snapshot of the current document plus a tail of pending deltas after the snapshot version.
Because only one editor exists, the OT / CRDT complexity collapses — the canonical insight to articulate aloud. With multiple editors, OT or CRDT would be required.
For code execution, sandbox each session's runtime (Firecracker / lightweight container); rate-limit per session.

steps: Derive propagation from the single editor
Snapshot plus log tail without gaps
solution.example: Example: text `cat` at v7 receives insert(position=3,text="s") at v8. A viewer at v7 applies once to get `cats`; a replay of v8 is ignored. A new viewer receiving snapshot v7 and a simultaneously broadcast v8 buffers/deduplicates by version and reaches the same text. No viewer is allowed to manufacture its own order from socket arrival time.
solution.trap: Only one editor means simple epoch/base-version delta serialization, snapshot+tail and replay; no OT/CRDT propagation machinery is invoked.
solution.teaching_notes_markdown:
### Derive propagation from the single editor

Only one authorized admin edits; viewers never submit mutations. Therefore the server can serialize a simple append-only delta stream without any concurrent-edit transformation algorithm. Session(id,admin_id,editor_epoch,head_version,snapshot_ref) and Delta(session,version,op_id,epoch,base_version,position,delete_length,insert_text) suffice. Define positions in a shared unit (assume Unicode code points) and validate ranges. A replacement is delete_length characters at position followed by insertion. Viewer presence is separate expiring state.

`POST /sessions` creates the session; the admin's authenticated WebSocket sends a unique op_id, current epoch and base_version. A per-session owner validates admin/epoch and base_version=head, applies the delta, appends it durably with version=head+1, then ACKs/broadcasts. Duplicate op_id returns the same version; a wrong base version gets the authoritative head/replay request. After an ACK loss the admin retries the same op, not another unversioned insertion. A reconnect/new admin connection increments an exclusive editor lease epoch so an old socket cannot remain a second writer.

### Snapshot plus log tail without gaps

The diagram is admin→versioned session log/state→socket fanout→viewers. On join, establish a stream/replay boundary, send a snapshot containing exact document text at version v, then deltas v+1..head, then live events. A viewer applies only its expected next version; duplicate old versions are ignored and a gap triggers `after_version` replay. If the log tail was compacted, send a newer snapshot. Build snapshots atomically at a committed version; serializing text while edits interleave without a version boundary can corrupt catch-up.

Example: text `cat` at v7 receives insert(position=3,text="s") at v8. A viewer at v7 applies once to get `cats`; a replay of v8 is ignored. A new viewer receiving snapshot v7 and a simultaneously broadcast v8 buffers/deduplicates by version and reaches the same text. No viewer is allowed to manufacture its own order from socket arrival time.

### Capacity and failures

With 10,000 sessions, assume twenty viewers/session: 200,000 viewer sockets. At an assumed ten edits/s/session and 100 bytes/delta, input is ten MB/s and fanout about 200 MB/s before framing/TLS. Regional gateways and per-session owner hashing keep a tens-of-ms local update target plausible; allocate, for example, 5 ms validation/append batching, 5 ms fanout and 20 ms network headroom, then benchmark durability latency. Don't store a full document copy on every keystroke; snapshots plus bounded deltas control cost.

A failed session owner recovers from committed snapshot/log under a new epoch; unacknowledged admin edits may be retried. Slow/offline viewers get bounded queues and replay/resnapshot rather than unlimited buffering. Access revocation closes subscriptions and replay endpoints enforce authorization. Optional execution captures document version and language, then runs in an isolated per-session sandbox with CPU/memory/time/network quotas; outputs are tagged with that version so later edits do not misattribute results. Execution is not needed to solve propagation. Test join during edit, duplicate/missing deltas, editor reconnect fencing and crash during snapshot. Introducing multiple independent writers changes the problem and requires a newly defined conflict protocol; it is not part of this single-admin design.

![W434 flow: Exclusive admin delta → Epoch / base-version check → Append-only session log → Versioned snapshot + tail → WebSocket viewer fanout → Gap replay / resnapshot.](../diagrams/W434_exact_review_426_450.svg)
