title: Real-Time Comment Threads (FigJam / Figma)
question:
Real-Time Comment Threads (FigJam / Figma)

Design the feature where a user clicks anywhere on a Figma/FigJam canvas to start a comment thread, and comments update in real time for everyone viewing the file. Often framed as 'design the data model first, then the server architecture' — explicitly not 'design Google Docs'.

Requirements

Design in-canvas commenting:

A user can click any point on the page to anchor a new comment thread; others can reply, forming threads.
Comments (new threads and replies) propagate to all current viewers of the file in real time.
Interviewers often structure it as: (1) design the data model, then (2) design the server architecture — so deliver a concrete schema before the distributed picture.
Notes
This is not "design Google Docs." Several candidates over-prepared a full collaborative-document/OT design and found it useless — the scope is comment threads anchored to canvas coordinates, nothing more. Go try the feature in FigJam before the interview.
Real scale is modest, so resist over-engineering. Nail the data model (thread anchored to a position, ordered replies, resolved state, author/timestamps) and a sane real-time path (WebSocket/SSE fan-out to file subscribers) before reaching for heavy distributed machinery.
Interviewers can interrupt and pivot the discussion anywhere mid-flow; keep your structure explicit so you can resume after a tangent.

steps: Schema first: comments anchored to a canvas
solution.example: No fixed scale is given. Assume 1,000 active files×twenty viewers×two comment events/minute: about 33 writes/s and 667 deliveries/s, easily modest relative to large document editing. Partition later by file/thread and retain reply indexes; do not introduce heavy text-merging machinery. On socket/broker outage saved comments remain readable and replay after reconnect; outbox retry prevents lost notifications. Slow viewers get bounded buffers and resync. Monitor commit-to-viewer lag, missed sequence recovery, anchor orphaning and authorization failures. Test object move/delete, pan/zoom transforms, duplicate reply, resolve race, reconnect between snapshot and subscription and file permission change. The product is anchored threads, so full document editing/formula/OT design would miss its core deliverable.
solution.trap: Thread anchors use page/world or object-local coordinates, not screen pixels; schema precedes file-scoped live comment architecture.
solution.teaching_notes_markdown:
### Schema first: comments anchored to a canvas

```text
Thread(id PK, file_id, page_id, anchor_kind, x, y,
       object_id nullable, local_x nullable, local_y nullable,
       resolved, created_by, created_at, updated_at, version)
Comment(id PK, thread_id FK, author_id, body, created_at, edited_at,
        deleted_at nullable, version, client_op_id UNIQUE per author)
FileChange(file_id, seq, event_id UNIQUE, thread_id, comment_id,
           kind, payload_ref, PRIMARY KEY(file_id,seq))
Outbox(event_id PK, file_id, seq, delivery_state)
```

Use page/world coordinates in documented units for a free-space anchor, independent of viewport pan/zoom. If anchored to an object, store stable object ID plus local coordinates and resolve through the object's current transform; if the object is deleted, retain an orphaned-position indicator or last world position rather than attach the thread to an unrelated replacement. Replies order by server created sequence/id within a thread; resolution is thread state, not a comment-body convention. Existing file ACLs authorize viewing/commenting/resolving, with edit/delete rights explicit.

### API and realtime architecture

`POST /files/{id}/threads` supplies page/anchor/comment/client key; `POST /threads/{id}/comments`, `PATCH /comments/{id}` and `POST /threads/{id}:resolve` use idempotency/version preconditions. `GET /files/{id}/threads?page_id=` pages thread summaries; `/threads/{id}/comments?before=` loads replies. A transaction writes the thread/comment/state change, file change sequence and outbox, then ACKs. This modest feature can use one replicated SQL database and a few stateless API/socket servers before sharding is needed.

The diagram's SQL change/outbox→file-scoped pub/sub→WebSocket/SSE gateways broadcasts to authorized current viewers. A joining viewer loads a snapshot at file-comment version v then replays changes after v before live subscription; sequence gaps reconnect through the durable change log. Callbacks/broadcast completion do not define whether the comment saved. Duplicate event IDs are ignored, and a stale edit version conflicts instead of silently overwriting newer text. File access revocation closes subscriptions and blocks history fetch; presence is optional.

### Examples, scale and failure handling

A user clicks at world (100,200) while zoomed 200%; storing screen (200,400) would move the anchor for other viewers, so convert before writing. Two users reply concurrently: server sequences both, and all clients converge without a collaborative-document algorithm. Two users toggle resolved state from version 4: one conditional update wins and the other reloads/version-conflicts according to the API contract.

No fixed scale is given. Assume 1,000 active files×twenty viewers×two comment events/minute: about 33 writes/s and 667 deliveries/s, easily modest relative to large document editing. Partition later by file/thread and retain reply indexes; do not introduce heavy text-merging machinery. On socket/broker outage saved comments remain readable and replay after reconnect; outbox retry prevents lost notifications. Slow viewers get bounded buffers and resync. Monitor commit-to-viewer lag, missed sequence recovery, anchor orphaning and authorization failures. Test object move/delete, pan/zoom transforms, duplicate reply, resolve race, reconnect between snapshot and subscription and file permission change. The product is anchored threads, so full document editing/formula/OT design would miss its core deliverable.

![W435 flow: Thread anchor + replies → File ACL / comment schema → Atomic file-change sequence → Outbox / file-scoped topic → Viewer socket subscribers → Snapshot + reconnect replay.](../diagrams/W435_exact_review_426_450.svg)

title: Subreddit Live Chat System
question:
Design Reddit's subreddit live-chat product (real-time chat anchored to a subreddit; rooms from tens to millions during live events). The Super Bowl scenario (~5M concurrent users in one subreddit chat) is the canonical scale follow-up.

Requirements
Functional: send/receive in real time, recent history on open, presence / active-user count, moderation (delete/mute/ban), reconnect + backlog.
Scale: typical thousands per room; pivots to 5M concurrent, sub-second fan-out latency.
Decisions: transport (WebSocket vs SSE vs long-poll), fan-out (push vs pull at peak), chat-server topology (single shard-per-room vs distributed gateway + pub/sub), message ordering (logical sequence per room), storage, moderation latency.

Key answers: per-room pub/sub topic, room-scoped sharding across gateway nodes at 5M, logical per-room sequence for ordering, heartbeat+TTL presence, backpressure via drop-and-resync (after_seq replay).

steps: Separate one room's order from millions of sockets
solution.example: Under a proposed subsecond local fanout budget, measure append, broker/relay, gateway and device lag separately. A gateway crash reconnects clients and replays from durable cursor; a broker outage retains committed messages and shows lag. Test celebrity/live-event ramps, sequencer failover, delayed delete, million-client slow queues and replay beyond retention. Monitor accepted send rate, room-seq lag, gateway egress, mute/delete delay, disconnect/resync and active-count uncertainty. These capacity limits determine the design before choosing transport acronyms.
solution.trap: 5M viewers receiving1000 msgs/s×200B requires1TB/s egress; pubsub alone does not remove fanout/UX limits. Slow-mode and gap/replay are explicit.
solution.teaching_notes_markdown:
### Separate one room's order from millions of sockets

Store Room(id,subreddit,next_seq,epoch,policy), Message(room,seq,sender,client_id,body,time,moderation_version), Membership/Role/Ban and DeviceCursor. A room ordering owner validates rate limits/mutes/bans, deduplicates client IDs and durably appends sequence+message+outbox before ACK. `GET /rooms/{id}/history?before|after_seq=` serves recent/reconnect history; WebSocket handles bidirectional sends/events (SSE plus HTTP send is an alternative for simpler receive-only clients). A room-scoped pub/sub topic carries committed events to many gateways, not one server with five million sockets.

### The five-million-viewer calculation

At an assumed 20,000 sockets/gateway, five million viewers need at least 250 gateways, plus headroom and regional placement. If the room accepts an assumed 1,000 messages/s of 200 encoded bytes and every viewer receives every message, delivery is **one billion bytes/s per 5,000 viewers**, or **1 TB/s total** (8 Tbit/s), before protocol overhead. More directly 5M×1,000×200=10^12 bytes/s. Each viewer would also receive 1,000 messages/s, a poor human interface. A single pub/sub topic does not eliminate this fanout/UX limit.

Define a moderated/slow-mode accepted stream, e.g. an assumed ten messages/s, which still costs 10 GB/s total at 200 bytes. Gateways receive one upstream copy and locally fan out; hierarchical regional relays, batch frames and dedicated capacity help. If the product still insists on all raw messages at arbitrary send rate with subsecond fanout, reject that as an unbounded requirement rather than silently drop data. A highlighted/sampled view is a separately labeled product mode, not “complete chat.”

### Backpressure, moderation and recovery

The diagram's logical room sequencer remains one ordering authority while delivery partitions by gateway audience. Gateways process seq order and buffer bounded gaps; clients ignore duplicates and request after_seq replay on a gap. Slow clients get drop-and-resync with an explicit gap marker, not unlimited RAM growth; catch-up can be paged/pulled even while new live frames arrive. Recent history is stored independently of sockets, with a stated retention/gap policy. Quorum/fenced failover protects the sequence from two room owners; multi-region fanout adds network latency and doesn't create independent conflicting room sequences.

Moderation actions are ordered tombstone/ban events with increasing versions. Send validation checks current bans, and delete events propagate through priority/control lanes so moderation is not trapped behind a huge message backlog. History/current reads suppress deleted messages; replayed old content cannot reverse moderation. Presence is approximate connection/session heartbeats with TTL, deduplicated across devices as defined; do not broadcast five million individual joins/leaves to everyone.

Under a proposed subsecond local fanout budget, measure append, broker/relay, gateway and device lag separately. A gateway crash reconnects clients and replays from durable cursor; a broker outage retains committed messages and shows lag. Test celebrity/live-event ramps, sequencer failover, delayed delete, million-client slow queues and replay beyond retention. Monitor accepted send rate, room-seq lag, gateway egress, mute/delete delay, disconnect/resync and active-count uncertainty. These capacity limits determine the design before choosing transport acronyms.

title: Credit Card Service with Points Earning and Redemption System
question:
Design a credit card service that offers points as the customer spends on the card. The customer can redeem their points at any time, with 1 point equating to USD 0.01 in value. Please provide your design.

Example

Input

customer1
100

steps: Define earning and redemption before accounting
solution.example: The prompt fixes redemption value at one point=$0.01, but gives no earning rate, eligible spend/refund policy, expiry or redemption destination. Those inputs are necessary for numeric rewards on the stray `customer1 / 100` example. For illustration assume one point per settled dollar of eligible purchases, transaction-level floor rounding, no expiry, and redemption as statement credit. A $100 settled purchase then earns 100 points worth $1, not $100. This is a chosen demonstration rule, not supplied economics.
solution.trap: One point equals one cent of redemption but does not define earning rate; settlement/refund/redeem are separate idempotent postings.
solution.teaching_notes_markdown:
### Define earning and redemption before accounting

The prompt fixes redemption value at one point=USD 0.01, but gives no earning rate, eligible spend/refund policy, expiry or redemption destination. Those inputs are necessary for numeric rewards on the stray `customer1 / 100` example. For illustration assume one point per settled dollar of eligible purchases, transaction-level floor rounding, no expiry, and redemption as statement credit. A USD 100 settled purchase then earns 100 points worth USD 1, not USD 100. This is a chosen demonstration rule, not supplied economics.

Store CardAccount/customer identity and card transaction states separately from RewardAccount and immutable PointsEntry(id,customer,source_event,rule_version,delta,kind,posted_at). A unique (source_event,entry_kind,rule_version) prevents duplicate earning/reversal. Record monetary entries in integer cents and rewards in integer points; never mix the two units. RewardBalance(customer,available,reserved,version) is a transactional projection of the points ledger, reconciled regularly. Earning happens on settlement, not each authorization/retry; a refund posts a linked compensating points reversal with an explicit policy for already-spent rewards/negative reward balance.

### API and atomic redemption

`GET /rewards` returns available/pending/reserved points and value; `POST /redemptions` takes customer, integer points, destination and idempotency key bound to body. Authenticate ownership, validate positive points, floor/minimum rules and balance, then lock the reward account and atomically reserve/debit points, create Redemption(id,key,state,cents=points,ledger_refs) and an outbox. Two concurrent 80-point redemptions against 100 cannot both commit. A matching retry returns the original result; changing the amount under the same key conflicts.

The diagram's spend-settlement events feed versioned earning postings, while redemption creates a durable state machine to a statement-credit/payment service. If statement credit shares the same database/ledger boundary, points and money postings can commit together. If external, use RESERVED→PROCESSING→SUCCEEDED or FAILED/UNKNOWN and a stable downstream operation ID. Timeout remains uncertain: query/retry that identity, not refund points then issue a second credit. Confirmed permanent failure releases the reservation through compensating entries once. No external transfer is made for zero redemption.

### Reconciliation and trade-offs

For a fictional starting 100 points, redeeming 80 creates an 80-cent credit and leaves 20; a duplicate request does not leave −60 or issue another credit. If the source purchase later refunds, append the policy-defined points reversal and expose any negative/recovery obligation rather than rewriting the original entry. Keep rule versions/effective dates so old transactions remain explainable.

Scale is absent. Assume ten million settled purchases/day: about 116 earning events/s average; store an assumed 100-byte points entry yields 1 GB/day logical before indexes/replicas. Shard by customer, use transactional outbox/inbox dedup, reserve retry capacity and reconcile points sum, balance projection and linked monetary credits daily. Monitor earn/redeem lag, negative balances, duplicate rejections, uncertain credits and drift. Protect card data through token references and audited access. Test refund-after-redemption, parallel redeem, duplicate settlement, rule changes and a lost credit ACK. The fixed point value alone cannot determine earning rules, solvency or all product policies; make those decisions explicit.

title: Credit Card System Design (OOD)
question:
Lightweight OOD design of a credit card system — card issuance, swipe/authorize transactions, repayment, statement generation, and minimal business rules.

Entities: Card, Account, Transaction, Statement (with explicit class definitions).

Operations: issueCard(account), authorize(card, amount), settle(transaction), repay(card, amount), generateStatement(card, period).

Business rules: credit-limit enforcement, pending vs settled balances, interest accrual on unpaid balance. Be explicit about pre-/post-conditions for each operation.

steps: Objects, units and chosen business policy
solution.example: The in-memory service uses an RLock to serialize account mutations and an operation-result map for retries; it is a working OOD exercise, not restart-durable banking storage. Production replaces dictionaries/locks with transactional durable tables, append-only balanced postings, expiry of holds, reconciliation, authenticated authorization and a complete contractual interest engine. Tests cover shared-limit races, duplicate settlement/repayment, void, interest/day dedup and immutable statements/backdating. This makes the requested classes and operation boundaries concrete without inventing financial terms.
solution.trap: Pending authorization holds and settled debt differ; shared-card limit serialization, once-daily interest and closed-period statement integrity are implemented/tested.
solution.teaching_notes_markdown:
### Objects, units and chosen business policy

`Account` owns credit_limit, settled debt and pending authorization holds in integer cents; multiple `Card`s may reference it, sharing the limit. `Transaction` records purchase/repayment/interest state and posting date. `Statement` is an immutable [start,end) snapshot of posted activity and closing debt. No card numbers/CVV are needed for this OOD model. Real issuance/token vault/network integrations are outside the toy class.

The prompt does not specify APR/grace/minimum-payment/rounding rules. The implementation explicitly assumes immediate daily simple accrual on nonnegative settled unpaid debt, a supplied integer parts-per-million daily rate, half-up cent rounding, no grace period and no overpayments. This is demonstration policy, not a claim about any real credit product. New accounts start at zero or need an explicit opening ledger posting; do not initialize an unexplained nonzero balance and expect statements to reconcile.

```python
"""Educational OOD model, integer cents; simplified daily interest and statement policy."""

from __future__ import annotations
from dataclasses import dataclass
from datetime import date
from threading import RLock
import uuid


@dataclass
class Card:
    id: str
    account_id: str
    active: bool = True


@dataclass
class Account:
    id: str
    credit_limit: int
    settled: int = 0
    pending: int = 0


@dataclass
class Transaction:
    id: str
    account_id: str
    card_id: str
    amount: int
    state: str
    posted_on: date | None = None
    kind: str = "PURCHASE"


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Statement:
    id: str
    account_id: str
    start: date
    end: date
    transaction_ids: tuple
    net_activity: int
    closing_balance: int


class CreditCardService:
    def __init__(self):
        self.accounts = {}
        self.cards = {}
        self.transactions = {}
        self.statements = {}
        self.keys = {}
        self.lock = RLock()

    def _once(self, key, signature, action):
        if key in self.keys:
            old, result = self.keys[key]
            if old != signature:
                raise ValueError("idempotency key reused with different parameters")
            return result
        result = action()
        self.keys[key] = (signature, result)
        return result

    @staticmethod
    def _amount(value):
        if type(value) is not int or value <= 0:
            raise ValueError("positive integer cents required")

    def issueCard(self, account):
        with self.lock:
            if account.credit_limit < 0:
                raise ValueError("invalid credit limit")
            if account.id in self.accounts and self.accounts[account.id] is not account:
                raise ValueError("conflicting account")
            self.accounts[account.id] = account
            card = Card(uuid.uuid4().hex, account.id)
            self.cards[card.id] = card
            return card

    def authorize(self, card, amount, key):
        self._amount(amount)
        with self.lock:

            def apply():
                if self.cards.get(card.id) is not card or not card.active:
                    raise ValueError("inactive or unknown card")
                account = self.accounts[card.account_id]
                if account.settled + account.pending + amount > account.credit_limit:
                    raise ValueError("credit limit exceeded")
                tx = Transaction(
                    uuid.uuid4().hex, account.id, card.id, amount, "PENDING"
                )
                self.transactions[tx.id] = tx
                account.pending += amount
                return tx

            return self._once(("authorize", key), (card.id, amount), apply)

    def _posting_allowed(self, account_id, day):
        if any(
            s.account_id == account_id and day < s.end for s in self.statements.values()
        ):
            raise ValueError("posting date belongs to a closed statement period")

    def settle(self, transaction, today):
        with self.lock:
            tx = self.transactions[transaction.id]
            if tx.state == "SETTLED":
                return tx
            if tx.state != "PENDING":
                raise ValueError("not pending")
            self._posting_allowed(tx.account_id, today)
            account = self.accounts[tx.account_id]
            account.pending -= tx.amount
            account.settled += tx.amount
            tx.state = "SETTLED"
            tx.posted_on = today
            return tx

    def void(self, transaction):
        with self.lock:
            tx = self.transactions[transaction.id]
            if tx.state == "VOID":
                return
            if tx.state != "PENDING":
                raise ValueError("only pending authorization may be voided")
            self.accounts[tx.account_id].pending -= tx.amount
            tx.state = "VOID"

    def repay(self, card, amount, key, today):
        self._amount(amount)
        with self.lock:

            def apply():
                if self.cards.get(card.id) is not card:
                    raise ValueError("unknown card")
                self._posting_allowed(card.account_id, today)
                account = self.accounts[card.account_id]
                if amount > account.settled:
                    raise ValueError("overpayment not supported in this demo")
                account.settled -= amount
                tx = Transaction(
                    uuid.uuid4().hex,
                    account.id,
                    card.id,
                    -amount,
                    "SETTLED",
                    today,
                    "REPAYMENT",
                )
                self.transactions[tx.id] = tx
                return tx

            return self._once(
                ("repay", key), (card.id, amount, today.isoformat()), apply
            )

    def accrue_interest(self, account_id, day, daily_rate_ppm):
        # Assumption: all unpaid settled principal immediately accrues, no grace; half-up cents.
        if type(daily_rate_ppm) is not int or daily_rate_ppm < 0:
            raise ValueError("invalid rate")
        with self.lock:

            def apply():
                self._posting_allowed(account_id, day)
                account = self.accounts[account_id]
                interest = (
                    max(0, account.settled) * daily_rate_ppm + 500000
                ) // 1000000
                account.settled += interest
                tx = Transaction(
                    uuid.uuid4().hex,
                    account_id,
                    "",
                    interest,
                    "SETTLED",
                    day,
                    "INTEREST",
                )
                self.transactions[tx.id] = tx
                return tx

            return self._once(("interest", account_id, day), (daily_rate_ppm,), apply)

    def generateStatement(self, card, period):
        start, end = period
        if not start < end:
            raise ValueError("period must be nonempty [start,end)")
        with self.lock:
            if self.cards.get(card.id) is not card:
                raise ValueError("unknown card")
            key = (card.account_id, start, end)
            if key in self.statements:
                return self.statements[key]
            txs = [
                t
                for t in self.transactions.values()
                if t.account_id == card.account_id
                and t.state == "SETTLED"
                and start <= t.posted_on < end
            ]
            closing = sum(
                t.amount
                for t in self.transactions.values()
                if t.account_id == card.account_id
                and t.state == "SETTLED"
                and t.posted_on < end
            )
            result = Statement(
                uuid.uuid4().hex,
                card.account_id,
                start,
                end,
                tuple(t.id for t in txs),
                sum(t.amount for t in txs),
                closing,
            )
            self.statements[key] = result
            return result
```

### Operation preconditions and postconditions

* `issueCard(account)` requires a valid nonnegative credit limit and a known/consistent account identity; returns an active card sharing that account's capacity.
* `authorize(card,amount,key)` requires a known active card and positive integer amount; atomically checks settled+pending+amount≤limit, reserves the hold and returns PENDING. Same key/parameters returns the original transaction; differing parameters conflict. It never adds settled debt yet.
* `settle(transaction,date)` requires its PENDING purchase and an open posting period; it moves amount from pending to settled once. Duplicate settlement returns the same record. `void` releases only a pending hold; settled refunds require separate compensating postings in a fuller model.
* `repay(card,amount,key,date)` requires a known card/account, positive cents≤settled debt and an open posting day; it reduces settled debt and creates one negative repayment transaction. In reality an external repayment is not credited as cleared until the provider contract permits; this local operation assumes funds have already been confirmed.
* `accrue_interest(account,day,rate)` posts once per day under a stable key and the declared rate/rounding; it may take settled debt above the limit and must not be silently dropped by purchase-limit checks.
* `generateStatement(card,(start,end))` returns the same immutable statement on retry, includes only SETTLED postings in the interval and computes closing from all postings before end. Pending holds are excluded; backdated new postings into a closed period are rejected, preventing silent rewrite of a prior statement.

### Worked behavior and limits

With an assumed USD 100 limit, authorizing USD 60 reserves 6,000 cents; another USD 50 is declined. Settling the USD 60 changes pending 6,000→0 and settled 0→6,000. Repaying USD 20 leaves 4,000. At assumed daily rate 100 ppm, daily interest is round_half_up(4,000×100/1,000,000)=0 cents, showing why rate/rounding policy matters; a larger balance/rate fixture tests nonzero accrual. Statement net activity/closing derive from those posted records, not current pending holds.

The in-memory service uses an RLock to serialize account mutations and an operation-result map for retries; it is a working OOD exercise, not restart-durable banking storage. Production replaces dictionaries/locks with transactional durable tables, append-only balanced postings, expiry of holds, reconciliation, authenticated authorization and a complete contractual interest engine. Tests cover shared-limit races, duplicate settlement/repayment, void, interest/day dedup and immutable statements/backdating. This makes the requested classes and operation boundaries concrete without inventing financial terms.

title: Design a Delayed Virtual-Currency Payment Scheduler
question: Design a system that lets a user schedule a virtual-currency transfer (e.g. Robux) from one account to another, to be executed automatically at a specified future time. The deep-dive is on durable scheduling under failure, exactly-once execution despite retries, and keeping the scheduler accurate when millions of payments are queued for the same wall-clock minute.

solution.example: Retry transient storage/worker faults with capped backoff while preserving the same transfer identity; invalid accounts/frozen state surface actionable failure and release/rescind holds under policy. A crash after reservation but before queue publish is repaired by the outbox; a crash after commit returns the existing transfer. Region promotion requires no acknowledged reservation/posting loss and fencing of the old scheduler/ledger authority. Reconcile holds against schedules and balanced postings, report stuck/overdue transfers and alert on clock skew. Test due/cancel races, repeated scheduling, worker death before/after commit, insufficient funds under the alternative policy and a same-minute million-item burst. “Exactly once” refers to the committed virtual-currency transfer, not once-only execution of worker instructions.
solution.trap: Due-time dispatch and atomic transfer are distinct; one million due/minute needs16667/s and arbitrary same-instant timing cannot be solved with minute-average capacity.
solution.teaching_notes_markdown:
### Durable schedule, atomic transfer

`POST /scheduled-transfers` accepts sender, recipient, positive integer virtual units, due_at UTC and idempotency key; status/cancel APIs expose the exact transfer state. Validate account/permission/currency/limits and clarify funds policy. Assume funds are **reserved at schedule time**, reducing spendable balance, so a valid due transfer is not later defeated by unrelated spending; if the product chooses execution-time funds checks instead, insufficient funds becomes a terminal/retryable policy decision. Never describe these choices interchangeably.

Store Schedule(id,key,hash,sender,recipient,amount,currency,due_at,state,version), Hold(schedule,account,amount,state), Attempt(schedule,n,token,lease_expiry), LedgerTransaction(id,transfer_id UNIQUE,currency) and balanced LedgerEntry rows, plus outbox. Scheduling commits the reservation and due row atomically. Cancellation locks the same schedule/hold, changes to CANCELED and releases once if not committed. Due scanners use time-bucket+hash partitions and database time, claim due READY rows and publish work transactionally; timer memory is only an acceleration layer.

The diagram's worker rechecks current schedule/lease and posts sender debit, recipient credit, hold consumption and SUCCEEDED in **one ledger transaction** where possible. Unique transfer_id is the exactly-once committed-effect guard. A worker retry after an ACK loss reads the same posting; it does not debit again. A lease alone cannot prevent an old physical process from still running, so downstream posting verifies token/state or deduplicates the logical transfer. Cross-shard accounts require a transactional ledger supporting atomic transfer or a reserved/pending saga with explicit exposure states, not two independent balance updates pretending to be atomic.

### Millions due in one minute

One million due transfers/minute is 16,667/s; five million is 83,333/s. If all are due at its first instant, minute-average capacity does not deliver zero lateness. Define an acceptable execution window, pre-stage eligible IDs, reserve processing capacity, hash shards within the time bucket and spread dispatch within the permitted minute. Early **execution** is forbidden even if prefetch/validation is early. At assumed 5,000 safe postings/s per shard, five million/minute needs at least seventeen shard-equivalents before headroom, and hot single senders still serialize on funds/limits.

Retry transient storage/worker faults with capped backoff while preserving the same transfer identity; invalid accounts/frozen state surface actionable failure and release/rescind holds under policy. A crash after reservation but before queue publish is repaired by the outbox; a crash after commit returns the existing transfer. Region promotion requires no acknowledged reservation/posting loss and fencing of the old scheduler/ledger authority. Reconcile holds against schedules and balanced postings, report stuck/overdue transfers and alert on clock skew. Test due/cancel races, repeated scheduling, worker death before/after commit, insufficient funds under the alternative policy and a same-minute million-item burst. “Exactly once” refers to the committed virtual-currency transfer, not once-only execution of worker instructions.

title: Design a Highly Reliable Account Balance System
question:
Design the backend that tells a bank customer their current account balance and records every change to it. Customers must never see money lost or counted twice, even when a whole cloud region fails. The ledger of transactions is the authoritative record, and the balance shown to customers must stay consistent with it.

Requirements

Functional:

1.
Read the current balance of an account.
2.
Apply a balance update (credit or debit) with a client-supplied idempotency key. A retried request with the same key must take effect once.
3.
Reconcile displayed balances against the authoritative ledger and surface any account where they differ (drift).

Non-functional, with the targets to design for:

Scale: 50 million accounts, up to 20,000 balance updates per second and 100,000 balance reads per second at peak.
Latency: 99th-percentile read at most 100 ms; 99th-percentile write at most 500 ms.
Consistency: writes are strongly consistent. A customer who has just made an update sees it in the next read (read-your-writes); other readers may see a balance at most 5 seconds old.
Durability and availability: after a single-region outage, RPO is 0 (no acknowledged update is lost or duplicated) and RTO is at most 5 minutes.
Reconciliation: drift for any account is detected within 24 hours, and within 1 hour for the 1% of accounts with the highest balances.
What to deliver
1.
The API, covering the read, the idempotent update and the reconciliation report.
2.
The data model for the ledger and the balance, and which one is the source of truth.
3.
A high-level design with the write path, the read path and the replication between regions.
4.
Failover: what happens to in-flight updates when the primary region fails, and what balance a customer sees afterwards.
5.
The reconciliation design: how drift is found, how often, and what happens when it is found.
6.
Capacity estimates for storage and throughput, using the scale above.
7.
Trade-offs and failure modes you accepted, for example the cost of RPO 0 on write latency.

solution.example: Monitor quorum commit/read p99, replication lag, unknown requests, token violations, per-account reconciliation deadlines, drift/repair age and failover time. Test concurrent debits, duplicate/conflicting keys, commit-then-ACK loss, stale read after own write, region death at every commit phase and reconciliation during concurrent updates. Availability is deliberately sacrificed where RPO zero and linearizable writes cannot otherwise be maintained.
solution.trap: RPO0 requires durable cross-region quorum before ACK; reconciliation compares identical ledger watermarks and high-balance coverage includes newly large accounts.
solution.teaching_notes_markdown:
### API and authoritative invariant

`GET /accounts/{id}/balance?min_version=` returns ledger/available balance, currency, account_version and as_of. A writer receives a consistency token/version; its next read is routed to a replica at least that version or the leader, giving read-your-writes. Other readers may use replicas only while lag≤five seconds; otherwise route to authority or fail rather than serve older data. `POST /accounts/{id}/updates` takes signed integer cents, currency, counteraccount/reference and idempotency key; store a request hash and reject conflicting reuse. `GET /reconciliation/reports?status=&from=` exposes authorized drift cases/actions.

LedgerTransaction(id,client_scope,key UNIQUE,request_hash,status,time), LedgerEntry(txn,line,account,currency,signed_amount), AccountBalance(account,currency,ledger_balance,holds,version,last_txn), Hold and ReconciliationCase make the model. Per-currency entry sums equal zero (external updates use designated clearing/counteraccounts), and the append-only ledger is authoritative. In one serializable/conditional transaction lock affected accounts in stable order, validate limits, append postings, update materialized balances/version, record idempotency response and outbox. Duplicate key returns the same version/result. Correct errors with new compensating entries, never edit historical money records.

### Replication, latency and failover

The diagram's write authority is a sharded consensus-replicated database/log spanning at least three independent regions/failure domains. Acknowledgment requires a durable cross-region quorum, so a single region cannot contain the only acknowledged copy. Async disaster-recovery replication cannot provide RPO zero. Place shard leaders near account traffic while ensuring WAN round-trip/durable commit fits the p99≤500 ms budget; actual regional geography and quorum performance must be measured. This trades partition availability and WAN cost for durability/consistency. Read caches contain version/as_of and cannot invent a current balance.

On primary loss, stop/fence its epochs, elect/promote only an up-to-date quorum and reroute gateways within a tested RTO≤five minutes. A request without ACK may already be committed; retry/query the same key, returning the preserved result or completing once. Never replay it as a fresh update. Customers after failover see the committed ledger-derived balance at/after their token; if authority cannot meet consistency, show unavailable/pending rather than an older post-write balance. No quorum means safe write unavailability. Failover drills must test routing, keys, dependencies and surviving-region capacity, not just database election.

### Reconciliation cadence and correction

At a consistent ledger watermark, independently sum postings per account/currency from a trusted opening checkpoint and compare with the balance projection **at that same version**. Comparing current balances to a yesterday-cutoff sum creates false drift. Incremental partition checks/checksums plus rotating full account coverage detect projection/processing corruption; periodically verify checkpoints against earlier immutable history. Track coverage explicitly for every account, not only changed ones.

Fifty million accounts/day is about **579 account checks/s** average. The highest-balance 1%=500,000 accounts/hour adds about **139/s** checks; maintain the high-balance set from authoritative values with conservative inclusion/re-ranking so newly large accounts enter promptly. These counts exclude underlying ledger I/O: incremental checkpoints and batch scans make it tractable, and sizing must use transaction history. A mismatch opens a case, flags the account, protects risky debit operations if warranted, investigates source corruption and repairs the projection through an audited version-checked rebuild. A valid ledger is not changed merely to match a wrong cache; uncertain ledger evidence requires escalation/reconstruction.

### Throughput and storage

Peak is 20,000 writes/s and 100,000 reads/s. Assuming a balance row of 100 bytes, 50 million rows are 5 GB logical before indexes/replicas. At an assumed **sustained peak** 20,000 updates/s, 1.728 billion updates/day; with a chosen 300-byte transaction plus two 100-byte entries, logical ledger growth is **864 GB/day** (~315.36 TB/year), excluding indexes/replicas/audit. Real average may be lower and must be measured. At an assumed safe 2,000 writes/s/shard, ten is a throughput lower bound; use substantially more for growth/hot accounts/failover and storage distribution. Read replicas/caches meet read load within version/lag constraints.

Monitor quorum commit/read p99, replication lag, unknown requests, token violations, per-account reconciliation deadlines, drift/repair age and failover time. Test concurrent debits, duplicate/conflicting keys, commit-then-ACK loss, stale read after own write, region death at every commit phase and reconciliation during concurrent updates. Availability is deliberately sacrificed where RPO zero and linearizable writes cannot otherwise be maintained.

title: Design a Ledger Service with Merchant Balance
question:
Onsite system design. Build a ledger with a record_transaction API and a merchant_balance query API. The interviewer drills heavily on money modeling and consistency under concurrent writes.

API:

recordTransaction(merchantId, Transaction) — append-only financial event. Transaction(txnId, amountCents, type, occurredAt), type ∈ {payment_received, payout, refund, ...}, amount in integer minor units (cents, never a float).
getBalance(merchantId) -> Balance{ available, pending } — settled/withdrawable vs recorded-but-not-cleared.

Constraints: balance reads must reflect all acknowledged writes; double-recording a txnId is forbidden; thousands of TPS, millions of txns/day; reads outnumber writes; money in integer minor units, currencies tracked separately.

solution.example: Example: record a $100 payment as 10,000 pending cents, then settlement moves 10,000 pending to available. Two simultaneous $80 payouts lock/condition the same balance: only one reserves 8,000, leaving 2,000 available. Re-delivering either event cannot add another $100 or subtract another $80. A provider timeout leaves payout UNKNOWN and its reservation in place until queried/reconciled, not released and resent with a new identity.
solution.trap: All acknowledged writes visible requires authority/version-gated reads, not an eventual cache; pending→available settlement and payout reservations are distinct.
solution.teaching_notes_markdown:
### Money and clearing states

Track each currency separately in integer minor units. A transaction ID is unique in the declared merchant/platform scope and bound to merchant/type/amount/currency/reference; a duplicate identical record returns its original result, while conflicting reuse is rejected. `recordTransaction` must include currency even if omitted from the abbreviated signature. `getBalance(merchant,currency)` returns available, pending and ledger_version; a default currency is an explicit product configuration, never a cross-currency sum.

Store FinancialEvent(txn_id,merchant,currency,amount_cents,type,occurred_at,posted_at,parent_txn_id,state), LedgerTransaction/Entry, MerchantBalance(merchant,currency,available,pending,version), ExternalOperation(provider_id,key,state) and Outbox. Payment receipt initially credits pending against a clearing receivable; a separate settlement event moves pending→available. Payout initiation reserves/debits available, confirmation moves it to payout clearing/settled; failure reverses/resolves the reservation. Refunds/chargebacks are linked compensating events, not negative overwrites of the original payment. State transitions and the available/pending deltas are defined per event type.

### Atomic append and balance query

The diagram's posting transaction locks the merchant/currency balance, verifies event uniqueness and sufficient spendable funds for payouts, appends balanced entries and updates the balance/version in one database commit. Event and outbox share that transaction. Acknowledge only after durable commit, and make `getBalance` a leader/quorum read or a replica read gated by the latest committed version. Plain eventually consistent caches cannot meet **all acknowledged writes** even for other readers. If the balance table is asynchronous, the API must wait for a commit watermark or calculate from authority; declaring it a cache does not weaken the requirement.

Example: record a $100 payment as 10,000 pending cents, then settlement moves 10,000 pending to available. Two simultaneous $80 payouts lock/condition the same balance: only one reserves 8,000, leaving 2,000 available. Re-delivering either event cannot add another $100 or subtract another $80. A provider timeout leaves payout UNKNOWN and its reservation in place until queried/reconciled, not released and resent with a new identity.

### Capacity, failure and audit

At an assumed five million events/day, average is about 58/s despite a stated thousands-TPS peak; provision shards and burst queue for peak. With chosen 300-byte events plus two 100-byte entries, about 2.5 GB/day logical precedes replicas/indexes. Partition by merchant/currency for local balance serialization and append transaction history by time; exceptionally hot merchants need dedicated shards or a carefully designed escrow/subledger model, not an unsafe split of one available balance.

Use multi-zone durable storage, scoped auth/RBAC, immutable audit history and idempotent provider adapters. Reconciliation compares balance at ledger watermark with summed postings and provider settlement statements, opening actionable cases and rebuilding projections under version checks. OccurredAt can be late but must not reorder already committed balance history ambiguously; retain both event/posting time and correction linkage. Test conflicting txn IDs, duplicate settlement, out-of-order provider status, concurrent payout, stale balance replica and currency crossover. Monitor posting p99, lock contention, pending age, unknown operations and drift; no queue retry is a new financial event by itself.

title: Design a Loan Payment Distribution System
question:
Design a simplified loan-payment distribution service. When a borrower payment is accepted, the service must create and track the payouts owed to the investors entitled to that payment. A third-party payment provider performs the actual movement of money; your system coordinates it and keeps an auditable record of the result.

What to design

Describe the APIs, data model, components, and end-to-end workflow for these inputs and outputs:

AcceptedPayment: a stable payment id, loan id, amount in an integer minor currency unit, currency, and acceptance time.
EntitlementSnapshot: the investor recipients and the amount each is owed from that accepted payment. This is supplied to your service; deriving investor ownership is outside the design.
ProviderUpdate: the third-party provider's acknowledgement or terminal result for a requested transfer.
Output: one durable distribution record per payment, transfer requests for entitled investors with positive allocations, and a queryable final or actionable status for every allocation, including those that require no transfer.
Rules
1.
Each distribution must durably reference the authoritative entitlement snapshot supplied for its accepted payment. The snapshot and the resulting allocations become immutable before transfer commands are created.
2.
The allocation amounts must use the same currency as the payment, be non-negative, and sum exactly to the accepted payment amount. Retain zero-cent allocations as part of the rounding and audit record, but mark them NO_TRANSFER_REQUIRED: do not create an outbox command or provider request for them. Invalid input must not initiate money movement.
3.
Re-delivery of an input event, a client retry, a timeout, or a repeated provider update must not create an extra payout.
4.
The provider executes transfers asynchronously. A timeout is an unknown outcome, not proof of failure, so the design must resolve it without blindly creating a replacement transfer.
5.
Preserve enough durable history to explain which payment, snapshot, allocation, request, and provider result produced every state transition.
Examples
Example 1: successful distribution

A 100-dollar payment arrives as 10,000 cents with an entitlement snapshot assigning 7,000 cents to Investor A and 3,000 cents to Investor B. The service creates two allocations, requests two transfers through the provider, and marks the distribution complete only after both transfers have terminal success results.

Example 2: retry after an uncertain response

A 50-dollar payment has one entitled investor. The transfer request reaches the provider, but the response times out. The request is retried with the same stable idempotency identity or queried by that identity; the system records one provider transfer, not a second payout, and eventually converges to the provider's terminal result.

Example 3: zero-cent audit allocation

A 100-dollar payment has allocations of 10,000 cents and 0 cents. The positive allocation requires a transfer and must reach terminal success. The zero-cent allocation is retained as NO_TRANSFER_REQUIRED and is never submitted. The distribution completes when both conditions hold.

Constraints
Interest, fees, principal accounting, amortization, delinquency, and other loan-accounting rules are out of scope.
Choosing investors, originating the loan, and computing investor ownership are out of scope; the entitlement snapshot is authoritative input.
Holding bank funds and executing money movement are out of scope; those actions belong to the third-party provider.
Monetary amounts use integer minor units. A payment can have one or more entitled investors.
No traffic volume or latency target is fixed. State explicit scale and availability assumptions, show how they affect partitioning and capacity, and avoid relying on a single global worker.
Explain consistency boundaries, idempotency, failure recovery, reconciliation, observability, privacy, and access control.

solution.example: Reconcile every nonterminal/unknown request against provider statements/status and compare successful amounts to immutable allocations. Maintain original idempotency keys beyond provider retry windows or stop before unsafe reuse. APIs enforce loan/tenant ownership and operator roles; encrypt recipient identifiers, authenticate webhooks and audit manual repair with dual review where configured. Monitor plan rejection/sum mismatch, zero-command violations, oldest pending/unknown, provider error/rate limits, partial distributions and reconciliation discrepancies. Test duplicate input, changed snapshot under same payment, zero allocation, worker crash before/after send, duplicate/reordered callback and provider success after timeout. Your service coordinates records and requests; it does not claim to hold funds or execute the provider's money movement.

solution.teaching_notes_markdown:
### Immutable allocation plan before any transfer

The supplied entitlement snapshot is authoritative; do not derive investor ownership, principal/interest/fees or amortization. `POST /distributions` takes AcceptedPayment plus snapshot ID/digest and allocations; `GET /distributions/{payment_id}` returns the immutable plan and each allocation's status/history. An authenticated provider webhook and a reconciliation poller deliver ProviderUpdate. Idempotency is payment-scoped and binds the complete payment/snapshot hash; a replay matches the existing plan, while conflicting same-payment inputs are quarantined/rejected before money moves.

```text
Distribution(id PK, payment_id UNIQUE, loan_id, amount_minor, currency,
             accepted_at, snapshot_id, snapshot_digest, plan_hash, state)
EntitlementSnapshot(id PK, immutable_ref, digest, currency, source_version)
Allocation(id PK, distribution_id FK, snapshot_recipient_id, investor_id,
           amount_minor, currency, state, UNIQUE(distribution_id,snapshot_recipient_id))
TransferRequest(id PK, allocation_id UNIQUE, provider_key UNIQUE,
                request_hash, provider_transfer_id nullable, state)
TransferAttempt(request_id, attempt_no, sent_at, response, error)
ProviderInbox(provider,event_id UNIQUE,payload_hash,received_at,applied_at)
AllocationTransition(id,allocation_id,from_state,to_state,evidence_ref,time)
Outbox(command_id PK, request_id UNIQUE, next_attempt_at, lease_token, state)
```

Validate stable IDs, same currency, nonnegative integer amounts and **exact sum=payment amount**. Persist/restrict the referenced authoritative snapshot and plan in the same acceptance transaction, rejecting invalid inputs with no outbox entries. Freeze all allocation amounts/recipients before creating commands. Zero-cent rows are retained with NO_TRANSFER_REQUIRED and **never** get TransferRequest/outbox/provider calls. Positive rows enter PLANNED with one stable transfer identity. Snapshot changes require a distinct audited correction/business process, not mutation of an already paying plan.

### Asynchronous transfer state machine

The diagram's immutable plan feeds partitioned transfer outboxes, provider adapters, signed result intake and reconciliation. Workers claim durable commands with leases, send provider_key and record attempt history. Acknowledgment/request acceptance yields SUBMITTED/PROCESSING, not success. Only explicit terminal provider success yields SUCCEEDED; definitive terminal failure becomes FAILED_ACTION_REQUIRED or another named actionable state. Timeout/connection loss yields UNKNOWN, retains the **same** request identity and schedules status lookup or idempotent resend. If a provider offers neither idempotency nor lookup by stable identity, one cannot safely guarantee automatic no-duplicate payout after timeout; stop for manual reconciliation rather than invent a replacement transfer.

ProviderInbox deduplicates callback events. Apply state transitions conditionally under an allocation/request lock, matching provider identity, amount, currency and recipient. Late PROCESSING cannot downgrade SUCCEEDED, duplicate success is a no-op, and contradictory terminal evidence opens an exception. Polling and webhook processing converge on the same state machine. A failed worker after provider success is repaired by querying/resending the original key. Lease expiry permits another **messenger**, not a second logical payout. Store enough request/response/evidence references to trace every transition without exposing bank details in ordinary logs.

### Completion, recovery and scale

Distribution COMPLETE means every positive allocation SUCCEEDED and every zero allocation NO_TRANSFER_REQUIRED. A terminal failed allocation makes the distribution actionable/partially failed; never report complete merely because all requests were sent. For 10,000 cents split 7,000/3,000, both provider successes are required. For 10,000/0, exactly one command is created and the zero row remains visible/auditable. Sum/count invariants validate the plan independently of delivery status.

Assume 100,000 payments/day×twenty recipients=two million allocations/day, about 23.1/s average; assume a 100× burst (~2,315/s) for queue/provider capacity. At 300 bytes/allocation this is 600 MB/day logical before history/indexes. Hash by payment/distribution for plan consistency, distribute transfer workers by provider/tenant and cap concurrent requests/rates; no global worker serializes every investor. Multi-zone database/queue replication, outbox replay, lease reconciliation and provider circuit breakers retain accepted plans through failure. Backpressure leaves commands pending with next_attempt_at rather than losing them.

Test duplicate input, changed snapshot under same payment, zero allocation, worker crash before/after send, duplicate/reordered callback and provider success after timeout. Your service coordinates records and requests; it does not claim to hold funds or execute the provider's money movement.

title: Design a Multi-Chain Crypto Ledger & Wallet History
question:
Design a crypto-asset ledger that tracks every transaction across chains and supports a 'wallet history' query: given a wallet address, return all transactions touching it, paginated and ordered by time. Requirements reported thinly:

Track multi-chain transactions in a single ledger surface.
Support per-wallet history queries (paginated, time-ordered).
Reasonable freshness — recent transactions appear within seconds.

Scale and durability targets were not fully specified in the source. The prompt mirrors an early internal Coinbase project.

solution.example: Indexer offsets commit with canonical block/application state or replay idempotently after crashes. Redundant providers catch missing/contradictory blocks; verify data consistency rather than treating one RPC response as unquestionable. API failure serves marked stale confirmed history or retries; it never invents missing transactions. Monitor chain-head lag, reorg depth, gap detection, projection counts/checksums and wallet query p99. Test duplicate logs, deep reorg, identical tx hashes on different chains, wallet hot keys and pagination during canonical changes. Finality, data rights and upstream reliability remain explicit chain-specific dependencies.
solution.trap: Per-chain address/transaction identity, canonical blocks and reorg-aware pagination/finality matter; cross-chain time is not one causal order.
solution.teaching_notes_markdown:
### Chain identity and wallet-oriented projection

Scope is transaction/transfer history, not private-key custody or trading. Ask which chains/assets, whether token/internal transfers count, retention, throughput and finality semantics; source gives no fixed scale. Store Chain(chain_id,adapter,finality_policy), Block(chain_id,height,hash,parent_hash,canonical,status), Transaction(chain_id,tx_hash,block_hash,index,raw_ref), Transfer(chain_id,tx_hash,event_index,block_hash,asset_id,from,to,amount_base_units,status), and WalletActivity(chain_id,address,block_time,block_height,tx_index,event_index,transfer_id,canonical). Native amounts/token quantities use integer base units plus asset/decimals metadata; the same address string on two chains is not one identity.

The diagram's chain adapters consume new blocks/mempool if supported, verify parent continuity and persist raw evidence, then a reorg-aware projector creates wallet activity rows for all touched addresses. Deduplicate event identity including chain and event/log/trace index: one transaction can contain multiple token transfers. Normalize addresses according to **that chain's** rules; don't lowercase every chain blindly. For an “all chains wallet” UI, require explicit verified address mappings instead of assuming identical strings belong to the same person.

### Query, order and freshness

`GET /wallets/{chain}/{address}/history?before=&limit=&status=` returns transaction/transfer grouping, amounts, confirmation/finality status and source freshness. Partition by (chain,address,time bucket) with a descending ordered activity index and hydrate transaction details in batch. A common chronological display uses (block_time,chain,height,tx_index,event_index,tx_hash) as deterministic tie-breaks; cross-chain timestamps are not one causal/consensus order. Cursor binds filters and canonical-view epoch; a reorg can invalidate the view, so return a refresh/resync marker or pin an old snapshot with its status rather than silently skip/duplicate activity.

Recent unconfirmed/canonical-but-not-final entries can appear within seconds, while finality may take longer and differs by chain. Never label “seconds fresh” as irreversible. On a parent-hash mismatch, find the common ancestor, mark orphaned records noncanonical, undo/rebuild affected projections and ingest the replacement branch. Keep raw orphan evidence for audit and reorg-depth alerts; an old ingestion replay must not make an orphan canonical again. Cross-chain bridges are linked observations with independent settlement/failure states, not atomic one-chain transfers.

### Capacity and failure choices

Assume 10,000 transfers/s and two wallet-index rows/transfer: 20,000 index writes/s. At chosen 250 bytes/transfer plus two 80-byte index rows, sustained logical growth is about 354.24 GB/day before raw receipts/index overhead/replicas. Shard by wallet hash/time with special handling for exchange/contract hot wallets; bucket and paginate them rather than create one unbounded partition. Recent data stays indexed/replicated, old immutable blocks/history move to cheaper storage with a query catalog, preserving the requested history.

Indexer offsets commit with canonical block/application state or replay idempotently after crashes. Redundant providers catch missing/contradictory blocks; verify data consistency rather than treating one RPC response as unquestionable. API failure serves marked stale confirmed history or retries; it never invents missing transactions. Monitor chain-head lag, reorg depth, gap detection, projection counts/checksums and wallet query p99. Test duplicate logs, deep reorg, identical tx hashes on different chains, wallet hot keys and pagination during canonical changes. Finality, data rights and upstream reliability remain explicit chain-specific dependencies.

title: Design a Payment Gateway System
question:
Design a payment gateway for merchants using POS machines. The POS scans a card and calls your API to validate the payment. Focus on card validation/authorization — not the full settlement/money-movement flow.

Requirements: support many card types (Visa, Mastercard, Amex, Discover, local), receive validation requests from POS machines, route each request to the correct bank based on the card number, and be highly available and low-latency.

Assumptions: ~10,000 merchants, ~10M transactions/day (~115 TPS avg, ~575 TPS peak), p95 < 200ms, 99.99% uptime.

Address: BIN-based bank routing, failure handling when a bank API is down/slow (retries + circuit breaker), PCI-DSS compliance (tokenization, encryption), rate limiting, idempotency (double-scan / double-click), monitoring, multi-region latency, local validation (Luhn / expiry) before calling the bank, Black-Friday spikes, and integrating hundreds of banks with different API formats.

solution.example: Tokenize/minimize PAN exposure, encrypt transport/storage, use managed keys/HSM boundaries and strict audited access/network segmentation. Sensitive authentication data such as CVV must not be stored after authorization even encrypted, as explained by the [PCI SSC guidance](https://www.pcisecuritystandards.org/faqs/1533/); tokenization is not a blanket exemption from assessment scope. Never log full card data. Monitor p95 by bank/network, approval/decline/unknown, circuit state, duplicate prevention and aged authorizations. Test malformed card/expiry, stale BIN configuration, issuer timeout after approval, lost ACK, double scan and regional failover. No settlement ledger is invented for this narrower prompt.
solution.trap: Local Luhn/expiry is not issuer approval; token/BIN adapters route authorization only, and bank timeout cannot trigger a fresh duplicate hold.
solution.teaching_notes_markdown:
### Authorization state before routing

Scope is validation/authorization, not settlement. `POST /authorizations` takes merchant/terminal identity, card token or protected card data, amount/currency and idempotency key; return APPROVED, DECLINED or PROCESSING/UNKNOWN plus authorization_id and issuer reference when present. “Luhn/expiry valid” is only local format plausibility, not available funds or issuer approval. Validate merchant/terminal credentials, positive integer money, supported card range/expiry and risk/rate limits before issuer calls.

Ten million/day is **115.7/s average**; use the supplied ~575/s peak. At an assumed 1 KB authorization audit record, raw intent/audit is 10 GB/day before replicas/indexes. A proposed p95<200 ms budget is 15 ms ingress/local checks, 5 ms BIN/adapter selection, 150 ms issuer path and 30 ms durable transition/network headroom. An issuer whose response p95 is already 300 ms makes the aggregate target infeasible for that route; negotiate SLO/timeouts and report PROCESSING rather than fabricate an approval. 99.99% gateway availability is distinct from every bank/network's approval availability.

### Routing and adapters

The diagram's secure ingress/token vault leads to a versioned BIN/IIN range table and network/issuer adapter layer. Use current authoritative range metadata supporting varying prefix lengths; longest applicable range plus network/co-brand rules determines the configured route. Card prefix identifies routing metadata, not necessarily a direct public issuer API: real integrations may go through an acquirer/network. Hundreds of bank adapters implement a common authorize/status/reversal contract, with protocol/error mapping, deadlines, credentials and capability flags separated from core orchestration. Update route tables atomically with validation/canary and last-known-good recovery.

Store Authorization(id,merchant,key,request_hash,amount,currency,token_ref,route_version,state), Attempt(id,authorization,downstream_key,issuer_ref,result) and outbox/audit. Commit intent before calling the bank, then persist explicit result. A double scan is safe only if the POS reuses the same logical purchase key; similar amount/time heuristics alone cannot prove identity. Timeout after send is UNKNOWN. Query/status or retry the **same downstream identity** when supported; do not reroute/re-authorize with a new identity that might create a second hold. Any compensating reversal is itself tracked/idempotent.

### Resilience and protected data

Per-bank circuit breakers, bulkheads and bounded queues contain slow routes. Retry only classified transient errors with a remaining latency budget and jitter; hard declines require customer/payment-method action. Active-active regional ingress routes each intent to one authoritative idempotency partition; synchronously replicate/fence failover if no acknowledged intent may be lost. Black Friday capacity uses prewarmed adapters/connections, merchant quotas and bank-specific rate limits; passing extra traffic to an already failing bank worsens success rate.

Tokenize/minimize PAN exposure, encrypt transport/storage, use managed keys/HSM boundaries and strict audited access/network segmentation. Sensitive authentication data such as CVV must not be stored after authorization even encrypted, as explained by the [PCI SSC guidance](https://www.pcisecuritystandards.org/faqs/1533/); tokenization is not a blanket exemption from assessment scope. Never log full card data. Monitor p95 by bank/network, approval/decline/unknown, circuit state, duplicate prevention and aged authorizations. Test malformed card/expiry, stale BIN configuration, issuer timeout after approval, lost ACK, double scan and regional failover. No settlement ledger is invented for this narrower prompt.

title: Design a Payment Webhook Delivery System
question:
Design a webhook delivery service for a payments platform that notifies merchants when payment events occur (payment success, refund, dispute). Emphasis is on reliability: at-least-once delivery, retries, idempotency, and signature verification.

The system must:

1.
Merchant registration — save a webhook URL and chosen event types (e.g., payment.success, refund.created).
2.
Send events — on a payment event, POST the data to all registered webhooks; the merchant replies HTTP 200 to confirm.
3.
Reliability — deliver even if the merchant's server is briefly down.

Discuss: delivery guarantees & duplicate handling, retry strategy, latency (merchants may take 10–15s to reply), signature verification (HMAC vs RSA), circuit breaking, event ordering, endpoint validation, SSRF prevention, observability, and backpressure/isolation.

solution.example: Shard by merchant/endpoint, keep per-tenant budgets and protect healthy endpoints from retry floods. Lease expiration reoffers the same Delivery; outbox/inbox dedup prevents fanout duplication. Monitor oldest undelivered age, attempt reasons, ACK latency, per-endpoint circuit/backlog and signature errors with redacted payloads. Test merchant success followed by lost response, 15-second latency, bad HMAC/key rotation, reordered resource events, DNS rebinding/redirect SSRF and worker crash after send. Manual replay preserves original event identity so it cannot silently request a new financial effect.
solution.trap: Stable event identity, receiver effect dedup and exact-byte signature verification are needed; validate actual egress DNS/redirects against SSRF and isolate15-second endpoints.
solution.teaching_notes_markdown:
### Durable event-to-delivery model

`POST /webhook-endpoints` stores merchant URL, event-type subscriptions, signing key version and enabled state; send a validation challenge and require authenticated merchant control. Committed payment changes create immutable Event(id,type,resource_id,resource_version,created_at,payload_schema) plus outbox atomically. Fanout snapshots applicable subscriptions into Delivery(event_id,endpoint_id UNIQUE,state,next_attempt_at,attempt_count,lease), with DeliveryAttempt(request,response,times,error) retained for debugging/replay. An event is distinct from each destination delivery.

The diagram is business outbox→durable fanout/scheduler→per-endpoint queues→HTTP workers→merchant ACK, with retries/reconciliation. The requested success condition is HTTP 200; other responses follow documented policy (common APIs accept other 2xx only if agreed). A timeout, even after the merchant committed the effect, leaves delivery unacknowledged and will be retried. Stable event_id/delivery_id let the merchant atomically deduplicate **and apply** its business effect; no network system can promise once-only callbacks through lost acknowledgments.

### Slow endpoints, order and signing

Workers use asynchronous I/O, bounded connections and endpoint-specific concurrency so a 10–15-second receiver does not consume every thread. At an assumed 10,000 deliveries/s×15 seconds, up to 150,000 HTTP requests are in flight before headroom; batch dispatch/rate limits/circuit breakers matter. Retry network/timeout/429/5xx with capped exponential backoff+jitter and bounded Retry-After; classify permanent errors, disable/alert on persistently broken endpoints and provide retained dead-letter/manual replay. At-least-once eventual delivery requires an eventually reachable accepting endpoint within retention; an indefinitely down endpoint cannot be guaranteed delivery by finite buffers.

Sign exact raw body bytes with timestamp, event/delivery ID and key ID. HMAC is efficient with a per-endpoint shared secret; RSA/asymmetric signatures let merchants verify using a public key without holding the signing secret, at greater key/crypto overhead. Constant-time verification, replay-window checks and event-ID dedup are all needed; timestamp checks alone don't stop in-window duplication. Retry keeps logical event identity but can use a fresh attempt timestamp/signature. Support overlapping key versions for rotation.

Ordering is normally not global. Include resource_version and provide a resource-fetch API so receivers ignore stale updates/refetch canonical state. If strict per-object/endpoint order is required, serialize that key and block later delivery behind retries, trading freshness for head-of-line blocking. A failed old callback must not downgrade a newer successful payment state.

### Endpoint safety and recovery

Validate HTTPS URLs, prohibit credentials and unsafe ports, resolve/check all IPs against private/link-local/metadata ranges, and enforce those checks on the actual outbound connection and every redirect/DNS refresh. Disable redirects or revalidate every hop; registration-only DNS validation is vulnerable to rebinding. Use a restricted egress proxy, allowlisted destinations where feasible, response/body size limits and no internal network access. Endpoint configuration changes are versioned; define whether old pending deliveries use old or new URL, and audit the choice.

Shard by merchant/endpoint, keep per-tenant budgets and protect healthy endpoints from retry floods. Lease expiration reoffers the same Delivery; outbox/inbox dedup prevents fanout duplication. Monitor oldest undelivered age, attempt reasons, ACK latency, per-endpoint circuit/backlog and signature errors with redacted payloads. Test merchant success followed by lost response, 15-second latency, bad HMAC/key rotation, reordered resource events, DNS rebinding/redirect SSRF and worker crash after send. Manual replay preserves original event identity so it cannot silently request a new financial effect.
