title: In-Memory KV Cache with Write-Ahead Log
question:
Design a single-machine, in-memory key-value cache for a web service. Then extend it:

1.
Persistence — add durability via a write-ahead log (WAL) so the cache can be recovered after a crash.
2.
Scaling — discuss how to scale the design via sharding and how to reduce lock contention under concurrent access.

Discuss the core data structures, the read/write path, and the tradeoffs of your persistence and concurrency choices.

steps: Log a mutation durably before publishing it in memory
solution.example: Extend SET/DELETE with a WAL record `(sequence,op,key,value,absolute_expiry,length,checksum)`. Under a defined write-order lock, append a framed record, flush/fsync under the durability policy, then publish the map update and acknowledge. A crash after durable append but before reply may replay an operation the client thinks failed; use request IDs if retries must recover the same result. For a durable DELETE, append a tombstone too; otherwise restart resurrects removed keys. A short/torn trailing record is ignored/truncated only at its validated boundary, while a checksum mismatch inside completed history requires investigation rather than silently dropping everything after it.
solution.trap: The core is a hash map of key→value/version/expiry plus a bounded eviction structure if this is an evictable cache. A mutex or striped locks serialize mutations; GET uses the same synchronization required by the language/runtime. Atomic INCR/CAS is a server operation, not client GET+SET. If acknowledged live entries must survive memory pressure, spill to durable storage rather than silently evicting them and calling the component a persistent store.
solution.teaching_notes_markdown:
### Log a mutation durably before publishing it in memory

The core is a hash map of key → value/version/expiry plus a bounded eviction structure if this is an evictable cache. A mutex or striped locks serialize mutations; GET uses the same synchronization required by the language/runtime. Atomic INCR/CAS is a server operation, not client GET+SET. If acknowledged live entries must survive memory pressure, spill to durable storage rather than silently evicting them and calling the component a persistent store.

Extend SET/DELETE with a WAL record `(sequence,op,key,value,absolute_expiry,length,checksum)`. Under a defined write-order lock, append a framed record, flush/fsync under the durability policy, then publish the map update and acknowledge. A crash after durable append but before reply may replay an operation the client thinks failed; use request IDs if retries must recover the same result. For a durable DELETE, append a tombstone too; otherwise restart resurrects removed keys. A short/torn trailing record is ignored/truncated only at its validated boundary, while a checksum mismatch inside completed history requires investigation rather than silently dropping everything after it.

Recovery loads the latest checksummed snapshot and replays complete newer WAL records in sequence, applying original absolute expiry so TTL does not restart after a crash. Snapshot creation captures a consistent map/sequence, writes/fsyncs a temporary, atomically publishes its manifest, and only then removes covered WAL segments. A crash at any stage leaves at least one valid snapshot+log chain. Background compaction retains tombstones until older state cannot return.

Syncing each write minimizes acknowledged-data loss but adds storage latency; group commit amortizes fsync while each acknowledgment still waits for its batch. Async flush trades a declared loss window for throughput, not equivalent durability. Memory update before WAL fsync can expose data that disappears on crash, so state whether reads of unacknowledged writes are permitted. Snapshot pause/copy-on-write choices trade latency, memory and implementation complexity.

For scale, shard keys and lock domains; each shard may have its own WAL/order, or a shared log needs a separate sequencer. GET-heavy LRU mutation can become a lock hotspot, so use sampled/segmented recency and monitor contention. Horizontal consistent hashing adds ownership/replication/rebalance protocols beyond this single-machine persistence design. For an assumed 100K writes/s with 1 KB values, WAL payload alone is 100 MB/s before framing; benchmark fsync and recovery time on actual disks. Test crash points, duplicate requests, tombstones, torn tails, expiry and snapshot rotation—not just process-restart success after a clean close.

title: Single-Machine Key-Value Store with Filesystem Spill
question:
Design a single-machine KV store that holds a billion keys and MB-scale values. Memory is bounded; on-disk format is append-only files; values cannot live entirely in memory. The round straddles system design and data-structure design — many candidates over-pivot to distributed systems and lose signal.

Functional

get(key) -> value / put(key, value) / delete(key).
Up to 1B keys live; each value is MB-scale.
Persistent across restarts.

Keep it single-node. Discuss the compaction strategy, not Raft.

steps: Keep value bytes on disk; the key index may also need disk
solution.example: Track live/dead bytes,write amplification,index cache hit,recovery time,checksum failures,reader pins and compaction debt. Batch tiny index updates and use a bounded writer queue; stripe locks or serialize one append with independent readers. Durability here covers process restart with intact disks; surviving disk/machine loss requires backups/redundancy outside this single-node exercise. Raft,global sharding and cross-region APIs do not solve the requested on-disk index/compaction problem.
solution.trap: At1B live keys×1MB values, logical payload is about1PB decimal. A single machine needs an unusually large attached storage system and substantial compaction bandwidth; the design can be single-node, but a normal workstation cannot physically hold the stated data. Even a32-byte in-memory pointer/index per key is32GB before key strings/hash overhead, so bounded memory may require a disk-resident sorted/B-tree/LSM index plus a hot cache. Do not promise a full in-memory hash index without its budget.
solution.teaching_notes_markdown:
### Keep value bytes on disk; the key index may also need disk

At 1B live keys×1 MB values, logical payload is about 1 PB decimal. A single machine needs an unusually large attached storage system and substantial compaction bandwidth; the design can be single-node, but a normal workstation cannot physically hold the stated data. Even a 32-byte in-memory pointer/index per key is 32 GB before key strings/hash overhead, so bounded memory may require a disk-resident sorted/B-tree/LSM index plus a hot cache. Do not promise a full in-memory hash index without its budget.

Append immutable records to segmented files: `(record_length,key_length,key,version,op,value_length,value,checksum)`. The current key index maps key→`(segment,offset,length,version,deleted)`; values are streamed from the referenced file, never loaded wholesale across the database. PUT appends/fsyncs according to acknowledgment policy, then atomically updates/recoverably logs the index mapping. DELETE appends a tombstone and publishes the new version. Recovery replays a checkpointed index plus later segment/index-journal records, rejecting torn tails/checksum errors. Stable request/version IDs define retry behavior.

GET checks the index, reads the exact range and verifies record/key/version/checksum. A reader pins its segment or generation so compaction cannot unlink it mid-read. The OS page cache/hot value cache helps repeated reads, but MB values imply significant random IO/network-copy cost; bound concurrent loads and maximum value/record length to avoid corrupt-length allocations.

Compaction selects segments with high dead-byte ratio, scans them sequentially and copies only records still current according to the index. CAS the index from the old `(segment,offset,version)` to the new location so a concurrent newer PUT cannot be overwritten. Publish the new compacted file/manifest durably before dropping old references; delete old segments only after all reader pins and checkpoints release them. Keep tombstones until every older record they suppress is outside the recovery/compaction horizon, or deleted keys resurrect. Reserve free space for rewrite amplification and throttle compaction so foreground writes do not stall.

Track live/dead bytes, write amplification, index cache hit, recovery time, checksum failures, reader pins and compaction debt. Batch tiny index updates and use a bounded writer queue; stripe locks or serialize one append with independent readers. Durability here covers process restart with intact disks; surviving disk/machine loss requires backups/redundancy outside this single-node exercise. Raft, global sharding and cross-region APIs do not solve the requested on-disk index/compaction problem.

### Follow the diagram

![W483 solution flow](../diagrams/review_451_500_W483.svg)

Read left to right: Append immutable value log → Durable disk key index → Exact ranged value read → Version-CAS compaction. Readers pin old segments; compaction cannot overwrite a concurrent newer key version.

title: Design a Concurrent Image Upload System
question:
Design a system (like Craigslist) that accepts a list of images and stores them concurrently, updating the user about the status of each upload as soon as possible.

Requirements:

Accept a batch of images from a client.
Upload/store them concurrently rather than sequentially.
Report per-image status (pending / uploading / succeeded / failed) to the user as early as possible.
Handle partial failures and retries.

steps: Give every image its own durable lifecycle
solution.example: `POST /upload-batches` accepts an authenticated list of `(client_image_id,name,size,type,checksum)` and an idempotency key. Return a batch ID plus per-image IDs and narrow multipart/signed upload URLs. Store `Batch(id,user,key,state)` and `ImageUpload(id,batch,client_id,state,attempt,bytes,checksum,object_key,error,version)`, unique `(batch,client_id)`. The client uploads with a bounded concurrency pool, for example4–8 images, rather than sequentially or opening hundreds of unbounded streams.
solution.trap: `POST /upload-batches` accepts an authenticated list of `(client_image_id,name,size,type,checksum)` and an idempotency key. Return a batch ID plus per-image IDs and narrow multipart/signed upload URLs. Store `Batch(id,user,key,state)` and `ImageUpload(id,batch,client_id,state,attempt,bytes,checksum,object_key,error,version)`, unique `(batch,client_id)`. The client uploads with a bounded concurrency pool, for example4–8 images, rather than sequentially or opening hundreds of unbounded streams.
solution.teaching_notes_markdown:
### Give every image its own durable lifecycle

`POST /upload-batches` accepts an authenticated list of `(client_image_id,name,size,type,checksum)` and an idempotency key. Return a batch ID plus per-image IDs and narrow multipart/signed upload URLs. Store `Batch(id,user,key,state)` and `ImageUpload(id,batch,client_id,state,attempt,bytes,checksum,object_key,error,version)`, unique `(batch,client_id)`. The client uploads with a bounded concurrency pool, for example 4–8 images, rather than sequentially or opening hundreds of unbounded streams.

The flow is metadata admission → parallel direct object uploads → completion/checksum validation → safe image decode/scan → publish. Per-image states are pending → uploading → succeeded/failed; define succeeded as verified/publishable, not merely bytes received. Client byte-progress is provisional; server completion events are authoritative. One failed image leaves the others successful. Retry only failed parts/images with stable IDs/keys, and do not create a second image row after a timeout. A cancelled/abandoned pending upload expires and cleans staged bytes.

`GET /batches/{id}/events?after_seq` uses SSE/WebSocket to stream `(image_id,state,version,error_code)` as each transition commits; `GET /batches/{id}` gives a full snapshot for reconnect. An outbox/change stream avoids losing a terminal event between DB commit and publish, and sequence IDs let clients dedup/replay. A stale uploading event cannot overwrite succeeded. Use row-version CAS to fence concurrent retry/completion workers; acknowledge duplicate completes with the current state.

Assume 100 batches/s×10 images×2 MB ≈ 2 GB/s ingress; image bytes should bypass API memory and go to scalable object storage, while workers cap CPU/decompression cost and queue depth. Validate actual magic bytes, dimensions/pixel count, checksums and authorization, not just filename MIME; re-encode/scan before public delivery. Store immutable object versions so a retried upload cannot overwrite another user's image. Report batch status as a summary of image states and return structured per-image failures, not one misleading all-or-nothing success. Monitor time-to-first-status, upload/verification latency, bytes, partial failures, retries and abandoned storage; test one slow image, one invalid image and a lost completion reply.

### Follow the diagram

![W484 solution flow](../diagrams/review_451_500_W484.svg)

Read left to right: Batch + per-image IDs → Bounded parallel byte upload → Verify / publish each image → Sequenced status stream. Partial failures and retry IDs are per image; successful siblings remain successful.

title: Design a URL Shortener
question:
URL Shortener

A URL shortener takes a long web address and turns it into a short link. When a user clicks the short link, they are redirected to the original page. Services like Bit.ly and TinyURL are examples of this.

The basic idea is simple, but there is enough depth to challenge a senior design: short-key generation (counter + base62, or hashing with collision handling), the read-heavy redirect path, durable mapping storage, caching the hottest links, and scaling reads globally.

steps: Durable code mapping with a cache-heavy redirect path
solution.example: A counter allocated in durable nonoverlapping ranges plus base62 encoding is collision-free if range ownership survives failover, but exposes sequence/enumeration. Random base62 codes are less predictable and need a unique insert/retry, because hashing/truncation alone is not collision-free. For a demonstration1M creates/day over5years,1.825B links at500bytes≈.91TB logical; eight base62 characters offer2.18e14 codes with low per-attempt occupancy, though birthday collisions across the population are expected and must be handled.
solution.trap: Expose `POST /links {url}` and `GET /{code}`. Store `Link(code PRIMARY KEY,url,owner,created_at,expires_at?,state,version)` in a durable partitioned database; only HTTP(S) destinations are accepted, with bounded length and no control-character/header injection. The redirect handler resolves code, checks state/expiry and returns302 Location. It does not fetch the destination, so do not add an unnecessary synchronous preview request.
solution.teaching_notes_markdown:
### Durable code mapping with a cache-heavy redirect path

Expose `POST /links {url}` and `GET /{code}`. Store `Link(code PRIMARY KEY,url,owner,created_at,expires_at?,state,version)` in a durable partitioned database; only HTTP(S) destinations are accepted, with bounded length and no control-character/header injection. The redirect handler resolves code, checks state/expiry and returns 302 Location. It does not fetch the destination, so do not add an unnecessary synchronous preview request.

A counter allocated in durable nonoverlapping ranges plus base62 encoding is collision-free if range ownership survives failover, but exposes sequence/enumeration. Random base62 codes are less predictable and need a unique insert/retry, because hashing/truncation alone is not collision-free. For a demonstration 1M creates/day over 5 years, 1.825B links at 500 bytes ≈ .91 TB logical; eight base62 characters offer 2.18e14 codes with low per-attempt occupancy, though birthday collisions across the population are expected and must be handled.

The hot path is regional edge/load balancer → local/shared hot-code cache → mapping shard. Positive entries carry version/expiry, and negative caches have short TTL to avoid hiding a newly created link. Prewarm/replicate hot links; a single celebrity URL can dominate a shard even when hashes balance normal traffic. Global replicas can be eventually consistent if create responses route early reads to the owner until replication catches up; state a bound and failover policy. Admin disable/delete invalidates caches and uses tombstones so old replica data does not resurrect links.

At an assumed 100M redirects/day, reads ≈ 1,157/s average, perhaps 10K/s peak; size from actual traffic and URL bytes, not just row count. Keep optional click analytics asynchronous and bounded, using stable event IDs if counts require dedup. Mapping writes use idempotency keys when the same client retry must return the same link. On database outage, serve only cached live entries under their policy and shed unsafe misses; a stale disabled link is not acceptable merely to improve availability. Monitor redirect p99, cache-hit rate, unknown/expired codes, abuse/reports and replica/invalidation lag. [W487](W487.md) includes a tested runnable core for collisions, aliases, expiry and create retries.

### Follow the diagram

![W485 solution flow](../diagrams/review_451_500_W485.svg)

Read left to right: Validate create request → Unique durable short mapping → Regional hot-link cache → 302 / expiry / controlled miss. Generated collisions retry; cached mutable state has a bounded invalidation policy.

- [F170: Design a cache without serving incorrect data.](../17_distributed_systems_depth.md#f170)

title: Design a URL Shortener (TinyURL)
question:
Design a URL shortener (TinyURL). Given a long URL, produce a short code that redirects to the original.

Cover the encoding scheme, collision handling, read-heavy caching, and click analytics. This is often used as a phone-screen warm-up.

steps: A phone-screen design with explicit collision behavior
solution.example: Click analytics emits `event_id,code,time,referrer_domain,country` into a bounded queue/outbox path and aggregates per-code/day asynchronously; drop/sampling/error policy is explicit so logging cannot stall redirects. Avoid storing full sensitive referrer URLs and label bot/duplicate estimates. For an illustrative1M creates/day and100M redirects/day, average rates are12 writes/s and1,157 reads/s; provision peak headroom and code/table retention accordingly. The [W487 implementation](W487.md) demonstrates the small core with real tests, while cache replication and analytics remain system components. This level is enough for the warm-up if you can trace a generated collision and a lost create reply.
solution.trap: Choose random eight-character base62 codes and a unique code primary key; retry a generated collision, never overwrite its destination. A monotonic ID→base62 alternative is shorter/simpler to guarantee uniqueness but enumerable and requires durable ID allocation. Hashing a URL then truncating does not avoid collisions and does not by itself guarantee repeat submissions map to the same link.
solution.teaching_notes_markdown:
### A phone-screen design with explicit collision behavior

Choose random eight-character base62 codes and a unique code primary key; retry a generated collision, never overwrite its destination. A monotonic ID → base62 alternative is shorter/simpler to guarantee uniqueness but enumerable and requires durable ID allocation. Hashing a URL then truncating does not avoid collisions and does not by itself guarantee repeat submissions map to the same link.

APIs are `POST /links {long_url,idempotency_key?} ->201 {code,short_url}` and `GET /{code} ->302 Location`, with 404 for unknown and 410 for expired/disabled under a stated retention policy. Store code, url, created/expiry, state, owner, version. Validate HTTP(S), length and header safety; enforce ownership for mutation and abuse quotas for public creation. Same URL may mint another code unless one-to-one mapping is explicitly requested as in W489.

A regional cache fronts a durable code-sharded database. Cache entries retain expiry/state/version and cap TTL at expiry; short negative caching handles random scans. Hot-code replication/edge caches reduce read amplification. A created code should be readable immediately through the owner/read-your-writes route, then global replicas converge. Disable/update invalidation needs a bounded consistency promise, not indefinite stale redirects.

Click analytics emits `event_id,code,time,referrer_domain,country` into a bounded queue/outbox path and aggregates per-code/day asynchronously; drop/sampling/error policy is explicit so logging cannot stall redirects. Avoid storing full sensitive referrer URLs and label bot/duplicate estimates. For an illustrative 1M creates/day and 100M redirects/day, average rates are 12 writes/s and 1,157 reads/s; provision peak headroom and code/table retention accordingly. The [W487 implementation](W487.md) demonstrates the small core with real tests, while cache replication and analytics remain system components. This level is enough for the warm-up if you can trace a generated collision and a lost create reply.

Read left to right: Create generated/custom code → Unique mapping + retry key → Cache then mapping shard → Redirect + async click event. The warm-up contract does not impose global long-URL deduplication.

title: Design a URL Shortener with Aliases, Expiry and Click Analytics
question:
Design a public link-shortening service. A user submits a long web address and gets back a short link; anyone who opens the short link is sent on to the original address. Opening links happens far more often than creating them, so the redirect must be fast and almost always available, and short codes should be hard to guess.

Requirements
1.
Create. POST /links {long_url, expires_at?} returns a short link such as https://sho.rt/<code>. The same long URL submitted twice may return two different short links.
2.
Redirect. GET /{code} redirects to the long URL. Unknown codes return 404; expired links return 410.
3.
Expiration. A link may carry an expiry time; after it, the link stops redirecting.
4.
Non-functional. Redirects are on the critical path of every click: p99 under 50 ms and very high availability. Codes should be short and should not be easy to enumerate.
What to deliver
1.
Back-of-envelope estimates: write and read rates, total links, storage, and the code length needed.
2.
The API and the data model.
3.
How short codes are generated without collisions, across many servers.
4.
The read path and its caching.
5.
How expiration is enforced.
6.
Failure modes and how the design scales further.
Examples
POST /links {"long_url": "https://example.com/a"}            -> 201 {"code": "<generated>"}
GET  /<generated code>                                       -> 302 Location: https://example.com/a
GET  /<code of a link that expired>                          -> 410
The first call mints a fresh generated code; opening it redirects to the stored long URL.
A link past its expiry time no longer redirects and answers 410 Gone, not 404.

With custom aliases (Follow-up 1):

POST /links {"long_url": "https://example.com/c", "custom_alias": "sale"} -> 201 {"code": "sale"}
POST /links {"long_url": "https://example.com/d", "custom_alias": "sale"} -> 409 (alias taken)
GET  /sale                                                   -> 302 Location: https://example.com/c
The first request for an alias wins; a second request for the same alias is refused with 409 Conflict.
Scale assumptions
100 million new links per day.
100 redirects per created link on average, with peaks 3 times the average.
Links are kept for 5 years unless they expire earlier.
About 500 bytes per stored link, including indexes.
Follow-up 1: custom aliases

A user may pass custom_alias to ask for a readable code such as sho.rt/sale. Aliases are unique, first come first served, may not have the same length as generated codes, and some words are reserved (api, admin, login, static). How are they stored and checked?

Follow-up 2: click analytics

The owner of a link can see click counts per day, with referrer and country. How are clicks recorded without slowing the redirect?

steps: Size the code space for the five-year population
solution.example: Click events are emitted asynchronously to a bounded log with event_id,code,time,referrer domain and coarse country, then dedup/aggregate into owner-authorized daily OLAP results. The redirect returns without waiting for a warehouse; declare sampling/loss semantics and protect privacy. A global event stream at the click rate is substantial and deserves its own partitions/retention. Retry failures use stable creation keys; a mapping-store outage serves cached still-live entries and returns a controlled error on unsafe misses. The runnable [W487 core](W487.md) can be configured with a10-character generator; distributed/cache/retention contracts are explicitly separate.
solution.trap: 100M creates/day≈1,157/s average and3,472/s at3× peak.100 redirects/link gives10B redirects/day≈115,741/s average and347,222/s peak under the stated ratio; retention/history can change the actual click-age distribution.5years×365days×100M≈182.5B links, at500bytes≈91.25TB logical, or273.75TB at3 replicas before overhead/backups. Eight base62 chars have2.18e14 possibilities, but choose **ten** (~8.39e17,~59.5bits) to lower occupancy/guessability. Even this is not a secret-access token; rate-limit enumeration and require separate auth for private destinations.
solution.teaching_notes_markdown:
### Size the code space for the five-year population

100M creates/day ≈ 1,157/s average and 3,472/s at 3× peak.100 redirects/link gives 10B redirects/day ≈ 115,741/s average and 347,222/s peak under the stated ratio; retention/history can change the actual click-age distribution.5 years×365 days×100M ≈ 182.5B links, at 500 bytes ≈ 91.25 TB logical, or 273.75 TB at 3 replicas before overhead/backups. Eight base62 chars have 2.18e14 possibilities, but choose **ten** (~8.39e17,~59.5 bits) to lower occupancy/guessability. Even this is not a secret-access token; rate-limit enumeration and require separate auth for private destinations.

`POST /links {long_url,expires_at?,custom_alias?}` returns 201 code. Store `Link(code PK,url,owner,created,expires_at,state,version)` with generated/alias codes in one namespace and reserved-word checks (api/admin/login/static). Generate cryptographically random codes on any server and conditionally insert; a collision retries, while an already-taken requested alias returns 409. A preliminary SELECT is insufficient under concurrent creates. The same URL can intentionally mint different codes; an optional idempotency key makes network retries repeat one creation without imposing global URL dedup.

GET resolves through regional edge/L1/L2 cache then durable code shard. A live hit returns 302 Location; missing 404; expired 410. Cache entries include absolute expiry/version, and the handler checks now>=expiry independently of cache TTL. Keep an expired-code tombstone/reservation for the defined retention so cleanup does not turn a promised 410 into 404 or reassign an old link. Cache TTL<=remaining life and response cache policy prevent a browser/CDN replaying a cached redirect after expiry; do not use an indefinitely cached 301 for mutable/expiring links. Negative caches are brief and invalidated on creation.

At 347K peak redirects/s, local cache/network dominate; shard backing storage by code hash, replicate hot links and separate creation quorum capacity from readers. A 50 ms p99 budget might allow 10 ms edge/route, 5 ms cache and 35 ms regional fallback/margin; a distant write quorum is not in every redirect. Replication lag after create needs an owner fallback/read token rather than a false 404. Disable/alias management needs versioned invalidation, audit and an outage policy that does not keep unsafe links live indefinitely.

Click events are emitted asynchronously to a bounded log with event_id, code, time, referrer domain and coarse country, then dedup/aggregate into owner-authorized daily OLAP results. The redirect returns without waiting for a warehouse; declare sampling/loss semantics and protect privacy. A global event stream at the click rate is substantial and deserves its own partitions/retention. Retry failures use stable creation keys; a mapping-store outage serves cached still-live entries and returns a controlled error on unsafe misses. The runnable [W487 core](W487.md) can be configured with a 10-character generator; distributed/cache/retention contracts are explicitly separate.

### Follow the diagram

![W488 solution flow](../diagrams/review_451_500_W488.svg)

Read left to right: Random ten-char / aliases → Unique insert + retention → Regional expiry-aware cache → Fast 302 + async analytics. 182.5B five-year links need explicit code-space, storage and expired-tombstone sizing.

title: Design Scalable TinyURL Service with One-to-One URL Mapping
question:
Design Scalable TinyURL Service with One-to-One URL Mapping

Design a TinyURL service where each long URL can only correspond to a single short URL. Consider scalability to support sharding and handling similar to DNS.

Example

Input

encode(http://example.com)
decode(a)

steps: The long URL needs its own uniqueness authority
solution.example: Assume1M unique URLs/day and1B resolutions/day: reverse-URL writes average12/s and resolutions11.6K/s, with chosen peak headroom. Store URL text once plus two lookup indexes; hash-routing avoids a global sequential counter bottleneck. Tests for this design must include exact duplicates,simultaneous same URL,deliberately colliding hash buckets and shard migration, not merely successful sequential encode/decode. The tiny example does not determine that the first code must literally be “a.”
solution.trap: Unlike the other variants, this service must return the same code for the same long URL, including simultaneous requests from different servers. Define equality first: use exact validated URL bytes or a conservative documented canonicalization (scheme/host case and default ports). Do not lowercase paths,sort arbitrary query parameters or remove fragments/tracking parameters without an explicit semantic policy; they can identify different destinations.
solution.teaching_notes_markdown:
### The long URL needs its own uniqueness authority

Unlike the other variants, this service must return the same code for the same long URL, including simultaneous requests from different servers. Define equality first: use exact validated URL bytes or a conservative documented canonicalization (scheme/host case and default ports). Do not lowercase paths, sort arbitrary query parameters or remove fragments/tracking parameters without an explicit semantic policy; they can identify different destinations.

Route create by a strong hash of the canonical URL to a home shard. That shard stores one transactionally unique `UrlMapping(canonical_url UNIQUE,code UNIQUE,url_hash,created,state)`. A hash is an index/routing aid; compare full URLs to handle hash collisions. Under a transaction, insert-or-return the existing mapping. Concurrent callers for the same URL receive the same code; a generated code collision tries another code, never changes an existing URL's code. Store both directions under the same authority rather than dual-writing unrelated URL/code databases.

One practical routing scheme prefixes the code with a stable virtual-shard ID plus random suffix; decode uses that prefix to find the authoritative shard via a versioned routing directory. This keeps URL and code uniqueness local to that shard while the full code remains globally unique. Migrations move virtual shards with ownership epochs/forwarding, not new user-visible codes. A global strongly consistent reverse-URL index is an alternative with different latency/cross-shard transaction costs.

`encode(url)` returns the stable short URL; `decode(code)` returns destination or 404/disabled status. Edge/regional caches resemble DNS in that cached mappings have TTLs and authoritative resolution on miss, but they are HTTP/database records, not necessarily one DNS record per short link. Cache invalidation/tombstones enforce disable policy and bounded staleness. Do not reassign expired/deleted codes if the one-to-one/stability contract is permanent; clarify reactivation and retention separately.

Assume 1M unique URLs/day and 1B resolutions/day: reverse-URL writes average 12/s and resolutions 11.6K/s, with chosen peak headroom. Store URL text once plus two lookup indexes; hash-routing avoids a global sequential counter bottleneck. Tests for this design must include exact duplicates, simultaneous same URL, deliberately colliding hash buckets and shard migration, not merely successful sequential encode/decode. The tiny example does not determine that the first code must literally be “a.”

### Follow the diagram

![W489 solution flow](../diagrams/review_451_500_W489.svg)

Read left to right: Canonical URL home shard → Unique URL and code row → Code-prefix shard resolver → TTL cached authoritative read. Simultaneous same-URL creates converge on the same code under one uniqueness authority.

title: URL Shortener With Click Tracking
question:
Design a URL-shortening service, then extend it to track clicks. Interviewers usually stay at overall architecture depth: encoding, redirect path, storage, collision handling, latency, and analytics write flow.

Requirements
Functional requirements:
Create a short URL for a long URL.
Redirect a short URL to the original destination with low latency.
Support custom or generated short codes, with collision handling.
Expire, disable, or update links when required by product policy.
Track each click for analytics as a bonus extension.
Scale / constraints:
Redirect reads dominate writes; design the redirect path as the hot path.
Click tracking should not slow down redirects.
Storage must preserve uniqueness of short codes and support fast lookup by code.
Design decisions to discuss:
random code generation vs counter / base62 encoding
cache placement for hot links
synchronous vs asynchronous analytics writes
abuse / invalid-link handling
Notes
A strong click-tracking extension emits an event after resolving the code, then returns the redirect immediately. Downstream analytics can aggregate by short code, timestamp bucket, user-agent, referrer, or geography.
Clarify whether the interviewer wants an API-level design or a higher-level component diagram. Several JPMorgan interviewers keep this prompt at the overall system level and do not push hard on database schema.
For custom aliases, add a uniqueness check and a reserved-word list; for generated aliases, make collision handling explicit.

A concurrent update uses optimistic version/If-Match; stale cache writes cannot republish an old destination indefinitely. A durable store outage can serve valid cached entries under policy, while misses return a controlled error rather than an invented destination.
solution.teaching_notes_markdown:
### Resolve first; meter analytics off the critical path

The architecture is client → regional redirect cache → durable mapping shard, with a separate bounded event collector → stream/batch aggregator → owner analytics store. `POST /links` creates generated/custom codes, `GET /{code}` redirects, `PATCH /links/{code}` changes destination/state/expiry under owner authorization and version preconditions, and `GET /links/{code}/stats` returns permitted aggregates. Store code, url, owner, expiry, state, version; a unique code index is the collision authority.

Random base62 codes hide simple sequences but need conditional insert/retry; counter ranges+base62 avoid collisions only if allocation is durable and fenced. Custom aliases share the namespace and reserved-word rules, returning 409 on conflict. Validate URL scheme/length/header safety and rate-limit creation/scan abuse. Same URL may produce distinct codes unless a one-to-one contract is explicitly added.

On GET, check unknown/disabled/expiry before 302, with absolute expiry in cached records and invalidation on update. A concurrent update uses optimistic version/If-Match; stale cache writes cannot republish an old destination indefinitely. Choose a bounded global propagation delay, with immediate local read-your-writes through the authoritative owner. Negative caches are short so new links are not hidden. A durable store outage can serve valid cached entries under policy, while misses return a controlled error rather than an invented destination.

After resolving, enqueue a click event with stable ID, code, time and privacy-minimized dimensions; do not wait for downstream aggregation. If the local buffer/log is unavailable, choose bounded loss/sampling and measure it, or pay a stated durable-enqueue latency budget if exact logging is required. “Emit after redirect” without a durable/bounded mechanism can lose all events on a process crash; “analytics never slows redirects and never loses a click” is not free. Dedup retries, distinguish bots/unique users from raw requests and retain a correction/replay path.

For an illustrative 100M redirects/day at 200 bytes/event, raw analytics is 20 GB/day before replicas; cache hot links and partition analytics independently from mapping writes. Monitor redirect p99/hit rate, stale state, unknown/expired codes, event drops and aggregation lag. [W487](W487.md) supplies a tested core; this prompt stays at API/system depth unless the interviewer requests implementation.

title: Ads Demand Intake Data Modeling
question:
Model the demand side of Netflix Ads: advertiser accounts, campaigns, ad groups, creative, targeting, orders, budgets, impressions, and measurement. Proactively cover bidding and targeting rather than waiting to be asked.

Requirements:

Model advertiser / business account ownership and permissions.
Model campaigns, ad groups / line items, creative assets, targeting rules, budgets, pacing, and order type.
Track serving events: eligible request, impression, click, conversion, and measurement attribution.
Support direct-sold demand as a special case where open-auction concepts may not apply.
Explain how config changes propagate to serving systems.
Discuss reporting tables and key campaign-health metrics.

steps: Separate advertiser configuration from serving facts and money
solution.example: Assume10K advertisers and100K requests/s: configuration volume is small relative to serving facts, so do not put every impression in one hot campaign row. Partition facts by time/campaign salt and aggregate minute/day totals. Campaign health includes eligible reach,fill/win rate,impressions,frequency,CTR,CVR,spend versus pace,budget remaining,creative rejection and attribution lag. Ratios use matching denominators/windows and disclose provisional late data. Direct-sold delivery/underfulfillment and auction clearing-price metrics remain separate. This is a demand model/design, not a claim of Netflix's internal schema.
solution.trap: Relational configuration starts with `BusinessAccount(id,billing_profile,currency)`, `AccountMember(account,user,role)` and `Campaign(id,account,objective,start,end,status,version)`. Each campaign owns `LineItem(id,campaign,order_type,targeting_version,bid_policy,budget,pacing,priority)` and joins reusable `Creative(id,asset_manifest,duration,format,review_state)` via placements. Store money as integer minor units with explicit currency; never add USD cents to another currency's cents. Budget changes and actual spend are distinct audited records.
solution.teaching_notes_markdown:
### Separate advertiser configuration from serving facts and money

Relational configuration starts with `BusinessAccount(id,billing_profile,currency)`, `AccountMember(account,user,role)` and `Campaign(id,account,objective,start,end,status,version)`. Each campaign owns `LineItem(id,campaign,order_type,targeting_version,bid_policy,budget,pacing,priority)` and joins reusable `Creative(id,asset_manifest,duration,format,review_state)` via placements. Store money as integer minor units with explicit currency; never add USD cents to another currency's cents. Budget changes and actual spend are distinct audited records.

Use `TargetingRule(id,version,expression_ast)` over canonical audience/geo/device/content IDs, with validated AND/OR/NOT semantics and a defined eligible-user universe. `BidPolicy(type,max_cpc/max_cpm,score_config)` specifies open-auction strategy; CPM and CPC have different cost units and expected-liability handling. `Order(id,type,contract,guaranteed_quantity,price,dates)` supports direct-sold guaranteed/non-guaranteed inventory where auction bids may be absent. Pacing/priority/allocation determine delivery under contract; do not fabricate a bid for every direct-sold line item.

Serving consumes compiled immutable campaign/targeting/creative snapshots from an outbox/change stream, with version manifests and atomic regional activation. Pause/revoke has a fast deny overlay plus a propagation SLO. The config API uses owner roles, optimistic version checks and approval/audit. Activation requires creative review, budget validity and consistent referenced versions; a partial update must not mix a new targeting rule with an old compliance state.

Record immutable `AdRequest`, `EligibilityDecision`, `Auction/Allocation`, `Impression`, `Click`, `Conversion` with event IDs, request/impression references, event/receive time, source and config version. Measurement attribution is its own versioned policy/window and can assign fractional credit; a conversion is not automatically one click. Dedup/fraud state and privacy/consent apply before billable ledger entries. A double-entry wallet/budget ledger and atomic reservations enforce spend, while event-time rollups support reporting.

Assume 10K advertisers and 100K requests/s: configuration volume is small relative to serving facts, so do not put every impression in one hot campaign row. Partition facts by time/campaign salt and aggregate minute/day totals. Campaign health includes eligible reach, fill/win rate, impressions, frequency, CTR, CVR, spend versus pace, budget remaining, creative rejection and attribution lag. Ratios use matching denominators/windows and disclose provisional late data. Direct-sold delivery/underfulfillment and auction clearing-price metrics remain separate. This is a demand model/design, not a claim of Netflix's internal schema.

![W491 solution flow](../diagrams/review_451_500_W491.svg)

Read left to right: Advertiser / campaign config → Targeting bid/order versions → Compiled serving snapshot → Facts / ledger / attribution. Direct-sold allocation is modeled separately from open-auction bidding.

title: Design Walmart Plus Membership System
question:
Design a paid-membership system (Walmart+ analog) covering signup, recurring billing, entitlement checks at read time, family/household plan sharing, and graceful handling of payment failures and cancellations.

Requirements
Functional: signup with plan selection (monthly/annual/family); recurring billing with retry on failure; entitlement check API used by checkout, shipping, and streaming flows; cancellation with end-of-period grace; family/household member invitation and management; transactional emails for renewal, failure, and cancellation.
Non-functional: entitlement check on the read path must be sub-50 ms p99 (called inline during cart and product-page loads); billing pipeline must be idempotent under payment-gateway retries; membership state must remain consistent across data-center failover; PCI scope limited to a tokenized payment vault.
Data model: Member, Subscription (plan, period, status active/past_due/canceled/paused, current_period_start/end), Entitlement (cached projection: member_id -> feature flags + expiry), PaymentMethod (token), BillingEvent (charge id, status, idempotency_key), HouseholdLink (primary_member_id, member_id, role).

steps: Billing is a durable state machine; entitlement is a versioned projection
solution.example: At an assumed10M members and100K peak entitlement checks/s,200-byte projections are2GB raw before replicas, while billing roughly monthly is much less frequent but correctness-critical. Replicate subscription/charge state with consensus/ownership fencing across data centers; a failed region cannot independently issue another renewal. Email delivery uses unique event/template keys and retries without duplicate charges. Monitor payment ambiguity,dunning,projection lag,entitlement p99,household churn and audit transitions; test failover after provider acceptance and cancellation at a period boundary.
solution.trap: `POST /subscriptions` validates plan and starts a charge with stable `(subscription,period,attempt-purpose)` idempotency. Webhooks and a reconciliation job advance pending→paid/failed under unique provider event IDs and a single subscription version owner. A lost charge reply is queried/reconciled, not paid again with a new key. Renewal reserves the next billing job; success advances the period once and emits entitlement/email outbox events. Retry transient payment failures under a bounded schedule/dunning policy, then past_due and eventually suspended/canceled according to the explicitly chosen grace period. Do not infer grace length from the word “membership.”
solution.teaching_notes_markdown:
### Billing is a durable state machine; entitlement is a versioned projection

Use the supplied entities with primary keys and ownership links: `Member`, `Plan(version,price_cents,currency,interval,features)`, `Subscription(member,plan_version,status,period_start,period_end,cancel_at_period_end,version)`, `PaymentMethod(vault_token)`, `BillingEvent(subscription,period,idempotency_key,provider_charge_id,state)` and `HouseholdLink(primary,member,role,state)`. An entitlement projection stores feature flags, expiry, source subscription/household versions. Store no raw card number; only the tokenized vault/provider boundary handles it.

`POST /subscriptions` validates plan and starts a charge with stable `(subscription,period,attempt-purpose)` idempotency. Webhooks and a reconciliation job advance pending → paid/failed under unique provider event IDs and a single subscription version owner. A lost charge reply is queried/reconciled, not paid again with a new key. Renewal reserves the next billing job; success advances the period once and emits entitlement/email outbox events. Retry transient payment failures under a bounded schedule/dunning policy, then past_due and eventually suspended/canceled according to the explicitly chosen grace period. Do not infer grace length from the word “membership.”

Cancellation marks end-of-period nonrenewal, keeps paid entitlements until period_end and returns that timestamp. Immediate fraud/admin suspension is a different transition with faster invalidation. Concurrent cancel/renew/payment callbacks serialize on subscription/version; a late paid webhook cannot silently reactivate a canceled future period without a defined policy. Pause/resume/proration are explicit plan rules, not ad hoc status strings.

`GET /entitlements/{member}?feature=shipping` authenticates the trusted caller and returns allow, expiry, version/reason in<50 ms p99 through regional in-memory/Redis projections. Absolute expiry is checked on every hit; an expired projection never extends access by resetting its TTL. Strict revocation needs a current version/lease authority; eventual outbox propagation requires a stated small bound and fail-closed behavior for unknown/stale state. A household invitation is unique, expires, requires acceptance and checks plan capacity; transactional links prevent the same dependent consuming multiple conflicting primary plans.

At an assumed 10M members and 100K peak entitlement checks/s, 200-byte projections are 2 GB raw before replicas, while billing roughly monthly is much less frequent but correctness-critical. Replicate subscription/charge state with consensus/ownership fencing across data centers; a failed region cannot independently issue another renewal. Email delivery uses unique event/template keys and retries without duplicate charges. Monitor payment ambiguity, dunning, projection lag, entitlement p99, household churn and audit transitions; test failover after provider acceptance and cancellation at a period boundary.

### Follow the diagram

![W492 solution flow](../diagrams/review_451_500_W492.svg)

Read left to right: Plan signup / renewal key → Payment reconciliation state → Versioned entitlement projection → Fast check / expiry / household. Duplicate webhooks or regional failover cannot create a second period charge.

title: Promotion Posting System Data Model
question:
Design the relational schema for Netflix's internal tool that posts trailers/clips/announcements to many social platforms (Facebook, YouTube, TikTok, Instagram, X) across regions and languages.

The schema must support:

Posting to many platforms, each with different rules (video length, aspect ratio, text length).
Different regions and languages (English in US, Japanese in Japan).
Money tracking (budgets and spend) rolled up by campaign / platform / region, stored in cents.
An approval workflow (managers approve before a post goes live).
Scheduling (post at a future time).
A full audit/history log of who changed what.

Scale: ~5K employees, ~20K campaigns/year, ~200K posts, ~30 translations each, ~30 regions, ~5–7 platforms. Read-heavy (dashboards + scheduler polling), not write-heavy.

Focus on tables, relationships, money handling, and extensibility (adding new platforms shouldn't break things).

steps: Model a creative concept, its translations and each actual delivery
solution.example: Append `AuditEvent(actor,entity,entity_id,old_version,new_version,action,patch,time,request_id)` in the same transaction/outbox as changes. At200K concepts×30 translations≈6M localization rows before revisions/deliveries, relational indexes and pagination are appropriate; this is read-heavy workflow data, not an excuse for a giant event-stream-only schema. Dashboards query indexed deliveries/materialized monetary aggregates. Foreign keys/unique constraints enforce ownership and revision links; add schema-compatible platform adapters/rules rather than hard-coded platform columns. Retain approval and provider evidence to explain who published exactly which content and why.
solution.trap: Use `Employee(id)`, `Campaign(id,name,owner,budget_cents,currency,version)` and `CampaignMember(campaign,employee,role)`. `PostConcept(id,campaign,source_locale)` owns `PostRevision(id,concept,revision,text,asset_manifest,author,created_at)`. `Localization(id,concept,locale,revision,text,asset_manifest,state)` stores each language variant rather than adding one column per language. `Region(id,code)` and `Platform(id,name,adapter_type)` are data rows so new platforms do not require schema branches.
solution.teaching_notes_markdown:
### Model a creative concept, its translations and each actual delivery

Use `Employee(id)`, `Campaign(id,name,owner,budget_cents,currency,version)` and `CampaignMember(campaign,employee,role)`. `PostConcept(id,campaign,source_locale)` owns `PostRevision(id,concept,revision,text,asset_manifest,author,created_at)`. `Localization(id,concept,locale,revision,text,asset_manifest,state)` stores each language variant rather than adding one column per language. `Region(id,code)` and `Platform(id,name,adapter_type)` are data rows so new platforms do not require schema branches.

`PlatformRule(platform,version,valid_from,max_video_seconds,aspect_ratios,max_text_length)` describes versioned constraints; validate a delivery against the rule version actually approved. `Delivery(id,localization_revision,platform,region,account_id,scheduled_at_utc,state,version,provider_post_id)` is one intended external post. Unique `(localization_revision,platform,region,account_id,purpose)` or a client idempotency key prevents accidental duplicates. A localization may be delivered to many platforms/regions without copying the whole campaign.

`Approval(delivery,revision,approver,decision,decided_at)` refers to exact content/rule revisions; changing approved text/media or schedule under policy returns it to review. States draft → pending_approval → approved → scheduled → publishing → published/failed. Scheduler claims due approved rows with lease/fence and an index on `(state,scheduled_at_utc,id)`, uses stable provider request keys and reconciles unknown external results. A retry cannot post a new revision that was never approved. Store source timezone for display, but schedule an unambiguous UTC instant.

Budget allocations live in `BudgetAllocation(campaign,platform,region,currency,amount_cents)`. Spend is an append-only `SpendEvent(id,delivery,currency,amount_cents,event_time,provider_reference)` with unique provider reference; credits are explicit signed events. Rollups group campaign/platform/region **and currency**, and reservations prevent overspend if required. Never sum cents across currencies without a versioned FX/reporting policy.

Append `AuditEvent(actor,entity,entity_id,old_version,new_version,action,patch,time,request_id)` in the same transaction/outbox as changes. At 200K concepts×30 translations ≈ 6M localization rows before revisions/deliveries, relational indexes and pagination are appropriate; this is read-heavy workflow data, not an excuse for a giant event-stream-only schema. Dashboards query indexed deliveries/materialized monetary aggregates. Foreign keys/unique constraints enforce ownership and revision links; add schema-compatible platform adapters/rules rather than hard-coded platform columns. Retain approval and provider evidence to explain who published exactly which content and why.

![W493 solution flow](../diagrams/review_451_500_W493.svg)

Read left to right: Concept + localized revisions → Platform/region delivery → Revision-bound approval → Due publish + spend audit. Editing approved content invalidates its approval; external retries retain identity.

title: Tagging System REST API
question:
Design a tagging system with REST APIs for creating tags, associating tags to resources, deleting tags, and finding tagged objects. Interviewers focus on API design details and edge cases more than broad architecture diagrams.

Requirements
Support creating tags.
Support associating and disassociating tags with resources.
Support deleting tags and defining what happens to existing associations.
Support finding resources by tag and finding tags for a resource.
Define REST APIs, request/response shapes, and error cases.
Cover pagination for large result sets.
Notes
This round is API-design heavy; the interviewer may drill every operation before there is time for a full system diagram.
Be explicit about uniqueness, case sensitivity, tag rename semantics, and authorization boundaries.

steps: Stable tag IDs, idempotent associations and explicit delete semantics
solution.example: Authenticate tenant and require tag-management permission for create/rename/delete plus resource-edit permission for attach/detach. Finding tagged resources filters by the caller's resource access; tag membership alone is not access. Use indexed `(tag_id,resource_type,resource_id)` and reverse `(resource_type,resource_id,tag_id)` within tenant. Keyset cursors bind tenant,query,sort and last key; limit maximum page size and define snapshot versus live pagination (choose live with immutable tie keys and documented concurrent-change behavior). A large tag must not return all associations in memory. Audit mutations and rate-limit expensive scans; unknown foreign-tenant IDs should not become an information oracle. This API-level precision matters more than a broad generic architecture.
solution.trap: Rename changes only tag display/normalized name, not association identity. Creation/deletion races serialize on the tag: attachment checks live state transactionally; a tombstoned tag cannot gain new associations during cleanup. Existing associations disappear from reads immediately through a live-tag join/filter, while a resumable worker deletes large join rows. State whether a recreated same name gets a new ID (here yes); old references do not silently reconnect.
solution.teaching_notes_markdown:
### Stable tag IDs, idempotent associations and explicit delete semantics

Choose tenant-scoped case-insensitive uniqueness using a documented Unicode normalization/casefold key, while preserving display case. Store `Tag(id,tenant,display_name,normalized_name,version,state)` unique `(tenant,normalized_name)` and `ResourceTag(tenant,resource_type,resource_id,tag_id,created_by,created_at)` unique on the full association. Tags reference resources by stable IDs; polymorphic resource existence/permission checks belong to the owning service or a resource registry.

| API | Request/result and errors |
|---|---|
| POST /tags | `{name}` →201 `{id,name,version}`; 400 invalid, 409 normalized duplicate |
| PATCH /tags/{id} | `{name}` plus If-Match →200 new version; 409 name conflict, 412 stale version |
| PUT /resources/{type}/{id}/tags/{tag_id} | Idempotently attach →204; 404 missing/inaccessible tag/resource, 403 where policy permits disclosure |
| DELETE /resources/{type}/{id}/tags/{tag_id} | Idempotently detach →204 even if absent |
| GET /tags/{id}/resources?cursor&limit | Ordered resource IDs/types and next cursor |
| GET /resources/{type}/{id}/tags?cursor&limit | Ordered tag IDs/names and next cursor |
| DELETE /tags/{id} | Tombstone immediately, then remove associations; 204 retry-safe |

Rename changes only tag display/normalized name, not association identity. Creation/deletion races serialize on the tag: attachment checks live state transactionally; a tombstoned tag cannot gain new associations during cleanup. Existing associations disappear from reads immediately through a live-tag join/filter, while a resumable worker deletes large join rows. State whether a recreated same name gets a new ID (here yes); old references do not silently reconnect.

Authenticate tenant and require tag-management permission for create/rename/delete plus resource-edit permission for attach/detach. Finding tagged resources filters by the caller's resource access; tag membership alone is not access. Use indexed `(tag_id,resource_type,resource_id)` and reverse `(resource_type,resource_id,tag_id)` within tenant. Keyset cursors bind tenant, query, sort and last key; limit maximum page size and define snapshot versus live pagination (choose live with immutable tie keys and documented concurrent-change behavior). A large tag must not return all associations in memory. Audit mutations and rate-limit expensive scans; unknown foreign-tenant IDs should not become an information oracle. This API-level precision matters more than a broad generic architecture.

![W494 solution flow](../diagrams/review_451_500_W494.svg)

title: Template & Instance System with Update Propagation
question:
Template & Instance System with Update Propagation

Design a template/instance model (Figma components, or online slide/PPT templates): a template defines a reusable object and instances customize it. When a template changes, instances should reflect the change — via a push notification letting the user choose whether to adopt the update.

Requirements

Two related framings have appeared:

Component template/instance representation. A template (e.g. a button) has instances that override properties (text, color). Choose an efficient representation (JSON-like) so that when the template changes, instances update accordingly while preserving their local customizations.
Online slide/PPT template system. Users generate document instances from templates. When a template is updated, notify users of affected instances and let each user decide whether to adopt the new version. Start with a simple version first.
Notes
Core design decisions: how an instance stores overrides versus inherited template values (so template edits propagate but local customizations survive), template versioning, and the notify-and-opt-in update flow for documents.
Real-world scale here is low — candidates who modeled it as a massive high-concurrency system were seen as over-engineering. Start from the simplest correct representation and add propagation/versioning incrementally.
Frequently bundled into the broader Figma system-design rotation alongside the trending and real-time-comments prompts.

steps: Pin the template version and store only local overrides
solution.example: For a simple version, store `Template(id,owner,latest_version)`, immutable `TemplateVersion(template,version,property_tree)` and `Instance(id,owner,template_id,base_version,overrides,revision)`. Properties/nodes have stable IDs, not fragile array positions. Effective rendering merges base properties with explicit overrides; “unset/inherit” differs from an explicit null/delete override. Example base button `{text:Buy,color:blue}` and override `{text:Pay}` renders Pay/blue. A template changing color to green should produce Pay/green **only after adoption** in the opt-in document framing.
solution.trap: Publishing a template inserts an immutable version and outbox `TemplateUpdated`. A small worker finds dependent instances, writes unique `UpdateOffer(instance,target_version,state)` and notifies owners. `GET /instances/{id}/update-preview?target=v` computes a diff; `POST /instances/{id}/adopt` includes expected instance revision and target version. The user can adopt,postpone or dismiss; a notification does not mutate their document. For live components, explicitly choose an auto-follow policy rather than silently reusing it for opt-in slides.
solution.teaching_notes_markdown:
### Pin the template version and store only local overrides

For a simple version, store `Template(id,owner,latest_version)`, immutable `TemplateVersion(template,version,property_tree)` and `Instance(id,owner,template_id,base_version,overrides,revision)`. Properties/nodes have stable IDs, not fragile array positions. Effective rendering merges base properties with explicit overrides; “unset/inherit” differs from an explicit null/delete override. Example base button `{text:Buy,color:blue}` and override `{text:Pay}` renders Pay/blue. A template changing color to green should produce Pay/green **only after adoption** in the opt-in document framing.

Publishing a template inserts an immutable version and outbox `TemplateUpdated`. A small worker finds dependent instances, writes unique `UpdateOffer(instance,target_version,state)` and notifies owners. `GET /instances/{id}/update-preview?target=v` computes a diff; `POST /instances/{id}/adopt` includes expected instance revision and target version. The user can adopt, postpone or dismiss; a notification does not mutate their document. For live components, explicitly choose an auto-follow policy rather than silently reusing it for opt-in slides.

Adoption uses a three-way merge: old template, local effective/overrides, new template. Preserve overridden properties; inherit changed unoverridden ones. If a template removes a node/property with local edits or changes its type, surface a conflict/orphan override and let the user keep a local copy or discard it. Renamed display labels keep the same stable property ID. Reset-to-template removes an override, rather than copying the current default and accidentally pinning it forever.

Transactionally update base_version and resolved overrides under instance revision CAS; concurrent local edit/adoption gets 412/conflict and a refreshed preview, not lost customization. Dedup offers/notifications by instance+target version, and newest offers can supersede older unadopted ones. Retain old versions for rendering/audit and rollback; deletion of a template must not break pinned instances. At an illustrative 10K templates and 100K instances, a relational index on template_id and a modest queue suffice. Start with JSON merge/diff plus explicit conflicts; avoid inventing a massive distributed propagation platform for the stated low-scale product.

### Follow the diagram

![W495 solution flow](../diagrams/review_451_500_W495.svg)

Read left to right: Immutable template version → Pinned instance + overrides → Update offer + merge preview → Opt-in CAS adoption. Local customizations survive adoption; conflicting removals require explicit resolution.

title: Design a Sales Tax Engine (Address + Date to Tax)
question:
Online stores must charge the right sales tax on every order, and in the United States the amount depends on exactly where the goods are delivered and on the date of the sale. Design the service a store calls at checkout: it takes a delivery address, a transaction date and the order's line items, and returns the tax owed, broken down by jurisdiction and tax type. Most of the discussion is about the data model, so settle the schema first; serving and scaling come after it.

What to design

Inputs:

A delivery address (street, city, state, postcode, country).
A transaction date.
The line items: an amount in cents and a product tax code for each (for example general or prepared_food). The amounts are needed to turn rates into money; assume they are always present.

Output:

The total tax in cents.
One line per applied tax: the jurisdiction, its level (state, county, city, special district), the tax type, the rate, and the amount.

title: Fee Calculation with Boolean Flag and Numeric Parameter
question:
Fee Calculation with Boolean Flag and Numeric Parameter

Suppose there are only two parameters: one can be a T/F flag and the other can be any number X. Under this condition, how would you design a mechanism to calculate three different fee schedules? The fee per share increases with longevity; let's say 0.2, 0.3, 0.4. The cap is 1.5.

steps: Two arguments are insufficient until their meanings are defined
solution.example: This code does **not** infer tenure from quantity: selecting young/middle/old requires the missing longevity policy or preconfigured account context. If X instead means tenure, define two thresholds and return .2/.3/.4 piecewise; a total order fee still needs quantity from somewhere, and a1.5 per-share cap never binds those three rates. If the interviewer demands a stateless two-input function where X simultaneously means an unconstrained quantity and a separate unconstrained tenure,that information is absent and cannot be recovered. State the missing contract rather than encode unexplained magic ranges or pretend one boolean selects three independent tiers.
solution.trap: This code does **not** infer tenure from quantity: selecting young/middle/old requires the missing longevity policy or preconfigured account context. If X instead means tenure, define two thresholds and return .2/.3/.4 piecewise; a total order fee still needs quantity from somewhere, and a1.5 per-share cap never binds those three rates. If the interviewer demands a stateless two-input function where X simultaneously means an unconstrained quantity and a separate unconstrained tenure,that information is absent and cannot be recovered. State the missing contract rather than encode unexplained magic ranges or pretend one boolean selects three independent tiers.
solution.teaching_notes_markdown:
### Two arguments are insufficient until their meanings are defined

The prompt gives three per-share rates .2/.3/.4 and cap 1.5, but omits longevity thresholds, what the boolean means, whether X is quantity or tenure, and whether the cap is per share/order/day. There is no unique fee formula. A boolean alone distinguishes two states, but the numeric input or configured policy can distinguish three or more schedules.

One explicit **demonstration contract** is: each schedule has a configured per-share rate selected from a known external longevity tier; the two runtime arguments are `(cap_enabled: bool,X: nonnegative share quantity)`. The fee is `min(rate*X,1.50)` when capped and `rate*X` otherwise, rounded to cents. A factory supplies three schedules without adding a third runtime argument:

```python
from decimal import Decimal, InvalidOperation, ROUND_HALF_UP


def make_fee_schedule(rate):
    """Configured rate; two runtime args: cap_enabled bool and quantity X."""
    rate = Decimal(str(rate))

    def fee(cap_enabled, X):
        if not isinstance(cap_enabled, bool):
            raise ValueError("boolean cap flag required")
        try:
            quantity = Decimal(str(X))
        except InvalidOperation:
            raise ValueError("numeric quantity required")
        if not quantity.is_finite() or quantity < 0:
            raise ValueError("finite nonnegative quantity required")
        total = rate * quantity
        if cap_enabled:
            total = min(total, Decimal("1.50"))
        return total.quantize(Decimal(".01"), rounding=ROUND_HALF_UP)

    return fee


fee_young, fee_middle, fee_old = (make_fee_schedule(r) for r in (".2", ".3", ".4"))
```

At X=4 with cap enabled, the three configured schedules return .80, 1.20, 1.50; with cap disabled they return .80, 1.20, 1.60. The 1.50 cap is per invocation in this demo. Tests verify those numbers, zero, invalid/nonfinite quantity and boolean validation.

This code does **not** infer tenure from quantity: selecting young/middle/old requires the missing longevity policy or preconfigured account context. If X instead means tenure, define two thresholds and return .2/.3/.4 piecewise; a total order fee still needs quantity from somewhere, and a 1.5 per-share cap never binds those three rates. If the interviewer demands a stateless two-input function where X simultaneously means an unconstrained quantity and a separate unconstrained tenure, that information is absent and cannot be recovered. State the missing contract rather than encode unexplained magic ranges or pretend one boolean selects three independent tiers.

title: Amusement Park Profitability Case
question:
Capital One Power Day case (Strategy & Data Analytics rotation), 45 minutes. Opens with conceptual questions about an amusement park business, then builds park profitability under different operating assumptions.

Phase 1: warm-up — define the levers of park profitability (ticket revenue, per-visitor in-park spend, operating costs, capacity constraints, seasonality).
Phase 2: build the P&L for a specified scenario (e.g. a 5,000-capacity park running 200 days/year at 70% utilization) — revenue, variable cost, fixed cost, net profit; mental math expected.
Phase 3: sensitivity / scenario analysis — e.g. "what happens if utilization drops 10%?" or "what is the break-even ticket price?" Identify the most impactful lever.

steps: Build visits and contribution before profit
solution.example: Capacity5000×200days×70% utilization gives700,000 annual visits (repeat visitors count as visits). The prompt supplies no prices/costs,so choose a labeled **illustrative scenario**: ticket$50,in-park revenue$20/visit,variable cost$25/visit and fixed annual cost$20M. Revenue is700K×70=$49M,variable cost$17.5M,contribution$31.5M and operating profit$11.5M. This excludes tax,interest,depreciation/capex unless explicitly included; define whether fixed cost already contains them.
solution.trap: Break-even ticket price at the original attendance is $P^*=F/(CDu)+v-S=20M/700K+25-20\approx\$33.57$. Break-even utilization is $F/[CD(P+S-v)]\approx44.44\%$. These are static calculations; reducing ticket price may change demand and in-park spending,which requires an elasticity assumption rather than holding everything fixed unnoticed.
solution.teaching_notes_markdown:
### Build visits and contribution before profit

Capacity of 5,000 visitors/day × 200 days × 70% utilization gives 700,000 annual visits; repeat visitors count as visits. Because prices and costs are not supplied, use this explicitly illustrative scenario: ticket 50 USD, in-park revenue 20 USD/visit, variable cost 25 USD/visit and fixed annual cost 20 million USD. Revenue is 49 million USD, variable cost 17.5 million, contribution 31.5 million and operating profit 11.5 million. Define whether fixed costs include depreciation; tax, interest and capex are excluded unless added explicitly.

Profit is $\Pi=CDu(P+S-v)-F$. Utilization dropping **10 percentage points** from 70% to 60% gives 600K visits and profit of 7 million USD, a 4.5 million USD decline. A **10% relative** drop means 63%, 630K visits and profit of 8.35 million USD, a 3.15 million USD decline. Clarifying the phrase avoids a common case error.

Break-even ticket price at the original attendance is $P^*=F/(CDu)+v-S=20M/700K+25-20\approx\$33.57$. Break-even utilization is $F/[CD(P+S-v)]\approx44.44\%$. These are static calculations; reducing ticket price may change demand and in-park spending, which requires an elasticity assumption rather than holding everything fixed unnoticed.

A one-percentage-point utilization increase adds 10,000 visits × 45 USD contribution, or 450,000 USD within capacity. A one-dollar ticket or variable-cost change affects 700,000 visits, about 700,000 USD. Compare feasible magnitudes and demand/quality effects, not derivatives in different units. Seasonality, weather, staffing, queues, safety, maintenance and peak-day capacity can make average utilization misleading. Segment weekdays/peak days and test pricing/bundling against margin and guest experience. Obtain actual cost, pass/repeat-visit and investment assumptions before using the illustration as a recommendation.

Analyzing Profitable Business Investment Opportunities and Market Dynamics

Can you describe a good business to invest in? Please detail aspects such as market size, key players and their profit margins, growth, and drivers.

solution.example: For a matchedFY2025 comparison,Visa reported$40.000B net revenue and$20.058B net income,implying a50.1% net margin; operating income derived from revenue minus$16.006B operating expenses is$23.994B,a60.0% operating margin. Revenue grew11%. Visa's2025 payments volume was$14.2T: transaction value flowing over a network is **not** its revenue. [Visa2025 Form10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1403161/000140316125000089/v-20250930.htm),[Visa2025 operational highlights](https://annualreport.visa.com/home/default.aspx).

That is a business-quality thesis,not a conclusion that today's stock price is attractive. Use comparable dated financial statements and a valuation model before deciding to invest.
solution.teaching_notes_markdown:
### An evidence-based example: payment-network economics

A business type worth studying is a scaled payment network, such as Visa or Mastercard, because interoperable acceptance, risk infrastructure and high incremental transaction volume can support strong economics. That is a business-quality thesis, not a conclusion that today's stock price is attractive. Use comparable dated financial statements and a valuation model before deciding to invest.

For a matched FY2025 comparison, Visa reported 40.000 billion USD net revenue and USD 20.058B net income, implying a 50.1% net margin; operating income derived from revenue minus USD 16.006B operating expenses is USD 23.994B, a 60.0% operating margin. Revenue grew 11%. Visa's 2025 payments volume was USD 14.2T: transaction value flowing over a network is **not** its revenue. [Visa 2025 Form 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1403161/000140316125000089/v-20250930.htm), [Visa 2025 operational highlights](https://annualreport.visa.com/home/default.aspx).

Mastercard FY2025 reported 32.791 billion USD net revenue, USD 14.968B net income and 57.6% operating margin; net margin is about 45.6% and revenue growth 16%. Their combined roughly USD 72.8B revenue is a scale reference for two firms including services, not an estimate of the whole payments TAM or unique addressable spend. [Mastercard 2025 Form 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1141391/000114139126000013/ma-20251231.htm).

For recency, Visa's fiscal 2026 release dated October 27, 2026 reported 45.9 billion USD revenue, growth 15%, and USD 23.5B GAAP net income. Keep that later period distinct from the matched 2025 comparison and distinguish GAAP from adjusted earnings. [Visa FY2026 release](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1403161/000140316126000126/q42026earningsrelease.htm).

The **investment reasoning** is conditional: card/digital transaction growth, cross-border mix and value-added fraud/data services may grow earnings, while network reliability, issuer/acquirer relationships and merchant acceptance are barriers to entry. Competitors/substitutes include the other global networks, domestic schemes and account-to-account rails; wallets can be partners or substitutes depending on how they route transactions. These are strategic hypotheses to test, not a guaranteed moat. Pricing/incentive competition, regulatory/litigation pressure, cyber outages and new routing technology can erode margins.

Size the market by segment: network service revenue/processed transactions is different from lending spreads, merchant-acquirer fees or total commerce volume. Build bear/base/bull forecasts for transaction growth, realized take rate, client incentives, operating expense, tax and reinvestment; value free cash flow under a range of discount/terminal assumptions. The break question is “what growth/margin is already priced in?” A high-margin business at an excessive valuation can be a poor investment. No valuation/current share-price inputs are supplied, so this answer supports a researched business thesis and diligence plan rather than an unsupported buy claim.
